parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the research method used by Piliavin et al. in their subway Samaritan study.
parts.answer: A field experiment.
parts.working: B1: field experiment (accept 'experiment carried out in a natural setting'). Not 'natural experiment' – the researchers manipulated the IVs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline two ways in which the victim's condition was varied in this study.
parts.answer: The victim either carried a black cane and appeared sober (cane/ill condition), or smelled of alcohol and carried a bottle of liquor wrapped in a brown paper bag (drunk condition).
parts.working: 1 mark for the cane condition with a detail (black cane, appeared sober/ill); 1 mark for the drunk condition with a detail (smelled of liquor, bottle in a brown paper bag).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the sample of passengers in Piliavin et al.'s study.
parts.answer: About 4450 men and women travelling on the New York subway (8th Avenue line) on weekdays between 11 a.m. and 3 p.m.; roughly 45% black and 55% white.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: about 4450 passengers; New York subway / 8th Avenue express line; weekdays, 11 a.m.–3 p.m.; about 45% black, 55% white; both men and women; an opportunity sample of whoever was in the carriage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of this sample.
parts.answer: The passengers were all from one city and one subway line in 1960s New York, so helping norms may differ in other cultures or in rural areas, which limits generalisability.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying a weakness (e.g. one location/culture, could not collect demographic details, same passengers may have seen more than one trial); 1 mark for explaining its effect on the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Piliavin et al. found that the cane victim received spontaneous help on 62 of 65 trials. Calculate this as a percentage. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The drunk victim received spontaneous help on 19 of 38 trials. Calculate this as a percentage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the cost–reward model, explain why the drunk victim was helped less often than the cane victim.
parts.answer: Helping a drunk victim has higher costs (disgust, possible embarrassment, fear he may be violent or vomit) and lower rewards/costs of not helping (others blame him less because his condition seems self-inflicted), so bystanders reduce their arousal in other ways, e.g. by leaving or ignoring him.
parts.working: 1 mark: costs of helping are higher for the drunk (any example: disgust, harm, embarrassment). 1 mark: costs of NOT helping are lower (he is seen as responsible for his state, less self-blame). 1 mark: link to arousal being reduced by a route other than helping (leaving the area, rationalising).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'diffusion of responsibility'.
parts.answer: The more bystanders there are, the less responsible each one feels for helping, so the less likely any one of them is to help.
parts.working: B1 for the idea that responsibility is shared/spread among bystanders so each feels less obliged to help.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether Piliavin et al.'s results supported the idea of diffusion of responsibility.
parts.answer: They did not support it: in this subway setting the victim was helped very quickly and often, and help was not reduced or delayed when more people were in the critical area. The researchers suggested this may be because the victim could clearly be seen and bystanders could not leave the moving train.
parts.working: 1 mark: not supported. 1 mark: evidence – high rate of help / help was not reduced or delayed when more passengers were present. 1 mark: reason – face-to-face situation, victim clearly visible, passengers could not easily leave between stations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how data were recorded in Piliavin et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Two female observers sat in the adjacent area of the carriage. One recorded the race, sex and location of every passenger in the critical area and adjacent area, and the number who helped. The other recorded the race, sex and location of every helper and timed how long it took for help to arrive (latency), including after the model's help. They also noted any spontaneous comments made by passengers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: two female observers; seated in the adjacent area; recorded number/race/sex/location of passengers; recorded race/sex/location of helpers; timed latency of first help (stopwatch); recorded latency after model acted; recorded comments by passengers; data were mostly quantitative with some qualitative comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the role of the model in Piliavin et al.'s study.
parts.answer: The model was a white male confederate who helped the victim if nobody else had, either after about 70 seconds (early) or about 150 seconds (late), standing either in the critical area or the adjacent area, to see whether his example increased helping by others.
parts.working: 1 mark: confederate who helped the victim if no one else did. 1 mark: detail of the conditions – early (70 s) or late (150 s); critical or adjacent area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the effect of the model could not be fully tested.
parts.answer: In most trials, especially with the cane victim, a passenger helped before the model was due to act, so there were too few trials in which the model actually intervened to compare conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: passengers often helped spontaneously before the model was due. 1 mark: so few model trials happened / not enough data for each model condition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two friends are discussing Piliavin et al.'s study. Farah says the study has high ecological validity. Hamza says its ethics are so poor that the results should not be used. Explain one point that supports each friend's view.
parts.answer: Farah: the study took place in a real subway carriage with real passengers who did not know they were being studied, so their helping behaviour was natural and reflects how people behave in everyday emergencies. Hamza: passengers did not give informed consent, were deceived into believing a real emergency was happening, could not withdraw, and were not debriefed, so some may have been distressed or felt guilty for not helping.
parts.working: 2 marks for Farah: real setting/real passengers (1) + unaware so natural behaviour, generalises to everyday life (1). 2 marks for Hamza: named guideline broken – no consent/deception/no right to withdraw/no debrief (1) + consequence, e.g. possible distress or guilt among passengers who did not help (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the findings of Piliavin et al.'s study about who helped the victim.
parts.answer: Most first helpers were male (about 90% of first helpers were men). There was a slight same-race effect: in the drunk condition, people were more likely to help a victim of their own race. Help was given more often and more quickly to the cane victim than to the drunk victim. More passengers left the critical area in the drunk trials than in the cane trials.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: about 90% of first helpers male; same-race helping more common, especially for the drunk victim; cane victim helped on 62 of 65 trials vs drunk 19 of 38; cane victim helped faster; spontaneous help occurred on 81 of the 103 trials; more people left the critical area with the drunk victim; there was no diffusion of responsibility.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way the findings about the gender of helpers could be applied in a public transport setting today.
parts.answer: Because women were less likely to give direct physical help (perhaps because of perceived costs), transport staff training or announcements could stress simple low-cost actions everyone can take, such as pressing the emergency alarm, so all passengers feel able to help.
parts.working: 1 mark: link to finding (men were much more likely to help directly). 1 mark: an ethical, practical application in a transport context (e.g. publicise easy help options, emergency buttons, training).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Piliavin et al.'s subway Samaritan study in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about the use of quantitative data.
parts.answer: Strengths: quantitative data (number of trials helped, latencies, percentages of helpers by sex/race) allowed objective comparison of the cane and drunk conditions and statistical analysis; high ecological validity as it was a real-life setting with real passengers; standardised procedure (same route, timings, victim clothing, 70 s collapse) improved reliability. Weaknesses: quantitative data did not explain why passengers chose to help or not – only a few spontaneous comments gave qualitative insight; ethics – no consent, deception, no debrief, possible distress; lack of control over passengers (some may have seen more than one trial, numbers in carriage varied); the drunk/cane conditions were unequal in number of trials; sample limited to New York.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): two strengths and two weaknesses, each well explained with examples from the study, quantitative data issue included and discussed thoroughly, balanced. Level 3 (5–7): four points, mostly explained, quantitative data issue included; or three detailed points. Level 2 (3–4): points identified with limited explanation or not linked to the study. Level 1 (1–2): brief or generic points. Points: quantitative data (objective, comparable vs lacks reasons), ecological validity, standardisation/reliability, ethics, control of extraneous variables, generalisability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the researchers chose the stretch of the subway between 59th Street and 125th Street.
parts.answer: There were no stops on this stretch for about 7½ minutes, so the passengers could not leave the carriage and the full trial could be observed under the same conditions each time.
parts.working: 1 mark: non-stop journey of about 7½ minutes. 1 mark: so passengers stayed in the carriage / trials were standardised / the whole incident could be observed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the participants in Milgram's (1963) study were recruited.
parts.answer: By a newspaper advertisement and direct-mail letters asking for men in the New Haven area to take part in a study of memory and learning at Yale University, for which they would be paid $4.50.
parts.working: 1 mark: newspaper advert and/or direct mail (volunteer/self-selected sample). 1 mark: detail – men aged 20–50 from New Haven, told it was about memory/learning, paid $4.50.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of participants who went to the maximum shock of 450 volts.
parts.working: B1: 26 (accept 65%).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the four verbal prods used by the experimenter in Milgram's study.
parts.answer: 'Please continue' (or 'Please go on'); 'The experiment requires that you continue'; 'It is absolutely essential that you continue'; 'You have no other choice, you must go on'.
parts.working: 1 mark for each prod in correct wording or a close paraphrase. Allow 1 mark max if the prods are listed without the idea that they were given in sequence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Milgram gave each participant a sample shock of 45 volts.
parts.answer: To convince the participant that the shock generator was real and that the shocks were painful, so that they believed they were really harming the learner.
parts.working: 1 mark: to make them believe the shocks/generator were genuine. 1 mark: so the obedience measured was real – they believed they were hurting the learner (increases validity).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one piece of qualitative data that Milgram recorded.
parts.answer: Many participants showed signs of extreme tension such as sweating, trembling, stuttering, groaning, biting their lips and digging fingernails into their flesh; 14 showed nervous laughter and three had uncontrollable seizures.
parts.working: 1 mark for a type of observation (signs of stress, nervous laughter, comments). 1 mark for detail (e.g. sweating, trembling, 14 nervous laughter, 3 full-blown seizures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before the study, Milgram asked 14 Yale psychology students to predict the results. Outline what they predicted and compare this with the actual result.
parts.answer: They predicted that only a very small proportion – between 0% and 3% (mean about 1.2%) – would go to 450 V. In fact 65% (26 of 40) did, far more than predicted.
parts.working: 1 mark: predictions 0–3% (or 'hardly anyone'). 1 mark: actual result 65%. 1 mark: comparison – actual obedience was much higher than expected (65 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 54, about 50 times more).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happened when the 'teacher' reached 300 volts in Milgram's study.
parts.answer: The learner (Mr Wallace) pounded on the wall of the room. After this he no longer gave answers to the word-pair questions, and the teacher was told to treat no answer as a wrong answer.
parts.working: 1 mark: learner pounded/banged on the wall. 1 mark: no further answers given / silence treated as wrong answer / five participants stopped at 300 V.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why this study is described as a controlled laboratory study even though Milgram did not compare conditions.
parts.answer: It was carried out in a controlled environment (a laboratory at Yale University) with a highly standardised procedure – the same script, prods, shock generator and confederates for every participant.
parts.working: 1 mark: controlled setting (Yale lab). 1 mark: standardised procedure/controls (same prods, same learner responses, same shock generator).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Milgram's study could be used to support a situational explanation of behaviour.
parts.answer: Most participants obeyed to 450 V even though they showed great distress, suggesting that features of the situation – the prestige of Yale, the experimenter's lab coat and authority, the prods and the gradual 15 V steps – rather than their personality caused the behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition – situational explanation = behaviour caused by the environment/setting. 1 mark: evidence – 65% obeyed to 450 V despite distress. 1 mark: named situational features (Yale, lab coat, prods, small increments, payment).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one piece of evidence from the study that suggests individual factors also played a part.
parts.answer: Not everyone obeyed: 14 of the 40 participants refused to continue at some point between 300 V and 450 V, so differences between people (e.g. personality, values) must have affected obedience.
parts.working: 1 mark: 14 (35%) disobeyed / five stopped at 300 V. 1 mark: same situation, different responses, so individual differences matter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether Milgram's study broke the ethical guideline of protection from harm, and describe what Milgram did to reduce any harm.
parts.answer: Yes: participants experienced extreme stress, e.g. sweating, trembling and three had seizures, more than they would meet in everyday life. To reduce harm, Milgram debriefed them, introduced them to the unharmed learner in a friendly reconciliation, and explained their behaviour was normal; follow-up questionnaires suggested most were glad to have taken part.
parts.working: 2 marks: guideline broken with evidence (stress signs, seizures). 2 marks: steps taken – debrief, reunion with learner, reassurance, follow-up questionnaire / psychiatric check.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Milgram's (1963) study in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about generalisability.
parts.answer: Strengths: standardised procedure (same prods, scripted learner responses, same generator) gives high reliability and allows replication; quantitative data (maximum voltage) allowed clear comparison, alongside rich qualitative data on stress which helps explain behaviour; deception meant participants believed the situation, raising internal validity. Weaknesses: generalisability – only 40 American men from New Haven, volunteers, so cannot generalise to women or other cultures; low ecological validity – an artificial task and an unusual setting; ethical problems – deception, harm, the prods undermined the right to withdraw.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): two strengths and two weaknesses, each well explained and linked to the study, generalisability included and fully discussed. Level 3 (5–7): four points with some explanation, generalisability included. Level 2 (3–4): limited explanation or few links to the study. Level 1 (1–2): brief, generic points. Valid points: generalisability (sample of 40 American males, volunteers; but wide age/occupation range), reliability/standardisation, validity (belief in shocks; artificial task), data type, ethics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the two confederates in Milgram's study and state one fact about each.
parts.answer: The experimenter – a 31-year-old biology teacher who wore a grey lab coat and appeared stern; the learner 'Mr Wallace' – a 47-year-old accountant, mild-mannered and likeable.
parts.working: 1 mark: experimenter with a detail (31-year-old, biology teacher, grey lab coat, impassive). 1 mark: learner with a detail (47-year-old, accountant, mild-mannered, of Irish-American appearance).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the tool-offering task used in Yamamoto et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Two chimpanzees were placed in adjacent booths with a window between them. One chimpanzee faced a task that needed a tool (a stick or a straw) to reach a juice reward, while the other had a set of seven objects, including the stick and straw. The researchers recorded whether the second chimpanzee passed a tool through the window and which tool it chose.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: two chimpanzees in adjacent booths; window/hole to pass objects; one needed a stick or straw to get juice; other had a tool box of seven objects; researchers recorded offers and which object was chosen; trials ended after a set time if no tool was offered.

author: HomiLabs
stem: Older-syllabus study: Yamamoto et al. was a core study up to 2023 and is not on the 2024 onward syllabus. Use this question with older past papers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the 'can-see' and 'cannot-see' conditions in Yamamoto et al.'s study.
parts.answer: In the can-see condition the helper could see through the panel into the partner's booth and so could see which tool task the partner faced. In the cannot-see condition the panel was made opaque (except for a hole for passing objects), so the helper could not see the partner's situation.
parts.working: 1 mark for each condition described.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the difference between the two conditions suggests about chimpanzees' ability to understand another's needs.
parts.answer: When they could see, helpers chose the correct tool more often, but when they could not see they offered tools more randomly. This suggests chimpanzees can understand what another chimpanzee needs when they can see its situation (targeted helping).
parts.working: 1 mark: correct tool chosen more often when able to see. 1 mark: conclusion – chimpanzees can work out a conspecific's needs from visual information / targeted helping.

author: HomiLabs
stem: Older-syllabus study: Yamamoto et al. was a core study up to 2023 and is not on the 2024 onward syllabus. Use this question with older past papers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of using chimpanzees from a research institute in Yamamoto et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Strength: the chimpanzees were used to taking part in cognitive tasks and to the booths, so they were less stressed and their behaviour could be tested under controlled, repeatable conditions. Weakness: captive chimpanzees raised with human contact and training may help differently from wild chimpanzees, so the findings may not generalise to chimpanzees in their natural habitat.
parts.working: 2 marks for strength (identified + linked to the study), 2 marks for weakness (identified + linked). Accept: ethics (well cared for, could be rewarded) or validity/generalisability points.

author: HomiLabs
stem: Older-syllabus study: Yamamoto et al. was a core study up to 2023 and is not on the 2024 onward syllabus. Use this question with older past papers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Yamamoto et al. found that chimpanzees rarely offered a tool unless their partner requested it. Explain how this finding helps answer the question of whether helping behaviour in humans is unique.
parts.answer: Chimpanzees did help each other and could select the correct tool (targeted helping), showing that helping based on understanding another's needs is not unique to humans. However, they mostly helped only after a request (e.g. the partner reaching through the hole), whereas humans often help spontaneously, as in Piliavin et al., so voluntary, unrequested helping may be more developed in humans.
parts.working: 1 mark: chimpanzees helped / showed targeted helping. 1 mark: so helping based on others' needs is shared with our closest relative (not uniquely human). 1 mark: but help was mostly in response to requests. 1 mark: humans help spontaneously, so this aspect may be more distinctive (accept comparison with a human study).

author: HomiLabs
stem: Older-syllabus study: Yamamoto et al. was a core study up to 2023 and is not on the 2024 onward syllabus. Use this question with older past papers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one assumption of the social approach in psychology.
parts.answer: The behaviour, feelings and beliefs of an individual are influenced by other individuals and groups, whether these people are actually present or only imagined.
parts.working: 1 mark: behaviour is influenced by other people/groups (or by culture/society). 1 mark: elaboration – e.g. real or imagined presence, social roles, norms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Milgram's study illustrates this assumption.
parts.answer: Participants gave what they believed were dangerous shocks because an authority figure (the experimenter) told them to, showing behaviour was shaped by another person.
parts.working: 1 mark: link to an authority figure/other person. 1 mark: specific evidence (prods, 65% went to 450 V).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Piliavin et al.'s study supports the assumption that behaviour is affected by the social situation.
parts.answer: Passengers' helping depended on features of the situation involving other people, such as whether the victim appeared drunk or ill (cane victim helped on 95% of trials vs about 50% for drunk) and the victim's race, showing that the behaviour of the people around us shapes our own behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark: statement of the assumption. 1 mark: evidence from the study (victim type / race / model). 1 mark: explanation linking the evidence to the assumption.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ayesha says Perry et al.'s study belongs in the social approach even though participants were given a hormone nasal spray. Explain one reason she could give.
parts.answer: The behaviour measured was how close participants were willing to let other people (such as a stranger or a friend) come to them, i.e. personal space, which is a response to other individuals, fitting the assumption that behaviour is influenced by others (real or imagined).
parts.working: 1 mark: behaviour studied is a response to other people (preferred distance from others / personal space). 1 mark: link to the study (approaching figures such as strangers or friends) or to the assumption (real or imagined presence of others).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why Perry et al.'s study gives only limited support to the assumptions of the social approach.
parts.answer: Differences in preferred distance were linked to oxytocin (a biological factor) and to each person's level of empathy (an individual trait), so the behaviour was not explained only by the influence of other people.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies a non-social cause in the study (oxytocin / biological; empathy / individual differences; only imagined figures on paper rather than real people). 1 mark: so the study does not show behaviour is shaped only by others / limited support.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the social approach with the cognitive approach, giving one similarity and one difference in their assumptions.
parts.answer: Similarity: both try to explain human behaviour by looking at influences beyond biology, and both mostly use controlled scientific methods such as experiments. Difference: the social approach assumes behaviour is shaped by other people and groups (external, situational influences), whereas the cognitive approach assumes behaviour is shaped by internal mental processes such as memory, attention and perception.
parts.working: 2 marks for a similarity (identified + explained, ideally with an example study). 2 marks for a difference (identified + explained, e.g. external social influence vs internal mental processes, with examples such as Milgram vs Andrade).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'personal space'.
parts.answer: The area immediately around a person's body which they feel belongs to them, and which they become uncomfortable if others enter without invitation.
parts.working: B1: the space around a person that they feel is theirs / the preferred distance kept from others.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Perry et al. gave each participant a nasal spray of oxytocin on one occasion and a placebo spray on another occasion. Explain why the placebo condition was included.
parts.answer: To provide a comparison: any difference in preferred interpersonal distance between the two sessions could then be caused by the oxytocin itself rather than by expectations or the experience of having a nasal spray, since both sessions were the same apart from the hormone (and neither participants nor researchers knew which spray was given).
parts.working: 1 mark: placebo acts as a control/comparison condition. 1 mark: so effects can be attributed to oxytocin, not to expectations/the procedure of being sprayed (accept reference to double-blind reducing demand characteristics).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why laboratory studies of personal space, such as Perry et al.'s, may lack ecological validity.
parts.answer: In real life a real person approaches us in a natural setting for a reason; in Perry et al.'s study participants only imagined a figure approaching and marked on paper where they would like it to stop, so their answers may not match how they react when a stranger really moves close in everyday life.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies an artificial feature of a lab study of personal space. 1 mark: explains why behaviour may differ from real life.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way findings about personal space could be applied in a crowded hospital waiting area in Lahore.
parts.answer: Seating could be arranged with small gaps or partitions between chairs so strangers are not forced too close, reducing discomfort and stress for waiting patients.
parts.working: 1 mark: practical, ethical suggestion. 1 mark: link to the idea that invasion of personal space causes discomfort/arousal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether a person's preferred personal space is better explained by individual or by situational factors. Use Perry et al.'s study and one other example in your answer.
parts.answer: Individual: Perry et al. investigated whether differences between people, such as their level of empathy, relate to how close they like others to be, finding that oxytocin led highly empathic people to prefer closer distances, so personal space depends partly on individual characteristics. Situational: preferred distance also changes with the situation – e.g. people tolerate being very close to strangers in a crowded bus but not in an empty park, and with friends rather than strangers. Both are needed: individual traits set a typical distance, which the situation then adjusts.
parts.working: 1 mark: defines individual vs situational explanations. 1 mark: individual side linked to Perry et al. (individual differences such as empathy, interacting with oxytocin). 1 mark: situational side with an example. 1 mark: reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the materials used in the Revised Eyes Test.
parts.answer: 36 black-and-white photographs of the eye region of different actors' and actresses' faces, taken from magazines. Each photo was surrounded by four words describing mental states: one target word and three foils. A glossary defined every word.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: 36 photographs; eye region only; black and white; from magazines; four words per photo (one target, three foils); foils of the same emotional valence as the target; glossary of word meanings; similar numbers of male and female faces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the four groups of participants in Baron-Cohen et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Group 1: 15 adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism; Group 2: 122 adults from the general population; Group 3: 103 students at Cambridge University; Group 4: 14 adults from the general population, matched on IQ with Group 1.
parts.working: 1 mark for each group. Numbers not required but credit them as detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The mean Eyes Test scores (out of 36) were: Asperger syndrome/high-functioning autism group 21.9, general population 26.2, students 28.0, IQ-matched group 30.9. Calculate the difference between the mean of the Asperger/autism group and the mean of the IQ-matched group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express the Asperger/autism group's mean as a percentage of the maximum score. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what these results suggest about theory of mind in adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism.
parts.answer: They scored lowest of all groups, even below people of the same IQ, which suggests adults with AS/HFA have a specific difficulty in attributing mental states to others from the eyes (a subtle theory of mind deficit), not just lower general intelligence.
parts.working: 1 mark: AS/HFA group lowest, including below IQ-matched group. 1 mark: conclusion – subtle theory of mind deficit that is not explained by IQ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline two problems with the original Eyes Test that Baron-Cohen et al. tried to solve in the revised version.
parts.answer: The original had only two answer choices, so participants could score 50% by guessing and many people scored near the top (ceiling effect); the revised test used four choices. The original had only 25 items, giving a narrow range of scores; the revised test had 36. (Also: original foils were often the semantic opposite of the target, making it too easy; some items could be solved by basic emotions or gaze direction; there were more female faces.)
parts.working: 2 marks per problem: 1 for the problem in the original, 1 for how the revision fixed it. Problems: two-choice forced format/guessing; ceiling effect; too few items (25 → 36); foils were opposites (→ same emotional valence); basic emotions/gaze direction cues; unequal male/female faces; no glossary (→ glossary added).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why participants in Baron-Cohen et al.'s study also completed the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ) questionnaire.
parts.answer: To measure autistic traits in all participants, so the researchers could test whether scores on the Eyes Test were related (negatively correlated) to the number of autistic traits a person has.
parts.working: 1 mark: AQ measures autistic traits/self-reported characteristics. 1 mark: to test the correlation with Eyes Test scores (prediction of a negative correlation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction of the correlation found between AQ scores and Eyes Test scores.
parts.answer: Negative – the higher the AQ score, the lower the Eyes Test score.
parts.working: B1: negative correlation (with explanation of meaning).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength of the sampling of the Asperger syndrome/high-functioning autism group in Baron-Cohen et al.'s study.
parts.answer: All had a clinical diagnosis of AS or HFA, so the researchers could be confident the group really had the condition being studied, which increases the validity of comparisons with the other groups.
parts.working: 1 mark: identified strength (diagnosed by clinicians / matched on IQ with Group 4). 1 mark: explained in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of this group's sample.
parts.answer: There were only 15 participants, all of them men, so the results may not represent all adults with AS/HFA, e.g. women, reducing generalisability.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness (small, 15 people; all male; volunteers). 1 mark: consequence for generalisability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two friends are arguing about the validity of the Revised Eyes Test. Bilal says it is a valid measure of theory of mind; Sana says it is not. Explain one argument for each friend.
parts.answer: Bilal: the test was carefully developed – target words were checked by judges, foils had the same emotional valence, a glossary removed vocabulary problems – and people with AS/HFA scored lower, as predicted, so it seems to measure the ability to read mental states. Sana: the photographs are static, black-and-white images of eyes only, whereas in real life we judge mental states from whole faces, voices, movement and context, so the test may not measure everyday theory of mind (low ecological/construct validity).
parts.working: 2 marks for Bilal (point + link to the test's design or results). 2 marks for Sana (point + link, e.g. static images, eyes only, no context, adults only).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Baron-Cohen et al.'s study in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about the use of quantitative data.
parts.answer: Strengths: quantitative data (scores out of 36, AQ scores) allowed objective comparison of the four groups and correlation with AQ; standardised procedure (same 36 photos, same instructions, glossary) increased reliability; inclusion of control groups (general population, students, IQ-matched) meant differences could be attributed to AS/HFA rather than IQ. Weaknesses: quantitative scores do not show why a participant chose a word or how they reasoned – no qualitative insight; low ecological validity – static photos of eyes only; small, mainly male AS/HFA group limits generalisability; the student group was not representative of the general population.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): two strengths and two weaknesses, each developed with examples from the study, quantitative data point discussed in detail, balanced. Level 3 (5–7): four points with some explanation including quantitative data, or three detailed points. Level 2 (3–4): limited explanation/links. Level 1 (1–2): brief generic points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'theory of mind'.
parts.answer: The ability to attribute mental states (beliefs, intentions, emotions) to oneself and to other people, and to understand that others' mental states can differ from one's own.
parts.working: B1 for the ability to understand/attribute mental states to others.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one way the findings of Baron-Cohen et al.'s study could be used in everyday life.
parts.answer: The Eyes Test could be used as part of an assessment to help identify adults who may have subtle difficulties understanding others' feelings, so they can be offered support or social skills training.
parts.working: 1 mark: application. 1 mark: explained, ethical and linked to the study (subtle deficits, adults, eyes).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the participants in the doodling condition were asked to do in Andrade's study.
parts.answer: While listening to a monotonous 2½-minute mock telephone message about a party, they shaded in printed squares and circles on a sheet of paper. They were told that speed and neatness did not matter. They also had to write down the names of people who would be coming to the party.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: shade printed shapes (squares and circles); while listening to the recording; told neatness/speed unimportant; write down names of party guests (monitoring task); same message as control group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and one dependent variable in Andrade's study.
parts.answer: IV: whether or not participants doodled (doodling group vs control group). DV: number of names correctly monitored (written down) OR number of names and places recalled in the surprise memory test.
parts.working: 1 mark IV; 1 mark DV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the experimental design used.
parts.answer: Independent measures design.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a surprise memory test the doodling group recalled a mean of 7.5 items and the control group recalled a mean of 5.8 items. Calculate the percentage by which the doodling group's mean recall was higher than the control group's. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the memory test was a surprise.
parts.answer: If participants had known they would be tested, they might have tried to rehearse the information, and the control group might have rehearsed more than the doodlers; a surprise test means recall reflects attention during the call rather than deliberate memorising.
parts.working: 1 mark: prevents deliberate rehearsal/memorising strategies. 1 mark: so the DV measures attention/incidental learning, increasing validity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the conclusion of Andrade's study.
parts.answer: Doodling while doing a boring task improves concentration and memory, perhaps because it reduces daydreaming, which would otherwise use up cognitive resources.
parts.working: 1 mark: doodling aids attention/recall. 1 mark: explanation – reduces daydreaming / keeps arousal at a suitable level.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the participants were tested after they had already taken part in another study.
parts.answer: Andrade wanted them to feel slightly bored or tired, so that the task would encourage daydreaming; this made it more likely that any benefit of doodling (reducing daydreaming) could show up.
parts.working: 1 mark: to make them bored/increase likelihood of daydreaming. 1 mark: needed to test the idea that doodling reduces daydreaming.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the sample in Andrade's study.
parts.answer: 40 adults aged 18–55 from the participant panel of a research unit in Cambridge (UK), who were paid for taking part; 20 were allocated to each condition.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: 40 participants; aged 18–55; from a Cambridge research unit's participant panel / volunteers; paid; 20 per condition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why this sample may limit the generalisability of the findings.
parts.answer: The participants were volunteers on a research panel who regularly take part in studies, and were all from one place in the UK, so people from other cultures or those unused to psychology tasks may respond differently to doodling.
parts.working: 1 mark: feature of sample. 1 mark: why it limits generalisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Andrade controlled extraneous variables in her study. Refer to two controls.
parts.answer: All participants heard the same recorded message read in the same monotonous voice at the same volume, so differences in recall could not be due to the message. Both groups were given the same instructions to write down names of people coming to the party, and were tested in the same conditions after another study, so tiredness/boredom was similar in both groups.
parts.working: 2 marks per control: 1 for identifying it, 1 for explaining why it matters. Controls: same recording/standardised message; same monitoring instructions; same pre-test conditions (after another study); doodle sheet the same for all; same surprise recall test; random allocation to conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Andrade's study in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about ecological validity.
parts.answer: Strengths: high control (same recording, instructions, conditions) allowed a cause–effect link between doodling and recall; quantitative data (names monitored, items recalled) allowed objective comparison; the task resembled an everyday situation (listening to a phone message), giving some ecological validity. Weaknesses: ecological validity is limited – doodling was imposed (shading shapes) rather than spontaneous, and people do not usually doodle on demand in a lab; independent measures design means participant variables (e.g. memory ability) might explain differences; sample of panel volunteers limits generalisability; mild deception about the memory test.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): two strengths and two weaknesses, each developed and linked to the study, ecological validity discussed in detail. Level 3 (5–7): four points with some explanation including ecological validity. Level 2 (3–4): limited explanation. Level 1 (1–2): brief generic points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mr Qureshi teaches a two-hour evening lecture in Karachi and notices that some students doodle in their notebooks. Using Andrade's study, suggest advice he could give his students.
parts.answer: He could tell students that simple doodling (such as shading shapes) during long, dull parts of the lecture is acceptable and may help them pay attention and remember more, because Andrade found doodlers recalled about 29% more than non-doodlers. He should advise that the doodling be simple so it does not distract from listening.
parts.working: 1 mark: advice allowing/encouraging simple doodling in boring tasks. 1 mark: link to findings (better recall / 29% more). 1 mark: explanation – reduces daydreaming, or caution that doodling must be simple and low demand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Andrade asked participants to write down the names of people coming to the party while they listened. Explain why this 'monitoring' task was included.
parts.answer: It gave a direct measure of attention during the call (how many target names were correctly detected), separate from the later memory test, so Andrade could see whether doodling affected concentration as well as recall.
parts.working: 1 mark: measures attention/concentration during the task. 1 mark: allows comparison with recall / shows if doodlers were paying attention.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a target-present line-up and a target-absent line-up.
parts.answer: In a target-present line-up the person (or character) the witness saw is included among the faces; in a target-absent line-up the person seen is not included, so the correct response is to reject the line-up.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a 'false positive' identification.
parts.answer: Choosing someone from a target-absent line-up, i.e. identifying an innocent person (foil) as the target.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pozzulo et al. compared young children with adults. Outline one finding about children's line-up identifications.
parts.answer: Children were less likely than adults to correctly reject a target-absent line-up – they made more false positive identifications, choosing a face even though the target was not there.
parts.working: 1 mark: children made more false positives / fewer correct rejections. 1 mark: comparison with adults and reference to target-absent line-ups.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way this finding could be applied by police in Pakistan when a child is a witness.
parts.answer: Police should warn the child clearly that the culprit may not be in the line-up and that saying 'not there' is a good answer, or use procedures that reduce pressure to choose, so that innocent suspects are less likely to be wrongly identified.
parts.working: 1 mark: practical suggestion. 1 mark: linked to reducing children's false positives.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pozzulo et al. used both cartoon characters and human faces as targets. Suggest one reason why cartoon characters were included.
parts.answer: Young children are familiar with cartoon characters and find them interesting, so including them allowed the researchers to see whether children's poor performance was due to unfamiliar human faces or to the line-up task itself.
parts.working: 1 mark: cartoons are familiar/engaging for young children. 1 mark: allows comparison to see whether target type affects children's accuracy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Researchers have suggested that children's false positive responding might have a cognitive explanation or a social explanation. Explain the difference between these two explanations.
parts.answer: Cognitive: the child's errors come from limits in mental processing – e.g. a weaker memory for the face, or difficulty comparing the faces with the memory and deciding that none matches. Social: the child may know the target is not there but chooses anyway because they feel pressure to give an answer to an adult, believe the adult expects them to pick someone, or want to be helpful.
parts.working: 2 marks cognitive (memory/recognition/decision-making limitation + elaboration). 2 marks social (pressure/compliance/expectation of adult + elaboration).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Pozzulo et al.'s study in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about the use of children as participants.
parts.answer: Strengths: comparing children with adults under the same controlled procedure allowed clear conclusions about age differences; quantitative data (correct identifications, false positives) were objective and easy to compare; the findings have useful applications to police line-up procedures. Use of children: findings are directly relevant to child witnesses, but children may misunderstand instructions or feel pressure, need parental consent, and must be protected from distress. Weaknesses: low ecological validity – seeing a target in a study is not the same as witnessing a real crime with stress and consequences; children's responses may be affected by demand characteristics; ethical issues with children.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): two strengths and two weaknesses, developed with examples from the study, the children issue discussed fully. Level 3 (5–7): four points with some explanation, including children. Level 2 (3–4): limited explanation. Level 1 (1–2): brief generic points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the false feedback given to participants in the 'love' group in Laney et al.'s study.
parts.answer: They were told that a computer analysis of their earlier questionnaire answers showed that, as a child, they had loved asparagus the first time they tried it.
parts.working: 1 mark: told the results came from a computer profile of their questionnaire answers. 1 mark: content – they loved asparagus the first time they tried cooked asparagus as a child.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one questionnaire used to measure the participants' attitudes towards asparagus.
parts.answer: Any one of: Food History Inventory; Food Preferences Questionnaire; Restaurant Questionnaire; Food Costs Questionnaire; Memory of Experience Questionnaire.

author: HomiLabs
stem: Older-syllabus study: Laney et al. was a core study up to 2023 and is not on the 2024 onward syllabus. Use this question with older past papers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Laney et al. included filler items about other foods in their questionnaires.
parts.answer: To hide the real aim (asparagus) from participants, reducing demand characteristics so they would not guess what the study was about and change their answers.
parts.working: 1 mark: to disguise the aim / mask the target item. 1 mark: reduces demand characteristics, increasing validity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way in which Laney et al.'s study broke the guideline on deception, and why this could be justified.
parts.answer: Participants were deliberately told a false 'fact' about their childhood. This could be justified because the false memory was positive (loving a healthy vegetable), was unlikely to cause harm, and the study could not be done without deception; participants were fully debriefed afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark: the deception described. 1 mark: justification (harmless/positive belief, necessary, debriefing).

author: HomiLabs
stem: Older-syllabus study: Laney et al. was a core study up to 2023 and is not on the 2024 onward syllabus. Use this question with older past papers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between 'believers' and 'non-believers' in Laney et al.'s study.
parts.answer: In the love group, believers were participants who came to believe/remember that they had loved asparagus as a child, after the false feedback; non-believers received the same feedback but did not come to believe it.
parts.working: 1 mark for each group defined.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one result about the believers.
parts.answer: Believers showed increased liking for asparagus and were more willing to eat it in a restaurant, and were willing to pay more for it in a shop, than controls.
parts.working: 1 mark: identified result (liking, intention to eat, willingness to pay). 1 mark: comparison with control/non-believers.

author: HomiLabs
stem: Older-syllabus study: Laney et al. was a core study up to 2023 and is not on the 2024 onward syllabus. Use this question with older past papers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ms Rizvi runs a school canteen in Islamabad and wants children to eat more spinach. Explain whether it would be ethical to use the findings of Laney et al.'s study to help her.
parts.answer: Deliberately planting false memories in children would be unethical: they cannot give fully informed consent, it involves deceiving them about their own past, and parents would need to agree. A more ethical application would be to use the idea that positive memories increase liking, e.g. by creating genuinely positive experiences with spinach (tasting days, praise) without deception.
parts.working: 1 mark: link to the study (false positive memories increased liking/eating). 1 mark: ethical problem – deception/consent. 1 mark: extra issue with children (parental consent, vulnerability). 1 mark: suggestion of an ethical alternative or reasoned conclusion.

author: HomiLabs
stem: Older-syllabus study: Laney et al. was a core study up to 2023 and is not on the 2024 onward syllabus. Use this question with older past papers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of the validity of Laney et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Strength: the use of filler items and a cover story ('food preferences and personality') reduced demand characteristics, so changes in liking are more likely to reflect a real effect of the false memory. Weakness: willingness to eat or pay for asparagus was measured by questionnaire, not real behaviour, so participants' answers may not show what they would actually eat (low ecological validity).
parts.working: 2 marks for strength (point + link). 2 marks for weakness (point + link). Accept: delayed second session; self-report bias; artificial setting.

author: HomiLabs
stem: Older-syllabus study: Laney et al. was a core study up to 2023 and is not on the 2024 onward syllabus. Use this question with older past papers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one assumption of the cognitive approach in psychology.
parts.answer: Cognitive processes such as perception, attention, memory and language influence behaviour, and these internal processes can be studied scientifically.
parts.working: 1 mark: internal mental processes influence behaviour. 1 mark: named examples or idea that differences between individuals can be explained by differences in mental processes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Andrade's study illustrates this assumption.
parts.answer: Doodling affected attention (reducing daydreaming), which improved the participants' memory for the phone message, showing that mental processes influence behaviour (recall).
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies attention/memory in the study. 1 mark: link to behaviour/assumption.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how both Baron-Cohen et al.'s and Pozzulo et al.'s studies support the assumption that differences between individuals can be explained in terms of differences in cognitive processes.
parts.answer: Baron-Cohen et al.: adults with Asperger syndrome/high-functioning autism scored lower on the Eyes Test than the other groups, including an IQ-matched group, so differences in social understanding can be explained by a difference in a cognitive process (theory of mind). Pozzulo et al.: children and adults differed in their line-up identifications (children made more false positives in target-absent line-ups), which can be explained by differences in memory or decision-making processes between age groups.
parts.working: 2 marks per study: 1 for the individual difference found, 1 for linking it to a cognitive process (memory, recognition, decision-making).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'informed consent'.
parts.answer: Agreement to take part in a study given by a participant who has been told enough about the aims and procedure to make a knowledgeable decision.
parts.working: B1: agreement to participate given with full knowledge of what the study involves.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A researcher secretly observes how people queue at a bank in Lahore. Explain why she cannot obtain informed consent in this study.
parts.answer: The observation is covert; if she asked customers for consent they would know they were being watched and might change how they queue, so the behaviour would no longer be natural.
parts.working: 1 mark: covert/naturalistic observation of strangers. 1 mark: asking would cause participant reactivity / demand characteristics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two pieces of information that should be given to participants in a debrief.
parts.answer: Any two of: the true aim of the study; whether any deception was used and why; that their data will be kept confidential; that they may withdraw their data; how to contact the researcher or find out the results; reassurance that their behaviour was normal.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: Dr Malik gives a 20-minute questionnaire about exam stress to 60 Grade 11 students in Faisalabad. Describe how Dr Malik should give the students the right to withdraw.
parts.answer: Before starting she should tell them clearly that they can stop answering at any time, without giving a reason and without any penalty, and that they can ask for their completed questionnaire to be removed and destroyed afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark: told before and during they may leave at any time without penalty/reason. 1 mark: can also withdraw their data afterwards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the right to withdraw is especially important in this study.
parts.answer: Questions about exam stress may upset some students, and as school pupils they may feel pressure to obey an adult researcher, so they need to know they can stop if they feel uncomfortable.
parts.working: 1 mark: sensitive topic may cause distress. 1 mark: young participants / power imbalance with researcher or teacher.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between confidentiality and privacy as ethical guidelines.
parts.answer: Confidentiality means participants' personal information and results must not be shared or published in a way that identifies them. Privacy means participants should not be observed or asked about things in situations where they would expect not to be watched, unless they have agreed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a correct explanation of each term.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a psychologist uses a confederate who pretends to drop her shopping in a busy street in Peshawar, and records whether passers-by help. Identify two ethical guidelines that may be broken in this study.
parts.answer: Any two of: informed consent; deception; right to withdraw; debriefing (passers-by usually leave before they can be debriefed).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct guidelines.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the researcher could reduce one of these ethical problems.
parts.answer: After a passer-by has helped or walked past, a researcher could approach them, explain the true purpose (debrief) and offer them the chance to have their data removed.
parts.working: 1 mark: suggestion. 1 mark: explained as reducing a named problem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'protection from harm' in psychological research.
parts.answer: Participants should not be exposed to more physical or psychological risk than they would meet in everyday life, and should leave the study in the same state as they entered it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hypothetical study: participants watch upsetting news clips about a flood before rating their mood. Suggest two ways the researcher could protect participants from harm.
parts.answer: Any two of: warn participants beforehand about the content and get consent; screen out people who have experienced floods; show a cheerful clip afterwards to restore mood; full debrief with contact details for support; remind them they may stop watching at any time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two suitable ways.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'deception' in psychological research.
parts.answer: Misleading participants, or withholding information, about the true aims or procedure of a study.
parts.working: B1: lying to or misleading participants (including withholding information).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why researchers sometimes need to use deception.
parts.answer: If participants knew the real aim they might change their behaviour to fit (demand characteristics), so deception keeps their behaviour natural and the results valid.
parts.working: 1 mark: participants would change their behaviour/demand characteristics. 1 mark: validity of findings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher wants to interview 9-year-old children in a Hyderabad primary school about bullying. Identify who must give consent for the children to take part.
parts.answer: Their parents or legal guardians (as well as permission from the school, and the children's own agreement).
parts.working: B1: parent/guardian consent (accept head teacher as well but not alone).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one other ethical issue the researcher must consider in this study.
parts.answer: Protection from harm: talking about bullying may upset the children, so the researcher should use gentle questions, allow them to stop at any time, and make sure a teacher or counsellor is available afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies an issue (harm, confidentiality vs safeguarding, right to withdraw, debriefing in simple language). 1 mark: explained in this context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the ethical guidelines of confidentiality and debriefing. Use any examples to support your answer.
parts.answer: Confidentiality: personal details and results must be kept secret and published anonymously, e.g. using participant numbers rather than names, storing questionnaires securely. In Baron-Cohen et al.'s study, participants' test scores would not be published with names. Debriefing: at the end of a study participants are told its true aim, any deception is explained, they are reassured and offered the chance to withdraw their data; e.g. Milgram introduced participants to the unharmed learner and explained the shocks were not real.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for each guideline: 1 for a definition, 1 for elaboration (how it is done), 1 for a relevant example (from a study or a suitable hypothetical one). Full marks require both guidelines and examples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a psychologist installs cameras in a hospital staff room in Karachi to record how nurses take breaks. The nurses agreed to take part in 'a study of working life' but were not told about the cameras. Explain which two ethical guidelines are most clearly broken.
parts.answer: Privacy: a staff room is a private space where nurses would not expect to be filmed, so recording them there invades their privacy. Informed consent/deception: they agreed to a general study but were not told about the filming, so their consent was not fully informed and they were deceived about the procedure.
parts.working: 2 marks per guideline: 1 for naming it, 1 for explaining why it is broken in this scenario.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: an online questionnaire asks 300 university students in Islamabad about their use of social media late at night. Explain two ways the researcher should maintain confidentiality.
parts.answer: Do not ask for names or student ID numbers – use code numbers so answers cannot be linked to individuals. Store the data on a password-protected computer and only report group results (e.g. averages), so no single student can be identified.
parts.working: 2 marks per way: 1 for the method, 1 for explaining how it protects identity. Accept: anonymous responses, coded IDs, secure storage, delete data after use, report only group data, do not share with university.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'presumptive consent'.
parts.answer: Asking a group of people similar to the participants whether they would find the study acceptable; if they would, it is presumed the real participants would also consent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one problem with using presumptive consent.
parts.answer: The people asked are not the actual participants, so individual participants may still object to what happened to them; they have not personally agreed to take part.
parts.working: 1 mark: real participants did not agree themselves. 1 mark: they may still feel upset/object once they find out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: participants are paid PKR 2000 for a 2-hour study on reaction times. The researcher tells them they will only be paid if they complete the whole study. Explain why this is unethical.
parts.answer: It undermines the right to withdraw: participants may feel they cannot leave because they would lose the money, so they are pressured to continue even if uncomfortable.
parts.working: 1 mark: right to withdraw. 1 mark: explanation – payment is conditional, so participants feel forced to continue.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the researcher could change the payment arrangement to be ethical.
parts.answer: Pay all participants the full amount (or pay for time spent) whether or not they complete the study, and make this clear at the start.
parts.working: 1 mark: payment not dependent on completing. 1 mark: participants told in advance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher interviews adults in Quetta who have recently lost a family member, to investigate coping. Suggest two ethical precautions the researcher should take.
parts.answer: Gain fully informed consent, explaining that the questions will be about their loss, and remind them they may stop at any time. Arrange support: provide contact details of a counsellor and end the interview gently with neutral questions, so participants are not left distressed.
parts.working: 2 marks per precaution: identified (1) + linked to the bereavement scenario (1). Accept: confidentiality of sensitive details, avoid probing questions, pilot the interview, trained interviewer, debrief.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'retrospective consent'.
parts.answer: Asking participants for their consent after they have taken part, usually during the debrief, when they know the true aims.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give an example of a study where retrospective consent would be appropriate, and explain why.
parts.answer: A field experiment on helping in a market, where passers-by cannot be told beforehand without spoiling the study; afterwards they are told what happened and asked whether their data may be used.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable example (field experiment, covert observation, deception study). 1 mark: explanation – prior consent would spoil natural behaviour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: Dr Khan tells half of a group of students in Lahore that they scored very low on an 'intelligence test' (false feedback) and then measures how long they persist at difficult puzzles. Explain two ethical guidelines broken in this study and describe what the debrief should include.
parts.answer: Deception: students were given false information about their intelligence. Protection from harm: being told they are of low intelligence could lower self-esteem and cause distress beyond everyday life. The debrief should: explain the true aim (effect of feedback on persistence); state clearly that the feedback was false and not their real score; reassure them that their performance was normal; offer the chance to withdraw their data; give contact details for questions or support.
parts.working: 2 marks per guideline (named + explained in context) = 4. 2 marks for the debrief: must include that the feedback was false + one other feature (true aim, reassurance, withdraw data, contact).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two researchers disagree about a planned covert observation of how people use their phones while walking in a shopping mall in Dubai. Researcher A says it is ethical; Researcher B says it is not. Explain one argument for each researcher.
parts.answer: A: the mall is a public place where people expect to be seen by strangers, so observing them does not invade privacy; no names are recorded and no one is harmed, so it is acceptable to observe without consent. B: people have not given consent and cannot withdraw; if the observers note details such as appearance, or record the content of screens or conversations, this could invade privacy, and they cannot be debriefed.
parts.working: 2 marks for each researcher's argument: 1 for the point (public place/privacy; no consent/right to withdraw), 1 for development in the scenario.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the need for valid results can conflict with ethical guidelines. Use one example from a psychological study.
parts.answer: To get valid results, participants often should not know the true aim, because knowing it could create demand characteristics. This conflicts with informed consent and deception guidelines. For example, Milgram told participants the study was about learning and that the shocks were real; if they had known it was about obedience and that no one was harmed, their behaviour would not have shown real obedience. So high validity was gained at an ethical cost (deception, distress).
parts.working: 1 mark: validity needs natural behaviour / avoid demand characteristics. 1 mark: conflicts with consent/deception. 1 mark: example from a study. 1 mark: explanation of the trade-off in that example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a 3-year longitudinal study follows 150 teenagers in Rawalpindi to see how part-time work affects school grades. The researchers need to link each teenager's data across the three years. Explain how they could keep the data confidential while still linking it.
parts.answer: Give each teenager a unique code number at the start, used on all questionnaires and records instead of names; keep a separate key linking names to codes in a locked or password-protected file that only the lead researcher can access; publish results only as group data and destroy the key at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark: code numbers instead of names. 1 mark: separate, secure key linking names and codes with restricted access. 1 mark: report group data only / destroy key / no identifiable details published.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one other ethical issue that is more of a problem in a longitudinal study than in a one-off study.
parts.answer: Consent must be renewed: the teenagers' circumstances change over three years and they may later wish to withdraw, so they should be reminded each year of their right to withdraw and asked to confirm consent (and their own consent sought when they become adults).
parts.working: 1 mark: issue (ongoing consent, withdrawal, long-term data storage, repeated testing stress). 1 mark: explained in a longitudinal context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: patients in a psychiatric ward in Lahore are asked to take part in a study of a new relaxation technique by the doctor who treats them. Explain two ethical problems with this procedure.
parts.answer: Consent: patients with mental health problems may not fully understand the information, so their consent may not be truly informed; extra checks or a guardian's agreement may be needed. Right to withdraw/pressure: because the request comes from their own doctor, patients may feel they must agree or that their treatment will suffer if they refuse or leave the study.
parts.working: 2 marks per problem: 1 for naming it, 1 for linking it to the vulnerable patients and their doctor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the ethical guidelines of deception and the right to withdraw. Use any examples to support your answer.
parts.answer: Deception: participants should not be misled about the aims or procedure unless it is necessary and is not likely to cause distress; any deception must be explained in the debrief. Example: in Andrade's study participants were not told about the surprise memory test, which was necessary so they would not rehearse the information, and was harmless. Right to withdraw: participants must be told they can leave at any time and remove their data, without penalty. Example: in Milgram's study the prods ('you have no other choice, you must go on') made it hard for participants to feel they could leave.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks per guideline: definition (1), elaboration – when allowed / how given (1), example (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of a cost–benefit analysis in deciding whether a study is ethical.
parts.answer: Before approving a study, an ethics committee weighs the possible costs to participants (distress, deception, loss of privacy) against the benefits of the knowledge gained for society; if the benefits clearly outweigh the costs, and harm is minimised, the study may go ahead.
parts.working: 1 mark: weighing costs to participants. 1 mark: against benefits to society/knowledge. 1 mark: decision made by an ethics committee / study approved only if benefits outweigh costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: In a Multan university, a lecturer asks the students in her own class to take part in her study on memory. She says it is voluntary but records the names of those who refuse. Evaluate the ethics of this procedure, referring to two guidelines.
parts.answer: Right to withdraw/voluntary participation: students may feel pressured to take part because their lecturer marks their work, and recording names of those who refuse suggests consequences, so participation is not truly voluntary. Confidentiality: recording names links individuals with their decision (and possibly their results), which should be kept anonymous. To be ethical, an independent person should recruit and no names of refusers should be kept.
parts.working: 2 marks per guideline: identified (1) + explained in scenario (1). Allow 1 of the 4 marks for a suitable improvement if one guideline is only weakly explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ethical guidelines that apply to research with animals.
parts.answer: Any two of: replacement; species and strain; number of animals; pain and distress; housing; reward, deprivation and aversive stimuli; anaesthesia, analgesia and euthanasia.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by the guideline of 'replacement'.
parts.answer: Researchers should consider whether animals can be replaced with other methods, such as computer simulations, videos or recordings of animals, before using live animals.
parts.working: 1 mark: use alternatives where possible. 1 mark: example of an alternative.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher plans to test maze learning in 60 rats, though a pilot study suggests 20 would give clear results. Explain which animal guideline is relevant.
parts.answer: Number of animals: researchers should use the smallest number of animals needed to get meaningful results, so the researcher should use about 20 rats, not 60.
parts.working: 1 mark: number of animals (reduction). 1 mark: applied – use the minimum needed (fewer rats).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: pigeons are kept at 80% of their normal body weight so that they will work for food rewards in a learning experiment. Explain which ethical guideline this raises and how the researcher could meet it.
parts.answer: Reward, deprivation and aversive stimuli: depriving animals of food can cause distress. The researcher should consider the species' normal feeding pattern, use the minimum deprivation needed, use highly preferred food treats as rewards instead, and monitor the birds' health.
parts.working: 1 mark: names guideline. 1 mark: explains the problem (deprivation causes distress/harm). 1 mark: suitable way to minimise it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: young monkeys are housed alone in small cages during a study of learning. Explain why this breaks the guideline on housing.
parts.answer: Monkeys are social animals; housing them alone in small cages can cause stress and abnormal behaviour, so they should be kept in suitable social groups with enough space and enrichment.
parts.working: 1 mark: social species/needs company or space. 1 mark: isolation/crowding causes distress; suggest appropriate housing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how poor housing could also reduce the validity of the study's results.
parts.answer: Stressed, isolated monkeys may learn or behave differently from normal monkeys, so the learning measured would reflect the effects of stress rather than normal ability.
parts.working: 1 mark: stress changes behaviour. 1 mark: results not representative/confounded.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the guideline on 'species and strain' when researchers select animals for a study.
parts.answer: Researchers should choose a species that is suited to the research purpose and that is likely to suffer least, considering the animals' background (e.g. bred for research vs caught in the wild); endangered species should not be used unless the research benefits their conservation.
parts.working: 1 mark: choose species suited to the aim and least likely to suffer. 1 mark: extra detail (wild-caught or endangered species, knowledge of the species' needs).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the animal ethical guidelines of 'pain and distress' and 'anaesthesia, analgesia and euthanasia'. Use any examples to support your answer.
parts.answer: Pain and distress: researchers should avoid or minimise pain, suffering and lasting harm to animals; any procedure causing distress must be justified by the value of the research and requires approval, e.g. a study using mild electric shocks must use the weakest shock that works and monitor the animal. Anaesthesia, analgesia and euthanasia: animals must be given appropriate anaesthetic during painful procedures and painkillers afterwards; if an animal suffers lasting pain it must be humanely killed by a trained person using an approved method, e.g. rats after brain surgery receive pain relief and are monitored.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks per guideline: definition (1), elaboration (1), example (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher studies fear learning in 12 zebrafish, which are bred in the laboratory, live in a large group tank, and are briefly startled by a tap on the tank. Evaluate whether this study meets two animal ethical guidelines.
parts.answer: Housing: met – the fish live in a large group tank, suitable for a social species, which reduces stress. Pain and distress: largely met – the startle is brief and mild rather than painful, though repeated startles could still cause stress, so the number of trials should be kept low. (Also: species – lab-bred fish rather than wild; number – only 12 used.)
parts.working: 2 marks per guideline: 1 for a judgement (met/not met), 1 for justification from the scenario. Accept replacement, species, number, aversive stimuli.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A psychologist wants to test whether listening to Qur'an recitation or calm instrumental music before an exam reduces anxiety more than sitting in silence. Describe how she could conduct a laboratory experiment to investigate this.
Your plan must include details about:
• the experimental design
• how anxiety would be measured
• controls.
parts.answer: Example plan: IV = 10 minutes of recitation, 10 minutes of instrumental music, or 10 minutes of silence before a timed 15-minute mental arithmetic test (an exam-like task). Independent measures design with random allocation (e.g. names drawn from a box), 30 university students per group, to avoid order effects and practice effects on the test. DV = anxiety, measured by a 10-item self-report rating scale (1 = not at all anxious, 5 = extremely anxious; total 10–50) completed just before the test, plus heart rate measured with a finger pulse monitor. Controls: same room, lighting and temperature; same headphones and volume (e.g. 60 dB); standardised instructions read from a script; same test paper; all tested at the same time of day; participants who are already on anxiety medication excluded. Procedure: consent, baseline heart rate, listening phase, rating scale + heart rate, test, debrief.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: design named and justified (independent measures with random allocation, or repeated measures with counterbalancing); IV conditions operationalised (duration, what is played); DV operationalised (rating scale with anchors and/or heart rate); controls (setting, volume, instructions, time of day); sample and procedure; ethics (consent, right to withdraw, debrief).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
