A researcher wants to find out whether the colour of the paper on which a test is printed (white or yellow) affects how many words students recall. Describe how she could conduct an experiment to investigate this using a repeated measures design.
Your plan must include details about:
• the materials
• how order effects will be controlled
• the sample.
parts.answer: Example plan: Materials – two lists of 20 concrete, two-syllable nouns of similar frequency (list A and list B), each printed in black 14-point font on either white or yellow A4 paper; a stopwatch; blank answer sheets. Procedure – each participant studies a list for 2 minutes, does a 1-minute distractor task (counting backwards in 3s), then writes down as many words as they remember in 2 minutes. They do this twice, once with each paper colour. Order effects – counterbalancing: half do white then yellow, half yellow then white; different but matched word lists in each condition, with list–colour pairing also counterbalanced; a 10-minute break between conditions to reduce fatigue. Sample – 40 Grade 12 students from two colleges in Lahore, chosen by random sampling from class lists (each name given a number, numbers drawn by computer), with parental consent for under-18s. DV – number of words correctly recalled out of 20.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: materials described (word lists matched for length/frequency, paper colour, font); counterbalancing explained (half each order) and matched lists; sample with technique and size; DV operationalised; standardised procedure; ethics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher tests whether chewing gum improves concentration during a 20-minute proofreading task. Write a directional (one-tailed) hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: Participants who chew gum during a 20-minute proofreading task will detect more spelling errors than participants who do not chew gum.
parts.working: 1 mark: both conditions of the IV stated (gum vs no gum). 1 mark: operationalised DV with a direction (more errors detected).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one control the researcher should use in this study.
parts.answer: All participants proofread the same passage containing the same number of errors (e.g. 30), in the same quiet room.
parts.working: B1 for any relevant control (same passage, same time limit, same flavour of gum, same room/time of day).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: an experiment tests whether students in Karachi solve more puzzles when working with background traffic noise or in silence. Explain one reason for using an independent measures design in this study.
parts.answer: Each student only does the puzzles once, so they cannot improve with practice or become bored between conditions (no order effects), and they are less likely to guess the aim of the study.
parts.working: 1 mark: avoids order effects (practice/fatigue) or demand characteristics. 1 mark: linked to the puzzles/noise scenario.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using an independent measures design in this study.
parts.answer: Differences in puzzle-solving ability between the two groups (participant variables) could cause the difference in scores rather than the noise.
parts.working: 1 mark: participant variables. 1 mark: in context (puzzle ability, intelligence, motivation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher wants to test whether a 'growth mindset' video increases how long 12-year-olds persist at a difficult maths task. Explain how she could use a matched pairs design in this study.
parts.answer: Give all children a pre-test of maths ability (and/or a measure of initial persistence). Rank them by score and pair children with the closest scores; then randomly allocate one child of each pair to watch the growth-mindset video and the other to watch a neutral video, before both attempt the maths task.
parts.working: 1 mark: pre-test on a relevant variable. 1 mark: pairing children with similar scores. 1 mark: one of each pair randomly allocated to each condition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how persistence could be operationalised.
parts.answer: The number of seconds a child keeps working on an impossible maths problem before choosing to stop (up to a maximum of 10 minutes).
parts.working: 1 mark: measurable unit (time in seconds/number of attempts). 1 mark: clear definition of start/stop or a maximum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher wants to compare the memory of people who sleep 8 hours with those who sleep 4 hours. Explain why this would be difficult to carry out as a laboratory experiment, and suggest one alternative way to study the question.
parts.answer: Restricting sleep to 4 hours in a lab may harm participants (tiredness, accidents travelling home) and is costly, as they must stay overnight under supervision; also sleeping in a lab is unnatural. Alternative: a natural/quasi-experiment comparing people who already sleep about 4 or 8 hours (measured with a sleep diary or wrist actigraph) on the same memory test.
parts.working: 1 mark: ethical problem (harm). 1 mark: practical problem (overnight, cost) or validity problem. 1 mark: alternative method named. 1 mark: alternative explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A psychologist wants to investigate whether there is a correlation between the number of hours that teenagers spend gaming each week and their sleep quality. Describe how she could conduct this correlational study.
Your plan must include details about:
• how both co-variables will be measured
• the sampling technique
• how the data will be analysed.
parts.answer: Example plan: Co-variable 1 – hours gaming per week, measured by a 7-day diary in which teenagers record minutes spent gaming each day (total converted to hours). Co-variable 2 – sleep quality, measured by a 10-item questionnaire with 1–5 rating scales (1 = very poor, 5 = very good), total 10–50, completed at the end of the week. Sample – 100 students aged 14–16 from four schools in Islamabad, using stratified sampling so that boys and girls and each school are represented in proportion; parental consent. Procedure – standardised instructions, diaries returned in sealed envelopes with code numbers. Analysis – plot a scatter graph (hours gaming on the x-axis, sleep quality score on the y-axis) to see direction and strength; calculate a correlation coefficient; a negative correlation is predicted. Note that no causal conclusion can be drawn.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: both co-variables operationalised; named sampling technique explained with size and population; data analysis (scatter graph with labelled axes, correlation coefficient, direction expected); ethics; recognises correlation ≠ causation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A researcher wants to investigate whether there is a relationship between how often older people in a care home in Lahore receive visitors and their level of happiness. Describe how this correlational study could be carried out using observation and self-report data.
Your plan must include details about:
• how visits would be recorded
• the self-report measure
• ethical issues.
parts.answer: Example plan: Visits – care staff keep a visitor log for 4 weeks, recording each resident's visitors (date, time, length); co-variable = total number of visits per resident. Happiness – a structured interview with a short rating scale read aloud: 5 questions such as 'How happy have you felt this week?' rated 1 (not at all) to 7 (extremely), total 5–35, asked at the end of the 4 weeks by the same trained interviewer. Sample – all 40 residents who are able to consent (opportunity sample). Ethics – informed consent from residents (and family if capacity is doubtful), right to withdraw explained simply and repeated, confidentiality by code numbers, privacy (log records only counts, not conversation content), protection from distress for lonely residents, debrief. Analysis – scatter graph and correlation coefficient; positive correlation predicted.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: visits operationalised (log, count); self-report measure with example question and scale; ethics specific to elderly/vulnerable participants; sample; analysis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher finds a correlation between the number of fruit portions students eat each day and their exam scores. Explain why she cannot conclude that eating fruit causes higher exam scores.
parts.answer: A correlation only shows that two variables are related; neither variable was manipulated, so a third variable (e.g. family income or a healthier lifestyle) could cause both.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation does not show cause/no IV manipulated. 1 mark: possible third variable or reverse direction in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a non-directional hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: There will be a correlation between the number of fruit portions eaten per day and percentage exam score.
parts.working: 1 mark: both co-variables operationalised. 1 mark: non-directional (correlation/relationship, no direction stated).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher measures 'confidence' using a 1–10 rating and 'public speaking performance' using judges' ratings. Suggest how the judges' ratings could be made reliable.
parts.answer: Use two or more judges who are trained with the same clear criteria (e.g. eye contact, fluency, clarity each rated 1–5) and practise on sample videos; each judge rates every speaker independently; then the judges' ratings are correlated to check inter-rater reliability (e.g. agreement of +0.8 or above).
parts.working: 1 mark: clear operationalised criteria/rating scale. 1 mark: training/practice. 1 mark: independent ratings compared to check inter-rater reliability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of using a correlational design for this study.
parts.answer: Confidence cannot ethically or easily be manipulated, so a correlation lets the researcher study the relationship between naturally occurring levels of confidence and performance.
parts.working: 1 mark: strength (variables cannot be manipulated / shows strength and direction / quick to collect). 1 mark: in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher collected data from 8 participants on hours of revision (x) and test score out of 50 (y): (2, 20), (4, 26), (5, 25), (6, 31), (7, 35), (9, 38), (10, 41), (12, 44). Describe how she should present these data in a graph.
parts.answer: A scatter graph with hours of revision on the x-axis (labelled, 0–12) and test score on the y-axis (labelled, 0–50); each participant plotted as a single point; a title such as 'Scatter graph showing the relationship between hours of revision and test score'.
parts.working: 1 mark: scatter graph. 1 mark: correctly labelled axes with units/scales. 1 mark: points not joined / suitable title.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction of the correlation shown by these data and give a reason.
parts.answer: Positive: as hours of revision increase, test scores increase (e.g. 2 hours → 20, 12 hours → 44).
parts.working: 1 mark: positive. 1 mark: reason with reference to the data.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A psychologist wants to study helping behaviour among children aged 5–7 during break time in a school playground in Hyderabad. Describe how she could conduct a naturalistic observation to investigate this.
Your plan must include details about:
• behavioural categories
• the sampling of behaviour (e.g. time or event sampling)
• whether the observation is overt or covert.
parts.answer: Example plan: Behavioural categories – helping a child who has fallen (helps them up, touches them), sharing (offers food/toy), comforting (puts an arm round a crying child), giving physical assistance (carries something with another child); each recorded on a tally chart. Sampling – time sampling: two observers each watch one target child for 30 seconds and record any category shown, then move to the next child, across 20-minute break times for 10 days; or event sampling – record every helping act seen in a defined zone. Observers – two trained observers, positioned at the edge of the playground (e.g. near the staff room window) so as not to interfere, recording independently to check inter-rater reliability. Overt/covert – overt with teachers' and parents' consent, but observers present for a week beforehand so children become used to them (habituation), reducing reactivity. Ethics – parental consent, confidentiality (no names), intervene if a child is at risk.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: at least three operationalised behavioural categories; time or event sampling explained with timings; overt/covert decision justified; observer position and inter-rater reliability; ethics for children.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A researcher wants to investigate how drivers in Karachi behave at a busy junction when the traffic light turns amber. Describe how this could be investigated using a structured covert observation.
Your plan must include details about:
• the location and timing
• how data would be recorded
• how reliability would be checked.
parts.answer: Example plan: Location – one busy four-way junction with traffic lights; observers seated in a parked car or a café overlooking the junction so drivers cannot tell they are being watched. Timing – 30-minute sessions at morning rush (8–8:30 a.m.), midday and evening rush, over five weekdays, so that different traffic conditions are sampled. Recording – event sampling: each time the light turns amber, record the behaviour of the first car in the lane facing it, using categories: stops before line; speeds up and crosses; crosses at normal speed; stops after the line; and record vehicle type (car, motorbike, rickshaw, bus). Tally chart/coded checklist. Reliability – two observers watch the same light changes independently, then compare their tallies; calculate percentage agreement or correlate their records; categories refined and observers trained in a pilot observation if agreement is low. Ethics – public place, no number plates recorded, so privacy is respected.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: covert position explained; timings and location; behavioural categories and sampling method; data recording sheet; inter-rater reliability method; ethics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: an observer watches customers in a shopping mall in Lahore. Explain the difference between a participant and a non-participant observation in this setting.
parts.answer: In a participant observation the observer joins in the activity being studied, e.g. acts as a shopper or works as a shop assistant; in a non-participant observation the observer watches from outside the activity, e.g. sitting at a café table without interacting with the shoppers.
parts.working: 1 mark for each type explained with reference to the mall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage of a non-participant observation in this study.
parts.answer: The observer can record behaviour more objectively/continuously because they are not distracted by taking part and are less likely to influence shoppers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: two observers rate aggression in a video of children playing. Their tallies for six 1-minute intervals were: Observer 1 – 4, 2, 5, 3, 6, 1; Observer 2 – 4, 3, 5, 3, 5, 1. Calculate the percentage of intervals in which the two observers gave exactly the same tally. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.working: M1: matches in intervals 1, 3, 4 and 6 = 4 of 6. A1: 4 ÷ 6 × 100 = 66.7 → 67%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the observers could improve their agreement.
parts.answer: Agree and write clear operational definitions of 'aggression' (e.g. hitting, pushing, kicking, grabbing a toy), then practise together on a pilot video and discuss differences before the real observation.
parts.working: 1 mark: clearer operationalised categories / training. 1 mark: explanation of how it reduces subjective judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between time sampling and event sampling, using an example of an observation of shoppers queuing at a supermarket checkout.
parts.answer: Time sampling: the observer records behaviour only at set time intervals, e.g. every 2 minutes records how many people are in the queue and whether anyone is using their phone. Event sampling: the observer records every time a particular behaviour occurs, e.g. every time someone leaves the queue or pushes in, whenever it happens during the session.
parts.working: 2 marks for each: 1 for explanation, 1 for a relevant example in the queue setting.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A psychologist wants to investigate the reasons why university students in Pakistan choose to study abroad. Describe how she could conduct an interview study to investigate this.
Your plan must include details about:
• the type of interview
• example questions
• how the data would be analysed.
parts.answer: Example plan: Type – semi-structured interview, so that every student is asked the same core questions but the interviewer can follow up interesting answers. Sample – 20 final-year students from three universities in Lahore and Islamabad who have applied to study abroad, recruited by volunteer sampling through a notice on student portals. Questions – closed: 'Have you applied to study in another country? Yes/No'; 'How important is the reputation of the university to you? 1 (not important) to 5 (very important)'; open: 'What are the main reasons you want to study abroad?'; 'How did your family influence your decision?'; follow-up probes: 'Can you tell me more about that?'. Procedure – 30-minute interviews in a quiet room, audio-recorded with consent; same trained interviewer for all to reduce interviewer effects. Analysis – closed and rating answers summarised as percentages/means; open answers transcribed and analysed by thematic analysis, coding recurring themes (career prospects, quality of education, family expectations, finance), with two researchers coding independently to check reliability. Ethics – consent, confidentiality (codes), right to withdraw.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: interview type named and justified; at least one open and one closed example question; sample; procedure (recording, setting, interviewer); analysis of quantitative and qualitative data; ethics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a questionnaire about phone use is given to 200 office workers. Write one closed question and one open question that could be included.
parts.answer: Closed: 'On average, how many hours per day do you use your phone for non-work purposes? (less than 1 / 1–2 / 2–3 / more than 3)'. Open: 'Describe how using your phone affects your concentration at work.'
parts.working: 1 mark for a closed question with fixed responses. 1 mark for a genuinely open question allowing free answers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why participants may not answer questionnaires about phone use honestly.
parts.answer: Social desirability bias – they may under-report non-work phone use to appear hard-working to their employer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a researcher designs a rating scale to measure job stress among nurses in Quetta. Write one rating-scale item, including the anchors, and explain how it would be scored.
parts.answer: Item: 'I feel exhausted at the end of my shift.' 1 = strongly disagree, 2 = disagree, 3 = neutral, 4 = agree, 5 = strongly agree. Scoring: the number chosen is the score for the item (higher = more stress); scores across all items are added to give a total stress score.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable item statement. 1 mark: labelled anchors at both ends (and/or each point). 1 mark: scoring explained (higher = more stress, items totalled; reverse-scored items if any).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why some items on the scale should be reverse-scored.
parts.answer: If all items are worded in the same direction, participants may tick the same answer down the page without reading (response set/acquiescence); mixing positively and negatively worded items, which are reverse-scored, reduces this bias.
parts.working: 1 mark: avoids response bias/acquiescence. 1 mark: explanation of how reverse-scoring works or why it matters.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A psychologist wants to investigate how children's friendships change between the ages of 6 and 10. Describe how she could conduct a longitudinal study to investigate this.
Your plan must include details about:
• the sample and how attrition would be reduced
• how friendships would be measured
• how often data would be collected.
parts.answer: Example plan: Sample – 120 six-year-olds from six primary schools in Lahore (both girls and boys), selected by stratified sampling from school registers, with parental consent. Attrition – collect several contact details, send newsletters about the study, give small gifts or certificates to children each year, and recruit extra participants at the start to allow for drop-out. Measures – each year, a short structured interview with the child ('Who are your best friends?', 'What do you like doing together?'), a sociometric nomination task (children name up to three classmates they like to play with), and a 15-minute playground observation of each child using time sampling (who they play with, in what kind of activity). Teachers complete a 5-point rating scale of each child's friendship quality. Frequency – once a year in the same month (e.g. October) from age 6 to 10, giving 5 data points, using the same measures and trained researchers each time. Analysis – compare number and type of friends across years (means, line graphs), and themes in interview answers.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): plan is detailed, coherent and could be carried out; all named features are included and explained; appropriate psychological terminology used throughout. Level 3 (5–7): plan is mostly clear and could be carried out with some gaps; most named features included; some terminology. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan, some features missing or unclear, limited terminology. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or not the method asked for. 0: no creditable response. Creditworthy content: sample with technique and size; specific attrition strategies; measures operationalised (interviews, nominations, observation, rating); intervals and duration; consistency of measures; ethics with children.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a 'longitudinal study'.
parts.answer: A study in which the same participants are tested or observed repeatedly over a long period of time (months or years).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of a longitudinal study compared with testing different age groups at one time.
parts.answer: Because the same people are followed, changes over time are not caused by differences between groups (participant variables / cohort effects), so the development of each person can be tracked.
parts.working: 1 mark: same participants compared with themselves. 1 mark: removes participant variables/cohort effects or shows individual development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: a 5-year study follows 400 teenagers' mental health. In year 1, 400 took part; by year 5, 292 remained. Calculate the percentage of the original sample lost by year 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this attrition could affect the validity of the findings.
parts.answer: If those who dropped out differ systematically from those who stayed (e.g. teenagers with worse mental health are more likely to drop out), the remaining sample is biased and may make mental health appear better than it really is.
parts.working: 1 mark: drop-outs may differ from those who stay. 1 mark: biased sample / distorted conclusions in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A student plans an experiment to see whether people remember more words in a quiet room than in a noisy room. She tests 10 friends in the quiet room in the morning and 10 different friends in the noisy room in the evening. Identify one weakness of this plan.
parts.answer: Time of day is a confounding variable (morning vs evening), or the sample of friends is small/biased.
parts.working: B1 for any valid weakness.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the weakness you identified could be overcome.
parts.answer: Test both conditions at the same time of day (e.g. all in the morning), allocating participants to rooms randomly, so time of day cannot explain any difference in recall.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable change. 1 mark: explanation of why it improves the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A researcher plans to measure aggression in teenagers using a single question: 'Are you an aggressive person? Yes/No'. Explain one weakness of this measure.
parts.answer: It is likely to produce socially desirable answers (few will admit aggression) and gives only a yes/no answer, so it cannot show different levels of aggression – low validity and sensitivity.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness identified (social desirability, limited detail, closed yes/no). 1 mark: explained in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improved measure of aggression.
parts.answer: A questionnaire of several items rated on a 1–5 scale (e.g. 'I lose my temper easily'), or an observation of aggressive acts (hitting, shouting) during a sports game, with clear behavioural categories.
parts.working: 1 mark: improved measure. 1 mark: detail showing it measures levels/behaviour objectively.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: Dr Ahmed plans an observation of students in a university library to see how often they check their phones. He will sit at a table with a clipboard and tell students he is observing them. Explain one strength and one weakness of this plan.
parts.answer: Strength: it is overt, so students know they are being studied, which is more ethical – consent can be obtained and privacy respected. Weakness: because students know they are being watched, they may check their phones less often than normal (participant reactivity), so the data would be less valid.
parts.working: 2 marks for strength (identified + explained in context). 2 marks for weakness (identified + explained in context).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A researcher wants to investigate whether a mindfulness app reduces stress in workers at a call centre in Lahore. She uses volunteers who respond to an email, asks them to use the app for 4 weeks, and then asks, 'Do you feel less stressed now?' Explain two weaknesses of this plan.
parts.answer: No control group or baseline: without a comparison group (e.g. workers who do not use the app) or a stress measure before the 4 weeks, any change could be due to other factors (e.g. a quieter month at work). Volunteer sample and leading question: volunteers may be keen on mindfulness and the question suggests the answer, so demand characteristics may produce biased results.
parts.working: 2 marks per weakness: identified (1) + explained in context (1). Accept: no baseline, no control group, volunteer bias, leading/closed question, self-report bias.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A psychologist plans a repeated measures experiment in which participants solve anagrams first after drinking water and then, 15 minutes later, after drinking a caffeinated drink. Explain one problem with this plan and how it could be overcome.
parts.answer: Order effects: all participants do the caffeine condition second, so they may do better because of practice with anagrams (or worse because of fatigue), not because of caffeine. It could be overcome by counterbalancing – half do water first, half caffeine first – on separate days, so caffeine from the first session cannot affect the second, with different but equally difficult anagram sets.
parts.working: 1 mark: order effects identified. 1 mark: explained in context (practice/fatigue/carry-over of caffeine). 1 mark: counterbalancing / separate days. 1 mark: explanation of how this solves the problem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A researcher plans a correlational study of the relationship between time spent reading for pleasure and vocabulary in 11-year-olds. She uses a 30-item vocabulary test and asks parents to estimate their child's weekly reading time. Explain one strength and one weakness of using parents' estimates as a measure of reading time.
parts.answer: Strength: parents see their child's daily routine at home and can report on reading that the child might forget, and it is quick and cheap to collect from many families. Weakness: estimates may be inaccurate – parents may not know about reading done in the child's room, or may exaggerate to appear good parents (social desirability), reducing validity. A reading diary could be more accurate.
parts.working: 2 marks for strength (identified + explained). 2 marks for weakness (identified + explained).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A researcher plans to study whether people help a stranger more in a small town than in a big city. She will have a confederate drop a bag of oranges in the main market of a small town in Punjab and in a busy market in Karachi, and record whether passers-by help. Evaluate this plan in terms of its validity.
parts.answer: Strength: it is a field setting with real passers-by who do not know they are being studied, so behaviour is natural and has high ecological validity. Weakness: other differences between the two markets (crowd size, time of day, the local language, how busy people are) are uncontrolled and could explain any difference in helping, so it is not certain that town/city size caused the difference; the confederate's behaviour should be standardised and the times of day matched.
parts.working: 2 marks for a point supporting validity (identified + explained). 2 marks for a point against validity (identified + explained), e.g. extraneous variables, sample bias, confederate inconsistency.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical plan: A psychologist plans to interview 6 employees about their experience of working night shifts, using an unstructured interview. Explain one strength and one weakness of using an unstructured interview, and suggest one improvement to the plan.
parts.answer: Strength: the interviewer can follow up whatever the employee says with new questions, gathering rich qualitative detail about their experience of night shifts that was not anticipated. Weakness: each interview is different, so answers are hard to compare and the data are harder to analyse and replicate (low reliability); the interviewer's own views may also influence the questions. Improvement: use a semi-structured interview with a fixed set of core questions plus follow-ups, and increase the sample to 20 employees from different shifts and companies.
parts.working: 2 marks strength, 2 marks weakness (each identified + explained in context). 2 marks improvement (suggestion + why it helps).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between rapid rotation and slow rotation shift systems.
parts.answer: In rapid rotation workers change shifts every few days (e.g. 2 mornings, 2 evenings, 2 nights); in slow rotation they stay on the same shift for longer, e.g. one to three weeks, before changing.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a correct description of each system.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a forward-rotating (morning → evening → night) shift system is thought to be better than a backward-rotating one.
parts.answer: The body clock naturally finds it easier to delay (stay up later) than to advance (go to sleep earlier), so moving shifts forward (phase delay) causes less disruption to circadian rhythms and sleep.
parts.working: 1 mark: link to circadian rhythms/body clock. 1 mark: phase delay is easier than phase advance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three types of human error that can lead to accidents at work.
parts.answer: Any three of: slips (doing the wrong action, e.g. pressing the wrong button); lapses (forgetting a step); mistakes (wrong plan or decision, e.g. misjudging a situation); violations (deliberately breaking a rule).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three; credit an example in place of a definition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Saima is the manager of a textile factory in Faisalabad where several minor accidents have happened on the night shift. Suggest how she could use a token economy to reduce accidents.
parts.answer: Workers (or teams) earn tokens/stamps for every week (or month) without an accident or safety violation, and for safety suggestions; tokens are lost if an accident happens. Tokens can be exchanged for goods or vouchers (e.g. groceries, phone credit). The scheme should be explained clearly to all workers, with tokens given promptly so safe behaviour is reinforced (operant conditioning).
parts.working: 1 mark: tokens earned for accident-free periods/safe behaviour. 1 mark: exchanged for rewards (named). 1 mark: practical detail (team tokens, lost after accident, prompt delivery). 1 mark: link to operant conditioning/positive reinforcement or to Fox et al.'s mining study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the debate about determinism versus free will.
parts.answer: Determinism is the view that behaviour is caused by factors outside the person's control (biological or environmental); free will is the view that people can choose how they behave.
parts.working: 1 mark for each side defined.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the Swiss cheese model of accidents can be seen as deterministic.
parts.answer: It explains accidents as the result of weaknesses ('holes') in organisational layers – management decisions, supervision, conditions – lining up, so an individual worker's error is caused by the system rather than freely chosen.
parts.working: 1 mark: model attributes accidents to system/organisational factors. 1 mark: so the worker's behaviour is determined by forces outside their control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the findings of research into the effects of open-plan offices on workers.
parts.answer: Oldham and Brass studied newspaper employees who moved from a conventional office to an open-plan office (a natural experiment), measuring them before and after the move. Employee satisfaction with work and internal motivation decreased after the move; workers reported fewer boundaries, more interruptions and less privacy, and found it harder to concentrate. Friendship opportunities did not increase as expected. Other research suggests open-plan offices increase noise and distraction but can make communication with supervisors easier, and that more private 'quiet zones' improve satisfaction.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): accurate, detailed description using psychological terms. Level 2 (3–4): mostly accurate, some detail. Level 1 (1–2): brief or partly inaccurate. Creditworthy: Oldham and Brass (natural/quasi-experiment, newspaper employees, measures before and after); decrease in satisfaction and motivation; reasons (lack of privacy, interruptions, no boundaries, distractions); other findings on noise/communication.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical data: A company introduced a token economy for safety. In the 12 months before, there were 48 lost-time accidents; in the 12 months after, there were 30. Calculate the percentage reduction in accidents.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why this reduction might not be caused by the token economy.
parts.answer: Other changes happened at the same time (e.g. new machinery, safety training, fewer hours worked or fewer workers), or workers may under-report accidents to keep their tokens, so the fall might not be due to the scheme itself.
parts.working: 1 mark: alternative explanation identified. 1 mark: explained (no control group / confounding variable / under-reporting).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one strength of using a token economy to improve safety.
parts.answer: It gives immediate, concrete rewards for safe behaviour, which reinforces it, and the tokens can be exchanged for rewards each worker values, so it can motivate a large workforce cheaply compared with the cost of accidents.
parts.working: 1 mark: strength identified. 1 mark: explained in a workplace context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate what psychologists have found about the effects of temporal conditions of work (shift work), including a discussion about the usefulness of research.
parts.answer: Usefulness: findings (e.g. Czeisler et al. – moving workers to forward-rotating, slower schedules improved satisfaction, health and productivity at an industrial plant) are directly applied to design better rotas; research on nurses (e.g. Gold et al.) showing more sleep problems and errors in rotating shifts helps hospitals reduce risks. Methodology: many studies are field studies with real workers (high ecological validity) but have many uncontrolled variables (family life, second jobs); self-report sleep diaries may be inaccurate. Generalisability: samples are often one factory or one profession. Individual differences: 'larks' and 'owls' adapt differently, so one rota may not suit everyone. Determinism: biological explanation (circadian rhythms) vs individual choice. Ethics: experimental changes to rotas affect workers' health and livelihoods. Conclusion: research is useful but recommendations should be tailored.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation with a range of points, the named issue discussed in depth, well supported by studies/examples, clear conclusion. Level 3 (6–8): good range of points, named issue included, mostly supported. Level 2 (3–5): some evaluation, may be one-sided or the named issue only touched on. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal points. Named issue: usefulness (applications to rota design, health, safety; limits).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: A psychologist wants to measure how noise in an open-plan call centre in Karachi affects workers' concentration. Suggest one objective way and one self-report way to measure concentration.
parts.answer: Objective: number of errors made when entering customer details per hour, taken from the call-centre computer system. Self-report: a rating scale at the end of each shift, e.g. 'How easy was it to concentrate today?' 1 = very difficult to 7 = very easy.
parts.working: 2 marks per measure: 1 for the method, 1 for operationalised detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between hygiene factors and motivators in Herzberg's two-factor theory.
parts.answer: Hygiene factors (e.g. pay, company policy, supervision, working conditions) prevent dissatisfaction when they are adequate but do not create satisfaction; motivators (e.g. achievement, recognition, responsibility, the work itself, advancement) create job satisfaction and motivation.
parts.working: 1 mark for each with an example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the method Herzberg used to develop the two-factor theory.
parts.answer: He interviewed engineers and accountants (about 200) in Pittsburgh using the critical incident technique, asking them to describe times when they felt exceptionally good and exceptionally bad about their jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark: interviews / critical incident technique. 1 mark: detail – engineers and accountants; times they felt very good or very bad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the five facets of job satisfaction measured by the Job Descriptive Index (JDI).
parts.answer: The work itself, pay, opportunities for promotion, supervision and co-workers.
parts.working: 3 marks for all five; 2 marks for four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of measuring job satisfaction using the JDI.
parts.answer: Workers may give socially desirable answers (e.g. not criticise their supervisor) if they fear the employer will see their responses, so the scores may not reflect their true satisfaction.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness (social desirability, fixed Yes/No/? answers lack detail, may not cover all aspects). 1 mark: explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal works on a mobile-phone assembly line in Lahore, fitting the same screen into each phone all day. His manager wants to improve his job satisfaction. Suggest how the manager could use job enrichment and job rotation.
parts.answer: Job enrichment: give Bilal more responsibility and control, e.g. assembling and testing the whole phone, checking quality of his own work, deciding the order of tasks, so the job becomes more meaningful (vertical loading). Job rotation: move Bilal between different stations (screen fitting, battery fitting, packing) every few days so he has more variety and less boredom.
parts.working: 2 marks for enrichment (idea + applied to Bilal). 2 marks for rotation (idea + applied to Bilal).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what psychologists have found about measuring job satisfaction, including the Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire (MSQ) and the Quality of Work Life (QWL) approach.
parts.answer: MSQ: a self-report questionnaire measuring satisfaction with many specific aspects (facets) of a job, such as ability utilisation, pay, co-workers, independence and working conditions; long form has 100 items, short form 20 items, each rated on a 5-point scale from very dissatisfied to very satisfied. QWL (Walton): judges a job against broad categories such as adequate and fair compensation, safe and healthy working conditions, opportunity to use and develop capacities, opportunity for growth and security, social integration, constitutionalism (rights), work and total life space, and social relevance. Other measures include the JDI (five facets, Yes/No/?).
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): accurate, detailed description using psychological terms. Level 2 (3–4): mostly accurate, some detail. Level 1 (1–2): brief or partly inaccurate. Credit accurate details of MSQ (facets, long/short form, 5-point scale) and QWL categories.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A psychologist wants to find out whether nurses in a large hospital in Islamabad are more satisfied with their jobs on day shifts or night shifts. Plan a study to investigate this using a questionnaire.
Your plan must include: the sampling technique; at least one rating-scale question; the type of data collected.
parts.answer: Example: Sample – stratified sample of 80 nurses: 40 who work mainly day shifts and 40 mainly night shifts, chosen randomly from staff rosters within each group, including different wards. Questionnaire – adapted from the JDI/MSQ facets: work itself, pay, supervision, co-workers, promotion; e.g. 'How satisfied are you with the support from your supervisor?' 1 = very dissatisfied to 5 = very satisfied (10 items, total 10–50); plus open questions such as 'What would improve your job satisfaction?'. Procedure – anonymous, distributed with sealed return boxes; same instructions for all. Data – quantitative (rating totals, compared using means and a bar chart) and qualitative (themes from open answers). Ethics – consent, confidentiality from hospital management, right to withdraw.
parts.working: Level 4 (8–10): detailed, coherent plan with all required features and justification. Level 3 (5–7): mostly clear plan, most features. Level 2 (3–4): basic plan with gaps. Level 1 (1–2): brief or confused.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the psychological knowledge on which your plan is based.
parts.answer: Herzberg's two-factor theory (hygiene factors such as working conditions vs motivators); job satisfaction measures (JDI five facets, MSQ, QWL); research on temporal conditions – shift work disrupts circadian rhythms and sleep and is linked to lower satisfaction and more errors (e.g. studies of nurses on rotating shifts); questionnaire design (rating scales, open/closed questions, social desirability).
parts.working: Level 3 (6–8): accurate, detailed and relevant knowledge clearly linked to the plan. Level 2 (3–5): some relevant knowledge, partly linked. Level 1 (1–2): brief, general.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason for your choice of sampling technique.
parts.answer: Stratified sampling ensures equal numbers of day and night nurses (and nurses from different wards) are included, so that the comparison is fair and the sample represents each group of the hospital's staff; random selection within strata reduces researcher bias. Because night-shift nurses are fewer and harder to reach, an opportunity sample would probably over-represent day staff and distort the comparison. A weakness is that full staff lists are needed and it takes longer.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): well-justified reason linked to the aim, with comparison to an alternative or acknowledgement of a weakness. Level 2 (3–4): reason explained with some link to the plan. Level 1 (1–2): reason stated with little justification.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate what psychologists have found about job design and job satisfaction, including a discussion about reductionism and holism.
parts.answer: Reductionism/holism: Herzberg reduces satisfaction to two sets of factors, which is easy to test and apply, but ignores how factors interact (e.g. pay can also be a form of recognition); job enrichment approaches (e.g. job characteristics model) look at several features together, which is more holistic. Methodology: Herzberg's critical incident interviews may be biased because people attribute good events to themselves and bad events to the company (self-serving bias); samples of engineers/accountants limit generalisability. Usefulness: job rotation, enlargement and enrichment are widely applied and practical. Individual differences: not everyone wants enriched jobs – some prefer routine. Cultural differences: research mainly Western. Conclusion.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation with a range of points, the named issue discussed in depth, well supported by studies/examples, clear conclusion. Level 3 (6–8): good range of points, named issue included, mostly supported. Level 2 (3–5): some evaluation, may be one-sided or the named issue only touched on. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal points. Named issue: reductionism vs holism, explained not just labelled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the three needs in Alderfer's ERG theory.
parts.answer: Existence – basic material and physical needs (food, pay, safe conditions); Relatedness – the need for relationships with others (colleagues, family, friends); Growth – the need for personal development and fulfilling one's potential.
parts.working: 1 mark for each need correctly named and described.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way ERG theory differs from Maslow's hierarchy of needs.
parts.answer: ERG allows more than one need to be active at once and includes frustration–regression (if a higher need is blocked, a person focuses more on a lower need), whereas Maslow says needs are satisfied in a fixed order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'intrinsic' and 'extrinsic' motivation.
parts.answer: Intrinsic motivation comes from within – doing the work because it is interesting or satisfying in itself. Extrinsic motivation comes from outside rewards or pressures – e.g. pay, bonuses, praise or avoiding punishment.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a non-monetary reward an employer could use.
parts.answer: Any one: praise/recognition (e.g. employee of the month), extra holiday, flexible hours, a better job title, training opportunities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hina manages a team of sales staff in a bank in Karachi. Using goal-setting theory, suggest how she could increase their motivation.
parts.answer: She should set specific goals (e.g. open 15 new accounts per month) rather than 'do your best'; goals should be difficult but achievable; she should involve staff in setting goals to increase commitment; and give regular feedback (e.g. weekly progress charts) so they can see how close they are to the goal.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four applied points: specific; challenging but achievable; commitment/participation in goal setting; feedback; deadline; rewards for reaching goals. Must be applied to Hina's team for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In Vroom's expectancy (VIE) theory, motivational force = expectancy × instrumentality × valence. An employee believes there is a 0.8 probability that extra effort will lead to high performance (expectancy), a 0.5 probability that high performance will lead to a bonus (instrumentality), and values the bonus at 0.9 (valence, scale 0–1). Calculate the motivational force.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the motivational force would be zero if the employee believed the bonus would never be paid.
parts.answer: Instrumentality would be 0; because the terms are multiplied, a zero for any one of them makes the whole motivational force zero, however high expectancy and valence are.
parts.working: 1 mark: instrumentality = 0. 1 mark: multiplication means the product is zero.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the nomothetic versus idiographic debate.
parts.answer: The nomothetic approach looks for general laws that apply to everyone, often using large samples and quantitative data; the idiographic approach focuses on understanding the unique individual in depth, often using qualitative methods such as case studies.
parts.working: 1 mark for each side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why McClelland's theory of needs (achievement, affiliation and power) could be seen as idiographic.
parts.answer: It recognises that individuals differ in the strength of each need – one employee may be driven mainly by achievement, another by affiliation – and needs are assessed for each person (e.g. through their stories on the Thematic Apperception Test), so motivation is understood at the individual level.
parts.working: 1 mark: emphasis on individual differences in need strength. 1 mark: elaboration, e.g. individual assessment with TAT, tailoring jobs to the person.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate need theories of motivation to work (such as Maslow, Alderfer and McClelland), including a discussion about cultural differences.
parts.answer: Cultural differences: Maslow's hierarchy reflects individualistic Western values (self-actualisation at the top); in collectivist cultures such as Pakistan, belonging/family or group needs may be ranked higher, so the order may not be universal. Evidence: little empirical support for a fixed order of needs; ERG is more flexible and better supported (frustration–regression). McClelland's needs are measurable (TAT) and useful for selection, but TAT scoring is subjective and has low reliability. Usefulness: managers can match rewards to needs (security, social events, development). Reductionism: need theories reduce complex motivation to a few needs and ignore cognitive factors such as goals and expectations (goal-setting, VIE). Individual differences: people vary in which needs dominate. Conclusion.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation with a range of points, the named issue discussed in depth, well supported by studies/examples, clear conclusion. Level 3 (6–8): good range of points, named issue included, mostly supported. Level 2 (3–5): some evaluation, may be one-sided or the named issue only touched on. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal points. Named issue: cultural differences, developed with examples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the two dimensions of leadership behaviour identified in the Ohio State studies.
parts.answer: Initiating structure – how far the leader defines and organises tasks, roles and goals for the group; consideration – how far the leader shows concern, trust and respect for followers' feelings and wellbeing.
parts.working: 1 mark for each dimension.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one problem with the 'great person' theory of leadership.
parts.answer: It assumes leaders are born with special traits, but research has not found a consistent set of traits shared by all effective leaders, and it ignores the situation and followers, so it cannot explain why a leader succeeds in one setting but fails in another.
parts.working: 1 mark: problem identified (no consistent traits, ignores situation, gender/cultural bias, retrospective). 1 mark: explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Muczyk and Reimann's four styles of leadership.
parts.answer: Directive autocrat – makes decisions alone and closely supervises how work is done. Permissive autocrat – makes decisions alone but lets subordinates decide how to carry them out. Directive democrat – involves subordinates in decisions but closely supervises how work is done. Permissive democrat – involves subordinates in decisions and gives them freedom in carrying out the work.
parts.working: 1 mark for each style correctly described (decision-making: autocratic/democratic; execution: directive/permissive).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mr Farooq has just been promoted to supervise a team of experienced software engineers in Islamabad who are working on a creative new app. Using Fiedler's contingency theory, suggest how he could decide on the most effective leadership style.
parts.answer: He could complete the Least Preferred Co-worker (LPC) scale to see whether he is task-oriented (low LPC) or relationship-oriented (high LPC). He should then judge how favourable the situation is: leader–member relations (new to the team, so may be moderate), task structure (a creative project is low in structure) and position power (as supervisor, moderate–high). In moderately favourable situations Fiedler predicts relationship-oriented leaders do best, so if he is task-oriented he might change the situation (e.g. build relations) since Fiedler sees style as fixed.
parts.working: 1 mark: LPC scale to identify style. 1 mark: three situational factors named. 1 mark: applied to Mr Farooq's situation. 1 mark: correct prediction/advice (relationship-oriented best in moderate; task-oriented in very favourable/unfavourable; change the situation not the leader).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hypothetical study: A researcher uses a questionnaire to measure whether employees in a Lahore factory see their supervisor as a transformational leader. Write two items the questionnaire could include, each linked to a different feature of transformational leadership.
parts.answer: Inspirational motivation: 'My supervisor talks enthusiastically about what our team can achieve' (1 = never to 5 = always). Individualised consideration: 'My supervisor spends time helping me develop my own skills' (1 = never to 5 = always). (Others: idealised influence – 'I am proud to work with my supervisor'; intellectual stimulation – 'My supervisor encourages me to find new ways of solving problems'.)
parts.working: 2 marks per item: 1 for a suitable item with a response scale, 1 for correctly linking it to a feature of transformational leadership (idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualised consideration).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what psychologists have found about leadership and the situation, including Fiedler's contingency theory.
parts.answer: Fiedler argued that a leader's effectiveness depends on the match between their style and the situation. Style is measured with the Least Preferred Co-worker (LPC) scale: low-LPC leaders are task-oriented, high-LPC leaders relationship-oriented. Situational favourableness depends on leader–member relations (good/poor), task structure (high/low) and position power (strong/weak). Task-oriented leaders are most effective when the situation is very favourable or very unfavourable; relationship-oriented leaders are best in moderately favourable situations. Style is seen as fixed, so the situation should be changed to fit the leader. Other situational approaches suggest leaders should adapt their style to followers' readiness/maturity.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): accurate, detailed description using psychological terms. Level 2 (3–4): mostly accurate, some detail. Level 1 (1–2): brief or partly inaccurate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate universalist and behavioural theories of leadership, including a discussion about individual and situational explanations.
parts.answer: Individual vs situational: great person and charismatic theories are individual explanations (leadership comes from traits), but they ignore the situation – the same leader may fail in a different context; behavioural theories (Ohio State) focus on what leaders do, which can be learned, and situational/contingency theories (Fiedler) show the interaction. Evidence: Ohio State used large questionnaire studies (LBDQ) – quantitative and reliable, but self-report/followers' ratings may be biased; transformational leadership is linked to follower satisfaction and performance. Usefulness: behavioural theories can be used to train leaders (consideration and structure); great person theory cannot. Cultural/gender bias: great person theory based on historical male leaders. Conclusion: a combination of individual and situational factors explains leadership best.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation with a range of points, the named issue discussed in depth, well supported by studies/examples, clear conclusion. Level 3 (6–8): good range of points, named issue included, mostly supported. Level 2 (3–5): some evaluation, may be one-sided or the named issue only touched on. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal points. Named debate: individual vs situational explanations, with examples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the stages of group development described by Tuckman.
parts.answer: Forming – members meet, are polite and uncertain, and depend on the leader. Storming – conflict over roles, power and ideas. Norming – agreement on rules, roles and ways of working; cohesion grows. Performing – the group works effectively towards its goals. (Adjourning – the group breaks up once the task is finished.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each of four stages correctly named and described; adjourning can replace one stage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A management committee at a cricket equipment company in Sialkot quickly agreed to launch a new bat without any member raising concerns, and the product failed. Suggest how groupthink might explain this and how it could be avoided in future.
parts.answer: Groupthink: in a cohesive group, members want agreement so much that they do not criticise ideas – e.g. self-censorship, illusion of unanimity, pressure on anyone who disagreed, and an illusion of invulnerability. To avoid it, the leader could hold back their own opinion at first, appoint a 'devil's advocate' to challenge the plan, invite outside experts, or use anonymous voting.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition/explanation of groupthink. 1 mark: named symptom applied to the committee. 1 mark: one way to avoid it. 1 mark: explanation of how it helps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the five conflict-handling styles described by Thomas.
parts.answer: Competing – assertive and uncooperative, pursuing one's own concerns at the other's expense. Collaborating – assertive and cooperative, working together to find a solution that satisfies both. Compromising – moderate on both, each side gives up something. Avoiding – unassertive and uncooperative, sidestepping the conflict. Accommodating – unassertive and cooperative, giving in to the other side.
parts.working: 1 mark for each style named and described (may refer to the dimensions of assertiveness and cooperativeness).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate what psychologists have found about group development and team roles (e.g. Tuckman, Belbin), including a discussion about the usefulness of research.
parts.answer: Usefulness: Tuckman's stages help managers anticipate conflict and support new teams; Belbin's team roles (e.g. plant, shaper, coordinator, monitor evaluator, teamworker, completer finisher) are used to build balanced teams and in training. Limitations: Tuckman's model was based on reviews of small, often therapy and laboratory groups, so may not apply to work teams; groups may not move through stages in order and may return to storming. Belbin's self-perception inventory is self-report and has been criticised for low reliability/validity; roles may change with the task. Reductionism: reducing team behaviour to set stages or nine roles ignores organisational context and culture. Cultural differences in how conflict is expressed. Conclusion: useful frameworks but should be applied flexibly.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation with a range of points, the named issue discussed in depth, well supported by studies/examples, clear conclusion. Level 3 (6–8): good range of points, named issue included, mostly supported. Level 2 (3–5): some evaluation, may be one-sided or the named issue only touched on. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal points. Named issue: usefulness, discussed with examples of application and its limits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of children who took part in Bandura et al.'s study of the imitation of aggression, and the nursery school they attended.
parts.answer: 72 children (36 boys and 36 girls) from the nursery school of Stanford University.
parts.working: 1 mark: 72 children (accept 36 boys and 36 girls). 1 mark: Stanford University nursery school.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline how the children were matched before being placed in the three conditions.
parts.answer: Each child was rated for pre-existing aggressiveness by the experimenter and a nursery teacher who knew the children well; children were then put into groups of three with similar aggression scores and one from each trio was assigned to each condition.
parts.working: 1 mark: rated on prior aggression by the experimenter and a teacher (rating scales for physical, verbal, object aggression and aggression inhibition). 1 mark: children with similar ratings were matched in threes and split across conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the adult model did in the aggressive-model condition of Bandura et al.'s study.
parts.answer: After about a minute of assembling toys, the model turned to the large inflated Bobo doll and attacked it for the rest of the session: laid it on its side and sat on it, punched it on the nose, struck it on the head with a mallet, tossed it in the air and kicked it about the room, while saying things such as 'Sock him in the nose', 'Hit him down', 'Kick him' and 'Pow'.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: model attacks the Bobo doll after about 1 minute; sits on Bobo / punches it on the nose; hits it with a mallet; tosses it in the air / kicks it around the room; repeated the sequence about three times; aggressive verbal comments (e.g. 'Sock him in the nose', 'Pow'); non-aggressive comments ('He keeps coming back for more').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what the model did in the non-aggressive condition.
parts.answer: The model quietly assembled the tinker toys for the whole session and ignored the Bobo doll.
parts.working: 1 mark: played quietly with tinker toys / ignored Bobo.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the children were mildly frustrated (Stage 2) before being observed in Bandura et al.'s study.
parts.answer: The researchers wanted all children to be in a similar state of mild arousal so that any aggression could be expressed; without this, children who had seen the non-aggressive model might be inhibited, and the frustration also ensured the control group had an equal chance to show aggression, so that differences were due to the model.
parts.working: 1 mark: to raise the chance of aggression being shown / arouse all children equally. 1 mark: so that differences in aggression could be attributed to the model condition (or so that the non-aggressive group's behaviour was not just due to inhibition).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline how this mild aggression arousal was produced.
parts.answer: Each child was taken to a room containing very attractive toys (e.g. a fire engine, a jet fighter, a doll set). After about two minutes of play the experimenter said these were her very best toys and she had decided to keep them for other children.
parts.working: 1 mark: child allowed to play with attractive toys briefly. 1 mark: told the toys were reserved for other children / taken away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the final stage of Bandura et al.'s study each child spent 20 minutes in the test room and was observed through a one-way mirror. Behaviour was recorded at 5-second intervals. Calculate the number of response units recorded for each child.
parts.answer: 240 response units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why using a one-way mirror improved the validity of the observation.
parts.answer: The children could not see the observers, so they were less likely to change their behaviour because they knew they were being watched; this reduced demand characteristics, so the aggression recorded was more likely to be the child's natural response to the model.
parts.working: 1 mark: observers hidden / covert observation. 1 mark: reduces participant reactivity / demand characteristics, so behaviour more genuine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two categories of behaviour that were recorded in the test room in Bandura et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Any two of: imitative physical aggression; imitative verbal aggression; imitative non-aggressive verbal responses; partially imitative responses (e.g. mallet aggression on other toys, sitting on Bobo without hitting); non-imitative aggression (e.g. punching Bobo, aggressive gun play).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two named categories.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how inter-rater reliability was checked in this study.
parts.answer: The male model watched every child, and a second observer independently scored half of the children; the two sets of scores were compared and were highly correlated, showing the coding was consistent.
parts.working: 1 mark: a second observer independently scored some children (half). 1 mark: scores compared / correlated and found to agree highly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one finding from Bandura et al.'s study about the sex of the child.
parts.answer: Boys produced more imitative physical aggression than girls, whereas the difference between boys and girls in imitative verbal aggression was much smaller.
parts.working: 1 mark: boys showed more (imitative) physical aggression than girls. 1 mark: comparison/detail, e.g. girls and boys similar in verbal aggression, or boys more influenced by the male model.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason, based on social learning, why children may be more likely to imitate a same-sex model.
parts.answer: Children identify more with models who are similar to them, and they may expect the same consequences (vicarious reinforcement) for behaviour shown by someone like themselves; also some behaviour is seen as sex-appropriate, e.g. physical aggression as 'masculine'.
parts.working: 1 mark: identification with a similar model. 1 mark: expansion – sex-typed behaviour seen as appropriate / expectation of similar consequences.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bandura et al.'s study is often said to be high in standardisation but low in ecological validity. Evaluate this claim.
parts.answer: High standardisation: every child experienced the same room layout, same toys, same 10-minute modelling period, same frustration procedure and the same 20-minute test, and models followed a set script of aggressive acts and phrases, so the study could be replicated and differences attributed to the IV. Low ecological validity: the child watched a stranger attack an inflatable doll that is designed to bounce back, alone in an unfamiliar room, for only a short time; hitting a Bobo doll is not the same as hurting a real person, so it may not reflect aggression in everyday life. However, it was set in a familiar nursery school with real toys, which partly supports validity.
parts.working: 1 mark: standardisation with example (same script/acts, timings, toys). 1 mark: benefit – replicable/reliable/control. 1 mark: low ecological validity with example (Bobo designed to be hit, stranger model, short exposure). 1 mark: balanced judgement or counterpoint (school setting, toys familiar).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one ethical issue raised by Bandura et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Protection from harm: young children were deliberately frustrated and exposed to an aggressive adult, which may have caused distress and taught them aggressive behaviour that could persist after the study.
parts.working: 1 mark: named issue (protection from harm / consent of children / right to withdraw). 1 mark: linked to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Bandura et al.'s study of the imitation of aggression in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about generalisability.
parts.answer: Strengths, e.g. (1) controlled lab setting with standardised procedure – same toys, timings, scripted model behaviour, so cause and effect between the model condition and imitation can be established; (2) quantitative data from time sampling every 5 s gave objective comparisons between groups, and inter-rater reliability was high; (3) matched-participants design on prior aggression controlled participant variables. Weaknesses, e.g. (1) generalisability – all children came from one university nursery (Stanford) and were aged about 3 to 5 years, so results may not apply to older children or other cultures; (2) low ecological validity – a Bobo doll is designed to be hit and the model was a stranger; (3) ethics – children were frustrated and exposed to aggression; (4) only short-term effects were measured.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): two strengths and two weaknesses, each developed with study detail, generalisability point clearly explained, well organised. Level 3 (6–8): four points, some lack detail or generalisability is brief. Level 2 (3–5): fewer points or mostly undeveloped/generic. Level 1 (1–2): one or two basic points. Generalisability must be included for top band.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one similarity and one difference between Bandura et al.'s study and Fagen et al.'s study of elephant learning.
parts.answer: Similarity: both studies investigate learning from the learning approach and produced quantitative data – Bandura recorded counts of imitative acts in 5-second intervals, Fagen recorded whether elephants performed each step of the trunk wash. Difference: Bandura investigated social learning (observational learning without direct reinforcement) in human children in a laboratory experiment with three conditions, whereas Fagen investigated operant conditioning using direct positive reinforcement (food) to shape behaviour in young Asian elephants in Nepal in a natural working setting with no control group.
parts.working: For each of similarity and difference: 1 mark identification, 1–2 marks explanation, 1 mark examples from each study (up to 4 marks each). Accept other valid similarities (e.g. both use non-adult participants; both standardised procedures) and differences (humans vs animals; lab vs field; social learning vs operant conditioning; experiment vs field study).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hamza's parents notice that their 6-year-old son copies the wrestling moves he sees on television on his younger cousin. Using Bandura et al.'s study, suggest two pieces of advice for Hamza's parents.
parts.answer: 1. Limit his viewing of aggressive role models, or watch with him, because Bandura found children who saw an aggressive adult copied specific aggressive acts, whereas those who saw a non-aggressive model did not. 2. Provide non-aggressive same-sex models (e.g. his father or older brother playing calmly and resolving conflict without force), because children in Bandura's study imitated the behaviour of the model they watched, and boys were especially influenced by male models.
parts.working: For each piece of advice: 1 mark for a suitable, ethical suggestion; 1 mark for a link to Bandura's findings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the research method used by Saavedra and Silverman.
parts.answer: A case study (of one child).
parts.working: 1 mark: case study.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the participant in Saavedra and Silverman's study, including how his phobia began.
parts.answer: A 9-year-old Hispanic-American boy with a phobia of buttons. It began when he was about 5 years old: in his kindergarten class he was reaching for buttons in a large bowl for an art activity, the bowl tipped and the buttons fell on him, which was very distressing.
parts.working: 1 mark: 9-year-old boy. 1 mark: button phobia. 1 mark: origin – buttons fell on him from a bowl at school when he was about 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how the boy's fear hierarchy was arranged in Saavedra and Silverman's study.
parts.answer: Button-related stimuli were ranked from least to most distressing: large denim jeans buttons were least distressing, and small plastic buttons were the most distressing.
parts.working: 1 mark: ranked list from least to most distressing. 1 mark: correct examples (large denim buttons low; small plastic buttons high).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the boy was asked to rate his distress on a 'feelings thermometer' throughout the therapy.
parts.answer: It gave a quick numerical measure of his distress for each step, so the therapist could check whether distress fell with exposure and decide when to move to the next item in the hierarchy.
parts.working: 1 mark: quantitative / self-rated measure of distress. 1 mark: to track change and guide progress up the hierarchy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the boy's button phobia could have been acquired through classical conditioning.
parts.answer: Before the incident buttons were a neutral stimulus. In kindergarten the buttons fell on him (unconditioned stimulus), causing distress and disgust (unconditioned response). Because buttons were paired with this experience, they became a conditioned stimulus that on their own produced fear/disgust (conditioned response), which then generalised to buttons on clothing.
parts.working: 1 mark: buttons as neutral → conditioned stimulus. 1 mark: the falling incident as UCS producing distress (UCR). 1 mark: association means buttons alone trigger fear/disgust (CR), with link to the case.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how positive reinforcement was used in the treatment.
parts.answer: The boy was rewarded (e.g. with praise and small agreed rewards) each time he completed a step of in-vivo exposure to buttons, which encouraged him to keep engaging with the feared items.
parts.working: 1 mark: rewards/praise given. 1 mark: contingent on successfully completing exposure steps (contingency management).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the disgust imagery exposure used with the boy.
parts.answer: The therapist guided the boy to imagine buttons in unpleasant, disgust-related ways, for example imagining buttons falling on him or touching his body, and thinking about how they look, feel and smell. He stayed with these images while his disgust was rated and was encouraged to see that the disgusting thoughts were not dangerous, so the disgust reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark: imagined (not real) button scenarios. 1 mark: focus on disgust-related sensations (touching, smell, feel). 1 mark: repeated / rated until disgust reduced, linked to cognitive change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the researchers concluded that targeting disgust was important for this child.
parts.answer: The boy's main reaction to buttons was disgust rather than fear, and behavioural exposure alone did not reduce it much; when the imagery focused on disgust his distress ratings fell and the gains lasted at follow-up.
parts.working: 1 mark: disgust was the dominant emotion. 1 mark: imagery that targeted disgust produced greater/lasting improvement than exposure with reinforcement alone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Saavedra and Silverman followed up the boy after treatment. State when the follow-ups took place and explain why follow-up is useful.
parts.answer: At 6 months and 12 months after treatment. Follow-up shows whether the improvement lasted rather than being a short-term effect, so the therapy can be judged effective in the long term.
