parts.working: 1 mark: 6 months and 12 months. 1 mark: shows whether improvement is long-lasting. 1 mark: e.g. rules out short-term demand effects / relapse check.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two friends are discussing Saavedra and Silverman's study. Nadia says the findings are useful for treating other children with phobias. Bilal says nothing can be generalised from a single case. Explain who you agree with.
parts.answer: Bilal is partly right: it was one 9-year-old boy with a rare phobia in which disgust was the main emotion, so other children (different ages, cultures or phobias) may not respond the same way. However, Nadia also has a point: the study gives detailed, in-depth evidence that adding disgust-focused imagery helped where exposure alone did not, which therapists can test with other children whose phobias involve disgust. Conclusion: the case is useful for generating ideas but needs replication before generalising.
parts.working: 1 mark: Bilal's point explained with study detail (one boy, unusual phobia). 1 mark: Nadia's point explained (in-depth data; practical application). 1 mark: link to disgust imagery/exposure. 1 mark: reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Saavedra and Silverman's study in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about the use of qualitative and quantitative data.
parts.answer: Strengths, e.g. (1) both quantitative data (feelings thermometer distress ratings at each step) and qualitative data (the boy's descriptions of feelings, parent interview data from the ADIS) were collected, giving a detailed and measurable picture; (2) case study gives in-depth insight into a rare phobia and the role of disgust; (3) useful application – disgust imagery added to exposure; (4) follow-ups at 6 and 12 months show lasting change. Weaknesses, e.g. (1) self-report ratings by a child may be affected by demand characteristics or limited understanding of the scale; (2) one participant limits generalisability; (3) therapist was also researcher – possible bias; (4) the cause of the original phobia was reconstructed from memory.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): two strengths and two weaknesses, each developed with study detail; named issue (qualitative/quantitative data) explicitly discussed. Level 3 (6–8): four points, some lack detail. Level 2 (3–5): limited or generic points. Level 1 (1–2): basic points only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ayesha, aged 10, is terrified of cotton wool after a bad experience at a clinic. Using Saavedra and Silverman's study, suggest how a therapist could help her.
parts.answer: Build a hierarchy of cotton-wool situations from least to most distressing (e.g. a picture of cotton wool, a closed bag, touching a ball, rubbing it on her arm). Expose her gradually to each step, asking her to rate her distress on a feelings thermometer and moving on only when ratings fall. Reward each completed step with praise or small prizes. If she reports disgust, add imagery exercises where she imagines touching cotton wool, as disgust imagery helped the boy in the study.
parts.working: 1 mark: hierarchy with relevant examples. 1 mark: gradual exposure. 1 mark: rating scale / positive reinforcement. 1 mark: disgust imagery, linked to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of learning used to train the elephants in Fagen et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Operant conditioning (positive reinforcement training).
parts.working: 1 mark: operant conditioning / positive reinforcement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how positive reinforcement and a bridging stimulus were used in the training.
parts.answer: Each time an elephant performed the target behaviour (or a step of it) it was given a food reward, which made that behaviour more likely to be repeated (positive reinforcement). A bridging stimulus (a signal such as a word or sound) was given at the exact moment the correct behaviour occurred, so the elephant could link that precise behaviour with the reward that followed a moment later.
parts.working: 1 mark: food reward given for the correct behaviour/step. 1 mark: reward increases the likelihood of the behaviour being repeated. 1 mark: bridging stimulus marks the exact moment of the correct behaviour / bridges the delay before the food.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it was useful to train the elephants to perform a trunk wash.
parts.answer: A trunk wash collects a sample of fluid from the elephant's trunk that can be tested for tuberculosis (TB). TB is a serious disease in captive elephants and can pass between elephants and people, so being able to test elephants safely helps protect both elephant and human health.
parts.working: 1 mark: trunk wash gives a sample to test for TB. 1 mark: elaboration – TB is a serious risk to elephants / can spread between elephants and humans, so screening protects health.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline why Fagen et al. wanted to show that positive reinforcement could replace traditional elephant-training methods.
parts.answer: Traditional training of working elephants often relies on punishment, dominance and fear (negative reinforcement), which harms welfare and can make elephants dangerous to handle. Showing that elephants can learn new behaviour with rewards alone offers a more humane and safer alternative.
parts.working: 1 mark: traditional methods use punishment/dominance/fear. 1 mark: positive reinforcement is more humane / better welfare / safer for handlers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Fagen et al.'s study could be considered ethical in terms of the guidelines for research with animals.
parts.answer: 1. No pain, punishment or distress was used: the elephants were trained only with food rewards, so the procedure was humane and caused no harm. 2. The research had clear benefits for the animals themselves – it allowed safe testing for tuberculosis and showed a kinder alternative to traditional training – so any small cost (e.g. time spent in training sessions) was outweighed by the benefits.
parts.working: For each reason: 1 mark identification (no harm/punishment – rewards only; benefits to elephants' health and welfare outweigh costs; elephants kept in their normal environment with familiar handlers), 1 mark explanation linked to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Fagen et al.'s study supports one assumption of the learning approach.
parts.answer: The learning approach assumes that behaviour is learned from the environment, for example through the consequences of behaviour (operant conditioning). The trunk wash is not a natural behaviour for elephants, but it was acquired because each step was followed by a food reward and the steps were shaped into the full sequence, showing that a completely new behaviour can be learned through reinforcement.
parts.working: 1 mark: states an assumption (behaviour learned through experience/consequences). 1 mark: the trunk wash is a new, not innate, behaviour. 1 mark: it was acquired through reinforcement/shaping.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Fagen et al.'s study of elephant learning in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about the use of animals in research.
parts.answer: Strengths, e.g. (1) animals in research: the study used only food rewards and no punishment, and it directly benefited the elephants (TB testing, a humane alternative to traditional training), so it meets ethical guidelines; (2) practical application – it shows handlers how to train useful health behaviours humanely; (3) carried out in the elephants' normal working environment, so it is high in ecological validity; (4) behaviour was broken into clearly defined steps, so progress could be recorded objectively. Weaknesses, e.g. (1) small sample of five juvenile elephants from one place in Nepal, so the findings may not generalise to adult elephants or other settings; (2) no control group (e.g. elephants trained traditionally), so it cannot show that positive reinforcement is better than other methods; (3) animals in research: findings from elephants may not generalise to human learning, and captive working elephants may differ from wild ones; (4) a field setting gives less control over extraneous variables (e.g. distractions, the elephants' daily workload).
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): two strengths and two weaknesses, each developed with study detail; animal issue clearly discussed. Level 3 (6–8): four points, some undeveloped. Level 2 (3–5): limited/generic. Level 1 (1–2): basic only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one similarity and one difference between Fagen et al.'s study and Saavedra and Silverman's study.
parts.answer: Similarity: both used positive reinforcement and broke the target behaviour into graded steps – the elephants were given food for each step of the trunk wash (shaping), while the boy was rewarded for completing each step of his fear hierarchy during exposure. Difference: Saavedra and Silverman carried out a case study of one 9-year-old boy to remove a learned phobia, using exposure with reinforcement and disgust imagery, whereas Fagen et al. trained five juvenile elephants in Nepal to acquire a completely new behaviour (the trunk wash) for health testing.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for the similarity and 4 for the difference: identification (1), explanation (1–2), examples from both studies (1). Accept other valid points (e.g. both have practical applications; human vs animal participants; one participant vs five; removing behaviour vs acquiring behaviour; self-report ratings vs observation of steps).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the aim of Fagen et al.'s study of elephant learning.
parts.answer: To find out whether young (juvenile) Asian elephants could be trained, using operant conditioning with positive reinforcement only, to perform a trunk wash – the behaviour needed to collect a sample to test for tuberculosis – showing a humane alternative to traditional training methods.
parts.working: 1 mark: train elephants to perform the trunk wash (for TB testing). 1 mark: using positive reinforcement / operant conditioning.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the participants in Fagen et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Five juvenile (young) Asian elephants living at an elephant facility in Nepal, cared for by their mahouts (handlers).
parts.working: 1 mark: five juvenile elephants. 1 mark: Asian elephants in Nepal / handled by mahouts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how shaping was used to train the elephants in Fagen et al.'s study.
parts.answer: The trunk wash was broken down into smaller steps – raising the trunk, keeping saline solution in the trunk, and lowering the trunk into a collection bag. Each step was reinforced with food as soon as it was performed, using a bridging signal to mark the exact moment of the correct behaviour. Once a step was reliable, rewards were given only for closer approximations, until the elephant performed the whole sequence on cue.
parts.working: 1 mark: behaviour broken into steps. 1 mark: named steps (trunk up, hold saline, trunk down into bag). 1 mark: immediate positive reinforcement with food / bridging stimulus. 1 mark: successive approximations combined into the full behaviour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether the elephants' learning in Fagen et al.'s study is better explained by individual or situational factors.
parts.answer: Situational: the learning was produced by the environment – the reinforcement schedule, the food rewards and the training sessions – which supports the learning approach's view that behaviour is shaped by consequences. Individual: the elephants did not all progress through the steps at the same speed, suggesting individual differences such as temperament, age or previous experiences with handlers also mattered. Conclusion: the situation (training) caused learning but individual characteristics affected how well it worked.
parts.working: 1 mark: defines individual vs situational. 1 mark: situational explanation linked to reinforcement in the study. 1 mark: individual explanation linked to differences between elephants. 1 mark: reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline two assumptions of the learning approach.
parts.answer: 1. Behaviour is learned through experience and interaction with the environment (nurture), rather than being innate. 2. Learning occurs through classical conditioning (association), operant conditioning (consequences such as reinforcement and punishment) and social learning (observing and imitating models).
parts.working: For each assumption: 1 mark identification, 1 mark expansion/example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Saavedra and Silverman's study supports one assumption of the learning approach.
parts.answer: The assumption that behaviour is learned through experience: the boy's phobia developed after a single distressing experience with buttons (classical conditioning), and it was reduced by new learning – exposure with positive reinforcement – showing that a learned behaviour can be unlearned.
parts.working: 1 mark: states assumption. 1 mark: acquisition of phobia through association with the button incident. 1 mark: treatment through reinforcement/exposure as evidence of learning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the learning approach, explain whether the nature or nurture side of the debate is more strongly supported. Refer to two studies from the approach.
parts.answer: The learning approach is on the nurture side. Bandura et al. showed that children who watched an aggressive adult reproduced specific acts and phrases they would not otherwise have shown, so aggression was learned by observation. Fagen et al. showed that elephants could acquire a completely new behaviour (the trunk wash) through shaping with food rewards. Saavedra and Silverman showed a phobia acquired through a frightening experience. However, nature also plays a part: boys in Bandura's study showed more physical aggression than girls, which may partly be biological, and individual animals differ in how quickly they learn. Conclusion: the studies strongly support nurture, but innate factors influence what is learned and how easily.
parts.working: 1 mark: defines nature/nurture. 2 marks: first study linked to nurture. 2 marks: second study linked. 1 mark: counterpoint for nature and conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'validity' in psychological research.
parts.answer: Validity is the extent to which a study or measure tests or measures what it claims to test or measure.
parts.working: 1 mark: measures what it intends to measure (accept 'accuracy of the findings / conclusions').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'ecological validity'.
parts.answer: The extent to which the findings of a study can be generalised to real-life settings and everyday behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark: findings apply to real-world situations / everyday life.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study tested memory by asking university students in Lahore to learn lists of 30 unrelated nonsense syllables in a quiet laboratory. Explain one reason why this study may be low in ecological validity.
parts.answer: Learning nonsense syllables in silence is not like everyday memory tasks, such as remembering a shopping list or a conversation in a noisy setting, so the results may not reflect how people remember in real life.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies artificial task/setting. 1 mark: explains why it differs from everyday memory, linked to the scenario.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one change that would increase the ecological validity of this study.
parts.answer: Ask participants to remember a realistic list, e.g. items to buy at a bazaar, while background market noise is played (or test them in a real shop).
parts.working: 1 mark: realistic task or setting. 1 mark: detail showing how it is more like everyday life.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'demand characteristics'.
parts.answer: Cues in a study that tell participants what the aim is, so they change their behaviour – for example to help the researcher (or to spoil the results) – rather than acting naturally.
parts.working: 1 mark: features/cues revealing the aim. 1 mark: participants change behaviour, reducing validity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a hypothetical experiment in Islamabad, participants drink either a caffeinated or a decaffeinated cola and then complete a reaction-time task. Suggest one way of reducing demand characteristics in this experiment.
parts.answer: Use a single-blind procedure: both drinks look and taste the same and participants are not told which one they received or that the study is about caffeine (e.g. say it is about 'drink preference and attention').
parts.working: 1 mark: single-blind / deception about aim / identical drinks. 1 mark: linked to the caffeine study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by 'social desirability bias' and suggest why it may affect a questionnaire about how often teenagers in Karachi help with household chores.
parts.answer: Social desirability bias is when participants give answers that make them look good rather than truthful ones. Teenagers may over-report how often they help at home because helping parents is seen as respectful and expected, so the results would overestimate helping.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition – answering to present oneself favourably. 1 mark: application – over-report chores. 1 mark: reason – helping is valued / expected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the researcher could reduce this bias.
parts.answer: Make the questionnaire anonymous (no names, sealed collection box).
parts.working: 1 mark: anonymity / confidentiality / filler questions / compare with parent reports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher wants to measure 'aggression' in children in a school playground in Peshawar. Explain why it is important to operationalise this variable, and give two examples of operationalised behaviours.
parts.answer: Operationalising means defining the variable in terms of specific, observable behaviours so it can be measured precisely; this means observers record the same thing, improving validity and reliability. Examples: pushing another child with both hands; hitting another child with a closed fist; shouting an insult at another child; kicking.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of operationalisation. 1 mark: why – precise/measurable, so the measure is valid/consistent. 1 mark each for two observable behaviours (max 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a single-blind and a double-blind procedure.
parts.answer: In a single-blind procedure the participants do not know which condition they are in (or the aim). In a double-blind procedure neither the participants nor the researcher who collects the data know which condition each participant is in.
parts.working: 1 mark: single-blind – participants unaware. 1 mark: double-blind – participants and data collector both unaware.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a double-blind procedure would improve the validity of a hypothetical trial testing whether a herbal tea improves sleep quality.
parts.answer: If the researcher rating sleep quality does not know who drank the herbal tea, their expectations cannot bias their ratings (researcher bias), and participants cannot react to knowing they received the 'real' tea (placebo/demand effects), so any difference is more likely due to the tea.
parts.working: 1 mark: removes researcher bias / expectations. 1 mark: removes participant expectation effects; difference due to IV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an extraneous variable and a confounding variable.
parts.answer: An extraneous variable is any variable other than the IV that might affect the DV. A confounding variable is an extraneous variable that has actually varied systematically with the IV, so it is impossible to tell whether the IV or the confound caused the change in the DV.
parts.working: 1 mark: extraneous – any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV. 1 mark: confounding – varies with the IV/conditions, so effect cannot be attributed to the IV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a hypothetical study, Class A in a Lahore school is taught spelling with a phone app in the morning, and Class B is taught with workbooks in the afternoon. Identify one confounding variable and explain how it reduces validity.
parts.answer: Time of day: pupils may be more alert in the morning, so if Class A scores higher it could be due to alertness rather than the app, so the study may not be measuring the effect of the teaching method.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies confound (time of day / different class / different teacher). 1 mark: explains why the DV difference cannot be attributed to the method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A psychologist designs a new 'exam stress' questionnaire for O Level students in Rawalpindi. Explain what is meant by 'face validity' and suggest how it could be checked for this questionnaire.
parts.answer: Face validity is whether a measure looks, on the surface, as if it measures what it claims to measure. It could be checked by asking experts (e.g. school counsellors or psychologists) and some students to read the questions and judge whether they appear to be about exam stress.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition – appears to measure what it should. 1 mark: method – experts/others judge items. 1 mark: application to exam stress questionnaire.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A new 10-item self-esteem questionnaire is given to 50 adults in Dubai, who also complete a well-established self-esteem scale. 46 of the 50 adults are placed in the same category (high or low self-esteem) by both measures. Calculate the percentage of adults placed in the same category.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name this way of checking validity and explain what the result suggests.
parts.answer: Concurrent validity (comparing a new measure with an established one taken at the same time). The high level of agreement (92 %) suggests the new questionnaire measures self-esteem in much the same way as the established scale, so it appears to be valid.
parts.working: 1 mark: concurrent validity. 1 mark: explanation of method – compare with an established measure. 1 mark: interpretation – high agreement supports validity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a laboratory experiment usually has high internal validity but may have low ecological validity. Use an example of a laboratory experiment in your answer.
parts.answer: In a lab the researcher controls extraneous variables (e.g. noise, lighting, instructions), so changes in the DV can be confidently linked to the IV – high internal validity. But the setting and tasks are often artificial, so behaviour may differ from real life – low ecological validity. Example: a lab study of distraction where participants solve puzzles while a recording of a phone ringing is played, which controls noise exactly but is unlike being distracted in a busy office.
parts.working: 1 mark: control of extraneous variables. 1 mark: cause and effect / internal validity. 1 mark: artificial setting/task reduces ecological validity. 1 mark: suitable example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe researcher bias and explain how it could affect a hypothetical observation of whether boys or girls share more toys at a nursery in Multan.
parts.answer: Researcher bias is when the researcher's expectations influence how they collect or interpret data. If the observer expects girls to share more, they may record ambiguous behaviour (e.g. a girl passing a toy) as sharing but code the same behaviour by a boy differently, so the data would be biased towards the hypothesis.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition. 1 mark: application – observer's expectation about girls/boys. 1 mark: effect – biased coding of ambiguous acts, findings invalid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing researcher bias in this observation.
parts.answer: Use observers who do not know the hypothesis (blind observers), or two observers with clear behaviour categories.
parts.working: 1 mark: blind observers / operationalised categories / inter-rater checks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by standardisation and explain why it improves validity. Use any examples.
parts.answer: Standardisation means keeping procedures, instructions and materials the same for every participant (e.g. the same written instructions, the same timing and the same room). This means differences in the DV are not caused by differences in how participants were treated, so the IV is more likely to be the cause; for example, if one group were given clearer instructions, their better scores might be due to the instructions rather than the IV.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition. 1 mark: example. 1 mark: reduces extraneous/situational variables. 1 mark: conclusions about the IV more valid (with example).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study in Nairobi asked shoppers to rate a new advertisement while a researcher stood beside them holding a clipboard with the company logo. Explain two threats to validity in this procedure.
parts.answer: 1. Demand characteristics / social desirability: shoppers can see the company logo and the researcher watching, so they may give more positive ratings to please the researcher. 2. Researcher (investigator) effects: the researcher's presence, tone or body language may influence how shoppers answer, so ratings may not reflect their true opinions.
parts.working: For each threat: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation linked to the scenario.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two researchers disagree. Sana says a field experiment is always more valid than a laboratory experiment. Haris says a laboratory experiment is more valid. Explain who you agree with.
parts.answer: Both are partly right because validity has different types. Sana: field experiments take place in natural settings, so participants behave more naturally and findings have higher ecological validity, and participants may not know they are in a study, reducing demand characteristics. Haris: laboratory experiments control extraneous variables more tightly, so they have higher internal validity – we can be more confident that the IV caused the DV. Conclusion: neither is 'always' more valid; the best choice depends on whether control or realism matters more for the research question.
parts.working: 1 mark: Sana's point explained. 1 mark: Haris's point explained. 1 mark: distinguishes internal vs ecological validity. 1 mark: reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study investigated whether a mindfulness app reduces stress in nurses at a hospital in Karachi. Nurses chose whether to use the app (20 did) or not (20 did not). After four weeks, all nurses rated their stress on a scale of 1 to 10. Explain three reasons why the conclusion 'the app reduces stress' may not be valid.
parts.answer: 1. Self-selection/participant variables: nurses who chose the app may already have been more motivated or less stressed, so differences may not be due to the app. 2. Demand characteristics / placebo: app users knew they were using a stress-reduction tool and may have rated themselves lower to fit expectations. 3. No baseline: stress was only measured afterwards, so we cannot tell whether stress actually changed. Also: other uncontrolled variables (e.g. different shifts or wards) may have affected stress.
parts.working: For each of three reasons: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation linked to the nurses/app study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by 'ecological validity' and 'demand characteristics', using any examples.
parts.answer: Ecological validity: how far findings can be applied to real-life settings; it depends on the setting, task and materials being realistic, e.g. a study of road-crossing decisions using a virtual-reality street is lower in ecological validity than observing pedestrians at a real crossing. Demand characteristics: cues that reveal the aim of the study so participants change their behaviour, e.g. if participants are asked about their mood before and after watching a comedy, they may guess the aim and report feeling happier. Both affect whether results reflect genuine behaviour.
parts.working: 3 marks for each concept: 1 mark definition, 1 mark elaboration, 1 mark example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a researcher could conduct a laboratory experiment to investigate whether background music affects reading comprehension, so that the study is as valid as possible. Include the IV and DV, the design, controls and how validity is protected.
parts.answer: IV: background music (instrumental music at a set volume vs silence). DV: reading comprehension score – number correct out of 20 multiple-choice questions on a 600-word passage. Design: independent measures (to avoid practice effects with the same passage), random allocation from a sample of e.g. 40 sixth-form students. Controls: same passage and questions, same 10-minute reading time, same room, lighting, time of day, headphones at same volume; standardised written instructions. Validity: single-blind cover story ('a study of reading speed') to reduce demand characteristics; the person marking answers does not know the condition (double-blind marking); exclude participants who are not fluent in the language of the passage; pilot study to check the questions measure comprehension (face validity). Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, debrief.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): IV and DV operationalised; appropriate design with allocation; several specific controls; at least two explicit validity measures; procedure replicable. Level 3 (6–8): most features with some detail. Level 2 (3–5): basic plan, little detail on validity. Level 1 (1–2): vague.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher measured 'helpfulness' in a hypothetical study by counting how many times participants said they would help a stranger in a questionnaire. Explain one reason why this measure may lack validity, and suggest a more valid measure.
parts.answer: What people say they would do is not necessarily what they actually do: they may overestimate their helpfulness because of social desirability, so the questionnaire may measure self-image rather than helping. A more valid measure would be to observe real helping, e.g. a confederate drops a bag of oranges in a shopping centre and the observer records whether passers-by help pick them up within 10 seconds.
parts.working: 1 mark: self-report vs actual behaviour. 1 mark: social desirability explanation. 1 mark: suggests behavioural measure. 1 mark: operationalised detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why using a placebo condition can improve the validity of a drug trial.
parts.answer: Participants in both conditions believe they may be receiving the drug, so any improvement due simply to expecting to get better (the placebo effect) occurs in both groups; a greater improvement in the drug group can therefore be attributed to the drug itself.
parts.working: 1 mark: controls for expectation/placebo effect. 1 mark: difference can then be attributed to the drug.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'reliability'.
parts.answer: Reliability is the consistency of a measure or procedure: whether it gives the same results if it is repeated.
parts.working: 1 mark: consistency / same results on repetition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline how the test-retest method could be used to check the reliability of a questionnaire on screen-time habits.
parts.answer: Give the same questionnaire to the same participants twice, a suitable time apart (e.g. two weeks), and compare (correlate) the two sets of scores; a strong positive correlation shows the questionnaire is reliable.
parts.working: 1 mark: same people, same test, two occasions with time gap. 1 mark: compare/correlate scores – high agreement = reliable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two observers recorded the number of times a toddler at a day-care centre in Islamabad made eye contact with a carer during 20 one-minute periods. They agreed on 18 of the 20 periods. Calculate the percentage agreement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what this result shows about the observation.
parts.answer: It shows high inter-rater (inter-observer) reliability: the two observers recorded the behaviour in a consistent way, so the behaviour categories were clear and the data are not just the opinion of one observer.
parts.working: 1 mark: inter-rater reliability is high. 1 mark: explanation – observers consistent / categories clear.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways of improving the inter-rater reliability of an observation of customer behaviour in a shopping mall.
parts.answer: 1. Operationalise the behaviour categories clearly (e.g. 'picks up a product and reads the label for at least 3 seconds'), so both observers know exactly what to record. 2. Train the observers together with practice recordings (e.g. video clips of shoppers) and compare scores until they agree highly before the real observation.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation linked to the mall context. Accept also: time sampling with fixed intervals; use of a coding sheet; video recording for later checking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between reliability and validity, using an example of a bathroom scale.
parts.answer: Reliability is consistency, validity is accuracy. A scale that shows 2 kg too heavy every time is reliable (it gives the same reading each time) but not valid (the reading is not the true weight). A valid scale must also be reliable, but a reliable scale is not necessarily valid.
parts.working: 1 mark: reliability = consistency. 1 mark: validity = measures what it should / accuracy. 1 mark: example showing reliable but not valid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical memory test was given to 140 students in Lahore and repeated three weeks later. 112 students were placed in the same score band (low, medium or high) both times. Calculate the percentage of students placed in the same band.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why some students may have been placed in a different band on the second occasion, even if the test is reliable.
parts.answer: 1. Practice effect: students may remember some items from the first test and score higher the second time. 2. Situational/participant changes: on one occasion a student may have been tired, ill or anxious (or the room was noisy), which changed their performance. Also: genuine change in memory over three weeks (e.g. learning).
parts.working: For each: 1 mark reason, 1 mark explanation linked to the test-retest situation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe 'test-retest reliability' and 'inter-rater reliability', using any examples.
parts.answer: Test-retest reliability: the same participants complete the same test on two occasions, separated by enough time to avoid remembering answers but not so long that the trait changes; scores are correlated and a strong positive correlation indicates consistency, e.g. an anxiety questionnaire taken two weeks apart. Inter-rater reliability: two or more observers or raters independently record or score the same behaviour; their scores are compared (correlation or % agreement), e.g. two observers coding aggressive acts in a playground. High agreement means the scoring is consistent and not based on one person's interpretation.
parts.working: 3 marks each: 1 mark definition, 1 mark how it is assessed, 1 mark example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'generalisability'.
parts.answer: The extent to which findings from a sample can be applied to the wider target population (and other settings).
parts.working: 1 mark: findings apply beyond the sample to the population/other people.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical study of sleep habits used 25 male medical students from one university in Peshawar. Explain one reason why the findings may not be generalisable.
parts.answer: The sample is all male, from one university and one course; medical students may have unusual sleep patterns because of long study hours and night shifts, so results may not apply to women, older adults or people in other jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies a sample bias (one gender/one institution/one course/small). 1 mark: explains why the wider population may differ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the sampling technique and sample size affect the generalisability of a study. Use examples.
parts.answer: A random sample gives every member of the population an equal chance of selection, so the sample is more representative, e.g. randomly selecting pupils from the register of every school in a district. An opportunity or volunteer sample may over-represent certain types of people, e.g. volunteers who are more confident. A larger sample reduces the effect of unusual individuals, so findings are more likely to apply to the population; a very small sample may be biased by chance.
parts.working: 1 mark: representative techniques explained. 1 mark: biased techniques explained. 1 mark: sample size effect. 1 mark: relevant examples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study in the UK found that children aged 8 to 10 remembered more words when they were presented as pictures. A teacher in Quetta wants to use the findings for her pupils. Evaluate whether the findings can be generalised to her class.
parts.answer: For: the memory processes studied (picture superiority) are likely to be similar in all children of this age, and her pupils are in the same age range, so the findings may apply. Against: the children were from a different culture and education system; they may differ in language, familiarity with pictures/screens and teaching style, and the sample size and sampling technique are unknown, so the results may not be representative. Conclusion: she could try it but should check whether it works with her own pupils.
parts.working: 1 mark: argument for generalising. 1 mark: cultural/educational differences. 1 mark: sample size/technique point. 1 mark: reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between objective and subjective data.
parts.answer: Objective data are not affected by the researcher's personal opinions or interpretations, e.g. reaction times measured by a computer. Subjective data depend on personal interpretation or feelings, e.g. a researcher's judgement of how 'friendly' a person seems.
parts.working: 1 mark: objective – free from personal bias, measured the same by anyone. 1 mark: subjective – depends on personal interpretation. Examples may be credited within either mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of an objective measure that could be used in a study of stress.
parts.answer: Heart rate measured with a monitor (or cortisol level in a saliva sample).
parts.working: 1 mark: any physiological or automatically recorded measure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical interview study in Lahore asked mothers open questions about how they cope with their child's illness. Explain why the analysis of these answers may be subjective, and suggest two ways of making it more objective.
parts.answer: Open answers produce qualitative data that must be interpreted; the researcher decides which themes are present, and their own views or expectations may influence this. Ways to increase objectivity: (1) use a clear coding scheme with defined themes decided in advance; (2) have two researchers code the answers independently and check inter-rater agreement (or convert themes into counts).
parts.working: 1 mark: qualitative data require interpretation. 1 mark: researcher's expectations/bias. 1 mark each for two suitable methods (max 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by an opportunity sample.
parts.answer: Participants are selected because they are available and willing at the time the researcher is collecting data, e.g. asking people who are in a college canteen at lunchtime.
parts.working: 1 mark: people who are available/convenient at the time. 1 mark: elaboration or example (researcher approaches them).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one strength and one weakness of opportunity sampling.
parts.answer: Strength: quick, cheap and easy to obtain participants. Weakness: likely to be unrepresentative because only people in one place at one time are sampled (and the researcher may choose people who look approachable), so findings may not generalise.
parts.working: 1 mark: strength. 1 mark: weakness with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a researcher could obtain a volunteer (self-selected) sample for a study of online gaming habits among young adults in Lahore.
parts.answer: Place an advertisement (e.g. on a university notice board or a gaming forum) describing the study and asking young adults aged 18 to 25 who play online games to contact the researcher if they would like to take part.
parts.working: 1 mark: advertisement/request for participants. 1 mark: participants choose to respond/sign up, linked to context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using a volunteer sample in this study.
parts.answer: People who reply may be especially keen gamers, or more confident and helpful, so the sample may over-represent heavy gaming and not reflect typical young adults (volunteer bias).
parts.working: 1 mark: volunteer bias. 1 mark: linked to the gaming study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a random sample of 25 pupils could be selected from a school of 250 pupils in Hyderabad.
parts.answer: Obtain a list of all 250 pupils, give each a number, then use a random number generator (or put all names in a container and draw out 25) to choose 25 pupils.
parts.working: 1 mark: list of the whole target population. 1 mark: random selection method (lottery/random number generator) giving each pupil an equal chance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the probability that any one pupil is selected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a snowball sample.
parts.answer: The researcher finds a few participants from the target population, then asks them to recommend or recruit other people they know who fit the criteria; those people recruit others, so the sample grows.
parts.working: 1 mark: initial small group found. 1 mark: they recruit/refer further participants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why snowball sampling would be useful for a study of people recovering from gambling problems.
parts.answer: People with gambling problems are hard to identify and may hide it; existing participants know others in a similar situation (e.g. from support groups) and can approach them with trust, so the researcher can reach a hidden population.
parts.working: 1 mark: hard-to-reach / hidden population. 1 mark: participants know and trust others like them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical snowball sample for a study of home-based tailors in Faisalabad, the researcher starts with 3 tailors. In each round of recruitment, every tailor recruited in the previous round (starting with the first 3) recruits exactly 2 new tailors. There are three rounds of recruitment. Calculate the total number of participants.
parts.answer: 45 participants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why this sample may be biased.
parts.answer: Tailors recruit people they know, so the sample will consist of connected friendship or family networks, possibly from the same area and with similar working conditions, and tailors outside these networks will be missed.
parts.working: 1 mark: participants recruit similar people / from own network. 1 mark: so sample unrepresentative of all home-based tailors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher placed an advertisement for a study about sleep in a newspaper read by about 4500 people in Rawalpindi. 300 people replied. Calculate the percentage of readers who replied. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the sampling technique and explain why the researcher should be cautious about generalising the results.
parts.answer: Volunteer (self-selected) sampling. Only a small proportion (6.7 %) replied, and those who reply may be different from other readers – e.g. people with sleep problems who are more interested in the topic, or people with more free time – and newspaper readers themselves may not represent the general population.
parts.working: 1 mark: volunteer sampling. 1 mark: respondents are a small, self-selected group with particular characteristics. 1 mark: readers of one newspaper not typical of whole population.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe 'random sampling' and 'opportunity sampling', using any examples.
parts.answer: Random sampling: every member of the target population has an equal chance of being selected; the researcher needs a complete list of the population and uses a lottery or random number generator, e.g. picking 30 staff numbers at random from a hospital's list of 600 nurses. It avoids researcher bias in selection but may still produce an unrepresentative sample by chance and can be time-consuming. Opportunity sampling: the researcher uses whoever is available and willing at the time, e.g. asking passengers waiting at a bus terminal; it is quick and convenient but likely to be biased towards certain types of people (e.g. those who use that terminal at that time).
parts.working: 3 marks each: 1 mark definition, 1 mark elaboration (how done / strength or weakness), 1 mark example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A psychologist wants to study the experiences of refugees from one region who have settled in a city. Explain which sampling technique would be most appropriate and why.
parts.answer: Snowball sampling: there is no complete list of refugees, so random sampling is not possible; refugees may be wary of strangers, but if a few trusted participants are found (e.g. through a community centre) they can introduce others, allowing the researcher to reach enough participants.
parts.working: 1 mark: snowball. 1 mark: no list / hard to reach. 1 mark: trust and referral explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a truly random sample is often difficult to obtain in psychology.
parts.answer: The researcher needs a complete list of everyone in the target population, which is often unavailable. Even if names are drawn randomly, some selected people may refuse or not be contactable, so the final sample becomes partly self-selected. It can also be time-consuming and costly to reach people who are spread over a wide area.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: need full list; refusals/non-response make it partly volunteer; time/cost; selected people may be hard to reach.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical study, a researcher stood outside a gym in Dubai at 7 a.m. and asked people leaving whether they would complete a questionnaire about healthy eating. Identify the sampling technique and explain two reasons why the results may be biased.
parts.answer: Opportunity sampling. 1. People leaving a gym early in the morning are probably more health-conscious than average, so they may report healthier eating than the general population. 2. Only people present at that time and place could be chosen (e.g. not shift workers or people who cannot afford gym fees), and the researcher may approach people who seem friendly, so the sample is not representative.
parts.working: 1 mark: opportunity sample. For each reason: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation linked to the gym context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one ethical advantage of using a volunteer sample compared with an opportunity sample.
parts.answer: Volunteers have actively chosen to take part after reading about the study, so they are more likely to have given genuine informed consent and feel free to refuse, whereas people approached face-to-face may feel pressured to agree.
parts.working: 1 mark: volunteers choose freely / informed. 1 mark: comparison – less pressure than being approached directly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A college in Karachi has 800 students. A researcher randomly selects 40 students for a study of exam stress, but 14 of the selected students refuse to take part. Calculate the percentage of selected students who refused.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this refusal rate affects the representativeness of the sample.
parts.answer: The final sample of 26 is no longer truly random because the people who agreed are, in effect, volunteers. Students who refused may be different – e.g. the most stressed students might avoid a study about stress – so the sample may underestimate exam stress, and the smaller sample is also more affected by individual differences.
parts.working: 1 mark: sample becomes partly self-selected. 1 mark: refusers may differ systematically (linked to stress). 1 mark: consequence – biased results / smaller sample.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare random sampling and snowball sampling in terms of representativeness and practicality.
parts.answer: Representativeness: random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance and avoids researcher bias, so it is more likely to be representative; snowball samples consist of linked social networks, so they are likely to be biased towards similar people. Practicality: random sampling needs a full list of the population and may be impossible for hidden groups (e.g. people with an addiction), whereas snowball sampling is practical for hard-to-reach populations because participants recruit others they know.
parts.working: 2 marks representativeness comparison (1 each side), 2 marks practicality comparison (1 each side).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a researcher could conduct a study using a questionnaire to investigate attitudes towards mental-health help-seeking among university students in Islamabad. Your plan must include the sampling technique, and you must explain how it would be carried out.
parts.answer: Sampling: random sample – obtain the list of all registered undergraduates from the university, number them, use a random number generator to select 100; contact by university email with information sheet and consent form; replace non-responders by drawing more names and record the response rate. Questionnaire: closed questions with a 5-point Likert scale (strongly agree to strongly disagree), e.g. 'I would see a counsellor if I felt low for two weeks'; some open questions, e.g. 'What would stop you seeking help?'; demographic questions (age, gender, course). Procedure: online or paper in a quiet room, standardised instructions, about 15 minutes, anonymous with ID codes, right to withdraw, debrief with details of the counselling service. Analysis: total attitude score (quantitative) compared between groups; themes from open answers. Pilot the questionnaire with a few students.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): sampling technique named and fully described (how selected, from what population, size, recruitment); questionnaire details with example items; procedure replicable; ethics. Level 3 (6–8): most features with some detail. Level 2 (3–5): basic plan, sampling vague. Level 1 (1–2): very limited.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study needs a sample of 60 shoppers at a large market in Peshawar. Ali suggests asking the first 60 people who walk past a stall. Fatima suggests putting up a poster asking shoppers to sign up. Evaluate each suggestion and recommend which is better for reducing bias.
parts.answer: Ali (opportunity): quick and gives a sample of people actually shopping, but only those passing one stall at one time are included, and passers-by in a hurry may refuse. Fatima (volunteer): participants choose freely, but only shoppers who notice the poster and have time or interest will sign up, creating volunteer bias and possibly a slow, small sample. Recommendation: e.g. Ali's method adapted – approach every 5th shopper at different stalls and times of day – reduces both selection by the researcher and self-selection bias; credit any justified recommendation.
parts.working: 1 mark: evaluation of Ali's suggestion. 1 mark: evaluation of Fatima's suggestion. 1 mark: clear recommendation. 1 mark: justification about bias.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a researcher might choose an opportunity sample even though it is likely to be unrepresentative.
parts.answer: It is the quickest and cheapest way of obtaining participants, and in some studies (e.g. a laboratory experiment on a basic process such as visual perception) the researcher assumes the process works the same in most people, so representativeness matters less.
parts.working: 1 mark: practicality (time, cost, ease). 1 mark: elaboration, e.g. universal processes or pilot studies.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify the sampling technique in each of the following hypothetical studies:
(i) A researcher posts on a social-media page asking for parents of toddlers to complete a survey.
(ii) A researcher asks the people sitting in a hospital waiting room to rate their anxiety.
(iii) A researcher draws 20 names from a box containing the names of every employee in a bank.
parts.answer: (i) Volunteer (self-selected) sample. (ii) Opportunity sample. (iii) Random sample.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe 'volunteer sampling' and 'snowball sampling', using any examples.
parts.answer: Volunteer sampling: participants select themselves, usually by responding to an advertisement, e.g. a poster in a library asking students to take part in a memory study; it gives willing and often committed participants but may be biased towards people who are more motivated or have more time. Snowball sampling: the researcher begins with a few participants who meet the criteria and asks them to recruit others they know, e.g. finding a few people who have recovered from a phobia, who then introduce others; it allows access to hard-to-reach groups, but the sample may contain people with similar characteristics because they come from the same networks.
parts.working: 3 marks each: 1 mark definition, 1 mark elaboration (strength/weakness or procedure), 1 mark example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher wants a random sample from all 1500 adults registered at a health clinic in Lahore. He chooses 90 adults using random numbers, and 54 of them complete his questionnaire. Calculate (i) the percentage of registered adults who were selected, and (ii) the percentage of selected adults who completed the questionnaire.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the researcher could increase the response rate without making the sample less random.
parts.answer: Send reminders to the selected adults who have not responded (or make the questionnaire shorter/available by phone or online), rather than replacing them with whoever is available, so that the original randomly chosen people are more likely to take part.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable method (reminders, convenience of format, short questionnaire, explanation of importance). 1 mark: keeps the originally selected random sample.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms 'target population' and 'sample'.
parts.answer: Target population: the whole group of people the researcher is interested in and wants the findings to apply to. Sample: the smaller group of people selected from the target population who actually take part in the study.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A researcher studies 30 nurses from one hospital in Multan to learn about stress among nurses in Pakistan. Identify the target population and the sample.
parts.answer: Target population: nurses in Pakistan. Sample: the 30 nurses from the hospital in Multan.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a representative sample and why it is important.
parts.answer: A representative sample has the same important characteristics as the target population (e.g. similar proportions of ages, genders and backgrounds), so findings from it can be generalised to the population.
parts.working: 1 mark: sample reflects the characteristics of the population. 1 mark: allows generalisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study wanted to investigate the reading habits of teenagers in Pakistan. The researcher's sample was 120 students from private English-medium schools in Islamabad, of whom 36 were girls. Calculate the percentage of the sample who were girls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which this sample may not represent the target population.
parts.answer: 1. Only 30 % were girls, whereas girls make up about half of teenagers, so girls' reading habits are under-represented. 2. All students came from private English-medium schools in one city; teenagers in government or Urdu-medium schools, in rural areas or not in school may have very different access to books and reading habits.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation linked to reading habits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a target population and a sampling frame (the list from which a sample is actually drawn), using an example.
parts.answer: The target population is everyone the researcher wants to generalise to, e.g. all adults with diabetes in Karachi. The sampling frame is the actual list available, e.g. patients registered at three diabetes clinics. The two may differ: people with undiagnosed diabetes or who do not attend these clinics are in the population but not on the list, so even a random sample from the list may be biased.
parts.working: 1 mark: target population definition with example. 1 mark: sampling frame / list definition with example. 1 mark: explains how the difference may cause bias.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment on the effect of caffeine on concentration used 20 psychology undergraduates from one university in the UK. Explain why the target population may be narrower than the researchers claim.
parts.answer: The researchers may claim the results apply to 'adults', but psychology undergraduates are mostly young, educated and from one country, and many may know about research aims. People who are older, from other cultures, or who rarely drink caffeine may react differently, so the findings really only generalise to similar students.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies the narrow sample characteristics. 1 mark: explains how other groups may differ in caffeine response or concentration. 1 mark: conclusion that the population the results apply to is limited.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher wants to investigate the experiences of women who run small home businesses in rural Punjab. Discuss how the definition of the target population affects the choice of sampling technique and the generalisability of findings.
parts.answer: Definition: the population must be defined precisely – e.g. women aged 18+ living in villages in Punjab who earn money from a business run from home – so it is clear who is included. Because there is no list of such women, random sampling is impractical; snowball sampling through community contacts or an opportunity sample at village markets may be used. These techniques are likely to produce samples biased towards connected women in accessible villages, so findings generalise best to similar women. A broad definition (e.g. 'women entrepreneurs in Pakistan') would make generalisation from such a sample inappropriate, whereas a narrow definition makes the sample more representative but the findings apply to fewer people.
parts.working: 1 mark: need to define population precisely (with example). 2 marks: link from definition/availability of a list to sampling technique choice. 2 marks: effect on representativeness/generalisability. 1 mark: trade-off between broad and narrow definitions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study of 60 commuters at a Lahore metro station found that 18 felt anxious in crowds. A newspaper reported: '30 % of people in Lahore suffer from crowd anxiety.' Calculate the percentage of the sample who felt anxious, and explain why the newspaper's claim is not justified.
parts.answer: 18 ÷ 60 × 100 = 30 %. The claim is not justified because the sample was 60 metro commuters at one station – not representative of all people in Lahore (e.g. people who avoid crowds may not use the metro at all, so anxiety may be underestimated, or the time of day may have affected results). The sample is also small, and 'felt anxious' is not the same as 'suffering' from an anxiety problem.
parts.working: B1: 30 %. 1 mark: sample not representative of the population of Lahore. 1 mark: specific reason (only metro users/one station/self-selection out of the metro). 1 mark: small sample or measurement issue (felt anxious ≠ disorder).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage of using a large sample in a psychological study.
parts.answer: Individual differences and unusual participants have less effect on the overall results, so the findings are more likely to be representative and generalisable to the target population.
parts.working: 1 mark: reduces effect of individual differences/anomalies. 1 mark: more representative / generalisable / reliable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of using a large sample.
parts.answer: It takes more time and money to recruit and test many participants, and it may be impractical, e.g. if each participant needs a one-hour interview.
parts.working: 1 mark: time/cost. 1 mark: elaboration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study compared the mean reaction times of two groups, each containing only 5 participants. In Group A the reaction times (in milliseconds) were 312, 298, 305, 640 and 301. Calculate the mean reaction time for Group A, and explain how the small sample size affects the conclusions that can be drawn.
parts.answer: Mean = 1856 ÷ 5 = 371.2 ms. One unusual score (640 ms) has a large effect on the mean of such a small group; without it the mean would be about 304 ms. With only 5 people, a single anomaly or individual difference can distort the comparison between groups, so the conclusion may not be reliable or generalisable.
parts.working: M1: sum 1856. A1: 371.2 ms. 1 mark: outlier 640 strongly affects a small sample. 1 mark: results less reliable/representative.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why case studies often use a sample size of one, and one consequence of this for the research.
parts.answer: Case studies investigate a single person (or small group) in great depth, often because the condition is rare or unusual (e.g. a person with a specific brain injury), so it may only be possible to study one. Consequence: detailed qualitative data are obtained, but the findings may not be generalisable because that individual may be unique.
parts.working: 1 mark: in-depth study of one person. 1 mark: rare/unusual cases. 1 mark: consequence – low generalisability (or rich detail).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher plans a questionnaire study about smartphone use among 9000 secondary-school pupils in a district. She can afford to survey either 30 pupils chosen at random or 300 pupils from the two schools nearest her office. Evaluate both options and recommend which she should choose.
parts.answer: 30 random pupils: every pupil has an equal chance, so there is no systematic selection bias, but the sample is small, so chance variation and individual differences may make it unrepresentative. 300 pupils from two nearby schools: the larger sample reduces the effect of individual differences, but it is biased – pupils from two schools in one area may share similar backgrounds, school phone rules and internet access. Recommendation: e.g. the random sample, because bias cannot be removed by increasing size, whereas the random sample's error is due to chance only; or a justified compromise (random selection of schools, then pupils). Credit any justified decision.
parts.working: 1 mark: evaluation of small random sample. 1 mark: evaluation of large biased sample. 1 mark: recommendation. 1 mark: justification (size does not cure bias).

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main characteristics of kleptomania.
parts.answer: Repeated failure to resist urges to steal objects that are not needed for personal use or for their money value; a rising sense of tension or arousal before the theft; and a feeling of pleasure, gratification or relief during or immediately after stealing. The stealing is not done out of anger or revenge, and the objects are often given away, hidden or thrown away.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: recurrent failure to control urge to steal; items not needed/of little value; tension before; relief/gratification during or after; not motivated by anger, revenge or delusion; items discarded/hoarded/returned.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one difference between kleptomania and pyromania.
parts.answer: In kleptomania the impulse is to steal objects, whereas in pyromania the impulse is to set fires (with a fascination with fire).
parts.working: 1 mark: stealing vs deliberate fire-setting.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal spends many hours a day on online betting apps, chasing his losses, and has borrowed money from his relatives without telling his wife. Suggest how operant conditioning could explain why Bilal continues to gamble.
parts.answer: Gambling is maintained by positive reinforcement – occasional wins give money and excitement (and a dopamine 'high'). Wins come on a variable-ratio schedule: they are unpredictable, so Bilal keeps betting in case the next bet pays out, and this schedule is very resistant to extinction. Near misses may also feel rewarding. Gambling may also be negatively reinforced if it lets him escape stress or worry about his debts, so 'chasing losses' continues.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive reinforcement from wins. 1 mark: variable-ratio / partial reinforcement schedule. 1 mark: resistance to extinction / near misses. 1 mark: negative reinforcement or application to Bilal's chasing losses.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe imaginal desensitisation as a treatment for gambling disorder.
parts.answer: Based on classical conditioning and systematic desensitisation. The client is first taught progressive muscle relaxation. Then, while relaxed, they imagine scenes that would normally trigger the urge to gamble (e.g. walking past a betting shop, having money in their pocket, seeing a match on TV), imagining themselves feeling the urge but not gambling and leaving the situation. Over several short sessions (often guided by recordings for practice at home), the relaxation response is paired with the cues, so the arousal and tension that drive the urge are reduced. It aims to break the link between gambling cues and arousal so the person can resist the urge.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 of: based on conditioning/reciprocal inhibition; relaxation training; imagined gambling cues/scenes; imagining resisting the urge and leaving; repeated sessions/audio recordings; reduces arousal/tension linked to cues; aim to weaken cue–urge association; may be compared with aversion therapy.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the feeling-state theory of behavioural addiction.
parts.answer: Miller's feeling-state theory proposes that an addictive behaviour (e.g. gambling or stealing) becomes linked with an intense positive feeling at a particular moment – such as a feeling of success, power or excitement – forming a 'feeling-state' (a memory combining the sensations, emotions, thoughts and the behaviour). Later, when the person experiences an unmet need or negative emotion, the feeling-state is triggered, producing an urge to repeat the behaviour to get that feeling again. Treatment (the feeling-state addiction protocol) aims to identify and break up these feeling-states, e.g. using eye-movement techniques.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive feeling linked to the behaviour. 1 mark: forms a feeling-state memory (sensations, emotions, cognitions). 1 mark: triggered later by negative emotions/unmet needs, producing the urge. 1 mark: treatment link (identify and process feeling-states).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the K-SAS (Kleptomania Symptom Assessment Scale) is useful for measuring kleptomania, and give one weakness of using it.
parts.answer: It is a self-report rating scale that asks about the key features of kleptomania over the past week, e.g. how strong and frequent urges to steal were, how much time was spent thinking about stealing, and how much distress was felt, giving a total score. Because it gives quantitative scores, it can be used to compare patients and to measure change before and after treatment. Weakness: it relies on honest self-report; people may under-report stealing because it is illegal and embarrassing (social desirability), so scores may not be valid.
parts.working: 1 mark: self-report rating scale of symptoms. 1 mark: example items (urges, thoughts, time, distress). 1 mark: strength – quantitative/compare/track change. 1 mark: weakness explained.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a study to investigate whether covert sensitisation reduces the urge to steal in people with kleptomania. Your plan must use a self-report rating scale and an experiment with an independent measures design.
parts.answer: Sample: e.g. 40 adults diagnosed with kleptomania, recruited through psychiatric clinics (volunteer/opportunity), with consent. Design: independent measures; randomly allocated to covert sensitisation or a waiting-list/relaxation control. IV: type of treatment. Covert sensitisation: patients imagine the urge to steal, then immediately imagine aversive consequences (e.g. being caught by security, embarrassment in front of family, or nausea), over 8 weekly sessions with home practice. DV: urge to steal measured by a self-report scale, e.g. the K-SAS or an urge rating of 0 (no urge) to 10 (overwhelming urge), completed weekly and at a 3-month follow-up; plus number of thefts reported. Controls: same number and length of sessions, same therapist training, rating completed in private. Ethics: informed consent, confidentiality (thefts are illegal), right to withdraw, controls offered treatment afterwards. Analysis: compare mean change scores.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): plan fully meets the requirements – independent measures with allocation, self-report scale with example items/anchors, covert sensitisation described, sample, procedure, controls, ethics; replicable. Level 3 (6–8): most features with some detail. Level 2 (3–5): basic plan, some requirements missing. Level 1 (1–2): very limited.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate explanations of impulse control disorders and non-substance addiction, including a discussion about reductionism.
parts.answer: Points may include: behavioural explanation (operant conditioning, variable-ratio reinforcement) is supported by the persistence of gambling and the design of gambling machines, and leads to treatments such as imaginal desensitisation; but it cannot explain why only some people who gamble develop a disorder. Biological explanations (dopamine reward pathways, possible genetic vulnerability) are supported by the use of opioid antagonists such as naltrexone reducing urges; but correlations between brain activity and gambling do not prove cause. Feeling-state theory explains individual differences in triggers but has limited research support and relies on subjective reports. Reductionism: biological and behavioural explanations reduce complex behaviour to single factors (neurotransmitters, reinforcement) – useful for treatment but ignore social, cultural and economic influences (e.g. availability of online betting); a more holistic, interactionist view combining biology, learning and cognition may be better. Also: nature/nurture, determinism, usefulness, cultural differences.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation of at least two explanations with evidence; reductionism explicitly and effectively discussed; well organised. Level 3 (6–8): reasonable evaluation; named issue discussed. Level 2 (3–5): limited, may be mostly descriptive; named issue brief. Level 1 (1–2): basic, anecdotal.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia, giving one example of each.
parts.answer: Positive symptoms are experiences or behaviours added to normal functioning, e.g. hallucinations (hearing voices) or delusions (false beliefs such as being persecuted). Negative symptoms are a loss or reduction of normal functioning, e.g. avolition (lack of motivation), alogia (poverty of speech) or flat affect.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive = additions to normal experience. 1 mark: example. 1 mark: negative = loss/reduction of normal function. 1 mark: example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia.
parts.answer: The hypothesis states that schizophrenia is associated with abnormal dopamine activity. Excess dopamine activity, or over-sensitive/too many D2 receptors, in the mesolimbic pathway is linked to positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions. Later versions suggest low dopamine activity in the mesocortical pathway (prefrontal cortex) is linked to negative and cognitive symptoms. Evidence: drugs that increase dopamine (e.g. amphetamines) can produce psychotic-like symptoms; typical antipsychotics block D2 receptors and reduce positive symptoms; the dose of antipsychotics needed relates to how strongly they bind to D2 receptors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 points: excess dopamine; D2 receptors (sensitivity/number); mesolimbic → positive symptoms; low prefrontal dopamine → negative symptoms; amphetamine evidence; antipsychotics block D2; L-dopa evidence; revised hypothesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline Frith's cognitive explanation of schizophrenia.
parts.answer: Frith proposed that schizophrenia involves a deficit in metarepresentation – the ability to reflect on our own thoughts and intentions. A failure of self-monitoring means the person does not recognise their own inner speech or actions as self-generated, so they experience them as coming from an outside source (auditory hallucinations, delusions of control). A deficit in central control (willed action) means they cannot suppress automatic responses, producing disorganised speech and thought (e.g. derailment) and possibly negative symptoms.
parts.working: 1 mark: metarepresentation deficit. 1 mark: self-monitoring failure → hallucinations/delusions of control. 1 mark: central control deficit. 1 mark: link to disorganised speech/negative symptoms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical twin study found that 28 of 60 identical (MZ) twin pairs were concordant for schizophrenia, compared with 5 of 55 non-identical (DZ) twin pairs. Calculate the concordance rate for each type of twin, as a percentage to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what these results suggest about the nature versus nurture debate in schizophrenia.
parts.answer: The much higher concordance for MZ twins, who share all their genes, than DZ twins, who share about half, suggests a genetic (nature) influence; but because MZ concordance is far below 100 %, environmental (nurture) factors must also play a part (diathesis–stress).
parts.working: 1 mark: higher MZ concordance supports genetic influence. 1 mark: concordance < 100 % shows environment also involved.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare typical and atypical antipsychotic drugs as treatments for schizophrenia.
parts.answer: Typical antipsychotics (e.g. chlorpromazine) mainly block dopamine D2 receptors and reduce positive symptoms, but often cause extrapyramidal side effects such as tremors and, with long-term use, tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements). Atypical antipsychotics (e.g. clozapine, risperidone) act on dopamine and serotonin receptors, can help some negative symptoms and cause fewer movement side effects, but may cause weight gain, and clozapine needs regular blood tests because of the risk of agranulocytosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: typical – D2 blockade, positive symptoms. 1 mark: typical side effects. 1 mark: atypical – dopamine and serotonin, broader effect. 1 mark: atypical side effects/fewer motor effects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) has 30 items, each rated by a clinician from 1 (absent) to 7 (extreme). Seven items form the positive scale. State the lowest and highest possible scores on the positive scale and on the whole PANSS.
parts.answer: Positive scale: 7 to 49. Whole PANSS: 30 to 210.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of using a clinician-rated interview scale such as the PANSS rather than a self-report questionnaire to assess schizophrenia.
parts.answer: Strength: trained clinicians can rate symptoms that patients may lack insight into (e.g. they may not see their delusions as unusual), and a structured interview with defined anchors gives standardised, quantitative scores that can track change. Weakness: ratings depend on the clinician's judgement, so they can be subjective or biased (e.g. by expectations of a treatment), and the interview is time-consuming and requires training.
parts.working: Strength: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation (insight/standardised). Weakness: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation (subjectivity/inter-rater reliability/time).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate treatment and management of schizophrenia, including a discussion about ethics.
parts.answer: Points may include: antipsychotics are effective in reducing positive symptoms and relapse, allowing many patients to live in the community; but side effects (tardive dyskinesia, weight gain) raise ethical concerns, and patients may lack capacity to consent or be treated compulsorily. Token economies (e.g. Paul and Lentz's social-learning programme) improved self-care and social behaviour in long-stay hospital patients, but behaviour may not generalise outside the institution and withholding privileges raises ethical issues about dignity and control. CBT helps patients challenge delusional beliefs and cope with voices; it respects autonomy and has fewer side effects, but needs insight and motivation and may not suit acute patients. Ethical discussion: informed consent and capacity, right to refuse, risk–benefit balance, coercion, stigma. Also: effectiveness, generalisability, reductionism, individual differences.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced evaluation of at least two treatments with evidence; ethics thoroughly discussed. Level 3 (6–8): reasonable evaluation; ethics included. Level 2 (3–5): limited/descriptive. Level 1 (1–2): basic.

parts.label: a
