parts.text: Outline the characteristics of generalised anxiety disorder (GAD).
parts.answer: Persistent, excessive worry about many everyday events (e.g. family, health, work or money) rather than one specific trigger, lasting for months (several months, most days), and difficult to control; with symptoms such as restlessness, muscle tension, sleep problems, difficulty concentrating, irritability and autonomic overactivity (racing heart, sweating), causing distress or impairment.
parts.working: 1 mark: general, excessive worry about many things. 1 mark: persistent (months, most days) / hard to control. 1 mark: physical or other symptoms (any two).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Zara faints whenever she sees blood or has an injection, so she has avoided going to the dentist for years. Suggest how applied tension could be used to treat her.
parts.answer: Applied tension targets the drop in blood pressure that causes fainting in blood-injection-injury phobia. Zara would be taught to tense the large muscles of her arms, legs and torso for about 10–15 seconds until she feels warmth in her face, then release (without fully relaxing), repeating this several times. Once she has learned the technique, she would practise it while being gradually exposed to blood-related stimuli – e.g. pictures of blood, a video of an injection, then a real finger prick – using tension at the first sign of a drop in blood pressure, so she can stay conscious and stop avoiding the dentist.
parts.working: 1 mark: aim – raise blood pressure / prevent fainting. 1 mark: tensing large muscle groups for a few seconds. 1 mark: practice with gradual exposure to blood/injury stimuli. 1 mark: application to Zara (dentist/injections).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how classical conditioning explains the development of phobias. Refer to Watson and Rayner's study in your answer.
parts.answer: A neutral stimulus becomes associated with an unconditioned stimulus that naturally causes fear, so the neutral stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus producing a conditioned fear response. Watson and Rayner studied 'Little Albert', an 11-month-old boy who initially showed no fear of a white rat. Each time he reached for the rat, a steel bar was struck loudly with a hammer behind him (UCS), causing fear and crying (UCR). After several pairings, the rat alone (CS) caused crying and attempts to crawl away (CR). Albert's fear then generalised to similar furry objects such as a rabbit, a dog, a fur coat and a Santa Claus mask. Avoidance of the feared object is then negatively reinforced because it reduces anxiety, which maintains the phobia (two-process model).
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 of: NS paired with UCS; becomes CS producing CR (fear); Albert, 11 months, no initial fear of rat; loud noise (steel bar) as UCS; rat alone produced fear after pairings; stimulus generalisation with examples; avoidance maintained by negative reinforcement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The GAD-7 questionnaire has 7 items, each scored 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day) for the past two weeks. A client's item scores are 2, 3, 1, 2, 2, 1 and 3. Calculate the client's total score and state the severity band, given the bands: 0–4 minimal, 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–21 severe.
parts.answer: 14 – moderate anxiety.
parts.working: B1: total = 14. B1: moderate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a clinician should not diagnose GAD from the GAD-7 score alone.
parts.answer: It is a short self-report screening tool; the client may over- or under-report symptoms (e.g. social desirability or misunderstanding), and the score does not check other diagnostic features such as duration, other causes or impairment, so a clinical interview is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: self-report bias / screening only. 1 mark: explanation – need for interview to check diagnostic criteria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe systematic desensitisation as a treatment for specific phobias.
parts.answer: Based on classical conditioning and reciprocal inhibition – a person cannot feel relaxed and anxious at the same time. Step 1: the client learns deep muscle relaxation (and breathing). Step 2: the client and therapist build an anxiety hierarchy of situations involving the feared object, ranked from least to most frightening (e.g. for spiders: the word 'spider', a cartoon, a photo, a spider in a closed jar, holding a spider). Step 3: the client works up the hierarchy while relaxed, either in imagination (in vitro) or with real stimuli (in vivo), moving to the next step only when they can stay relaxed. The fear response is replaced (counter-conditioned) by relaxation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 of: classical conditioning/counter-conditioning; reciprocal inhibition; relaxation training; hierarchy built with client; example items; gradual progression only when relaxed; in vivo/in vitro; several sessions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical trial for GAD in a clinic in Karachi, 35 patients received CBT and 40 patients received medication. After 12 weeks, 14 CBT patients and 6 medication patients were classed as 'recovered'. Calculate the percentage recovered in each group.
parts.answer: CBT: 40 %; medication: 15 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why it would be wrong to conclude from these results alone that CBT is more effective than medication for GAD.
parts.answer: 1. Patients may not have been randomly allocated – e.g. those with milder anxiety or more motivation may have chosen CBT, so participant variables could explain the difference. 2. The measure of 'recovered' may have been made by clinicians who knew which treatment each patient received (no blinding), introducing bias; also the follow-up was short (12 weeks) and the groups were small, so long-term effectiveness is unknown.
parts.working: For each reason: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation linked to the trial.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the nature versus nurture debate, and explain one reason why explanations of anxiety and fear-related disorders can be seen as supporting nurture.
parts.answer: The nature–nurture debate concerns whether behaviour is mainly caused by inherited, biological factors (nature) or by experiences and the environment (nurture). Explanations of phobias such as classical conditioning support nurture because fear is learned through experiences: Little Albert's fear of the rat was created by pairing it with a loud noise, and fears can be learned by observing others (social learning). However, some fears (e.g. of snakes) may be easier to acquire because of evolved preparedness, which supports nature.
parts.working: 2 marks: outline of the debate (nature = genes/biology; nurture = environment/experience). 2 marks: reason supporting nurture explained with example (conditioning/modelling).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between obsessions and compulsions, giving an example of each.
parts.answer: Obsessions are persistent, intrusive and unwanted thoughts, images or urges that cause anxiety, e.g. a recurring thought that one's hands are contaminated with germs. Compulsions are repetitive behaviours or mental acts that a person feels driven to perform to reduce the anxiety caused by obsessions, e.g. washing hands many times in a particular way, or checking the door is locked again and again.
parts.working: 1 mark: obsessions defined. 1 mark: example. 1 mark: compulsions defined (reduce anxiety). 1 mark: example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) has 10 items: 5 about obsessions and 5 about compulsions, each scored 0 to 4. A patient's obsession item scores are 3, 3, 2, 4 and 3, and the compulsion item scores are 3, 4, 2, 3 and 3. Calculate the obsession subtotal, the compulsion subtotal and the total score, and state the severity band (0–7 subclinical, 8–15 mild, 16–23 moderate, 24–31 severe, 32–40 extreme).
parts.answer: Obsessions 15, compulsions 15, total 30 – severe.
parts.working: B1: 15 and 15. B1: total 30. B1: severe.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of using the Y-BOCS to measure OCD.
parts.answer: It is administered by a trained clinician in a semi-structured interview, so ratings are standardised and give a quantitative score; this allows the severity of different patients to be compared and changes during treatment to be measured.
parts.working: 1 mark: standardised/quantitative/clinician-administered. 1 mark: allows comparison or measurement of progress.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ahmed checks the gas stove up to 30 times before leaving home, because he fears that if the house burns down it will be his fault. Suggest how exposure and response prevention (ERP) could be used to treat Ahmed.
parts.answer: The therapist and Ahmed build a hierarchy of situations that make him anxious about the stove, from leaving after checking 10 times up to leaving the house after not checking at all. He is exposed to each situation (e.g. turning the stove off once and walking away) and prevented from carrying out the compulsion (checking again). He stays with the anxiety until it falls (habituation), learning that the feared disaster does not happen. He moves up the hierarchy over sessions and practises as homework.
parts.working: 1 mark: hierarchy. 1 mark: exposure to anxiety-provoking situation. 1 mark: response prevention – not checking. 1 mark: habituation/learning feared outcome does not occur, linked to Ahmed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Lovell et al. compared CBT (exposure and response prevention) for OCD delivered by telephone with the same treatment delivered face to face. Explain one strength and one weakness of delivering therapy by telephone, using evidence from this study.
parts.answer: Strength: Lovell et al. found telephone-delivered ERP was about as effective as face-to-face treatment in reducing OCD symptoms (measured with the Y-BOCS), while saving travel time and costs and making treatment accessible to people who live far away or find it hard to leave home. Weakness: the therapist cannot see the patient's body language or carry out exposure exercises together in person, and some patients may feel less supported, so it may not suit everyone (e.g. those with severe symptoms).
parts.working: Strength: 1 mark identification, 1 mark linked to Lovell's finding of equivalence/accessibility. Weakness: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate explanations of obsessive-compulsive disorder, including a discussion about determinism.
parts.answer: Biological: low serotonin activity is supported by the effectiveness of SSRIs in reducing symptoms; family and twin evidence suggests a genetic component; but SSRIs do not help everyone and correlation does not show cause. Cognitive (e.g. Salkovskis's inflated responsibility): intrusive thoughts are normal, but people with OCD interpret them as meaningful and feel responsible for preventing harm, leading to neutralising compulsions; supported by the success of CBT/ERP, but it is unclear whether faulty thinking causes OCD or results from it. Behavioural: compulsions maintained by negative reinforcement (anxiety reduction). Determinism: biological explanations are hard-determinist (genes/neurotransmitters cause OCD), which may reduce blame but suggests the patient has little control; cognitive explanations are softer – patients can learn to change their thoughts – which supports therapy and personal responsibility. Also: reductionism, nature/nurture, usefulness.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): detailed, balanced evaluation of at least two explanations with evidence; determinism explicitly discussed. Level 3 (6–8): reasonable evaluation; determinism included. Level 2 (3–5): limited/descriptive. Level 1 (1–2): basic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between a depressive disorder and bipolar disorder.
parts.answer: Depressive disorder involves episodes of low mood and/or loss of interest only. Bipolar disorder involves episodes of mania or hypomania (elevated or irritable mood, increased energy, reduced need for sleep), usually alternating with depressive episodes.
parts.working: 1 mark: depression – low mood/loss of interest only. 1 mark: bipolar – manic/hypomanic episodes (often with depression).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe Beck's cognitive triad.
parts.answer: Beck proposed that depressed people have three types of negative automatic thoughts: a negative view of the self (e.g. 'I am worthless'), a negative view of the world/experiences (e.g. 'everyone is against me') and a negative view of the future (e.g. 'things will never get better').
parts.working: 1 mark each for self, world and future (with example or explanation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) has 21 items, each scored 0 to 3. State the maximum possible score.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A patient's item scores add up to 22. Using the bands 0–13 minimal, 14–19 mild, 20–28 moderate and 29–63 severe, state the patient's level of depression.
parts.answer: Moderate depression.
parts.working: B1: moderate (22 lies in 20–28).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one weakness of the BDI as a measure of depression.
parts.answer: It is a self-report questionnaire, so patients may exaggerate or minimise symptoms (e.g. social desirability, or stigma about mental illness), and it only covers the last two weeks, so scores may not be valid.
parts.working: 1 mark: self-report bias / snapshot of two weeks. 1 mark: explanation of effect on validity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mehreen has felt low for months since failing her university entrance exam. She now believes she is a failure at everything and refuses to apply for any course. Suggest how cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) could help her.
parts.answer: The therapist would help Mehreen identify her negative automatic thoughts (e.g. 'I fail at everything') and challenge them by looking for evidence against them, such as subjects she has done well in (reality testing). She would learn to replace them with more balanced thoughts ('I failed one exam, but I can prepare differently'). Behavioural tasks such as scheduling enjoyable activities and taking small steps towards applying to a course would provide evidence of success and improve mood. Homework such as a thought diary would help her practise between sessions.
parts.working: 1 mark: identify negative thoughts. 1 mark: challenge/dispute with evidence. 1 mark: behavioural activation/homework. 1 mark: application to Mehreen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the biological (biochemical) treatment of mood disorders, including a discussion about individual differences.
parts.answer: Antidepressants such as SSRIs increase the availability of serotonin in the synapse; many patients improve, they are relatively cheap and easy to take, and they can be combined with therapy. Weaknesses: they take several weeks to work; side effects (e.g. nausea, sleep problems) can lead to stopping treatment; relapse is common when they are stopped; some trials suggest only small advantages over placebo for mild depression; they treat symptoms rather than causes such as negative thinking or life events. Mood stabilisers (e.g. lithium) are used for bipolar disorder but need blood monitoring. Individual differences: patients respond very differently – some need several drugs before one works, genetics and severity affect response, and some prefer psychological therapy; a nomothetic, one-size approach may not suit everyone, so combining medication with CBT tailored to the person may be best. Also: reductionism, ethics, comparison with CBT.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, detailed evaluation with evidence; individual differences explicitly discussed. Level 3 (6–8): reasonable evaluation; named issue included. Level 2 (3–5): limited/descriptive. Level 1 (1–2): basic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how participants in Dement and Kleitman's study were woken during the night and how they reported their dreams.
parts.answer: A doorbell rang near the bed to wake the participant. The participant then spoke into a tape recorder beside the bed, saying whether they had been dreaming and, if so, describing the content of the dream. There was no direct contact with the experimenter, who later came in to ask questions if needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: doorbell used to wake; spoke into a recorder by the bed; reported whether dreaming and the dream content; no contact with the experimenter while reporting (experimenter could enter afterwards to question).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify two things participants were asked to avoid on the day of the study, and explain why.
parts.answer: They avoided caffeine (e.g. coffee) and alcohol, because these drugs affect sleep and could change the sleep stages being measured (a control for extraneous variables).
parts.working: 1 mark for both caffeine and alcohol; 1 mark for the reason (they affect sleep patterns / would be confounding variables).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how the EEG was used to measure sleep in Dement and Kleitman's study.
parts.answer: Electrodes were attached to the scalp to record brain activity (to identify the stage of sleep) and near the eyes to record eye movements, so that REM and NREM sleep could be identified objectively.
parts.working: 1 mark: electrodes on scalp record brain waves/sleep stage; 1 mark: electrodes near the eyes record eye movements to identify REM.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of using the EEG as a measure in this study.
parts.answer: The EEG gives objective, quantitative data: whether a participant was in REM or NREM sleep when woken did not depend on the participant's or researcher's opinion, so the classification was reliable and could be repeated.
parts.working: 1 mark for identifying a strength (objective / quantitative / reliable / not open to demand characteristics); 1 mark for linking it to identifying REM vs NREM at the point of waking.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using the EEG as a measure in this study.
parts.answer: Participants slept with electrodes attached in an unfamiliar laboratory, which may have changed how they slept, so sleep and dreaming may not reflect normal sleep at home (low ecological validity).
parts.working: 1 mark for the weakness (equipment is unnatural / uncomfortable / may disturb sleep); 1 mark for the effect on the validity of the sleep or dream data in this study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the part of Dement and Kleitman's study that tested whether participants could judge how long they had been dreaming.
parts.answer: Participants were woken either 5 minutes or 15 minutes after the start of a REM period. They were asked to say whether they had been dreaming for 5 or 15 minutes. Their choice was compared with the actual REM duration; they were correct most of the time, which suggests dream time is related to real time.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: woken after 5 or 15 min of REM; asked to choose 5 or 15 min; choice compared with actual REM time; most estimates correct / a forced choice of two options.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why giving participants only two options (5 or 15 minutes) may be a weakness.
parts.answer: With only two choices a participant has a 50 % chance of being right by guessing, so some correct answers may not reflect real awareness of dream length.
parts.working: 1 mark: guessing / 50 % chance; 1 mark: so accuracy may be overestimated / data less valid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how Dement and Kleitman investigated the link between the direction of eye movements in REM sleep and dream content.
parts.answer: Participants were woken after a clear pattern of eye movements had been recorded – mainly vertical, mainly horizontal, both, or very little movement – and asked to describe their dream. The dream content was then compared with the pattern of eye movements.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: EEG/EOG recorded the direction of eye movements; woken after a distinct pattern (vertical / horizontal / mixed / little movement); asked to describe dream; content compared with the pattern.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a dream report that matched a pattern of eye movements.
parts.answer: Mainly vertical movements – a dream of climbing up a series of ladders and looking up and down (or: horizontal movements – watching two people throwing tomatoes at each other).
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct matched example (vertical: looking up/down e.g. climbing ladders, looking up at cliffs; horizontal: two people throwing tomatoes at each other).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this part of the study gives only limited support for the idea that eye movements reflect what the dreamer is 'looking at'.
parts.answer: Only a small number of awakenings showed a clear single pattern and the dream report relied on self-report, which may be incomplete or influenced by what participants thought was expected; so the link is based on few, subjective cases.
parts.working: 1 mark: few clear-pattern awakenings / small sample; 1 mark: dream reports are subjective / could be affected by demand characteristics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Dement and Kleitman's study of sleep and dreams, including a discussion of ecological validity.
parts.answer: Strengths could include: objective EEG measurement of REM/NREM; standardised procedure (same doorbell, recorder, instructions) giving reliability; controls such as no caffeine/alcohol; quantitative data allowing comparison of dream recall in REM vs NREM. Weaknesses could include: low ecological validity (sleeping in a laboratory with electrodes, woken repeatedly, so sleep may not be natural); small sample of nine adults limits generalisability; dream recall is self-reported and may be affected by demand characteristics; individual differences in recall.
parts.working: Mark points (any 4, developed and linked to the study): ecological validity – lab setting, electrodes, being woken by a doorbell are unlike normal sleep (weakness) although participants slept at night at their normal bedtime (partial strength); EEG objective; standardisation/reliability; controls (caffeine, alcohol); quantitative data; small sample; self-report dreams subjective; ethics (sleep disturbed but participants consented). Level 4 (9–10): two developed strengths and two developed weaknesses, the named issue included, all clearly linked to the study, good range. Level 3 (6–8): evaluation is mostly developed and linked; the named issue is present. Level 2 (3–5): limited range or mostly undeveloped points; the named issue may be missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief, general or muddled points. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ayesha tells her friend, 'I never dream. I sleep the whole night and remember nothing.' Using the findings of Dement and Kleitman, explain what her friend could tell her.
parts.answer: Dement and Kleitman found that dreaming occurs mainly in REM sleep, which happens several times each night, and that people woken during REM usually reported dreams. People woken in NREM, or later on, rarely remembered dreams. So Ayesha probably does dream but forgets her dreams because she wakes from NREM sleep or some time after a REM period.
parts.working: 1 mark: dreams mainly linked to REM sleep; 1 mark: REM occurs regularly (several times) every night; 1 mark: recall is much lower when woken outside REM / dreams are forgotten, so she probably does dream.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Dement and Kleitman's study can be used in the debate about individual and situational explanations of behaviour.
parts.answer: Individual explanations say behaviour comes from factors within the person (biology, personality); situational explanations say it comes from the environment. The regular REM cycles found in all participants suggest dreaming is an internal biological process (individual). However, dream recall depended on the situation – whether the person was woken during REM or NREM, and how soon – which supports a situational influence on what is reported.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of individual explanation; 1 mark: definition of situational explanation; 1 mark: individual example from the study (REM cycles / biological rhythm within each person, or differences between participants in recall); 1 mark: situational example (timing of the doorbell awakening affected recall).

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the participants in Hölzel et al.'s study of mindfulness and brain structure.
parts.answer: Healthy adult volunteers with no previous meditation experience who were planning to take a Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) course; about 16 took the course (experimental group) and about 17 formed a waiting-list control group.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 2: healthy adults; no previous meditation experience (meditation-naive); volunteers recruited from people planning to join MBSR courses; small groups of about 16–17 each (MBSR and waiting-list control); right-handed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using volunteers who had chosen to take a mindfulness course.
parts.answer: They were motivated and expected the course to help them, so they may have practised more and changed their lifestyle in other ways; the results may not generalise to people who are not interested in mindfulness.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness (motivation/expectations, volunteer bias, not representative); 1 mark: linked to the study (e.g. may not generalise to unmotivated people, or expectations rather than mindfulness may explain changes).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Hölzel et al. used participants who had no previous experience of meditation.
parts.answer: If participants had meditated before, their brains might already have been changed by meditation, so the baseline scan would not be a true starting point; using beginners means any change after eight weeks can be linked to the MBSR programme.
parts.working: 1 mark: earlier meditation could already have affected grey matter / acts as a confounding variable; 1 mark: so changes can be attributed to the eight-week programme.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one ethical reason why the control group was offered the MBSR course after the study ended.
parts.answer: The control group had also wanted to reduce stress; offering them the course afterwards meant they were not denied a potentially beneficial programme just because they took part in the research (fair treatment / protection from harm).
parts.working: 1 mark: control participants should not lose out on a benefit; 1 mark: linked to fairness/protection of participants who also wanted the course.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one result from Hassett et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Male monkeys interacted much more with wheeled toys than with plush toys, whereas female monkeys interacted with both kinds of toy and showed a much weaker preference.
parts.working: 1 mark: male preference for wheeled toys; 1 mark: females interacted with both / weaker or more varied preference.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one conclusion from the study and explain how it differs from a result.
parts.answer: Conclusion: sex differences in toy preference can develop without human gender socialisation, so biological factors (e.g. hormones) may contribute to boys' and girls' toy choices. A result is what was actually measured in this group of monkeys; a conclusion is the general claim drawn from it.
parts.working: 1 mark: appropriate conclusion (biological/hormonal influence on sex differences in toy preference, independent of human socialisation); 1 mark: result = data found in this study, conclusion = general statement drawn from it.

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one ethical issue that the researchers had to consider when scanning participants with MRI in Hölzel et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Protection from harm: lying in a narrow, noisy scanner can cause anxiety (especially for people with claustrophobia), and people with metal implants could be harmed, so participants had to be screened and told they could stop the scan at any time.
parts.working: 1 mark: named issue (protection from harm/distress, screening for metal, right to withdraw, confidentiality of brain scans); 1 mark: linked to MRI scanning in this study.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why MRI scanning is usually considered an ethically acceptable measure.
parts.answer: MRI is non-invasive: it uses a magnetic field and radio waves rather than radiation or surgery, so a scan before and after the course causes no lasting harm.
parts.working: 1 mark: non-invasive / no radiation / no injections; 1 mark: so repeated scanning carries little risk to participants.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Hölzel et al.'s study of mindfulness and brain scans, including a discussion of validity.
parts.answer: Strengths: MRI gives an objective, quantitative measure of grey matter that participants cannot fake; scans before and after plus a waiting-list control group mean changes are unlikely to be due to time or repeated scanning (internal validity); the mindfulness questionnaire showed the programme really changed mindfulness; the standardised MBSR course can be replicated. Weaknesses (validity): there was no active control group (e.g. a relaxation class), so changes could be due to expectations, social contact or general stress reduction rather than mindfulness itself; home practice was self-reported; small samples of volunteers who wanted the course limit generalisability; increased grey matter concentration does not directly show better memory or emotion regulation.
parts.working: Mark points (any 4, developed and linked): validity – control group and pre/post scans (strength); no active control / expectations / social support as confounds (weakness); construct validity of the mindfulness questionnaire; self-reported practice; objective MRI; standardisation/replicability; small, motivated volunteer sample; usefulness of findings. Level 4 (9–10): two developed strengths and two developed weaknesses, the named issue included, all clearly linked to the study, good range. Level 3 (6–8): evaluation is mostly developed and linked; the named issue is present. Level 2 (3–5): limited range or mostly undeveloped points; the named issue may be missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief, general or muddled points. 0: no creditworthy response.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one similarity and one difference between Hölzel et al.'s study and Dement and Kleitman's study.
parts.answer: Similarity: both used a physiological measure of the brain alongside self-report – Hölzel et al. used MRI scans of grey matter together with a mindfulness questionnaire; Dement and Kleitman used the EEG (and eye-movement recordings) together with dream reports spoken into a recorder – so both combined objective and subjective data. Difference: Hölzel et al. measured brain structure (grey matter) before and after an eight-week programme and compared an experimental group with a waiting-list control group, whereas Dement and Kleitman measured brain activity during single nights in the laboratory and had no control group (participants were compared across REM and NREM awakenings).
parts.working: Similarity (4 marks): 1 identify; 1–2 for description in each study with detail; 1 for comparison/link. Difference (4 marks): same structure. Accept other valid points: both small samples; both biological approach; both quantitative data; structure vs activity; longitudinal over 8 weeks vs overnight recordings; control group vs repeated measures.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Hassett et al.'s study supports one assumption of the biological approach.
parts.answer: The biological approach assumes behaviour is influenced by genes, hormones and evolution. Male rhesus monkeys, which have no human gender stereotypes, preferred wheeled toys as boys do, suggesting the sex difference has a biological (e.g. hormonal or evolutionary) basis.
parts.working: 1 mark: assumption (behaviour influenced by genes/hormones/evolution, shared with other species); 1 mark: link to male monkeys' preference for wheeled toys without socialisation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one everyday application of Hassett et al.'s findings.
parts.answer: Parents and teachers could offer children a wide range of toys without pressure and not assume that a preference is only the result of upbringing, since some differences in preference may be partly biological.
parts.working: 1 mark: plausible application (parenting, education, toy design/marketing, debates on gender-neutral toys); 1 mark: justified by the finding that preferences appear without human socialisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why Hassett et al. studied monkeys rather than human children.
parts.answer: Children learn from parents, peers and the media which toys are 'for boys' or 'for girls', so their preferences may be caused by socialisation; monkeys do not experience human gender stereotypes about toys, so any sex difference is more likely to be biological.
parts.working: 1 mark: children are affected by gender socialisation; 1 mark: monkeys lack this, so the effect of biology can be separated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why rhesus monkeys were a suitable species for this research.
parts.answer: They are closely related to humans and show similar hormone-linked sex differences in behaviour (e.g. young males do more rough-and-tumble play).
parts.working: 1 mark: close evolutionary relatives / similar hormonal sex differences / similar sex differences in play / live in social groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the background to Hassett et al.'s study of toy preferences in monkeys.
parts.answer: Boys and girls show clear differences in toy choice (e.g. boys choose vehicles, girls choose dolls). It is debated whether this is caused by socialisation or by biology. Girls exposed to high levels of male hormones before birth (congenital adrenal hyperplasia) tend to play more with boys' toys, suggesting a hormonal influence. An earlier study found that male vervet monkeys spent more time with 'masculine' toys and females with 'feminine' toys. Hassett et al. aimed to see whether rhesus monkeys show similar sex differences with wheeled and plush toys.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: sex differences in children's toy choice; nature vs socialisation debate; hormonal evidence (e.g. CAH girls prefer male-typical toys); earlier vervet monkey study found similar sex differences; aim – test whether rhesus monkeys show sex differences in preference for wheeled vs plush toys.

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hölzel et al. used the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire. Name two of the facets of mindfulness it measures.
parts.answer: Any two of: observing; describing; acting with awareness; non-judging of inner experience; non-reactivity to inner experience.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct facets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why participants in the MBSR group were asked to record how much time they spent practising at home.
parts.answer: To check that they actually carried out the daily practice (the programme was followed as planned), and so the amount of practice could be related to changes in mindfulness or grey matter.
parts.working: 1 mark: checks adherence / that the IV was carried out; 1 mark: allows amount of practice to be compared with the outcome measures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one problem with these practice records.
parts.answer: They were self-reported, so participants may have overestimated their practice to look committed (social desirability).
parts.working: 1 mark: self-report inaccuracy / social desirability / forgetting.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of awakenings that produced a dream report in each condition. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether these results are consistent with Dement and Kleitman's findings. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Yes – like Dement and Kleitman, dreams were reported far more often after REM awakenings than after NREM awakenings.
parts.working: 1 mark: consistent, because dream recall was much higher in REM than in NREM.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a few dream reports were given after NREM awakenings.
parts.answer: The participant may have been woken soon after a REM period had ended, so a recent dream could still be recalled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one similarity and one difference between Hassett et al.'s study and Hölzel et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Similarity: both collected quantitative data – Hassett et al. recorded the frequency and duration of each monkey's interactions with wheeled and plush toys; Hölzel et al. measured grey matter concentration from MRI scans and mindfulness scores on a questionnaire – so both allowed statistical comparison between groups. Difference: Hassett et al. studied animals (rhesus monkeys) in their social group by observation, whereas Hölzel et al. studied human volunteers in an experiment with scans before and after an eight-week mindfulness course and a waiting-list control group.
parts.working: Similarity (4 marks): 1 identify; 1–2 for description in each study with detail; 1 for comparison/link. Difference (4 marks): same structure. Accept other valid points: both biological approach; both compare groups (males/females; MBSR/control); animals vs humans; observation vs experiment; natural group setting vs laboratory scanner; self-report used only by Hölzel.

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Hölzel et al.'s findings relate to the nature versus nurture debate.
parts.answer: Nature is the view that behaviour and brain structure are determined by inherited biology; nurture is the view that they are shaped by experience and the environment. Hölzel et al. found that eight weeks of mindfulness practice (an experience) were followed by increases in grey matter in areas such as the hippocampus, which suggests the adult brain can be changed by nurture (neuroplasticity). However, the brain is a biological organ and people may differ biologically in how much it can change, so the findings show nature and nurture interacting.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of nature/nurture; 1 mark: mindfulness practice as an environmental/learning experience (nurture); 1 mark: brain structure changed (grey matter increase / neuroplasticity); 1 mark: conclusion that biology and experience interact.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the species of animal used by Hassett et al. in their study of toy preferences.
parts.answer: Rhesus monkeys.
parts.working: 1 mark: rhesus monkeys (accept rhesus macaques).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the two types of toy used in the study.
parts.answer: Wheeled toys (seen as stereotypically 'masculine'), such as a wagon or a truck, and plush toys (seen as stereotypically 'feminine'), such as soft stuffed toys.
parts.working: 1 mark: wheeled toys with an example/description; 1 mark: plush (soft) toys with an example/description.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the monkeys' behaviour with the toys was recorded in Hassett et al.'s study.
parts.answer: A wheeled toy and a plush toy were placed together in the group's outdoor enclosure for a fixed trial period. Sessions were video-recorded and the recordings were coded for each monkey's interactions with each toy, giving the frequency and the duration of interaction.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: one wheeled and one plush toy presented at the same time; in the monkeys' home enclosure / social group; video-recorded; coded for frequency and duration of contact with each type of toy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one finding about the male monkeys.
parts.answer: Male monkeys interacted with the wheeled toys much more than with the plush toys.
parts.working: 1 mark: males showed a clear preference for wheeled toys.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Outline one finding about the female monkeys.
parts.answer: Female monkeys interacted with both types of toy and showed a much weaker (more varied) preference than the males.
parts.working: 1 mark: females played with both / no strong preference compared with males.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how Hassett et al.'s study contributes to the nature versus nurture debate about sex differences in toy preferences.
parts.answer: The nurture view says children choose sex-typed toys because of social learning, e.g. parents and media. Monkeys do not experience human gender stereotypes about trucks and dolls, yet male monkeys preferred wheeled toys, like boys do. This suggests a biological (nature) influence, such as prenatal hormones, on toy preference. However, the monkeys lived in social groups, so some learning cannot be ruled out.
parts.working: 1 mark: nature/nurture defined; 1 mark: monkeys lack human socialisation about toys; 1 mark: male preference for wheeled toys mirrors boys → biological factors; 1 mark: development/caveat (pattern in females less clear, or social influences in groups, or similarity to human data shows evolutionary basis).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength of observing the monkeys in their usual social group rather than alone in a cage.
parts.answer: The monkeys behaved in a natural social setting with their own group, so their choice of toys is more likely to reflect normal behaviour (higher ecological validity) and they were less stressed.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies natural setting/ecological validity or animal welfare; 1 mark: explanation linked to the study.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difficulty in generalising Hassett et al.'s findings to human children.
parts.answer: Monkeys differ from humans in brain development, cognition and culture; children's toy play involves pretend play and social meaning that monkeys do not have, so the reasons behind the preferences may differ.
parts.working: 1 mark: species differences; 1 mark: explained with a relevant example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Hassett et al.'s study of monkey toy preferences, including a discussion of the use of animals in psychological research.
parts.answer: Strengths: avoids the human gender socialisation that makes child studies hard to interpret; non-invasive observation in the monkeys' normal social groups (good welfare and ecological validity); video recording allows coding to be checked for inter-rater reliability; quantitative frequency and duration data allow comparisons between sexes. Weaknesses: generalising from monkeys to humans is limited; the classification of toys as masculine/feminine is based on human stereotypes; individual differences such as rank or age could influence access to toys; findings for females were less clear-cut.
parts.working: Mark points (any 4, developed): use of animals (the named issue) – ethical (non-invasive, natural groups, welfare guidelines) and generalisation problems; ecological validity; reliability of video coding; quantitative data; confounds such as social rank; toy categories based on human views. Level 4 (9–10): two developed strengths and two developed weaknesses, the named issue included, all clearly linked to the study, good range. Level 3 (6–8): evaluation is mostly developed and linked; the named issue is present. Level 2 (3–5): limited range or mostly undeveloped points; the named issue may be missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief, general or muddled points. 0: no creditworthy response.

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the programme that the experimental group took part in during Hölzel et al.'s study.
parts.answer: The Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) programme.
parts.working: 1 mark: MBSR / mindfulness-based stress reduction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline what this programme involved.
parts.answer: An eight-week course with weekly group meetings and a one-day retreat, teaching mindfulness exercises such as body scan, sitting meditation and mindful yoga; participants were also asked to practise at home every day using audio recordings and to record their practice.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: eight weeks; weekly group sessions; one-day retreat; mindfulness exercises (body scan / meditation / yoga); daily home practice with recordings; logged home practice.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Hölzel et al. scanned participants' brains both before and after the programme.
parts.answer: To measure change in grey matter within each participant: the scan before gave a baseline, so any difference afterwards could be attributed to the eight-week programme rather than pre-existing brain differences.
parts.working: 1 mark: baseline / comparison within participants; 1 mark: shows the change was due to the programme (not prior differences).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the study included a control group who did not do the programme until later (a waiting list).
parts.answer: The control group were scanned at the same times; if their brains did not change, changes in the MBSR group could not be due to time passing or repeated scanning, strengthening the causal conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark: comparison/control for time or repeated testing; 1 mark: so changes can be attributed to mindfulness.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one finding from Hölzel et al.'s study.
parts.answer: The MBSR group showed an increase in grey matter concentration in the left hippocampus (also in areas such as the posterior cingulate cortex, temporo-parietal junction and cerebellum) that was not found in the control group.
parts.working: 1 mark: increase in grey matter concentration in the hippocampus or another named region in the MBSR group (not in controls).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hölzel et al. used a self-report questionnaire measuring mindfulness alongside MRI scans. Explain one strength and one weakness of using the self-report measure.
parts.answer: Strength: it measures participants' own experience of mindfulness (e.g. observing, acting with awareness), giving data the scan cannot provide and allowing a check that the programme actually changed mindfulness. Weakness: participants who had committed to an eight-week course might report more mindfulness to please the researchers or justify their effort (social desirability/demand characteristics).
parts.working: 2 marks for strength (identify + link); 2 marks for weakness (identify + link).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Imran works in a busy call centre in Karachi and feels stressed. Using Hölzel et al.'s study, suggest advice that could be given to him.
parts.answer: He could join an eight-week mindfulness course like MBSR, attending weekly sessions and practising at home daily (e.g. body scan or sitting meditation with an audio recording). Hölzel et al. found that this kind of programme was linked to increased grey matter in brain regions involved in learning, memory and emotion regulation, which may help him cope with stress.
parts.working: 1 mark: suggests a mindfulness programme/practice; 1 mark: specific details (weekly sessions, daily home practice, named exercises); 1 mark: justified by the finding about grey matter changes / emotion regulation.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two students disagree. Zara says Hölzel et al.'s study shows that mindfulness causes brain changes. Bilal says it cannot show this. Explain one argument for each view.
parts.answer: Zara: the study used a longitudinal design with scans before and after and a control group; grey matter increased only in the MBSR group, so the programme was the likely cause. Bilal: participants were volunteers who wanted to reduce stress; other changes during eight weeks (e.g. reduced stress, lifestyle, expectations, group social support) could explain the grey matter difference, and the sample was small.
parts.working: 2 marks for Zara's argument (before/after + control group; change only in MBSR group); 2 marks for Bilal's (confounding variables such as motivation, social contact, lifestyle; small sample; volunteers).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A hypothetical study in a Lahore college tested whether background music affects revision. Students learned a list of 30 words either with pop music playing or in silence and then recalled as many words as possible.
Condition | Mean number of words recalled
Music | 14.2
Silence | 17.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of graph that should be used to display the results in the table. Give one reason for your choice.
parts.answer: A bar chart, because the IV (music or silence) is made of separate categories, and the bars show the mean for each condition.
parts.working: 1 mark: bar chart; 1 mark: reason – discrete/categorical conditions (bars do not touch) / comparing two means.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable title, a label for the x-axis and a label for the y-axis for this graph.
parts.answer: Title: 'Mean number of words recalled when revising with music and in silence'. x-axis: 'Condition (music or silence)'. y-axis: 'Mean number of words recalled (out of 30)'.
parts.working: 1 mark each: title mentioning both variables; x-axis = conditions of the IV; y-axis = mean words recalled (must say 'mean').

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the two means.
parts.answer: 3.4 words

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A hypothetical correlational study recorded the average daily screen time and average nightly sleep of eight teenagers in Islamabad.
Teenager | Screen time (hours) | Sleep (hours)
A | 1 | 8.5
B | 2 | 8.0
C | 3 | 7.6
D | 4 | 7.4
E | 5 | 6.8
F | 6 | 6.9
G | 7 | 6.1
H | 8 | 5.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of graph that should be used to display these data.
parts.answer: A scatter graph (scattergram).
parts.working: 1 mark: scatter graph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two features your graph should have.
parts.answer: Daily screen time (hours) on one axis and sleep duration (hours) on the other, both labelled with units; each teenager plotted as a single point (no lines joining the points); a title stating both co-variables.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: both axes labelled with co-variables and units; points plotted not joined; suitable title; sensible scales starting from a stated value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of correlation shown by the data and explain what it means here.
parts.answer: A (strong) negative correlation: the more hours of screen time a teenager has, the fewer hours they sleep.
parts.working: 1 mark: negative (strong); 1 mark: interpretation in context.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why these data do not show that screen time causes less sleep.
parts.answer: A correlation only shows that two variables change together. A third variable, such as exam stress or a late bedtime routine, might increase screen use and reduce sleep, or poor sleep could lead to more screen use.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation ≠ causation / no manipulation of variables; 1 mark: example of a third variable or reverse direction.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Reaction times (in milliseconds) of drivers in a hypothetical simulator study were grouped as follows.
Reaction time (ms) | Frequency
200–249 | 3
250–299 | 7
300–349 | 12
350–399 | 9
400–449 | 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one difference between a bar chart and a histogram.
parts.answer: A bar chart shows separate categories (or means of conditions), so the bars have gaps between them; a histogram shows continuous data split into class intervals, so the bars touch and the x-axis is a continuous scale.
parts.working: 1 mark: bar chart = discrete categories, gaps; 1 mark: histogram = continuous data, bars touch / frequency on y-axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which type of graph is suitable for the reaction-time data in the table.
parts.answer: A histogram.
parts.working: 1 mark: histogram (data are continuous and grouped into intervals).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the modal class.
parts.working: 1 mark: 300–349 ms (frequency 12).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the number of participants in the study.
parts.answer: 35 participants

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a hypothetical field experiment in a Karachi shopping mall, a confederate dropped a pile of papers near 80 passers-by. For 50 passers-by the confederate was smartly dressed and for 30 scruffily dressed. 35 people helped the smartly dressed confederate and 12 helped the scruffily dressed confederate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of people who helped in each condition.
parts.answer: Smartly dressed: 70 %; scruffily dressed: 40 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Draw a results table to summarise these findings. Your table should show the number and percentage of people who helped and did not help in each condition (describe the rows and columns in words).
parts.answer: Rows: smartly dressed; scruffily dressed. Columns: number who helped | number who did not help | % who helped. Smart: 35 | 15 | 70 %. Scruffy: 12 | 18 | 40 %. Title: 'Number and percentage of passers-by who helped a person who dropped papers, by how the person was dressed'.
parts.working: 1 mark: rows/columns correctly organised by condition; 1 mark: helped and not-helped numbers correct (35/15, 12/18); 1 mark: percentages correct; 1 mark: informative title / headings with units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why percentages are more useful than raw numbers for comparing the two conditions in this study.
parts.answer: The conditions had different numbers of passers-by (50 and 30), so raw numbers of helpers cannot be compared directly; percentages put both on the same base (out of 100), so the comparison is fair.
parts.working: 1 mark: common base / standardised; 1 mark: allows fair comparison between unequal groups.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A hypothetical time-sampling observation of children's play at break time in an Islamabad primary school recorded the following behaviour categories.
Behaviour | Frequency
Running | 18
Chasing | 12
Sitting and talking | 24
Ball games | 30
Playing alone | 6
Give percentages correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of observations recorded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of observations that were ball games.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how these data should be displayed as a graph.
parts.answer: A bar chart with the five behaviour categories along the x-axis, with gaps between bars, and the frequency (number of observations) on the y-axis starting from zero; with a title such as 'Frequency of play behaviours observed during break time'.
parts.working: 1 mark: bar chart; 1 mark: categories on x-axis with separated bars; 1 mark: frequency on labelled y-axis from 0 / suitable title.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In a hypothetical study, patients attending a support group in Peshawar rated their anxiety each week on a scale from 0 (no anxiety) to 10 (extreme anxiety).
Week | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
Mean rating | 7.5 | 6.1 | 5.3 | 4.7 | 4.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name a type of graph that could show the change in anxiety ratings across the five weeks.
parts.answer: A line graph (accept a bar chart of the weekly means).
parts.working: 1 mark: line graph (time on x-axis); accept bar chart.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the trend shown in the data.
parts.answer: Mean anxiety fell each week, from 7.5 in week 1 to 4.2 in week 5, with the biggest drop between weeks 1 and 2 (1.4 points) and smaller drops later.
parts.working: 1 mark: anxiety decreased across weeks; 1 mark: use of data (start/end values or largest fall early).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in mean anxiety rating from week 1 to week 5. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Sana drew a bar chart of the mean test scores (out of 100) of students who revised on paper (mean 52) or on a tablet (mean 56). Her y-axis begins at 40 and has no label. The two bars touch each other and the graph has no title.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three problems with Sana's graph.
parts.answer: 1) The y-axis starts at 40, not 0, so the difference between the two conditions looks far larger than it is. 2) The y-axis has no label, so it is not clear that it shows mean scores out of 100. 3) The bars touch, which wrongly suggests continuous data, and there is no title.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: truncated y-axis exaggerates the difference; missing y-axis label/units; bars touching for categorical data; no title; x-axis categories not named.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the problem with the y-axis could mislead a reader.
parts.answer: The means of 52 and 56 differ by only 4 marks, but starting the axis at 40 makes one bar look about 1.3 times taller in relation to the axis (12 vs 16 units above 40), so a reader may think the effect of the IV is large.
parts.working: 1 mark: exaggerates a small difference; 1 mark: use of the data (only 4 points apart / bar heights from 40 are 12 and 16).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In a hypothetical experiment, each participant chose one of two brands of juice, X or Y. In the 'with friends' condition, the participant shopped with two friends who (as secretly instructed) chose brand X first. In the 'alone' condition, the participant shopped alone but saw a sign saying that most shoppers chose brand X.
Condition | Chose brand X | Chose brand Y
With friends | 22 | 8
Alone | 12 | 18
Give percentages correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how many participants took part in the study.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of participants in the 'with friends' condition who chose the same brand as their friends.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using the data, state one conclusion from this study.
parts.answer: People are more likely to choose the same brand as others when they shop with friends who choose it (73.3 %) than when they shop alone and only see others' choices (40.0 %), suggesting friends exert stronger social influence on choices.
parts.working: 1 mark: conclusion about social influence/conformity; 1 mark: supported with comparative data (73.3 % vs 40 %).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In a hypothetical repeated-measures study of memory in Multan, six participants learned shapes and recalled them after no nap and after a 20-minute nap.
No nap: 12, 15, 9, 14, 11, 17
Nap: 18, 20, 16, 21, 19, 15
Give means to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the range for each condition.
parts.answer: No nap: mean = 13.0, range = 8; Nap: mean = 18.2, range = 6
parts.working: M1 mean method; A1 both means correct (13.0 and 18.2 to 1 d.p.); M1 range = highest − lowest; A1 both ranges (8 and 6).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a summary table of these results should be organised.
parts.answer: Rows for the two conditions (no nap / nap) and columns for the mean and range of the number of shapes remembered, with a title naming the IV and DV.
parts.working: 1 mark: conditions as rows (or columns) with mean and range headings; 1 mark: title/units (number of shapes recalled).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hypothetical study of 20 university students in Kuala Lumpur plotted hours of sport played per week (x-axis, 0–14) against a self-rated mood score (y-axis, 1–10). Most points rise from the bottom left to the top right of the graph. One student who played 12 hours of sport per week had a mood score of 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the two variables shown by the scatter graph.
parts.answer: There is a positive correlation: students who reported more hours of sport per week generally reported higher mood scores, though the points are moderately spread, so it is not perfect.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive; 1 mark: interpretation in context, with strength (moderate/not perfect).

parts.label: b
parts.text: One student (12 hours of sport, mood 3) does not fit the pattern. Suggest two reasons why a researcher might find a point like this.
parts.answer: The student may have had a personal problem (e.g. a family illness) that lowered mood that week; or they may have misread the rating scale or recorded their answer wrongly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two plausible reasons: individual circumstances / other variables; recording or self-report error; misunderstanding the scale; social desirability.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the researcher should not simply remove this point from the data.
parts.answer: Removing data that do not fit the hypothesis is researcher bias; it would make the correlation look stronger than it really is and reduce the validity of the conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark: bias / dishonest reporting; 1 mark: the correlation would be misrepresented.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two observers watched the same 10-minute video of children in a playground and tallied aggressive behaviours (hypothetical data).
Category | Observer 1 | Observer 2
Hitting | 5 | 5
Grabbing toys | 8 | 7
Pushing | 3 | 3
Verbal threat | 6 | 6
Excluding others | 4 | 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: For how many of the categories did the two observers record exactly the same tally?
parts.working: Same tally for hitting (5), pushing (3) and verbal threat (6): 3 categories.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of behaviours recorded by each observer.
parts.answer: Observer 1: 26; Observer 2: 26
parts.working: B1 each: 26 and 26.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what these data suggest about the inter-rater reliability of the observation, and suggest how it could be improved.
parts.answer: The totals are identical and three of five categories match exactly, with the other two differing by 1, so inter-rater reliability appears high. It could be improved by giving the observers more practice with the operationalised categories (e.g. clearer definitions of 'grabbing' versus 'pushing') before the study, and by video-recording so tallies can be checked.
parts.working: 1 mark: reliability is high/good with reference to data; 1 mark: identifies the discrepancies (grabbing toys and excluding others each differ by 1); 1 mark: improvement (clearer operational definitions, training, recording).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher is investigating how working night shifts affects nurses at a hospital in Rawalpindi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'quantitative data'.
parts.answer: Numerical data, such as scores, counts or ratings.
parts.working: 1 mark: data in the form of numbers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define 'qualitative data'.
parts.answer: Descriptive data in words (or pictures), such as detailed answers about thoughts and feelings.
parts.working: 1 mark: data in the form of words/descriptions, not numbers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of each type of data that the researcher in this study could collect.
parts.answer: Quantitative: the number of hours per day each nurse sleeps, or a rating of tiredness from 1 to 10. Qualitative: each nurse's description of how night shifts affect family life.
parts.working: 1 mark each; must be linked to the nurses / shift-work context.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Students in Hyderabad were asked an open question: 'Describe how you felt before your last exam.' Seven answers were:
1 I was too nervous to eat
2 My mind went blank
3 I prayed and felt calmer
4 My hands were shaking
5 I could not sleep the night before
6 I talked to my friends and felt better
7 My heart was racing

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sort the seven answers into two categories: 'physical symptoms' and 'coping strategies' (any answer that is neither should be identified).
parts.answer: Physical symptoms: too nervous to eat; hands shaking; could not sleep; heart racing (4). Coping strategies: prayed and felt calmer; talked to friends (2). Neither (cognitive symptom): my mind went blank (1).
parts.working: 1 mark: physical symptoms correct (4 answers; accept 'could not sleep' or 'too nervous to eat' in either a physical or 'other' category); 1 mark: coping strategies correct (2); 1 mark: 'mind went blank' identified as a cognitive symptom/neither.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how sorting answers into categories changes the type of data collected.
parts.answer: Counting how many answers fall into each category turns qualitative data (words) into quantitative data (frequencies), which can be compared and graphed but loses some detail.
parts.working: 1 mark: converts qualitative to quantitative (frequencies); 1 mark: consequence – easier comparison/analysis but loss of depth/meaning.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hypothetical study interviewed 30 elderly people living in Faisalabad about their experiences of loneliness, recording their answers in full.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength of collecting qualitative data in this study.
parts.answer: Unstructured answers let the elderly participants explain in their own words why they feel lonely (e.g. children moving abroad), giving detailed insight that fixed questions might miss, which increases validity.
parts.working: 1 mark: depth / detail / participant's own words; 1 mark: linked to loneliness context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of collecting qualitative data in this study.
parts.answer: It is difficult to compare participants or summarise 30 long interviews objectively; the researcher's interpretation of what counts as loneliness may be biased.
parts.working: 1 mark: hard to analyse/compare or subjective interpretation; 1 mark: linked to the study.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by quantitative data and qualitative data, using any examples.
parts.answer: Quantitative data are numerical: e.g. the number of aggressive acts counted in an observation, reaction times in ms, or scores on a rating scale. They are easy to summarise with means and graphs and to compare objectively, but can lack depth. Qualitative data are descriptive: e.g. interview transcripts about how a patient experiences anxiety, or diary entries. They give rich insight into reasons and meanings but are harder to analyse and may be interpreted subjectively.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for each type: 1 for definition, 1 for a relevant example, 1 for elaboration (feature, strength or weakness). Examples may come from any study (e.g. Milgram's voltage = quantitative, participants' comments = qualitative).

stem:
A questionnaire for gym members in Dubai contains four items:
1 How many times did you exercise last week? ____
2 Describe what motivates you to come to the gym.
3 Rate your fitness: 1 (very poor) to 7 (excellent).
4 Do you prefer exercising alone or with others? (tick one)

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each item, state whether it collects quantitative or qualitative data.
parts.answer: 1 – quantitative; 2 – qualitative; 3 – quantitative; 4 – quantitative (it gives a frequency/category count).
parts.working: 1 mark each. Item 4 is a closed question giving nominal (count) data, so quantitative.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher wrote detailed notes describing how children in two nurseries in Quetta behaved when there were not enough toys for everyone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two behavioural categories the researcher could use to turn her notes into quantitative data. Make sure each is operationalised.
parts.answer: 'Sharing' – child hands an object to another child without being asked. 'Snatching' – child takes an object out of another child's hands.
parts.working: 1 mark for each clearly operationalised, observable category relevant to sharing/toys.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of turning her notes into quantitative data.
parts.answer: Frequencies of each category can be compared between the two nurseries and checked for inter-rater reliability, which is hard with descriptive notes.
parts.working: 1 mark: advantage (objectivity / comparison / reliability / graphs); 1 mark: linked to the study.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hypothetical study asked patients recovering from knee surgery in a Toronto hospital to rate their pain each evening from 0 to 10 and also to write a short diary entry about their day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why collecting both quantitative and qualitative data could improve the validity of this study.
parts.answer: The rating scale gives comparable numbers showing whether pain changed over the week, while the diary explains why (e.g. pain worse after physiotherapy). If both show the same pattern, the conclusions are supported by two kinds of evidence (triangulation); the diary can also reveal if numbers were misunderstood.
parts.working: 1 mark: quantitative allows comparison/objectivity; 1 mark: qualitative gives reasons/depth; 1 mark: combining checks one against the other (triangulation) to increase validity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one problem the researcher may have when analysing the diaries.
parts.answer: Diaries will vary greatly in length and detail, and deciding which themes appear requires interpretation, so two researchers might code them differently (low inter-rater reliability).
parts.working: 1 mark: problem (time-consuming, subjective interpretation, differing detail); 1 mark: consequence for the study.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Employees at a bank in Lahore rated 'How satisfied are you with your job?' on a scale from 1 to 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the data from the 1–5 rating scale are quantitative.
parts.answer: Each answer is a number that can be added up or averaged.
parts.working: 1 mark: numerical scores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the data are still subjective.
parts.answer: Each employee judges what '4' means for themselves; two people with similar satisfaction might choose different numbers, so the score depends on personal interpretation.
parts.working: 1 mark: based on personal opinion/interpretation; 1 mark: example of different interpretations of the scale points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of making the scale less open to interpretation.
parts.answer: Label every point with a description (e.g. 1 = very dissatisfied, 3 = neither satisfied nor dissatisfied, 5 = very satisfied).
parts.working: 1 mark: anchor/label every point, or give examples for each point.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Seven participants in a hypothetical memory study recalled the following number of items: 4, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean, median and mode of the scores. Give the mean to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Mean = 8.14; median = 8; mode = 7
parts.working: B1 mean: 57 ÷ 7 = 8.14; B1 median = 8 (4th of 7 ordered values); B1 mode = 7.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of the mean as a measure of central tendency.
parts.answer: It uses every score in the data set, so it is the most sensitive measure and represents all participants' performance.
parts.working: 1 mark: uses all scores; 1 mark: elaboration (most sensitive/representative when there are no extreme scores).

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a hypothetical study, seven shoppers in a Karachi supermarket were timed (in minutes) from entering the store to reaching the checkout: 15, 18, 17, 16, 19, 20, 95.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the median for these data. Give the mean to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Mean = 28.6 minutes; median = 18 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which measure gives the better summary of these data.
parts.answer: The median, because the extreme value of 95 minutes distorts the mean, making it higher than six of the seven scores; the median is not affected by this outlier.
parts.working: 1 mark: median; 1 mark: reason linked to the outlier of 95 inflating the mean.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Eight customers rated a new tea brand on a scale from 1 (strongly dislike) to 7 (strongly like): 4, 6, 3, 4, 2, 5, 4, 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the median rating.
parts.working: M1: ordered 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6 – median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values; A1: (4 + 4) ÷ 2 = 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the median is more appropriate than the mean for these rating-scale data.
parts.answer: Rating-scale data are ordinal: the gap between 'agree' and 'strongly agree' is not necessarily the same as between other points, so averaging the numbers is not meaningful; the median only uses rank order.
parts.working: 1 mark: data are ordinal / intervals not equal; 1 mark: median uses order only, mean assumes equal intervals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the only appropriate measure of central tendency for the question 'Which is your favourite brand of tea?' and explain why.
parts.answer: The mode, because the answers are categories (nominal data) that cannot be ordered or averaged.
parts.working: 1 mark: mode; 1 mark: nominal/categorical data.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In a hypothetical independent-measures study in a Lahore school, Group 1 learned a word list and Group 2 learned pictures of the same items. Correct answers:
Group 1: 6, 8, 5, 9, 7
Group 2: 10, 9, 12, 11, 8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of correct answers for each group.
parts.answer: Group 1 (word lists): 7; Group 2 (pictures): 10

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the means suggest about the hypothesis that pictures are remembered better than words.
parts.answer: The picture group had a higher mean (10 vs 7), which supports the hypothesis.
parts.working: 1 mark: supports, with reference to the means.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: The mean of eight participants' scores is 12.5. Seven of the scores are 10, 14, 12, 11, 15, 13 and 9. Calculate the eighth score.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the median of all eight scores.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the mean and median are equal here and what this suggests about the distribution of the scores.
parts.answer: The scores are spread evenly (one at each value from 9 to 16), with no extreme values, so the distribution is symmetrical; in a symmetrical distribution the mean and median are equal.
parts.working: 1 mark: evenly spread / no outliers; 1 mark: symmetrical distribution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three features of a normal distribution.
parts.answer: It is bell-shaped and symmetrical about the centre; the mean, median and mode are all equal and at the highest point; the tails extend in both directions and get closer to the x-axis without touching it; most scores lie near the middle.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: bell-shaped; symmetrical; mean = median = mode at the peak; tails approach but never touch x-axis; about 68 % of scores within one standard deviation of the mean.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what should be shown on each axis when sketching a normal distribution of reaction times.
parts.answer: x-axis: reaction time (ms), the measured variable/score; y-axis: frequency (number of participants).
parts.working: 1 mark: x-axis = score/variable measured with units; 1 mark: y-axis = frequency.

stem: A hypothetical concentration test was given to a large group of Pakistani secondary-school students. The scores were normally distributed with a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Between which two scores would you expect about 68 % of the students to fall?
parts.answer: 42 and 58
parts.working: M1: one standard deviation either side of the mean (50 ± 8); A1: 42 and 58.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Approximately what percentage of students would you expect to score above 66?
parts.answer: About 2.5 % (accept 2–2.5 %)
parts.working: 66 is two standard deviations above the mean; about 95 % lie within ±2 SD, so about 2.5 % lie above (exact 2.3 %).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Out of 400 students, approximately how many would you expect to score between 42 and 58?
parts.answer: About 272 students

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a hypothetical proof-reading task in Singapore, the numbers of errors missed by 50 participants had a mean of 14, a median of 11 and a mode of 10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether this distribution is normal, positively skewed or negatively skewed. Explain your answer using the three measures.
parts.answer: Positively skewed. The mean (14) is greater than the median (11), which is greater than the mode (10); a few participants made many errors, pulling the mean towards the long tail on the right.
parts.working: 1 mark: positively skewed; 1 mark: mean > median > mode; 1 mark: explanation – a few high scores create a long tail to the right/pull the mean up.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what the graph of this distribution would look like.
parts.answer: The peak (highest frequency) is towards the left (at low numbers of errors) and there is a long tail stretching out to the right towards high numbers of errors.
parts.working: 1 mark: peak to the left; 1 mark: long tail to the right.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the distribution of errors might not be normal in this study.
parts.answer: The task may have been easy for most people, so most made few errors (a floor effect), while a few tired or distracted participants made many.
parts.working: 1 mark: plausible reason (floor effect, task too easy, a few outliers, small sample).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two groups of trainee drivers in Islamabad completed a hazard-perception test (hypothetical scores).
Group A: 22, 25, 24, 23, 26
Group B: 10, 35, 18, 30, 27

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the range for each group.
parts.answer: Group A: 4; Group B: 25

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean for each group.
parts.answer: Both groups have a mean of 24
parts.working: 120 ÷ 5 = 24 for each group.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answers, explain what the results show about the two groups.
parts.answer: Although both groups have the same mean, Group B's scores are much more spread out (range 25 vs 4), so performance in Group B varied a great deal between individuals while Group A performed consistently.
parts.working: 1 mark: same mean; 1 mark: Group B much more variable/less consistent with data.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a hypothetical study in Melbourne, workers who did a mindfulness course had a mean stress score of 32 (standard deviation 2.1). A control group also had a mean of 32 (standard deviation 7.8).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'standard deviation'.
parts.answer: A measure of spread showing the average amount by which scores differ from the mean; a larger standard deviation means scores are more spread out.
