parts.working: 1 mark: spread/variation around the mean; 1 mark: larger SD = more spread (or calculation idea: based on every score's distance from the mean).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare the two groups using the means and standard deviations.
parts.answer: Both groups have the same mean stress score (32), but the mindfulness group has a much smaller standard deviation (2.1 vs 7.8), so their scores were closer together and more consistent; the control group varied more.
parts.working: 1 mark: same mean; 1 mark: mindfulness group less spread/more consistent, quoting SDs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one advantage of the standard deviation compared with the range.
parts.answer: It uses every score, so it is not distorted by a single extreme score as the range is.
parts.working: 1 mark: uses all data / less affected by one outlier.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Five participants in a hypothetical study in Cairo rated their sleep quality: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean of the scores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation of the scores, using the sample formula s = √(Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A second group had the same mean but a standard deviation of 0.71. Explain what this tells you.
parts.answer: The second group's scores were much closer to the mean of 8, so participants in that group were far more similar to each other than in the first group.
parts.working: 1 mark: less spread / more consistent; 1 mark: comparison with 3.16.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher plans a questionnaire to investigate mobile phone use among college students in Lahore.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write one closed question the researcher could include in the questionnaire.
parts.answer: 'Do you use your phone during meals with your family? Yes / No'
parts.working: 1 mark: a question with fixed response options relevant to phone use.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write one open question the researcher could include in the questionnaire.
parts.answer: 'Describe how using your phone affects the time you spend with your family.'
parts.working: 1 mark: a question that allows participants to answer in their own words; must not be answerable with yes/no.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using closed questions in this study.
parts.answer: Students must choose from fixed answers that may not fit their real experience (e.g. they use the phone only sometimes), so the data may lack validity and detail.
parts.working: 1 mark: forced choice / lack of detail; 1 mark: linked to phone use.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe structured interviews and unstructured interviews, using any examples.
parts.answer: A structured interview uses a fixed list of questions asked in the same order to every participant, e.g. asking every patient the same ten questions about symptoms; it is easy to compare and replicate but the interviewer cannot follow up interesting answers. An unstructured interview has no fixed questions beyond a topic: the interviewer follows the conversation, e.g. a therapist asking a client to talk about childhood; it gives rich, detailed data but answers cannot easily be compared, and interviewer bias is more likely.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for each type: 1 for a description, 1 for an example, 1 for an elaboration (strength/weakness or feature such as standardisation, replicability, rapport, depth).

stem: A researcher interviews parents in Karachi face to face about how they discipline their children.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'social desirability' in self-report research.
parts.answer: When participants give answers that make them look good or match social norms, rather than the truth.
parts.working: 1 mark: answers to appear favourable/acceptable; 1 mark: rather than truthful, so data are invalid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why social desirability is a particular problem in this study.
parts.answer: Asking parents face to face how often they shout at or smack their children is sensitive; parents may underreport harsh discipline to avoid being judged by the interviewer.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies the sensitive behaviour; 1 mark: direction of bias (under-reporting) linked to face-to-face interview.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to reduce this problem.
parts.answer: Use an anonymous postal or online questionnaire instead of a face-to-face interview, so parents feel their answers cannot be traced back to them.
parts.working: 1 mark: anonymity/confidentiality/online questionnaire/filler questions; 1 mark: explanation of why it reduces the bias.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a rating-scale question that could be used to measure how stressed teachers feel at work. Your scale must have labelled anchor points.
parts.answer: 'How stressed do you feel at work most days?' 1 = not at all stressed, 2, 3, 4, 5 = extremely stressed.
parts.working: 1 mark: question about stress with a numerical scale; 1 mark: both ends (anchor points) labelled.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of using a rating scale rather than an open question.
parts.answer: It gives numerical (quantitative) data, so the mean stress of teachers in different schools can be compared easily and objectively.
parts.working: 1 mark: quantitative / easy comparison; 1 mark: linked to teachers.

stem: A researcher in Jeddah has written a questionnaire to measure attitudes to healthy eating.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the researcher could test the reliability of her questionnaire using the test–retest method.
parts.answer: Give the same questionnaire to the same participants twice, with a gap of a few weeks (long enough that they don't remember their answers but not so long that their real attitudes change). Correlate the two sets of scores; a strong positive correlation (e.g. above +0.8) shows the questionnaire is reliable.
parts.working: 1 mark: same participants, same questionnaire, twice; 1 mark: suitable time gap with justification; 1 mark: compare/correlate scores – a strong positive correlation indicates reliability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a reliable questionnaire may still not be valid.
parts.answer: It may consistently measure something other than intended – e.g. items about 'healthy eating' may really measure knowledge of nutrition rather than what people actually eat, so answers are consistent but not accurate.
parts.working: 1 mark: consistency ≠ accuracy; 1 mark: example in context (e.g. social desirability gives the same false answers each time).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hypothetical study interviews patients at a diabetes clinic in Islamabad about why they do or do not follow their doctor's advice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength of using a semi-structured interview in this study.
parts.answer: The interviewer can ask set questions to all patients, giving some comparable data, but also follow up interesting answers (e.g. why a patient stopped taking medication), giving more detail.
parts.working: 1 mark: combination of fixed questions and flexibility; 1 mark: linked to patients.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using a semi-structured interview in this study.
parts.answer: Different follow-up questions are asked to different patients, so answers are harder to compare, and the interviewer's own views may influence which points are explored (interviewer bias).
parts.working: 1 mark: less standardised / interviewer bias / time-consuming; 1 mark: linked to the study.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one ethical issue the researcher must consider and how to deal with it.
parts.answer: Confidentiality: patients may disclose personal health information, so their names must not be recorded and data stored securely.
parts.working: 1 mark: issue (confidentiality, privacy, right to withdraw, protection from distress); 1 mark: how to deal with it.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A psychologist wants to investigate the relationship between sleep habits and concentration in university students.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how this study could be conducted as a self-report using a questionnaire. Include details of the sampling technique, the types of questions with examples, and how the data would be analysed.
parts.answer: A possible plan: opportunity or stratified sample of 100 university students (e.g. equal numbers of first- and final-year students) from different faculties of a university in Lahore; online anonymous questionnaire with standardised instructions and consent page; closed questions (e.g. 'How many hours a night do you usually sleep on weekdays? less than 5 / 5–6 / 7–8 / more than 8'), rating scales (e.g. 'Rate your ability to concentrate in lectures: 1 = very poor to 7 = excellent'), and open questions (e.g. 'Describe what stops you sleeping before exams'); filler questions to reduce demand characteristics; pilot study to check clarity; quantitative data analysed as means/medians and bar charts by year group; qualitative answers coded into themes; ethics – informed consent, right to withdraw, confidentiality, debrief with sleep advice.
parts.working: Mark points: sampling technique and sample detail; recruitment; questionnaire format (online/paper, anonymous); at least two question types with examples; rating scale with anchors; filler questions/pilot; standardised instructions; analysis (descriptive statistics, graphs, thematic coding); ethics. Level 4 (9–10): a detailed, well-reasoned, coherent plan covering all the required features, with clear operationalisation and justified choices. Level 3 (6–8): a clear plan with most required features and some detail; minor omissions. Level 2 (3–5): a basic plan; several features missing or vague. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or largely irrelevant. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of your plan and suggest how it could be improved.
parts.answer: Weakness: self-reported sleep hours may be inaccurate because students guess or overestimate, reducing validity. Improvement: ask students to keep a sleep diary for a week, or wear an activity tracker that records sleep, and compare the measures (triangulation).
parts.working: 1 mark: identify a weakness of the plan; 1 mark: explain it in context; 1 mark: suggest an improvement; 1 mark: explain how the improvement helps.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Dr Malik asks recently widowed women in Multan to talk about their experiences. She has no list of questions and simply follows what each woman wants to talk about.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which type of interview Dr Malik is using.
parts.answer: An unstructured interview.
parts.working: 1 mark: unstructured (no fixed questions, follows the conversation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why this type of interview is suitable for this topic.
parts.answer: Grief is a sensitive and individual experience; an unstructured interview allows each widow to talk freely about what matters to her, building rapport and giving detailed, valid data.
parts.working: 1 mark: flexibility / rapport / depth; 1 mark: linked to the sensitive topic.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Hamza is writing a questionnaire about public transport in Karachi. Three of his questions are:
1 Don't you agree that the new bus service is excellent?
2 Are the buses cheap and clean? Yes / No
3 Do you often use public transport? Yes / No

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two problems with the questions written by Hamza.
parts.answer: Question 1 is a leading question ('Don't you agree…'), pushing respondents towards 'yes'. Question 2 is a double-barrelled question asking about two things at once (price and cleanliness).
parts.working: 1 mark each: leading question (Q1); double-barrelled (Q2). Accept: Q3 uses ambiguous terms ('often').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rewrite question 3 so that it produces clearer data.
parts.answer: 'How many times did you use public transport in the last 7 days? 0 / 1–3 / 4–6 / 7 or more'
parts.working: 1 mark: removes the vague word 'often'; 1 mark: gives specific, mutually exclusive response options.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hypothetical telecommunications company with 2,000 employees in branches across Pakistan wants to find out how employees feel about their managers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of collecting data with questionnaires rather than interviews in this study.
parts.answer: Strength: questionnaires can be sent to all 2,000 employees across the country quickly and cheaply, and anonymity may make employees more honest about their managers. Weakness: there is no chance to clarify unclear questions or follow up answers, and response rates may be low, so those who reply (e.g. very unhappy staff) may not be representative.
parts.working: 2 marks for strength (identify + link to the large company / anonymity); 2 marks for weakness (identify + link).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The response rate was 18 %. Calculate how many questionnaires were returned.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A neuropsychologist in Lahore studies a man who lost the ability to recognise faces after a stroke.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define 'case study'.
parts.answer: An in-depth investigation of a single individual, or a small group, usually using several methods.
parts.working: 1 mark: detailed study of one person/small group (or one event/organisation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of the case study method for studying this patient.
parts.answer: It gives detailed, rich information about a rare condition that could not be studied with a large sample, and can be followed over time to see changes.
parts.working: 1 mark: depth / rare cases / longitudinal; 1 mark: linked to the patient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one weakness of the case study method for studying this patient.
parts.answer: The findings come from one unique person whose brain damage and life history are different from others, so they cannot be generalised to other people.
parts.working: 1 mark: generalisability / researcher bias / hard to replicate; 1 mark: linked to the patient.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A school psychologist in Islamabad carries out a case study of a 12-year-old boy who refuses to attend school.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'triangulation' in a case study.
parts.answer: Using several different methods or sources of data (e.g. interviews, observations, tests, records) to study the same case, and checking whether they agree.
parts.working: 1 mark: several methods/sources; 1 mark: comparing them to check consistency/validity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three different sources of data the researcher could use to triangulate in this case study.
parts.answer: An interview with the boy about how he feels in class; an observation of his behaviour in lessons; school records of attendance and grades (or a questionnaire for his parents/teachers, or a psychometric test).
parts.working: 1 mark each for three different, appropriate sources linked to the boy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why triangulation increases the validity of the case study.
parts.answer: If different sources give the same picture, the conclusion does not rely on one possibly biased source.
parts.working: 1 mark: agreement between sources makes conclusions more accurate/less dependent on one method's bias.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher spent eighteen months visiting one family of refugees settling in Peshawar, interviewing them and observing their daily life.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the researcher's close relationship with the family could be a problem in this case study.
parts.answer: After months of contact she may become less objective and interpret the family's behaviour in a way that supports her own expectations (researcher bias), reducing validity.
parts.working: 1 mark: loss of objectivity / bias; 1 mark: effect on interpretation in this case.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one ethical issue that is particularly important in this case study.
parts.answer: Confidentiality: a detailed account of one family could easily identify them in a small community, so names and identifying details must be changed.
parts.working: 1 mark: issue (confidentiality/privacy/right to withdraw); 1 mark: why it is especially important in a case study.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A psychologist wants to carry out a case study of a child who is gifted at mathematics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how this case study could be conducted. Include at least two methods of data collection, how long it would last, and one ethical consideration.
parts.answer: A possible plan: one gifted 9-year-old girl in a Lahore school; volunteer/parental consent; longitudinal over one school year; methods: semi-structured interviews with the child (e.g. 'Tell me what you enjoy doing in maths lessons'), interviews or questionnaires with parents and teachers; structured observations in class (event sampling for categories such as 'asks a question', 'helps a classmate'), standardised tests of ability at the start and end; school records; triangulation of findings; qualitative data analysed into themes, quantitative test and observation data summarised; ethics – informed consent from parents and assent from child, right to withdraw, confidentiality (pseudonym), protection from stress from being labelled.
parts.working: Mark points: participant and how chosen; duration/longitudinal; at least two methods described in detail with examples; triangulation; types of data and analysis; ethics specific to a child. Level 4 (9–10): a detailed, well-reasoned, coherent plan covering all the required features, with clear operationalisation and justified choices. Level 3 (6–8): a clear plan with most required features and some detail; minor omissions. Level 2 (3–5): a basic plan; several features missing or vague. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or largely irrelevant. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of your plan.
parts.answer: Strength: using interviews, observations and test scores (triangulation) means that conclusions about the girl's abilities are supported by several sources, reducing the effect of bias from any one method (e.g. a teacher's opinion), so the case study has higher validity. The year-long duration also shows how her behaviour changes over time.
parts.working: 1 mark: identify; 1–2 marks: explain with reference to the plan; 1 mark: why it improves the study.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher studied a survivor who was trapped for three days after a building collapsed, to understand how she coped.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the case study method was used rather than an experiment.
parts.answer: The situation (surviving a building collapse) is rare and could not ethically be created by a researcher, so the only way to study it is to investigate the few people it has happened to in depth.
parts.working: 1 mark: rare / naturally occurring event; 1 mark: cannot be manipulated ethically in an experiment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify one type of data, qualitative or quantitative, the researcher is likely to collect most and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Qualitative, because the researcher wants a detailed account of the survivor's thoughts, feelings and experiences, which are best captured in words.
parts.working: 1 mark: qualitative (accept quantitative with justification, e.g. symptom scores); 1 mark: justification.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher wants to observe how waiting staff in a busy Karachi restaurant deal with rude customers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a participant and a non-participant observation, using this study as an example.
parts.answer: In a participant observation the researcher joins the group, e.g. works as a waiter alongside the staff; in a non-participant observation the researcher watches without joining in, e.g. sits as a customer and records the staff's behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark for each type with a link to the restaurant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of an overt observation in this study.
parts.answer: The staff know they are being observed and have agreed, so the study is ethical (informed consent and no invasion of privacy).
parts.working: 1 mark: ethical/informed consent; 1 mark: linked to the restaurant staff.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe event sampling and time sampling, using any examples.
parts.answer: Event sampling: the observer records every time a particular behaviour occurs, e.g. tallying each time a child hits another in the playground; useful for infrequent behaviours but may be hard if many events happen at once. Time sampling: the observer records behaviour only at set intervals, e.g. noting what a shopper is doing every 30 seconds; reduces the amount of data, but behaviour between intervals is missed.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for each: description, example, elaboration (strength/weakness).

stem: In a hypothetical study, observers stood near the checkout in a Lahore hypermarket and secretly recorded how shoppers behaved while waiting in queues.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why the observation was covert.
parts.answer: If shoppers knew they were being watched they might change how they behave in the queue (e.g. queue more politely), so a covert observation reduces demand characteristics and gives more valid data.
parts.working: 1 mark: avoids participant reactivity/demand characteristics; 1 mark: linked to queue behaviour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one ethical problem with this covert observation and suggest whether it is acceptable.
parts.answer: Shoppers did not give informed consent; however, the observation took place in a public place where people would expect to be seen by strangers, so it is usually considered acceptable as long as individuals are not identified.
parts.working: 1 mark: no consent/deception; 1 mark: justification about public place and anonymity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two behavioural categories the observers could use. Each must be operationalised.
parts.answer: 'Pushing in' – joining the queue in front of someone who arrived earlier. 'Complaining' – making a verbal comment about waiting time to another person.
parts.working: 1 mark each for operationalised observable categories.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher wants to investigate road rage in drivers waiting at traffic signals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how this study could be conducted as a structured observation. Include the setting, the type of observation, behavioural categories, the sampling of behaviour and how reliability would be checked.
parts.answer: A possible plan: naturalistic, non-participant, covert observation of drivers at a busy signal-controlled junction in Islamabad during rush hour (e.g. 5–7 p.m., weekdays over two weeks); two observers positioned on the pavement (or video recording from a public place, number plates not recorded); event sampling of each car arriving at a red light; operationalised categories: 'hooting' (horn used while stopped at red light), 'aggressive gesture' (hand gesture towards another driver), 'jumping the light' (crossing stop line after light turns red), 'calm waiting' (no hooting or movement until green); tally chart; quantitative data as frequencies compared between drivers of different vehicle types or sexes if visible; inter-rater reliability – both observers code the same cars and correlate tallies, training beforehand with practice video; ethics – public place, no identification of drivers.
parts.working: Mark points: setting and time; naturalistic/controlled; participant/non-participant; overt/covert with justification; behavioural categories operationalised; event or time sampling; recording method (tally/video); inter-rater reliability; data type and analysis; ethics. Level 4 (9–10): a detailed, well-reasoned, coherent plan covering all the required features, with clear operationalisation and justified choices. Level 3 (6–8): a clear plan with most required features and some detail; minor omissions. Level 2 (3–5): a basic plan; several features missing or vague. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or largely irrelevant. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of your plan.
parts.answer: Weakness: observers can see behaviour but not the reasons for it – a driver who hoots may be warning another driver rather than being aggressive, so the category may be misinterpreted, reducing validity. This could be improved by stopping a sample of drivers at a nearby petrol station to interview them, or by refining the category definitions.
parts.working: 1 mark: identify weakness; 1–2 marks: explain with reference to the plan; 1 mark: consequence for validity/reliability or improvement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one difference between a naturalistic and a controlled observation.
parts.answer: A naturalistic observation watches behaviour in its usual setting without changing anything (e.g. children in their own classroom); a controlled observation takes place in a setting arranged by the researcher, often a laboratory, where variables are standardised.
parts.working: 1 mark for each type; must show the contrast (normal setting vs researcher-controlled).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The researcher used a one-way mirror to observe children in a playroom set up at a university. State one advantage of this.
parts.answer: The children cannot see the observer, so their behaviour is less likely to change because they know they are being watched.
parts.working: 1 mark: reduces reactivity/demand characteristics.

stem: A researcher in Singapore asks teenagers how many hours they spend playing violent video games each week and gives them a questionnaire measuring aggression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a non-directional hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: There will be a correlation between the number of hours spent playing violent video games per week and the score on an aggression questionnaire.
parts.working: 1 mark: states a relationship/correlation without direction; 1 mark: both co-variables operationalised (e.g. hours per week, questionnaire score).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this study is a correlation and not an experiment.
parts.answer: Neither variable is manipulated by the researcher: both violent video game hours and aggression are measured as they already are, so we are looking for a relationship between two co-variables rather than the effect of an IV on a DV.
parts.working: 1 mark: no manipulation of an IV; 1 mark: two measured co-variables.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A head teacher in Hyderabad found a correlation coefficient of −0.72 between the number of days students were absent and their final exam scores (hypothetical data).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a correlation coefficient of −0.72 shows about the relationship between the two variables.
parts.answer: A fairly strong negative correlation: as the number of days absent increases, exam scores tend to decrease.
parts.working: 1 mark: strength (fairly strong/strong); 1 mark: negative direction described in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what a correlation coefficient of +0.05 would have shown instead.
parts.answer: There is almost no relationship between absence and exam scores.
parts.working: 1 mark: no (or extremely weak) correlation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the head teacher cannot conclude that absence causes lower exam scores.
parts.answer: A third variable such as illness, family problems or poor motivation may cause both absence and low scores.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation cannot show cause/effect; 1 mark: suitable third variable or reverse direction.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A psychologist wants to investigate whether there is a relationship between how much people exercise and how happy they feel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how this study could be conducted as a correlation. Include how each co-variable would be measured, the sample and how the results would be presented.
parts.answer: A possible plan: volunteer or opportunity sample of 60 adults aged 18–60 attending a gym and a community centre in Karachi; co-variable 1 – self-reported average daily minutes of exercise over the last month (or a fitness tracker's daily step count over one week); co-variable 2 – score on a happiness/wellbeing rating questionnaire (e.g. ten items rated 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree, total 10–50); standardised instructions, informed consent, confidentiality; scores plotted on a scatter graph with exercise on the x-axis and wellbeing score on the y-axis; look for a positive correlation; directional hypothesis stated; ethics – right to withdraw, debrief.
parts.working: Mark points: both co-variables operationalised; measurement tools with example items; sampling technique and size; procedure/standardisation; hypothesis; scatter graph with axes; direction of expected correlation; ethics. Level 4 (9–10): a detailed, well-reasoned, coherent plan covering all the required features, with clear operationalisation and justified choices. Level 3 (6–8): a clear plan with most required features and some detail; minor omissions. Level 2 (3–5): a basic plan; several features missing or vague. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or largely irrelevant. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of your plan and one reason why it could not show that exercise causes happiness.
parts.answer: Strength: measuring exercise with a fitness tracker gives objective data, so it is not affected by people overestimating how much they exercise. Causation: happier people may simply be more motivated to exercise, or a third variable such as free time or income could increase both, so the direction of cause is unknown.
parts.working: 2 marks: strength identified and explained with reference to the plan; 2 marks: causation problem explained with reverse causality or a third variable.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify the type of correlation in each statement:
(i) The more coffee a student drinks, the fewer hours they sleep.
(ii) The more hours a nurse works overtime, the higher her stress score.
parts.answer: (i) Negative correlation; (ii) positive correlation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of using a correlation to study the link between overtime and stress in nurses.
parts.answer: It would be unethical to make nurses work extra hours to see if they become stressed; a correlation allows the relationship to be studied using the hours they already work.
parts.working: 1 mark: ethical/practical (variables cannot be manipulated) or can show the strength of the relationship; 1 mark: linked to nurses.

stem: In a hypothetical experiment in a university laboratory in Lahore, 20 students chewed gum while learning and recalling a list of 25 words and another 20 students did not chew gum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this experiment.
parts.answer: IV: whether the students chewed gum or not during the test. DV: the number of words correctly recalled.
parts.working: 1 mark each; DV must be operationalised.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the type of experiment used.
parts.answer: A laboratory experiment.
parts.working: 1 mark: laboratory experiment (controlled setting, IV manipulated).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one strength of this type of experiment.
parts.answer: Extraneous variables such as noise and test time can be controlled, so differences in recall are more likely to be caused by chewing gum (cause and effect).
parts.working: 1 mark: control of variables; 1 mark: allows a causal conclusion in context.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher compared the general knowledge of children in a village in Gilgit-Baltistan that had recently received internet access with children in a similar village that had not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this is a natural experiment.
parts.answer: The researcher did not manipulate the IV (whether the village had internet access or not); the difference already existed naturally and she only measured its effect.
parts.working: 1 mark: IV not manipulated by the researcher; 1 mark: occurs naturally, linked to internet access.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of a natural experiment in this study.
parts.answer: Participants cannot be randomly allocated to conditions, so the two villages may differ in other ways (e.g. wealth, schooling), which could explain differences in children's general knowledge.
parts.working: 1 mark: no random allocation/confounding variables/no control; 1 mark: example linked to the villages.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher wants to find out whether offering free food samples increases sales of a new product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how this field experiment could be conducted. Include the IV, the DV, the design, and controls.
parts.answer: A possible plan: field experiment in a large Islamabad supermarket; IV – whether a free-sample stall for a new biscuit is present at the end of an aisle (condition A) or absent (condition B), alternating on matched weekdays over four weeks; DV – number of packets of the biscuit sold per hour from the store's sales records (or the proportion of shoppers passing who pick up a packet, observed by two researchers); independent measures (different shoppers each day); controls – same price, same shelf position, same times (5–8 p.m.), same days of the week, same stall assistant with a standard script; shoppers unaware (covert); ethics – public place, no identification of individuals, debrief not possible so no personal data kept.
parts.working: Mark points: field setting; IV operationalised with two conditions; DV operationalised; design (independent/repeated) with justification; controls (time, day, price, script); sampling of participants; procedure; ethics. Level 4 (9–10): a detailed, well-reasoned, coherent plan covering all the required features, with clear operationalisation and justified choices. Level 3 (6–8): a clear plan with most required features and some detail; minor omissions. Level 2 (3–5): a basic plan; several features missing or vague. Level 1 (1–2): brief, muddled or largely irrelevant. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of your plan and how it could be improved.
parts.answer: Weakness: other factors that change from day to day, such as weather or special offers in another aisle, could affect sales and cannot be fully controlled in a field setting, reducing internal validity. Improvement: run the study over more days, alternating conditions randomly, and note any special events so those days can be excluded.
parts.working: 1 mark: identify; 1 mark: explain in context; 1 mark: improvement; 1 mark: how it helps.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher wants to investigate whether rickshaw drivers in Lahore are more stressed during rush hour than at quieter times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two physiological measures the researcher could use to measure stress in the drivers.
parts.answer: Heart rate and cortisol level in saliva (accept blood pressure, skin conductance/galvanic skin response).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid physiological measures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one strength of using physiological measures rather than self-report to measure stress.
parts.answer: Physiological measures are objective: a driver cannot easily fake their heart rate, so the data are not affected by social desirability (e.g. not wanting to admit being stressed).
parts.working: 1 mark: objective / not affected by demand characteristics or social desirability; 1 mark: linked to drivers.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what an fMRI scan measures.
parts.answer: It measures changes in blood flow (oxygenated blood) in the brain, which shows which areas are more active while a person performs a task.
parts.working: 1 mark: blood flow/oxygen use; 1 mark: shows brain activity in specific areas during a task.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using fMRI scans in psychological research.
parts.answer: Participants must lie still inside a noisy, enclosed scanner, so tasks are unlike real life (low ecological validity) and some people find it stressful, which may change brain activity.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness (low ecological validity, cost, small samples, only shows correlation, stressful); 1 mark: explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how an MRI scan (structural) differs from an fMRI scan.
parts.answer: A structural MRI shows the physical structure of the brain (e.g. size of regions or grey matter), whereas fMRI shows activity over time.
parts.working: 1 mark: structure vs function/activity.

stem: In a hypothetical study in Dhaka, participants gave a short speech to an audience. Their heart rate was measured with a monitor and they also rated their anxiety from 1 to 10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the researcher measured the participants' heart rate as well as asking them to rate their anxiety.
parts.answer: The rating is subjective and participants might under- or overstate their anxiety; heart rate gives an objective measure of arousal, so the two can be compared to check validity.
parts.working: 1 mark: self-report subjective/biased; 1 mark: physiological measure objective, allows triangulation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one problem with using heart rate as a measure of anxiety.
parts.answer: Heart rate can rise for reasons other than anxiety, such as excitement, physical movement or caffeine, so a high heart rate does not definitely mean the participant was anxious.
parts.working: 1 mark: not specific to anxiety; 1 mark: example of another cause.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The mean heart rate rose from 72 beats per minute before the speech to 99 beats per minute during it. Calculate the percentage increase. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two types of retail store layout.
parts.answer: Grid layout: shelves arranged in long parallel aisles at right angles, as in most supermarkets; shoppers move up and down aisles, and it is efficient for finding everyday items. Freeform layout: displays and racks are placed in irregular, flowing patterns, as in fashion boutiques; it encourages browsing and relaxed movement around the store. (Accept racetrack/loop layout: one main path leads shoppers past all departments, as in large furniture stores.)
parts.working: 2 marks per layout: 1 for naming/identifying it with a key feature, 1 for a further detail or example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why a freeform layout might suit a small clothing boutique better than a grid layout.
parts.answer: Customers in a boutique want to browse and try items rather than find things quickly; a freeform layout encourages them to wander, look at more displays and stay longer, which can increase unplanned purchases.
parts.working: 1 mark: browsing/exploration/longer time in store; 1 mark: link to more purchases or customer enjoyment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nadia is opening a clothing store for young adults in a Lahore shopping mall. Suggest how she could use music to influence customers' behaviour in her store.
parts.answer: She could play music that fits the store's image and her young customers, such as current pop music, because music congruent with the store and audience creates a positive mood and approach behaviour. She could use slower-tempo music at quiet times so customers move more slowly and browse longer (research found slow music in a supermarket slowed shoppers and increased sales). She should keep the volume moderate so customers can talk and are not driven away.
parts.working: 1 mark per relevant, justified suggestion, up to 4; suggestions must be linked to psychological evidence (tempo, congruence/fit, volume, mood) and applied to Nadia's store; max 2 if no link to evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the procedure of North et al.'s study of music in a restaurant.
parts.answer: The study took place in a real restaurant over a number of evenings. On different evenings either classical music, pop music or no music was played in the background. The bills of diners were used to record how much was spent per head on starters, main courses, desserts, coffee, drinks and in total, and this was compared across the three music conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: field setting (a real restaurant); three conditions – classical, pop, no music; conditions varied between evenings; spending per person measured from bills, including different courses/items.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the main finding of this study.
parts.answer: Customers spent more in total when classical music was played than when pop music or no music was played.
parts.working: 1 mark: classical music led to the highest spending.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one weakness of the way the conditions were organised in this study.
parts.answer: Different evenings had different customers, so differences in spending may be due to the kind of diners on each evening (e.g. people celebrating special occasions) rather than the music; customers could not be randomly allocated to conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness (participant variables / independent measures / no random allocation / other changes between evenings); 1 mark: explained in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe research into the effects of sound (music) on consumer behaviour.
parts.answer: North et al. found that restaurant diners spent more when classical music was played than with pop music or no music, possibly because classical music creates an upmarket image (a 'sophisticated' priming effect). North, Hargreaves and McKendrick played French or German music on alternate days next to a supermarket wine display: French wine outsold German wine when French music played, and German wine outsold French when German music played; few shoppers said the music had influenced them. Milliman found that slow-tempo music in a supermarket slowed shoppers' movement and increased sales compared with fast-tempo music.
parts.working: Credit named studies with procedure and findings; theory such as priming/congruence/arousal. Marks: 1 mark per accurate point, or 2 for a well-detailed point, up to 6; the answer should name the research and its findings in detail for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate research into the effects of sound on consumer behaviour, including a discussion of ecological validity.
parts.answer: Strengths: field studies in real restaurants and supermarkets have high ecological validity – real customers spending their own money; useful applications for retailers. Weaknesses: lack of control in field settings – other variables (weather, day of the week, special offers) may affect spending; customers cannot be randomly allocated; ethical concerns – shoppers are influenced without awareness or consent (unconscious manipulation); cultural differences – musical associations (e.g. classical = expensive) may not hold in other cultures such as Pakistan; results are often small and may depend on the type of product; reductionism – music is only one part of the atmosphere; determinism vs free will – suggests consumers are passive.
parts.working: Must include ecological validity (named issue); credit other issues and debates (application, ethics, control, generalisability, culture, determinism). Level 4 (9–10): a range of well-developed evaluative points, including the named issue, with effective use of examples from research; clear structure. Level 3 (6–8): several evaluative points, mostly developed; the named issue covered. Level 2 (3–5): limited evaluation, mostly undeveloped; the named issue may be missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief, general points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the conditions in North, Hargreaves and McKendrick's study of in-store music and wine choice.
parts.answer: On alternate days, French accordion music or German Bierkeller (beer-hall) music was played beside a display of French and German wines in a supermarket.
parts.working: 1 mark: French vs German music; 1 mark: alternated between days, at a wine display in a supermarket.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline the results of the study.
parts.answer: More French wine than German wine was sold when French music was played, and more German wine than French wine when German music was played.
parts.working: 1 mark for each direction of the result.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some shoppers were asked whether the music had influenced their choice. Explain what their answers suggested.
parts.answer: Very few shoppers said the music had influenced their choice, suggesting that the music affected their decisions without conscious awareness (it primed thoughts of the country).
parts.working: 1 mark: few shoppers aware/mentioned music; 1 mark: influence was unconscious/priming.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the determinism versus free will debate.
parts.answer: Determinism is the view that behaviour is caused by factors outside a person's control (internal or external), whereas free will is the view that people can choose how to behave.
parts.working: 1 mark: determinism; 1 mark: free will.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why research into store atmospherics (such as music and scent) can be seen as deterministic.
parts.answer: It suggests customers' choices – what they buy and how much they spend – are caused by environmental cues like music tempo or scent that they are not aware of, rather than by free, conscious choices.
parts.working: 1 mark: environmental cues cause behaviour; 1 mark: example from research (e.g. French music → French wine) and lack of awareness/control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a field experiment to investigate whether a pleasant scent in a bakery increases the amount customers spend. Your plan must include an independent measures design and a way of measuring the dependent variable from sales records.
parts.answer: A possible plan: field experiment in a bakery in Islamabad; IV – a vanilla/fresh-bread scent released from a diffuser near the entrance vs no added scent; conditions alternate on matched days (e.g. Mondays and Wednesdays scent, Tuesdays and Thursdays no scent) over four weeks; independent measures – different customers in each condition; DV – mean spending per customer from till receipts (total sales ÷ number of transactions), plus the number of items per receipt; controls – same opening hours, prices, staff, displays and music, no promotions during the study, scent intensity kept the same; ethics – scent safe and mild, no personal data recorded, public setting.
parts.working: Mark points: IV operationalised; independent measures with how conditions are allocated; DV from sales records operationalised; controls; sample/setting; duration; ethics. Level 4 (9–10): detailed, coherent plan covering all the required features with clear operationalisation. Level 3 (6–8): clear plan with most features. Level 2 (3–5): basic plan, several features missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief/muddled. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the psychological knowledge on which your plan is based.
parts.answer: Research on scent in retail: pleasant ambient scent can improve mood and evaluations of a store, increasing approach behaviour such as browsing longer and spending more. Spangenberg et al. found that a Christmas scent improved evaluations of a store when combined with Christmas music, but not with non-Christmas music – showing the importance of congruence between scent and setting; a bread or vanilla scent is congruent with a bakery. Mehrabian–Russell model: environmental stimuli produce pleasure and arousal, leading to approach or avoidance behaviour.
parts.working: Credit relevant theories and studies on scent/atmospherics and their link to the plan. Level 4 (7–8): accurate, detailed psychology (named theory/studies) clearly linked to the plan. Level 3 (5–6): mostly accurate and linked. Level 2 (3–4): basic or partly relevant. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons for choosing the features of your plan.
parts.answer: Independent measures: customers each visit only once, so a repeated measures design is not practical and order effects are avoided; alternating days balances out weekday differences. Sales records: objective, quantitative and already collected by the bakery, so customers are unaware they are being studied (no demand characteristics) and the measure is reliable.
parts.working: 3 marks for each of two choices: 1 identifies the choice, 1 explains why it is appropriate, 1 links to the plan or psychological evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the findings of research by Milliman on music tempo in a supermarket.
parts.answer: When slow-tempo music was played, shoppers moved through the store more slowly and sales were higher than when fast-tempo music was played.
parts.working: 1 mark: slow music slowed shoppers' pace; 1 mark: higher sales with slow music.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how a Karachi supermarket manager could apply these findings, and give one reason why this might not work.
parts.answer: Play slow music during quiet weekday hours to encourage longer browsing; however, at busy times slow movement may cause crowding and annoy shoppers, so faster music might be better then (or local shoppers may prefer different music).
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable application; 1 mark: limitation (crowding, cultural differences, customer purpose such as quick top-up shopping).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'congruence' between scent and other features of a store, using research to support your answer.
parts.answer: Congruence is when the scent fits the store, its products or other atmospheric cues such as music. Spangenberg et al. found that a Christmas scent produced more favourable evaluations of a store when Christmas music was also played, but less favourable evaluations with non-Christmas music.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of congruence; 1 mark: supporting research evidence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ali owns a perfume and attar shop in Rawalpindi. Suggest two ways he could use the physical environment to increase sales during Eid.
parts.answer: 1) Use a light, festive scent congruent with his products (e.g. a mild rose or oud attar) diffused in the shop, as congruent scents improve evaluations and approach behaviour. 2) Use warm lighting and an uncluttered layout with testers displayed at the front, so customers can browse comfortably; play quiet traditional music congruent with Eid, as music that fits the setting creates a positive mood.
parts.working: 2 marks per suggestion: 1 for a suitable suggestion, 1 for justification from psychology.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which packaging can influence consumer choice.
parts.answer: Colour: colours carry associations, e.g. green packaging suggests a natural or healthy product, so consumers may judge the product as healthier. Shape and size: a tall, slim bottle may look as if it holds more, or an attractive shape stands out on a crowded shelf and attracts attention, increasing the chance of purchase.
parts.working: 2 marks each: 1 for the feature (colour, shape, size, labels/information, material), 1 for how it influences perception or choice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how McClure et al. investigated the effect of brand knowledge on preferences for cola drinks.
parts.answer: Participants tasted cola drinks in a brain scanner (fMRI). In some trials they did not know which brand they were drinking (blind tasting); in others they were told or shown the brand (e.g. a Coke label) before tasting. Their preferences and brain activity were compared across these conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: blind tasting vs brand-labelled tasting; drinks delivered while in an fMRI scanner; preferences/stated choices recorded; brain activity compared.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one finding of this study.
parts.answer: Knowing that the drink was Coke increased people's preference for it, compared with blind tasting.
parts.working: 1 mark: brand knowledge (Coke) biased preferences; accept activation of brain areas linked to memory and higher thinking (e.g. hippocampus, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex) when the brand was known.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the blind-tasting condition was needed.
parts.answer: It showed preference based on taste alone, so any change when the brand was known could be attributed to brand knowledge rather than the taste of the drink.
parts.working: 1 mark: baseline/control based on taste only; 1 mark: allows effect of brand to be isolated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal is launching a new brand of packaged chai for busy young professionals in Pakistan. Suggest how he could use psychology to design the product's name and packaging.
parts.answer: Name: choose a short, easy-to-pronounce name that is easy to remember and conveys the benefit (e.g. a word suggesting energy or speed), because easy-to-process names are liked more and remembered better. Packaging: use colours associated with warmth and energy (e.g. deep red or gold) and a modern, simple design that stands out on the shelf and matches the young professional image; include clear information about preparation time to show convenience.
parts.working: 1 mark per relevant suggestion with justification, up to 4; suggestions must apply to Bilal's product and use psychology (memorability, colour associations, brand image, attention).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the individual versus situational explanations debate.
parts.answer: Individual explanations say behaviour is caused by characteristics of the person (e.g. personality, preferences, biology); situational explanations say behaviour is caused by features of the environment (e.g. packaging, price, store setting).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how research on the product supports a situational explanation of consumer choice.
parts.answer: Blind taste tests show that preferences change when the brand label is visible, so the choice is driven by information in the situation (the packaging/brand) rather than only by the person's own taste.
parts.working: 1 mark: situational feature of the product influences choice; 1 mark: example from research.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe research into how product information, such as brand or price, affects how consumers experience a product.
parts.answer: McClure et al. used fMRI while participants tasted colas: when they knew a drink was Coke, their preference for it increased compared with blind tasting, and brain areas linked to memory and higher thinking were more active – brand associations changed the experience. Plassmann et al. found that when the same wine was presented with a higher price, participants rated it as more pleasant and activity in an area of the brain linked to pleasure (medial orbitofrontal cortex) increased – a price–quality heuristic. Blind taste tests in general show that people often cannot identify their 'favourite' brand without the label.
parts.working: Credit named studies, procedure, findings and explanations (brand associations, price–quality heuristic, expectation). Marks: 1 mark per accurate point, or 2 for a well-detailed point, up to 6; the answer should name the research and its findings in detail for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate research into how product information affects how consumers experience a product, including a discussion of the use of physiological measures.
parts.answer: Physiological measures (fMRI): objective evidence that brand/price information changes brain responses, not just what people say – avoids social desirability; but scanners are artificial (lying still, drinks via tubes), samples are small and costly, and brain activity is correlational and open to interpretation (reverse inference). Other points: laboratory control allows causal conclusions about the label; low ecological validity – tasting tiny amounts is unlike real consumption; generalisability across cultures and brands (Coke is unusually familiar); application – explains why branding and pricing are effective; ethics – raises concerns about 'neuromarketing'; reductionism – reduces preference to brain areas.
parts.working: Must include physiological measures (named issue). Level 4 (9–10): a range of well-developed evaluative points, including the named issue, with effective use of examples from research; clear structure. Level 3 (6–8): several evaluative points, mostly developed; the named issue covered. Level 2 (3–5): limited evaluation, mostly undeveloped; the named issue may be missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief, general points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

stem: A researcher at a university in Faisalabad asked 30 students to taste three mango juices from unlabelled cups and to rank them in order of preference.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the taste test was carried out 'blind'.
parts.answer: So that participants rated the juices on taste alone; if they could see the brands, their existing brand loyalty and expectations would affect their ratings.
parts.working: 1 mark: brand not visible; 1 mark: removes the effect of expectations/brand image.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the order in which the three juices were tasted was varied between participants.
parts.answer: To counterbalance order effects – e.g. the first juice might seem better because the participant was thirsty, or later juices worse because of aftertaste – so these effects are spread equally across the juices.
parts.working: 1 mark: counterbalancing/order effects; 1 mark: example of an order effect in tasting.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of measuring participants' preferences, other than asking them to rank the juices.
parts.answer: Ask them to rate each juice from 1 (very unpleasant) to 9 (very pleasant), or measure how much of each juice they drink when offered freely.
parts.working: 1 mark: a different, operationalised measure (rating scale, amount consumed, choice of a free bottle).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe utility theory and satisficing as explanations of consumer decision-making.
parts.answer: Utility theory: consumers are rational; they consider all available options and their features, and choose the one that gives the greatest overall value (utility). Satisficing (Simon): consumers do not have the time or ability to compare every option, so they choose the first option that meets their minimum requirements – 'good enough' rather than the best.
parts.working: 2 marks per theory: 1 for the basic idea, 1 for elaboration or example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of satisficing in an everyday purchase.
parts.answer: When buying a pen at a stationery shop, a student picks the first one that writes well and costs under Rs 100 rather than comparing every brand.
parts.working: 1 mark: everyday example; 1 mark: shows a minimum standard accepted without full comparison.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Farah visits an electronics market in Karachi to buy a mobile phone. The shop shows her more than 40 models, and she leaves without buying anything. Suggest how psychology could explain her behaviour and how the shop could make a sale more likely.
parts.answer: Choice overload: when there are too many options, comparing them is difficult and people worry about making the wrong choice, so they may delay or avoid deciding (Iyengar and Lepper found more people bought jam when 6 rather than 24 varieties were offered). The shop could ask Farah about her needs and budget and then show only three or four suitable phones, or group phones into clear categories (e.g. 'best for camera', 'best battery'), making comparison easier.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies choice overload; 1 mark: explains why (difficult comparison/anticipated regret); 1 mark: evidence; 1 mark: practical suggestion for the shop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the procedure of Iyengar and Lepper's jam study.
parts.answer: A tasting booth was set up in an upmarket grocery store. On some occasions it offered 24 varieties of jam (extensive choice) and on others 6 (limited choice). Researchers recorded how many passing shoppers stopped at the booth and how many later used the discount coupon they were given to buy a jar of jam.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: field setting in a grocery store; 24 vs 6 jams; conditions alternated over time; number stopping recorded; purchases measured by use of discount coupons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline the findings of the study.
parts.answer: More shoppers stopped at the booth with 24 jams, but a much higher proportion of those who saw only 6 jams went on to buy one.
parts.working: 1 mark: extensive choice attracted more shoppers; 1 mark: limited choice led to more purchases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one strength of this study.
parts.answer: It was a field experiment with real shoppers making real purchases, so it has high ecological validity and they were unaware of being studied, so demand characteristics were low.
parts.working: 1 mark: identify (ecological validity, realistic behaviour, no demand characteristics, objective measure via coupons); 1 mark: explain in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe prospect theory as an explanation of consumer decision-making.
parts.answer: Kahneman and Tversky proposed that people evaluate outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, not in terms of final wealth. Losses are felt more strongly than equal gains (loss aversion), e.g. losing Rs 1,000 feels worse than gaining Rs 1,000 feels good. People are risk-averse for gains but risk-seeking to avoid losses. This explains framing effects: '20 % off' or 'save Rs 500' (a gain) and 'avoid paying Rs 500 extra' (a loss) can lead to different choices though the outcome is the same; and why 'free trial' offers work – once owned, giving up a product feels like a loss.
parts.working: Credit: reference point; gains vs losses; loss aversion; risk attitudes; framing with examples; application to consumers. Marks: 1 mark per accurate point, or 2 for a well-detailed point, up to 6; the answer should name the research and its findings in detail for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate prospect theory as an explanation of consumer decision-making, including a discussion of the usefulness of the theory.
parts.answer: Usefulness: explains and predicts real behaviour such as framing of discounts, free trials, money-back guarantees; marketers and policymakers use it (e.g. framing health messages). Strengths: supported by many experiments showing loss aversion and framing; more realistic than utility theory, which assumes rational choice. Weaknesses: much evidence comes from hypothetical choices in laboratory experiments with students, so low ecological validity; does not explain individual differences (experts, wealthy people may be less loss averse) – individual vs situational; cultural differences in risk attitude; describes rather than fully explains why losses loom larger; reductionist about emotion and social influences; ethics of using framing to manipulate consumers.
parts.working: Must include usefulness (named issue). Level 4 (9–10): a range of well-developed evaluative points, including the named issue, with effective use of examples from research; clear structure. Level 3 (6–8): several evaluative points, mostly developed; the named issue covered. Level 2 (3–5): limited evaluation, mostly undeveloped; the named issue may be missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief, general points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shoe shop in Lahore labels a pair of shoes 'Was Rs 9,000 – now Rs 5,499'. Explain how the anchoring heuristic could influence customers.
parts.answer: The original price (Rs 9,000) acts as an anchor; customers judge the new price relative to it, so Rs 5,499 seems like a bargain even if it is the normal market price.
parts.working: 1 mark: anchor = first number seen; 1 mark: later judgement made relative to it → perceived bargain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The shop also displays a sign: 'Only 3 pairs left in your size!' Explain why this might increase sales.
parts.answer: Scarcity heuristic: people assume items that are scarce are more valuable and fear missing out (a potential loss), so they decide quickly without comparing alternatives.
parts.working: 1 mark: scarcity heuristic/value; 1 mark: urgency/fear of loss → faster decision.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one ethical issue with using these techniques.
parts.answer: If the 'was' price was never really charged or the stock is not actually low, customers are being deceived and pushed into decisions they might regret, which exploits cognitive biases.
parts.working: 1 mark: deception/manipulation; 1 mark: consequence for consumers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a study to investigate whether the number of options displayed affects the likelihood of customers buying a product in a Pakistani supermarket. Your plan must include a field experiment and quantitative data.
parts.answer: A possible plan: field experiment in a large Lahore supermarket; IV – a promotional stand displaying either 5 or 20 varieties of a new brand of biscuits (all equally priced); conditions alternate in four-hour blocks over two weeks, balanced across days and times; DV – (i) the percentage of passing shoppers who stop at the stand (counted by two covert observers) and (ii) the percentage of stoppers who buy, measured by a numbered discount voucher redeemed at the till; independent measures; controls – same location, same staff member with a standard script, same price and discount, no other promotions; ethics – public place, no personal data, store manager's permission.
parts.working: Mark points: IV with two operationalised levels; DV quantitative and operationalised; field setting; design and allocation; controls; data recording; sample; ethics. Level 4 (9–10): detailed, coherent plan covering all the required features with clear operationalisation. Level 3 (6–8): clear plan with most features. Level 2 (3–5): basic plan, several features missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief/muddled. 0: no creditworthy response.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the psychological knowledge on which your plan is based.
parts.answer: Choice overload: Iyengar and Lepper found more shoppers stopped at a 24-jam display but a higher proportion bought when only 6 jams were offered; too many options make comparison hard and increase fear of choosing wrongly, leading to decision avoidance. Satisficing (Simon) suggests consumers accept a 'good enough' option when options are limited; utility theory would predict more choice is always better, which the study tests. Bounded rationality – limited cognitive capacity for comparing many attributes.
parts.working: Credit relevant theory and evidence linked to the plan. Level 4 (7–8): accurate, detailed psychology (named theory/studies) clearly linked to the plan. Level 3 (5–6): mostly accurate and linked. Level 2 (3–4): basic or partly relevant. Level 1 (1–2): brief or anecdotal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons for choosing the features of your plan.
parts.answer: Field experiment: shoppers make real decisions with their own money, giving high ecological validity, and are unaware of being studied, reducing demand characteristics. Discount voucher: provides objective, quantitative evidence of purchase that can be linked to the condition, rather than relying on shoppers saying what they intend to buy.
parts.working: 3 marks for each of two choices: 1 identifies the choice, 1 explains why it is appropriate, 1 links to the plan or psychological evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the AIDA model of advertising.
parts.answer: AIDA describes the stages an advert should take a consumer through: Attention – the advert must first be noticed (e.g. bright colours, a celebrity); Interest – it must keep the consumer engaged with information about the product; Desire – it must make the consumer want the product by showing its benefits; Action – it must prompt the consumer to buy (e.g. 'order today').
parts.working: 1 mark for each stage correctly described; naming the four stages without description earns 1 mark at most.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one weakness of the AIDA model.
parts.answer: It assumes consumers move through the stages in a fixed order, but many purchases (e.g. cheap snacks) are made on impulse without passing through interest and desire.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness (linear, ignores impulse buying, emotional responses, post-purchase stage); 1 mark: explanation/example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'high self-monitor' and a 'low self-monitor' in Snyder and DeBono's research.
parts.answer: High self-monitors pay close attention to social situations and change their behaviour to create the right image; low self-monitors act according to their own inner values and attitudes regardless of the situation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the two types of advertisement used in Snyder and DeBono's research.
parts.answer: Image-oriented adverts, which linked the product with a desirable image or lifestyle; and quality-oriented adverts, which made claims about the quality, taste or performance of the product itself.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Outline the main findings of this research.
parts.answer: High self-monitors responded more favourably to image-oriented adverts (and were willing to pay more for products advertised that way), whereas low self-monitors responded more favourably to quality-oriented adverts.
parts.working: 1 mark: high self-monitors – image; 1 mark: low self-monitors – quality.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sara works for an agency planning an advertising campaign for a new running shoe aimed at young people in Karachi. Suggest how she could use psychology to make the campaign effective.
parts.answer: She could use product placement in popular local web dramas or music videos watched by young people, because repeated exposure in an entertaining context builds familiarity and positive attitudes. She could use a well-liked young athlete or influencer, as an attractive, credible source increases persuasion and links the shoe with a desirable image (appealing to high self-monitors), while also stating quality features such as grip and comfort (appealing to low self-monitors, as Snyder and DeBono found).
parts.working: 1 mark per relevant, justified suggestion, up to 4; must apply to Sara's campaign and use psychology.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the nomothetic versus idiographic debate.
parts.answer: The nomothetic approach looks for general laws that apply to all or most people, usually using large samples and quantitative data; the idiographic approach focuses on the unique individual and their detailed experiences, often using qualitative methods.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how Snyder and DeBono's research on advertising combines nomothetic and idiographic ideas.
parts.answer: It is nomothetic because it seeks general rules about how types of people respond to types of advert, using a standard self-monitoring scale; but it recognises that individuals differ in personality, so it moves away from a single rule for everyone towards matching adverts to individual differences.
parts.working: 1 mark: nomothetic elements (general rules, scale scores, groups); 1 mark: recognition of individual differences (closer to idiographic).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe research into product placement in films and television.
parts.answer: Product placement is when a brand appears in a film or programme as part of the content rather than as an advert. Auty and Lewis showed children a film clip in which a well-known cola brand appeared, while a control group saw a clip without it; children who had seen the brand were more likely to choose that cola when later offered a drink, suggesting placement influences choice even without explicit advertising. Explanations include mere exposure (familiarity increases liking) and priming – the brand is more accessible in memory at the point of choice. Placements that are central to the plot are remembered better than background ones.
parts.working: Credit definition, named research with procedure and findings, explanations (mere exposure, priming). Marks: 1 mark per accurate point, or 2 for a well-detailed point, up to 6; the answer should name the research and its findings in detail for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate research into product placement, including a discussion of the use of children in research.
parts.answer: Children: they are an important target audience, so research with them has high usefulness for regulating advertising aimed at children; but they cannot give fully informed consent (parental consent needed), may be more easily influenced, and may give answers to please adults (demand characteristics). Other points: experimental control shows cause and effect; low ecological validity – short clips and immediate choice differ from watching a whole film at home; effects may be short-lived; cultural differences in brands; ethics of influencing children without awareness; application to policy (e.g. limiting placement in children's programmes).
parts.working: Must include use of children (named issue). Level 4 (9–10): a range of well-developed evaluative points, including the named issue, with effective use of examples from research; clear structure. Level 3 (6–8): several evaluative points, mostly developed; the named issue covered. Level 2 (3–5): limited evaluation, mostly undeveloped; the named issue may be missing. Level 1 (1–2): brief, general points. 0: nothing creditworthy.

stem: A company in Pakistan has launched a television advert for a new washing powder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two ways the company could measure the effectiveness of its television advert.
parts.answer: 1) A recall test: a day after the advert is broadcast, telephone a random sample of viewers and ask which washing powder adverts they remember (unaided recall), giving a percentage who recall the brand. 2) Compare weekly sales of the washing powder in shops in the region for four weeks before and four weeks after the campaign starts.
parts.working: 2 marks each: 1 for the method, 1 for an operationalised detail (who, when, how measured).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using sales figures to measure the effectiveness of an advert.
parts.answer: Sales may change for other reasons, such as a price cut, a competitor's product being unavailable or seasonal changes, so an increase cannot definitely be attributed to the advert.
parts.working: 1 mark: confounding factors; 1 mark: example.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Customers at a bank in Lahore complain about long waits. Suggest how the bank could use psychology to make waiting feel shorter.
parts.answer: Occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time, so the bank could provide a television, reading material or forms to fill in while customers wait. Uncertain waits feel longer, so a token system with a display showing how many people are ahead and the expected waiting time would help. Unfair waits feel longer, so a single queue with numbered tokens (first come, first served) prevents people pushing in.
parts.working: 1 mark per relevant, justified suggestion, up to 4 (occupy time, reduce uncertainty, explain delays, ensure fairness, start the service process early).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Research on menu design found that diners spent more when prices were shown as plain numbers (for example '12') than when they included a currency sign or were written in words. Suggest one explanation for this finding.
parts.answer: The currency sign reminds diners that they are spending money, which may make them feel the 'pain of paying' and choose cheaper items; plain numbers make prices less noticeable.
parts.working: 1 mark: currency sign makes spending/cost salient; 1 mark: leads to more cautious choices (pain of paying).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a restaurant in Islamabad could design its menu to increase spending, using psychological principles.
parts.answer: Place high-profit dishes where diners look first or at the top of a section (primacy), or box/highlight them to attract attention; use descriptive names (e.g. 'slow-cooked Peshawari lamb karahi') to make dishes seem more appealing; include a very expensive 'decoy' dish so the next most expensive item seems reasonable (anchoring); list prices without currency signs and without lining them up in a column, so diners do not compare on price alone.
parts.working: 1 mark per relevant suggestion with justification, up to 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how personal space and crowding can affect customers' behaviour in a restaurant.
parts.answer: When tables are placed close together, diners' personal space is invaded; they may feel uncomfortable, unable to have a private conversation and less satisfied, and may leave sooner or not return. Perceived crowding (a psychological feeling, not just density) increases stress and reduces enjoyment, especially when people feel they lack control; however, some lively, low-cost restaurants may benefit from a busy atmosphere, which signals popularity.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: invasion of personal space; discomfort/privacy concerns; behavioural effects (shorter stay, lower satisfaction, avoidance); perceived crowding vs density / perceived control; context-dependent effects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why it may be difficult to generalise research on personal space in restaurants to different cultures.
parts.answer: Norms about comfortable distances differ between cultures; for example, in some cultures people sit close together and see closeness as friendly, while in others greater distance is expected, so findings from one country may not apply in Pakistan or elsewhere.
parts.working: 1 mark: cultural differences in personal space norms; 1 mark: consequence for generalisation with example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one similarity between the samples used by Milgram (obedience) and Piliavin et al. (subway Samaritans).
parts.answer: Both samples were drawn from the USA (Americans living in or near a city), so both studied American adults.
parts.working: 1 mark for the similarity (e.g. both American / both adults); 1 mark for linking it to both studies (Milgram: men from the New Haven area; Piliavin: passengers on the New York subway).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one difference between the samples used in these two studies.
