parts.answer: Milgram's 40 participants were all male volunteers who answered an advertisement; Piliavin's participants were thousands of male and female passengers who did not volunteer and did not know they were in a study.
parts.working: 1 mark for the difference identified (gender mix / volunteer vs unaware / sample size); 1 mark for detail from both studies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the procedure of the study by Hölzel et al. (mindfulness and brain scans).
parts.answer: Participants who joined an 8-week Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) course were given MRI brain scans before and after the course; a waiting-list control group was scanned at the same times without doing the course. Participants recorded their home meditation practice and completed a mindfulness questionnaire. Grey matter concentration in chosen brain areas (e.g. the hippocampus) was compared before and after.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to four points: 8-week MBSR course (weekly group sessions plus daily home practice); MRI scans before and after; waiting-list control group; home practice recorded / mindfulness questionnaire; comparison of grey matter concentration in regions of interest such as the left hippocampus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one similarity and one difference between the study by Hölzel et al. and the study by Dement and Kleitman (sleep and dreams).
parts.answer: Similarity: both used objective physiological measuring equipment (MRI scans in Hölzel; EEG recordings of brain waves and eye movements in Dement and Kleitman), giving quantitative data less open to bias. Difference: Hölzel et al. compared an MBSR group with a separate control group (independent measures), whereas Dement and Kleitman had no separate control group – each of the nine participants was woken in different sleep stages (repeated measures).
parts.working: Similarity (4): identified 1; explained 1; example from Hölzel 1; example from Dement and Kleitman 1. Difference (4): identified 1; explained 1; example from each study 1 + 1. Other creditworthy points: both biological approach; both small samples; difference in setting (sleep laboratory overnight vs scans at a hospital/medical centre plus normal daily life).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the sample used in the study by Baron-Cohen et al. (eyes test).
parts.answer: Several groups of adults were tested: a group of adults with Asperger syndrome or high-functioning autism, a large group of adults from the general population, a group of university students, and a small group of adults with Tourette syndrome. Most participants were from the UK.
parts.working: 1 mark for each group correctly described (AS/HFA adults; general population adults; UK university students; adults with Tourette syndrome as a comparison group); credit sample sizes if correct (15, 122, 103, 14).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one similarity and one difference between the study by Baron-Cohen et al. and the study by Andrade (doodling).
parts.answer: Similarity: both collected quantitative data from a test (number of correct answers on the 36-item Eyes Test; number of names and places recalled in Andrade), which makes comparison between groups straightforward. Difference: Andrade randomly allocated participants to a doodling or non-doodling condition (a laboratory experiment with a manipulated IV), whereas Baron-Cohen et al. compared pre-existing groups such as adults with and without Asperger syndrome (a quasi-experiment; the IV was not manipulated).
parts.working: Similarity (4) and difference (4): 1 identify, 1 explain, 1 + 1 examples from each study. Accept other valid points, e.g. both cognitive approach; both done in controlled conditions; Andrade used deception (surprise memory test) whereas the Eyes Test aim was clear.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one similarity and one difference between the study by Bandura et al. (aggression) and the study by Saavedra and Silverman (button phobia).
parts.answer: Similarity: both studied children and both explain behaviour as learned rather than innate – Bandura showed aggression is imitated from a model; Saavedra and Silverman showed a phobia (and its disgust response) can be learned and changed through conditioning-based therapy. Difference: Bandura et al. used a large sample (72 children) in a controlled laboratory experiment with groups, whereas Saavedra and Silverman was a case study of one 9-year-old boy, so it gave detailed, idiographic data that cannot be generalised in the same way.
parts.working: Similarity: identified 1, explained 1, example from Bandura 1, example from Saavedra and Silverman 1. Difference: identified 1, explained 1, examples 1 + 1. Credit: method (experiment vs case study), type of learning (social learning vs classical/evaluative conditioning), data (observation counts vs self-rated distress such as a fear thermometer).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the results of the study by Hassett et al. (monkey toy preferences).
parts.answer: Male rhesus monkeys showed a consistent and strong preference for wheeled (masculine) toys over plush (feminine) toys. Female monkeys showed more varied preferences, interacting with both types of toy, with some preferring plush toys. The pattern was similar to the toy preferences found in human children.
parts.working: 1 mark per point: males preferred wheeled toys; females' preferences more variable / interacted with both; some females preferred plush; similarity to human children; conclusion credited only if linked to results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one similarity and one difference between the study by Hassett et al. and the study by Fagen et al. (elephant learning).
parts.answer: Similarity: both studied non-human animals living in a social/managed setting (rhesus monkeys at a field station; juvenile elephants in Nepal), which raises the question of how far findings generalise to humans. Difference: Hassett et al. supports a nature explanation – the monkeys showed gender-typed toy preferences without human socialisation – whereas Fagen et al. shows nurture: the elephants' new behaviours were trained using positive reinforcement with food rewards and a bridging stimulus.
parts.working: Similarity 4 marks (identify, explain, two examples); difference 4 marks (identify, explain, two examples). Accept: observation of free choice (Hassett) vs training procedure (Fagen); both raise animal welfare issues handled carefully.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one similarity between the study by Milgram (obedience) and the study by Perry et al. (personal space) in terms of the research method.
parts.answer: Both were controlled laboratory studies with a standardised procedure, so all participants experienced the same conditions (e.g. the same prods in Milgram; the same nasal spray procedure and distance task in Perry et al.).
parts.working: 1 mark for the similarity; 1 mark for an example from both studies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between these two studies in terms of the type of explanation they support.
parts.answer: Milgram's results support a situational explanation (obedience produced by the authority of the experimenter and the setting), whereas Perry et al. looked at a biological factor (oxytocin) and how its effect depended on an individual difference (the participant's level of empathy).
parts.working: 1 mark for each study's explanation, clearly contrasted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one feature that the studies by Pozzulo et al. (line-ups) and Andrade (doodling) have in common.
parts.answer: Both measured memory performance (recognition/identification accuracy in Pozzulo et al.; recall of names and places in Andrade).
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid shared feature: both cognitive; both measured memory; both laboratory-based; both quantitative data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one difference between the participants in the two studies.
parts.answer: Pozzulo et al. tested both children and adults, so age was the independent variable and was not manipulated; Andrade tested only adults (aged 18–55), and the IV (doodling or not) was manipulated by the researcher.
parts.working: 1 mark for the difference identified; 1 mark for Pozzulo detail; 1 mark for Andrade detail / effect on the type of experiment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the studies by Dement and Kleitman (sleep and dreams) and Piliavin et al. (subway Samaritans) in terms of ecological validity.
parts.answer: Piliavin et al. has higher ecological validity: it was a field experiment on a real New York subway train and passengers behaved naturally because they did not know they were being studied. Dement and Kleitman has lower ecological validity: participants slept in an unfamiliar laboratory, attached to electrodes, and were woken by a doorbell during the night, which is unlike normal sleep at home.
parts.working: 1 mark for the comparison (Piliavin higher); 1 mark Piliavin explanation; 1 mark Dement and Kleitman explanation; 1 mark for linked detail (doorbell / electrodes / avoided caffeine and alcohol vs real commuters).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ms Sana teaches at a school in Lahore. Her pupils must listen to long, dull morning announcements and forget most of them. Suggest one piece of advice Ms Sana could take from the study by Andrade (doodling).
parts.answer: Allow pupils to doodle (e.g. shade shapes on a sheet) while listening, because in Andrade's study doodlers recalled more information from a boring message than non-doodlers.
parts.working: 1 mark for advice; 1 mark for the link to Andrade's finding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why this advice might not work for Ms Sana's pupils.
parts.answer: Andrade's participants were adults (18–55) listening to a monotonous telephone message in a quiet room; school children may find doodling distracting or turn it into drawing, so the effect may not generalise.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reason; 1 mark for explanation linked to Andrade's sample or task.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The manager of a shopping mall in Karachi is worried that shoppers do not help people who collapse. Using the study by Piliavin et al. (subway Samaritans), suggest two ethical ways the manager could increase helping.
parts.answer: 1) Lower the 'costs' of helping: clear signs and a help button / trained staff so shoppers know helping is quick and safe. 2) Make the person in need seem deserving and not responsible for their state (e.g. publicity showing that people who collapse are often ill, not drunk), because in Piliavin's study the ill victim with a cane was helped far more often than the drunk victim. The campaign must not deceive or frighten shoppers.
parts.working: For each suggestion: 1 mark practical idea, 1 mark link to Piliavin (cost–reward model; ill victim helped more than drunk victim; helping was quicker for the cane victim). Max 2 if not ethical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mr and Mrs Qureshi let their six-year-old son watch cartoons in which characters hit each other. Using the study by Bandura et al. (aggression), explain one piece of advice you could give the parents.
parts.answer: Limit the aggressive cartoons and choose programmes with non-aggressive role models, because Bandura et al. found that children who watched an adult model hitting a Bobo doll imitated specific aggressive acts, especially when the model was the same sex as the child.
parts.working: 1 mark advice; 1 mark Bandura result; 1 mark explanation of observational learning / imitation of same-sex model.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The keepers at a wildlife park in Islamabad need their elephants to keep still while blood samples are taken. Using the study by Fagen et al. (elephant learning), suggest how the keepers could train the elephants.
parts.answer: Use positive reinforcement: reward each small step towards the target behaviour (e.g. presenting an ear or leg) with a preferred food. Pair the food with a bridging stimulus (a sound such as a whistle) so the elephant knows exactly which action earned the reward, and shape the full behaviour gradually over short daily sessions.
parts.working: 1 mark each: positive reinforcement with food; bridging stimulus / secondary reinforcer; shaping in small steps; link to Fagen (juvenile elephants in Nepal trained for a trunk-wash procedure using positive reinforcement instead of negative methods).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A software company in Bengaluru wants to reduce stress among its staff. Using the study by Hölzel et al., suggest how the company could do this.
parts.answer: Offer an 8-week mindfulness course (like MBSR) with weekly group sessions and short daily home practice, because Hölzel et al. found increases in grey matter concentration in areas such as the hippocampus, linked to learning, memory and emotion regulation, after such a course.
parts.working: 1 mark suggestion; 1 mark detail of programme; 1 mark link to findings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why taking part in the course must be voluntary.
parts.answer: Staff must give informed consent and have the right to withdraw; forcing them would break ethical guidelines and could itself cause stress.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A police officer in Faisalabad plans to ask a seven-year-old girl, who saw a theft, to pick the thief from a line-up. Using the study by Pozzulo et al. (line-ups), explain two pieces of advice you would give the officer.
parts.answer: 1) Tell the child clearly that the thief may not be in the line-up and that it is fine to say 'not there', because Pozzulo et al. found children were more likely than adults to choose someone when the culprit was absent (more false identifications). 2) Treat a child's identification with caution and look for other evidence, because children's identification accuracy in target-absent line-ups was poorer than adults'. The child should be supported and not pressured.
parts.working: Each advice: 1 mark for the advice, 1 mark for link to Pozzulo's finding that children made more errors than adults in target-absent line-ups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether Milgram (obedience) followed the ethical guideline of the right to withdraw.
parts.answer: It was not fully followed: participants were told they could keep the money whatever happened, but when they tried to stop, the experimenter used verbal prods (e.g. 'You have no other choice, you must go on'), making it hard to withdraw.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark evidence from the study.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether Milgram followed the ethical guideline of debriefing.
parts.answer: It was followed: after the session participants met the unharmed learner and were told the shocks were not real; they were later sent a report and a follow-up questionnaire.
parts.working: 1 mark decision; 1 mark evidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two students disagree. Ayesha says the study by Piliavin et al. (subway Samaritans) was unethical. Hamza says it was ethical. Explain one point that supports Ayesha and one point that supports Hamza.
parts.answer: Ayesha: passengers did not give informed consent and were deceived – they believed a real person had collapsed, which may have caused distress, and they were not debriefed. Hamza: the situation was one that could happen in everyday life, the ride lasted only a few minutes, the 'victim' was helped by the model if no one else did, and consent would have destroyed the natural behaviour being studied.
parts.working: 2 marks for each side: 1 for the point, 1 for linking to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one way in which Hassett et al. (monkey toy preferences) protected the welfare of their animals.
parts.answer: The monkeys lived in their normal social groups in a large outdoor enclosure at a field station and were simply offered toys to play with, so they were not isolated, deprived or harmed.
parts.working: 1 mark point; 1 mark detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one way in which the study by Bandura et al. (aggression) may have broken the ethical guideline of protection from harm.
parts.answer: Children were exposed to an adult hitting a Bobo doll and were then deliberately frustrated (attractive toys taken away), which may have upset them or encouraged aggressive behaviour that lasted after the study.
parts.working: 1 mark point; 1 mark detail.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the researchers could have reduced this risk.
parts.answer: Return the children to play with the attractive toys and a friendly adult afterwards, and explain to parents/teachers what happened so they could watch for and correct any copied aggression.
parts.working: 1 mark suggestion; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the study by Andrade (doodling) involved deception.
parts.answer: Participants were not told that their memory would be tested; the recall test was a surprise so that they would not deliberately rehearse the names, which would have made the results invalid.
parts.working: 1 mark: memory test was a surprise / true aim hidden; 1 mark: reason (avoid rehearsal / demand characteristics).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way this deception could be justified.
parts.answer: The deception was mild and unlikely to cause distress, and participants could be debriefed afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the study by Milgram (obedience) in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about ethics.
parts.answer: Strengths could include: high internal validity through a standardised procedure (same prods, same 15 V steps, scripted learner responses); quantitative data (65% went to 450 V) allowing clear comparison; usefulness in explaining real obedience; debriefing and follow-up questionnaire showed most participants were glad to have taken part. Weaknesses could include: ethical problems – deception about the shocks, psychological distress (sweating, nervous laughter) and pressure from prods against the right to withdraw; a sample of 40 American men only, limiting generalisability; low ecological validity of giving shocks to a stranger.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): four developed points, each well linked to Milgram, ethics point detailed and two-sided; balanced. Level 3 (6–8): four points, mostly developed, or three well developed. Level 2 (3–5): points identified with limited development or link. Level 1 (1–2): vague or one point. Max 6 if no ethics point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by the individual versus situational explanations debate.
parts.answer: Whether behaviour is caused by factors within the person (personality, attitudes, biology, e.g. empathy) or by factors in the environment around them (e.g. setting, other people, rewards).
parts.working: 1 mark individual side; 1 mark situational side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a situational explanation and one example of an individual explanation from the study by Piliavin et al. (subway Samaritans).
parts.answer: Situational: the type of victim – the ill victim with a cane was helped more often than the drunk victim. Individual: the passenger's own race / gender – helpers were more often male, and same-race helping tended to be higher for the drunk victim.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the study by Fagen et al. (elephant learning) can be used to support both sides of the individual versus situational debate.
parts.answer: Situational: the elephants learned the new behaviours because of the training environment – positive reinforcement with food and a bridging stimulus changed their behaviour. Individual: the elephants did not all learn at the same speed or reach the same level, showing that differences between individual animals (e.g. temperament, motivation) also affected learning.
parts.working: 2 marks each side: 1 point, 1 link to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether the results of Milgram's study (obedience) support a situational explanation more than an individual explanation.
parts.answer: Mostly situational: 65% of ordinary men gave the maximum 450 V when ordered by an experimenter in a lab-coat at Yale, and all went to at least 300 V, suggesting the authority and setting rather than personality produced obedience. But 35% defied the experimenter and participants varied in the point at which they stopped and in their tension, so individual differences also mattered; the conclusion is that the situation had a strong effect but did not fully determine behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark situational evidence; 1 mark explanation; 1 mark individual evidence; 1 mark reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two psychologists disagree about the validity of the Revised Eyes Test used by Baron-Cohen et al. One says it validly measures theory of mind; the other says it does not. Explain one point for each view.
parts.answer: Valid: adults with Asperger syndrome/high-functioning autism scored lower than the comparison groups, as theory predicts, and scores correlated negatively with the Autism Spectrum Quotient. Not valid: the test uses still, black-and-white photographs of the eye region only, whereas in real life people read emotions from whole moving faces, tone of voice and context, so it may lack ecological validity.
parts.working: 2 marks each: 1 point, 1 link to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one feature of the study by Dement and Kleitman (sleep and dreams) that increased its reliability.
parts.answer: A standardised procedure: every participant was attached to the same EEG equipment, woken by the same doorbell and asked to speak into a recording device, so the study could be repeated in the same way.
parts.working: 1 mark feature; 1 mark explanation of why that improves reliability (consistency / replicability).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the study by Andrade (doodling) in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about generalisability.
parts.answer: Strengths: controlled procedure (same recorded monotonous message, same shading task, same recall test) gives high reliability and internal validity; quantitative recall scores allow objective comparison of doodlers and non-doodlers; useful application to classrooms and meetings. Weaknesses: generalisability – a small sample of 40 adults from one participant panel in the UK, recruited after another study, may not represent children or other cultures; the task (a boring phone message about a party) lacks ecological validity; the surprise memory test involved deception, which raises ethical issues.
parts.working: Levels as for 10-mark evaluation: L4 9–10 four detailed, linked points, generalisability discussed in depth; L3 6–8; L2 3–5; L1 1–2. Max 6 without a generalisability point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of using children as participants in the study by Bandura et al. (aggression).
parts.answer: Strength: young children (aged about 3–5) have had less exposure to social norms, so researchers could see whether aggression is learned by observation without much prior learning getting in the way. Weakness: children cannot give fully informed consent and are more vulnerable to harm, e.g. being frustrated and possibly learning aggressive acts.
parts.working: 2 marks each: point + link to Bandura.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the study by Pozzulo et al. (line-ups) needed to use children as participants, and describe one ethical issue this raised.
parts.answer: The aim was to compare children's and adults' eyewitness identification, so child participants were essential – children do act as real witnesses and their accuracy must be understood. Ethical issue: consent – children cannot give fully informed consent, so parental consent is needed as well as the child's agreement, and the procedure (seeing a staged event and a line-up) must not frighten them; they must be able to stop at any time.
parts.working: 2 marks reason linked to aim; 2 marks ethical issue explained with link to study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the study by Hassett et al. (monkey toy preferences) supports the nature side of the nature versus nurture debate.
parts.answer: Male rhesus monkeys preferred wheeled toys, like human boys, even though the monkeys had not been taught gender roles by human society; this suggests a biological (possibly hormonal) basis for gender-typed preferences.
parts.working: 1 mark result; 1 mark link to nature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the study by Bandura et al. (aggression) supports the nurture side.
parts.answer: Children who watched an aggressive model copied specific aggressive acts they had not shown before, so aggression was learned from the environment through observation.
parts.working: 1 mark result; 1 mark link to nurture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one way in which the study by Dement and Kleitman (sleep and dreams) relates to the nature versus nurture debate.
parts.answer: It supports nature: all participants showed the same regular cycles of REM and NREM sleep through the night, and dream recall was linked to REM sleep, suggesting that sleep stages and dreaming are biologically determined. However, dream content (what the person dreams about) is likely to be influenced by experience, which is nurture.
parts.working: 1 mark position; 1 mark evidence; 1 mark further explanation or counterpoint.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'operationalising' a variable.
parts.answer: Defining a variable precisely in terms of how it will be manipulated or measured, so that it can be tested and the study repeated.
parts.working: 1 mark: clear/precise definition; 1 mark: in measurable / testable terms (or example).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical field experiment at a bus station in Lahore tests whether people are more helpful when the person asking is smiling. Suggest how 'helpfulness' could be operationalised.
parts.answer: Whether the passer-by stops and gives directions to the bus stand within 10 seconds of being asked (recorded as helped / did not help).
parts.working: 1 mark for a measurable behaviour; 1 mark for precise detail (time limit / what counts).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study asks students how anxious they feel before a mathematics test. Write a rating scale question to measure anxiety. Your scale must have labelled anchors.
parts.answer: 'How anxious do you feel right now about the test? Circle one number: 1 = not at all anxious, 2, 3, 4, 5 = extremely anxious.'
parts.working: 1 mark for a question with a numbered scale; 1 mark for labelled anchors at both ends.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one weakness of measuring anxiety in this way.
parts.answer: Students may give socially desirable answers (e.g. boys under-reporting anxiety), so the score may not reflect their real anxiety.
parts.working: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark explanation in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher plans a hypothetical observation of aggression among children in a school playground in Rawalpindi. Suggest two behavioural categories for 'physical aggression' and two for 'verbal aggression'.
parts.answer: Physical: pushing another child with one or both hands; kicking another child. Verbal: calling another child a rude name; shouting a threat such as 'I'll hit you'.
parts.working: 1 mark for each clearly observable, operationalised category (vague terms such as 'being mean' get 0).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the categories need to be operationalised before the observation starts.
parts.answer: So that every observer records the same behaviours in the same way, which improves inter-observer reliability and makes the data objective.
parts.working: 1 mark: consistency between observers; 1 mark: reliability / objectivity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical experiment, students in Nairobi either listen to music or work in silence while learning a list of 30 words. Suggest how the dependent variable 'memory' could be operationalised.
parts.answer: The number of words (out of 30) correctly written down in 3 minutes of free recall immediately after the learning period.
parts.working: 1 mark: number of words recalled; 1 mark: detail (out of 30 / time limit / spelling rule).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the independent variable could be operationalised.
parts.answer: Music condition: an instrumental piece played through headphones at the same volume for the 5-minute learning period; silence condition: the same headphones worn with no sound.
parts.working: 1 mark for each condition clearly defined.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study investigates sleep quality among night-shift nurses in Karachi. Describe one objective and one subjective way of operationalising 'sleep quality'.
parts.answer: Objective: a wrist activity monitor records the number of minutes of sleep and the number of awakenings each night for a week. Subjective: each morning nurses rate 'How well did you sleep?' on a scale from 1 (very badly) to 10 (very well).
parts.working: 2 marks each: 1 for the method, 1 for precise measurement detail.

stem: A hypothetical experiment tests whether background traffic noise affects concentration. Each participant proofreads a page of text containing 40 planted spelling errors, once in a quiet room and once with recorded traffic noise. They have 10 minutes for each page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the researcher has operationalised 'concentration'.
parts.answer: Concentration is measured as the number of planted errors (out of 40) correctly found in the 10-minute proofreading task.
parts.working: 1 mark: number of errors found; 1 mark: out of 40 / in 10 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One participant found 34 errors in the quiet condition and 26 in the noisy condition. Calculate the percentage of errors found in each condition.
parts.answer: Quiet: 85%; noisy: 65%.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one problem with this way of measuring concentration.
parts.answer: Finding errors also depends on reading and spelling ability, not only concentration, so it may lack validity (or participants may remember error positions if the same passage is reused).
parts.working: 1 mark problem; 1 mark explanation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study investigates whether volunteers at a charity in Manchester have higher empathy than non-volunteers. Describe how 'empathy' could be operationalised in two different ways.
parts.answer: 1) Self-report: a questionnaire of 10 statements (e.g. 'I feel upset when I see someone in pain') each rated 1–5 from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree', giving a total score out of 50. 2) Behavioural/task: the number of correct emotions identified when shown 20 photographs of faces, or whether the participant offers help when a researcher 'accidentally' drops a pile of papers.
parts.working: 2 marks each: method + precise scoring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which of your two ways would give more valid data.
parts.answer: The behavioural measure may be more valid because it records what people actually do and is less affected by social desirability, which is likely to be strong for a quality such as empathy in charity volunteers.
parts.working: 1 mark choice; 1 mark justification (accept the reverse with a good reason).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study tests whether a breathing exercise reduces stress before a driving test in Dubai. Suggest how stress could be operationalised physiologically and by self-report.
parts.answer: Physiological: heart rate in beats per minute measured with a finger pulse monitor for one minute just before the test. Self-report: 'How stressed do you feel?' on a 0–10 scale where 0 = completely calm and 10 = extremely stressed.
parts.working: 2 marks each: method + unit/scale detail.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of using both measures.
parts.answer: If both measures show the same pattern, the researcher can be more confident the result is valid (triangulation); the self-report also shows how the person feels, which heart rate cannot.
parts.working: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical field experiment tests whether pupils obey a teacher more when the teacher wears a formal suit than casual clothes. The teacher asks each pupil to pick up a piece of litter. Operationalise 'obedience' so that it could be recorded reliably.
parts.answer: Obedience = the pupil picks up the litter and puts it in the bin within 15 seconds of the instruction, without the instruction being repeated. Recorded as obeyed / did not obey.
parts.working: 1 mark: specific behaviour; 1 mark: time limit; 1 mark: clear rule for what does not count (repeated request, partial compliance).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way the operationalisation of the IV could be standardised.
parts.answer: The same teacher wears the same dark suit and tie (formal) or the same jeans and T-shirt (casual) on every trial.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher in Singapore wants to measure how long teenagers spend on social media each day. Describe two ways of operationalising this variable.
parts.answer: 1) Read the phone's screen-time report for social media apps, recorded in minutes per day averaged over 7 days. 2) Ask the teenager: 'On a normal school day, about how many minutes do you spend on social media?' recorded as a number of minutes.
parts.working: 2 marks each: method + unit/time period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain which way is more likely to be reliable.
parts.answer: The screen-time report, because it is recorded automatically and the same each time it is checked, whereas teenagers' estimates may change from one occasion to the next and depend on memory.
parts.working: 1 choice; 1 reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study states: 'The dependent variable is how happy people feel after exercising.' Explain why this variable has not been operationalised.
parts.answer: It does not say how happiness will be measured (no scale, score or behaviour), so another researcher could not repeat the measurement in the same way.
parts.working: 1 mark: no measurement stated; 1 mark: consequence (not replicable / subjective).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rewrite the dependent variable so that it is operationalised.
parts.answer: The score from 1 (very unhappy) to 7 (very happy) that each participant circles on a mood scale 5 minutes after finishing a 20-minute walk.
parts.working: 1 mark measure; 1 mark timing / anchors.

stem: A hypothetical experiment tests whether caffeine improves reaction time. The IV is operationalised as either 3 mg of caffeine per kilogram of body mass, dissolved in a fruit drink, or the same fruit drink with no caffeine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the caffeine dose a participant of mass 72 kg would receive.
parts.answer: 216 mg

parts.label: b
parts.text: A drink contains 80 mg of caffeine per can. Calculate how many cans' worth of caffeine the 72 kg participant receives. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 2.7 cans

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the researcher operationalised the IV as a dose per kilogram rather than giving everyone the same amount.
parts.answer: The same amount would have a stronger effect on lighter people than heavier people, which would be a participant variable; a dose per kilogram makes the effect more equal across participants, so differences in the DV are more likely due to caffeine itself.
parts.working: 1 mark: body mass affects the effect; 1 mark: controls a participant variable / improves validity.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical observation at a farm in Punjab investigates play in young goats. Suggest two operationalised behaviour categories for 'play'.
parts.answer: Jumping with all four feet leaving the ground at once; head-butting another kid gently without injury (no chasing away afterwards).
parts.working: 1 mark each clearly observable category.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the researcher could use time sampling to record these behaviours.
parts.answer: Every 30 seconds for 20 minutes, the observer looks at a focal goat and records which category (if any) it is showing at that moment, giving 40 observations per goat.
parts.working: 1 mark: record at fixed intervals; 1 mark: detail of interval and duration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'participant variable'.
parts.answer: A characteristic of an individual participant, such as age, intelligence or personality, that could affect the DV.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment compares two methods of teaching reading to children in Hyderabad, using two different groups. Give two participant variables that could affect the results.
parts.answer: Children's existing reading ability; their age / how much English is spoken at home.
parts.working: 1 mark each, must be plausible for reading.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical laboratory experiment tests whether noise affects mental arithmetic. Identify two situational variables that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Room temperature; time of day the test is taken (also accept lighting, instructions, the experimenter).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how one of these could be controlled.
parts.answer: Test all participants in the same room with the air conditioner set to 22 °C so temperature cannot explain differences in arithmetic scores.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why participant variables are a particular problem in an independent measures design.
parts.answer: Different people are in each condition, so a difference in the DV could be caused by differences between the groups (e.g. one group being more able) rather than by the IV.
parts.working: 1 mark: different people in each condition; 1 mark: confounds the result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how random allocation could reduce this problem.
parts.answer: Put each participant's name on a slip, mix the slips in a box and draw them out, putting alternate names in condition A and B, so every participant has an equal chance of being in either group and participant variables should be spread evenly.
parts.working: 1 mark method; 1 mark how it helps.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each of the following, state whether it is a participant variable or a situational variable:
(i) a participant's handedness
(ii) the brightness of the lighting in the testing room
(iii) the friendliness of the experimenter
(iv) how tired the participant was before arriving
parts.answer: (i) participant (ii) situational (iii) situational (iv) participant
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical field experiment in a market in Karachi tests whether shoppers are more likely to take a free leaflet from a smiling or a neutral-faced researcher. Explain two situational variables that would be hard to control.
parts.answer: 1) Crowding – on busy days shoppers may hurry past and take fewer leaflets regardless of facial expression. 2) Weather – heat or rain may change how willing shoppers are to stop. These could vary between the conditions and confound the results.
parts.working: 2 marks each: variable + effect in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe participant variables and situational variables, using any examples.
parts.answer: Participant variables are characteristics of the people taking part that might affect the DV, e.g. age, IQ, gender, mood, prior experience. They matter mainly in independent measures designs and are controlled by random allocation, matched pairs or repeated measures. Situational variables are features of the environment or procedure, e.g. noise, temperature, time of day, instructions, experimenter's behaviour. They are controlled by standardisation – keeping these features the same for every participant.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks each: definition (1), example (1), how controlled / why a problem (1).

stem: A hypothetical experiment with 40 students in a college in Kuala Lumpur compares two revision techniques (flashcards and re-reading) on a French vocabulary test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a matched pairs design could be used to control participant variables in this study.
parts.answer: Give all 40 students a vocabulary pre-test; rank them by score; pair the top two, the next two and so on; then randomly put one member of each pair into the flashcard group and the other into the re-reading group. The groups then have similar starting ability.
parts.working: 1 mark pre-test on a relevant variable; 1 mark pairing; 1 mark random allocation within pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many participants would be in each condition.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one participant variable that matching on the pre-test would not control.
parts.answer: Motivation to revise / amount of revision done at home.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical experiment, a male researcher tested participants in the morning and a female researcher tested participants in the afternoon. Explain why this is a problem.
parts.answer: The researcher is a situational variable that changes with the condition/time, so any difference could be caused by the researcher (or the time of day) rather than the IV – it is a confounding variable.
parts.working: 1 mark: identify uncontrolled situational variable; 1 mark: confounding explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how this could be avoided.
parts.answer: Use one researcher for all participants, testing at the same time of day, or have each researcher test equal numbers in each condition and read from the same script.
parts.working: 1 mark suggestion; 1 mark detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical online experiment lets participants in Pakistan and Canada complete a memory task at home at any time. Explain two situational variables that the researcher cannot control.
parts.answer: 1) Time of day – some do it late at night when tired, others in the morning, which affects memory. 2) Distractions – family noise, television or phone notifications may interrupt some participants, lowering their scores.
parts.working: 2 marks each: variable + effect.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to reduce the effect of one of these variables.
parts.answer: Ask participants to complete the task between 9 am and 12 noon local time, in a quiet room with their phone switched off, and record the time from the website.
parts.working: 1 mark suggestion; 1 mark detail.

stem:
A hypothetical study compares memory scores of people using a memory-training app with people using a paper workbook. Participants chose which method to use. Their ages (years) were:
App group: 19, 21, 23, 20, 28
Paper group: 35, 41, 30, 38, 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean age of each group. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: App group: 22.2 years; paper group: 36.8 years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using your answers, explain why the researcher cannot conclude that the app caused better memory scores.
parts.answer: The app group was about 14.6 years younger on average; age is a participant variable that is linked to memory and familiarity with apps, so it is a confounding variable – the younger age, not the app, may explain the better scores.
parts.working: 1 mark: groups differ in age (with numbers); 1 mark: age could affect memory/app use; 1 mark: confounding variable so cause unclear.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the design could be improved.
parts.answer: Randomly allocate participants to conditions, or match pairs on age.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment tests whether students in Peshawar who sleep for at least 8 hours remember more facts than students who sleep for less than 5 hours. Write a directional (one-tailed) hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: Students who sleep for at least 8 hours will recall more facts (out of 20) the next morning than students who sleep for less than 5 hours.
parts.working: 1 mark: direction stated; 1 mark: both IV levels and operationalised DV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: There will be no difference in the number of facts recalled the next morning by students who sleep at least 8 hours and those who sleep less than 5 hours; any difference will be due to chance.
parts.working: 1 mark: no difference; 1 mark: IV and DV included.

stem: A hypothetical field experiment in Cairo records whether drivers stop at a zebra crossing for a pedestrian who is either a child or an elderly person.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a non-directional (two-tailed) hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: There will be a difference in the number of cars that stop (out of 100) for a pedestrian waiting at the crossing depending on whether the pedestrian is a child or an elderly person.
parts.working: 1 mark: difference without direction; 1 mark: IV and DV clear.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the researcher might choose a non-directional hypothesis.
parts.answer: Previous research does not clearly predict which pedestrian will receive more help – drivers might stop more for a child (seen as vulnerable) or for an elderly person – so the direction cannot be predicted.
parts.working: 1 mark: no clear previous research / contradictory findings; 1 mark: linked to context.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an aim and a hypothesis.
parts.answer: An aim is a general statement of what the study intends to investigate; a hypothesis is a precise, testable prediction about the expected result.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical study investigates whether players of fast action video games have quicker reaction times than non-players. Write an aim for this study.
parts.answer: To investigate whether playing fast action video games is related to reaction time.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write a directional hypothesis for the same study.
parts.answer: People who play fast action video games for at least 5 hours a week will have faster mean reaction times (in milliseconds, on a computer test) than people who never play.
parts.working: 1 direction; 1 operationalised variables.

stem: A hypothetical study with office workers in Lahore investigates whether longer commuting time is related to lower job satisfaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a directional hypothesis for this correlational study.
parts.answer: There will be a negative correlation between the number of hours per week employees spend commuting and their job satisfaction score (out of 50).
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation and direction; 1 mark: both co-variables operationalised. Do not credit wording about difference or cause.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a null hypothesis for this study.
parts.answer: There will be no correlation between hours per week spent commuting and job satisfaction score; any relationship found will be due to chance.
parts.working: 1 mark: no correlation; 1 mark: co-variables.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the researcher cannot conclude that commuting causes low job satisfaction.
parts.answer: A correlation does not show cause and effect: a third variable (e.g. lower pay meaning people live further away and are also less satisfied) could explain both.
parts.working: 1 mark: correlation not causation; 1 mark: example of a third variable or reverse direction.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hypothetical experiment in Toronto: one group chews mint gum while learning 25 words; another group does not. Both groups write down as many words as they can remember 10 minutes later.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the independent variable.
parts.answer: Whether participants chewed gum or not while learning.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the dependent variable.
parts.answer: The number of words (out of 25) recalled after 10 minutes.
parts.working: 1 mark (must be operationalised for credit).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hypothetical experiment in a sports centre in Islamabad allocates participants to sit still, walk slowly or jog, each for 15 minutes. Afterwards each person rates their mood on a scale from 1 (very low) to 10 (very good).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the three levels of the independent variable.
parts.answer: Sitting still for 15 minutes, walking slowly for 15 minutes, jogging for 15 minutes.
parts.working: 1 mark for all three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the dependent variable and state how it was measured.
parts.answer: Mood, measured by the score circled on a 1–10 mood scale (1 = very low, 10 = very good) after the activity.
parts.working: 1 mark DV; 1 mark measurement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify one variable that should be controlled and explain why.
parts.answer: Time of day / temperature – it could affect mood independently of the activity, so it must be kept the same for all conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark variable; 1 mark reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hypothetical study collects data from 60 secondary-school pupils in Mumbai on the hours of homework they do per week and their score on the end-of-term science test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the two co-variables in this study.
parts.answer: Hours of homework per week; score (%) on the end-of-term science test.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these are called co-variables rather than an independent and dependent variable.
parts.answer: Neither variable is manipulated by the researcher; both are simply measured as they occur, to see whether they change together, so neither can be said to be the cause.
parts.working: 1 mark not manipulated / measured naturally; 1 mark no cause and effect.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by an independent measures design.
parts.answer: Different participants take part in each condition of the experiment.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment in Quetta compares memory for pictures and memory for words using an independent measures design. Explain one weakness of this design for this study.
parts.answer: Participant variables such as natural memory ability may differ between the picture group and the word group, so differences in recall may be due to the people rather than the type of material.
parts.working: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark linked to context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an 'order effect' in a repeated measures design.
parts.answer: A change in performance caused by the order in which the conditions are done rather than by the IV, e.g. doing better in the second condition through practice, or worse through fatigue or boredom.
parts.working: 1 mark definition; 1 mark example (practice / fatigue / boredom).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how counterbalancing could be used in a repeated measures experiment on whether people type faster on a laptop keyboard or a phone screen.
parts.answer: Split participants into two halves: one half types on the laptop first and then the phone; the other half uses the phone first and then the laptop, so order effects are balanced across the conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: two groups in opposite orders; 1 mark: in context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a researcher could use a matched pairs design in a hypothetical experiment comparing two diets for weight loss among adults in Lagos.
parts.answer: Measure each volunteer's starting weight (and perhaps age and sex); pair people with similar starting weight; randomly allocate one member of each pair to diet A and the other to diet B.
parts.working: 1 mark: pre-measure a relevant variable; 1 mark: form pairs; 1 mark: one of each pair to each condition (randomly).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of using a matched pairs design in this study.
parts.answer: It is time-consuming to measure and match people, and if one member of a pair drops out the other's data may be lost (or matching cannot be perfect on all variables).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe repeated measures design and matched pairs design, using any examples.
parts.answer: Repeated measures: the same participants do every condition, e.g. each person takes a memory test in silence and with music. It removes participant variables between conditions and needs fewer participants, but suffers from order effects (practice, fatigue) and demand characteristics, controlled by counterbalancing. Matched pairs: different participants in each condition but each participant is paired with another who is similar on a key variable (e.g. IQ or age), one of each pair going into each condition. It reduces participant variables without order effects, but matching is time-consuming and never perfect.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks each: description (1), example (1), strength/weakness or control (1).

stem: A hypothetical experiment with 48 participants in Hong Kong tests whether people compare shop prices faster when the prices are shown as a vertical bar chart or as a horizontal bar chart. Each participant does both conditions; half do vertical first and half do horizontal first.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many participants should do the order 'vertical chart first, then horizontal chart'?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the technique the researcher is using and state its purpose.
parts.answer: Counterbalancing (ABBA / two orders); to balance out order effects such as practice and fatigue between the two conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark name; 1 mark purpose.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hypothetical repeated measures experiment with 36 students in Riyadh tests concentration in three conditions: silence, instrumental music, and speech playing in the background.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of different orders in which the three conditions could be presented.

parts.label: b
parts.text: If each order is used equally, how many participants complete each order?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How many participants do the 'speech' condition first?
parts.working: 2 of the 6 orders start with speech: 2 × 6 = 12 (or 36 ÷ 3).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why full counterbalancing of all orders is better than just using a single order for everyone.
parts.answer: With one order, the last condition would always benefit from practice or suffer from fatigue, confounding the results; using every order equally means each condition appears in each position equally often, so order effects cancel out.
parts.working: 1 mark problem with single order; 1 mark how full counterbalancing solves it.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study in Islamabad investigates whether students learn new Urdu poetry better when they study it at 8 am or at 8 pm. Explain which experimental design you would choose and why.
parts.answer: Matched pairs (or independent measures): the same poem cannot be learned twice by the same person, so repeated measures would cause practice effects; matching on a pre-test of memory ability reduces participant variables between the 8 am and 8 pm groups.
parts.working: 1 mark design; 1 mark reason against repeated measures (practice/learning the same material); 1 mark reason for chosen design.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the researcher could use a repeated measures design instead.
parts.answer: Use two different but equally difficult poems (one for each time) and counterbalance which poem is learned at which time.
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: A hypothetical experiment tests whether visitors find their way through a large hospital in Kuala Lumpur faster using a printed map or a phone map. The measure is the time taken to walk from the entrance to the eye clinic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the researcher should not use a repeated measures design.
parts.answer: After the first condition participants would already know the route, so their time in the second condition would be quicker because of learning (a practice effect), not because of the type of map.
parts.working: 1 mark practice/learning effect; 1 mark linked to route.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which design should be used and give one strength of it for this study.
parts.answer: Independent measures: each participant uses only one map, so there are no order effects and they cannot work out the aim by comparing conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark design; 1 mark strength.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study compares the spatial ability of left-handed and right-handed people. Explain why it must use an independent measures design.
parts.answer: Handedness is a characteristic of the participant that cannot be changed, so each person can only be in one condition (left-handed or right-handed).
parts.working: 1 mark: IV is a participant characteristic / not manipulated; 1 mark: so cannot be in both conditions.

stem: In a hypothetical driving-simulator study in Sydney, each participant drives for one hour while talking on a hands-free phone and then for one hour while using a hand-held phone. Reaction time to hazards is measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a fatigue effect could affect the results of this study.
parts.answer: In the second hour participants will be tired and bored, so their reaction times will be slower whatever the condition; since the hand-held phone condition always comes second, it will appear worse than it really is.
parts.working: 1 mark tiredness slows reactions; 1 mark confounds the second condition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways of reducing this problem.
parts.answer: Counterbalance the order (half do hands-free first); give a rest break between conditions / shorten each session.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a researcher could randomly allocate 30 participants to two conditions.
parts.answer: Give each participant a number from 1 to 30, put the numbers in a hat and draw them out; the first 15 drawn go to condition A and the remaining 15 to condition B (or use a random number generator).
parts.working: 1 mark random method; 1 mark equal groups / how it is used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why random allocation is used.
parts.answer: So that each participant has an equal chance of being in either condition, spreading participant variables evenly and avoiding researcher bias in choosing groups.
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: A hypothetical experiment in schools in Karachi tests whether children aged 8–10 choose a healthy snack more often after watching a cartoon advert for fruit than after watching a cartoon advert for toys.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of using an independent measures design rather than a repeated measures design in this study.
parts.answer: Strength: each child sees only one advert, so they cannot compare the adverts and guess the aim (fewer demand characteristics) and there are no order effects such as boredom. Weakness: the two groups may differ in participant variables, e.g. some children may already like sweet snacks more, which could explain any difference in snack choice instead of the advert.
parts.working: 2 marks each: point + context (children, adverts, snack choice).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a laboratory experiment to investigate whether chewing gum improves short-term memory, using a matched pairs design. Your plan should include details of the variables, the matching procedure, controls and how the data will be analysed.
parts.answer: Example plan: IV – chewing sugar-free mint gum vs not chewing; DV – number of digits recalled in the correct order on a digit-span test (strings of increasing length, read out by recording). Sample: 40 university students; pre-test on a digit-span test, rank by score, pair adjacent participants, randomly allocate one of each pair to each condition. Controls: same room, same time of day, same recorded instructions and digit lists, gum given 2 minutes before the test, no other food or drink. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, check for allergies, debrief. Data: compare mean (or median) digit span of the two conditions; bar chart.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): accurate and detailed plan covering IV and operationalised DV, clear matching procedure with random allocation within pairs, several controls, ethics and data analysis; replicable. Level 3 (6–8): most features with some detail. Level 2 (3–5): basic plan with matching mentioned but vague. Level 1 (1–2): little relevant detail. Max 4 if design is not matched pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of your plan and suggest how it could be improved.
parts.answer: Weakness: matching only on digit span leaves other participant variables, such as anxiety, unmatched. Improvement: also measure anxiety with a short rating scale and match on both, or use repeated measures with two equivalent digit lists and counterbalancing.
parts.working: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark explanation; 1 mark improvement; 1 mark why improvement helps.

stem:
A hypothetical repeated measures experiment tests reading comprehension (score out of 25) with phone notifications switched off (condition A) or on (condition B). The order was counterbalanced.
Order 1 (A then B): A scores 18, 16, 19, 17, 20; B scores 14, 13, 15, 12, 16
Order 2 (B then A): B scores 11, 12, 10, 13, 14; A scores 19, 20, 18, 21, 22

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean score for condition A and for condition B, using all ten participants.
parts.answer: Condition A: 19; condition B: 13.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain whether there is evidence of an order effect.
parts.answer: Yes, a practice effect: condition A mean was 18 when done first and 20 when done second; condition B mean was 12 when done first and 14 when done second, so each condition scored 2 more when done second.
parts.working: 1 mark: A first 18 vs second 20; 1 mark: B first 12 vs second 14; 1 mark: names practice effect / both improve when second.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the researcher can still draw a conclusion about the IV.
parts.answer: Because the design was counterbalanced, the practice effect was spread equally over both conditions, so the 6-point difference between A and B is still due to the notifications.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A hypothetical experiment in an office training centre in Lahore compares a new keyboard layout with a standard layout. Twelve learners took a typing pre-test and were formed into 6 matched pairs; one member of each pair was randomly allocated to each layout. After two weeks of practice, their typing speeds (words per minute) were:
Pair 1: new 42, standard 38
Pair 2: new 35, standard 36
Pair 3: new 50, standard 44
Pair 4: new 28, standard 25
Pair 5: new 46, standard 41
Pair 6: new 31, standard 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean typing speed for each layout. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: New layout: 38.7 words per minute; standard layout: 35.7 words per minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State in how many of the pairs the learner using the new layout was faster.
parts.answer: 5 of the 6 pairs (all except pair 2).
parts.working: Pairs 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6 = 5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a matched pairs design was used here rather than a repeated measures design.
parts.answer: With repeated measures each learner would practise on both layouts, so skill learned on the first layout would carry over to the second (an order/practice effect, and the layouts could interfere with each other); matched pairs avoids this while still controlling typing ability, because the pairs were matched on the pre-test.
parts.working: 1 mark: order/practice or interference effect with repeated measures, in context; 1 mark: matching on the pre-test still controls the main participant variable.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one problem that would arise if the learner using the new layout in pair 4 left the study before the final test.
parts.answer: The other member of pair 4 has no partner to be compared with, so their data are also lost (or must be excluded), reducing the sample to 5 pairs.
parts.working: 1 mark: partner's data cannot be used / sample reduced.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a hypothetical independent measures experiment in Doha, 60 adults were randomly allocated to an 8-week group exercise programme or an individual exercise programme (30 in each). Six people dropped out of the group programme and one dropped out of the individual programme.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of participants who dropped out of each condition.
parts.answer: Group exercise: 20%; individual exercise: 3.3% (to 1 d.p.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of all participants who completed the study. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the uneven drop-out could affect the validity of comparing the two groups.
parts.answer: The people who stayed in the group-exercise condition may be the most motivated, so the groups are no longer equivalent; any difference in fitness may be due to motivation (a participant variable) rather than the type of exercise.
parts.working: 1 mark groups no longer equal; 1 mark participant variable confounds result.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hypothetical experiment tests whether students in a school in Accra understand a passage better when it is printed on paper or shown on a tablet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the repeated measures and independent measures designs for this study, and explain which you would recommend.
parts.answer: Repeated measures removes differences in reading ability between conditions and needs half as many students, but students would read two passages and could guess the aim or improve with practice; independent measures avoids order effects and guessing, but differences in reading ability between groups could confound the result. Recommendation: repeated measures with two passages of equal difficulty and counterbalancing, because reading ability varies widely between students and is the biggest threat to validity.
parts.working: 1 mark repeated strength; 1 mark repeated weakness; 1 mark independent strength/weakness; 1 mark justified recommendation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'standardisation' in an experiment.
parts.answer: Keeping the procedure, instructions and conditions the same for every participant.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment tests whether colour of ink (red or blue) affects how well students in Multan remember a list of words. Give two ways the procedure could be standardised.
parts.answer: Every participant is given the same list of 20 words printed in the same font size; every participant gets exactly 2 minutes to study the list (also: same instructions, same room).
parts.working: 1 mark each, linked to the study.

stem: A hypothetical experiment in Ankara tests whether a cup of coffee increases alertness in the afternoon. Alertness is measured by a reaction-time test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the researcher should include a placebo condition.
parts.answer: Participants who know they have had caffeine may expect to feel more alert and try harder; a placebo (decaffeinated coffee that looks and tastes the same) controls for these expectations, so any difference is due to caffeine itself.
parts.working: 1 mark expectations / demand characteristics; 1 mark placebo isolates effect of caffeine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a double-blind procedure could be used in this study.
parts.answer: A colleague prepares coded cups so that neither the participants nor the researcher who gives the drinks and measures alertness knows which cups contain caffeine until all the data are collected.
parts.working: 1 mark participants unaware; 1 mark researcher unaware (with method).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of a control condition in an experiment.
parts.answer: It provides a baseline in which the IV is absent, so the experimental condition can be compared with it to see whether the IV had an effect.
parts.working: 1 mark baseline/no IV; 1 mark for comparison.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical study tests whether a 10-minute meditation app reduces exam anxiety in Karachi students. Suggest a suitable control condition.
parts.answer: Students listen to a 10-minute recording of neutral information (e.g. a weather report) through the same app at the same time.
parts.working: 1 mark (same length / same setting, no meditation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a set of standardised instructions for participants in a hypothetical experiment in which they solve anagrams under time pressure.
parts.answer: 'You will be shown 15 jumbled words, one at a time, on the screen. Rearrange the letters to make a real English word and type it in the box. You have 20 seconds for each word. If you cannot solve one, press Next. Please work alone and do not use your phone. You may stop at any time. Press Start when ready.'
parts.working: 1 mark task explained; 1 mark time limit/what to do if stuck; 1 mark clear, neutral, includes right to withdraw; must not reveal the hypothesis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why standardised instructions are important.
parts.answer: So all participants receive the same information and differences in the DV are not caused by differences in what they were told.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe controls and standardisation, using any examples.
parts.answer: Controls are ways of keeping extraneous variables from affecting the DV, so that only the IV changes, e.g. keeping room temperature, noise and time of day the same, using a control group or placebo, random allocation, counterbalancing. Standardisation is a type of control in which the procedure is identical for everyone, e.g. the same instructions read from a script, the same materials and timing. Both increase validity (the effect is due to the IV) and reliability (the study can be repeated).
parts.working: Up to 3 marks each: description (1), example (1), why it matters (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it is harder to control variables in a field experiment than in a laboratory experiment.
parts.answer: In a natural setting the researcher cannot control things like noise, crowds or weather, which may vary between conditions, whereas a lab lets these be kept the same.
parts.working: 1 mark: real setting variables vary; 1 mark: contrast with lab.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical field experiment in a park in Lahore tests whether a dog increases the number of people who smile at a walker. Suggest two controls the researcher could use.
parts.answer: The same walker, wearing the same clothes, walks the same 200 m path at the same time of day in both conditions; trials are done only on dry days.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical memory experiment, all participants see the same 20 pictures. Explain why the researcher presents the pictures in a different random order to each participant.
parts.answer: Pictures near the start and end of a list are usually remembered better; randomising the order stops particular pictures always benefiting from their position, so position does not bias the results.
parts.working: 1 mark position effects; 1 mark randomising spreads them out.

stem: A hypothetical laboratory experiment in Singapore tests whether people change their answers to match others in an online group chat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the researcher could use a cover story to reduce demand characteristics.
parts.answer: Tell participants the study is about which colours people prefer for a new website, so they do not know conformity is being measured and behave naturally when they hear others' answers.
parts.working: 1 mark cover story example; 1 mark explanation of how it reduces demand characteristics.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one ethical problem with using a cover story and how it could be dealt with.
parts.answer: It is deception, so participants cannot give fully informed consent; they should be debriefed fully afterwards, told the real aim and offered the chance to withdraw their data.
parts.working: 1 mark problem; 1 mark solution.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical study, the same researcher read the same script to every participant in a calm, neutral voice. Explain why.
parts.answer: To standardise the procedure: different researchers or tones of voice could affect participants' behaviour (experimenter effect), which would be an extraneous variable.
parts.working: 1 mark standardisation; 1 mark avoids experimenter effects.

stem: A hypothetical experiment in Dhaka tests whether children who learn spelling with tablets do better than children who learn with books. The researcher believes tablets are better and personally tests every child.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the researcher's expectations could affect the results.
parts.answer: The researcher may unconsciously give more encouragement or extra time to the children with tablets, making their scores higher because of the researcher's behaviour rather than the tablets.
parts.working: 1 mark unconscious bias / cues; 1 mark effect on scores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two controls that would reduce this experimenter effect.
parts.answer: Give instructions by a recording; have the tests marked by someone who does not know which group each child was in (blind marking).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of strict controls in laboratory experiments. Refer to one strength and one weakness.
parts.answer: Strength: strict controls (same room, time, instructions) remove extraneous variables, so the researcher can be confident that the IV caused the change in the DV (high internal validity) and the study can be replicated. Weakness: the more controlled the situation, the more artificial it becomes, so participants may behave differently from real life (low ecological validity) and may respond to demand characteristics.
parts.working: 2 marks each: point + explanation (example credited).

stem: A hypothetical study at a bird sanctuary in Sindh records how often parrots interact with two types of enrichment toy (a puzzle feeder or a hanging rope).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two controls the researcher should use when observing the parrots.
parts.answer: Observe at the same time each day (e.g. 30 minutes after the morning feed); use the same observer standing at the same distance behind a screen so the birds are not disturbed.
parts.working: 1 mark each, in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why controlling the time of observation is important.
parts.answer: Birds are more active at certain times (e.g. early morning, before feeding), so observing at different times in different conditions could change the number of toy interactions regardless of the toy type.
parts.working: 1 mark activity varies with time; 1 mark confound.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hypothetical experiment tests whether a radio advert for a juice drink is more persuasive when it uses a famous singer's voice or an unknown person's voice. Participants rate how much they want to buy the drink from 1 to 10.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two variables, other than the IV, that should be kept the same in the two conditions.
parts.answer: The length and content of the advert / the volume at which it is played; the room and time of day (also: the same products shown on the rating sheet).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the researcher should allocate participants to the conditions randomly.
parts.answer: So that participant variables such as age or liking for the product are spread equally between the conditions, and the researcher does not unconsciously put certain people in one group.
parts.working: 1 mark spread participant variables; 1 mark avoid researcher bias.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dr Farah runs a dental clinic in Multan and wants to persuade teenagers to stop chewing gutka. Using psychological research on fear appeals, suggest how she could design her health promotion message.
parts.answer: Use a low-to-moderate level of fear rather than very frightening images, because research on fear arousal (Janis and Feshbach) found the minimal-fear message produced the most change in dental behaviour while strong fear produced least (people may avoid or deny a very frightening message). Combine the warning with clear, specific, achievable advice (e.g. where to get help to quit, what to chew instead), so teenagers feel able to act.
parts.working: 1 mark: moderate/low fear; 1 mark: research evidence; 1 mark: give clear specific actions; 1 mark: explanation (defensive avoidance / self-efficacy) applied to Dr Farah's clinic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the study by Janis and Feshbach on fear arousal in health promotion.
parts.answer: Aim: to see whether the amount of fear in a health message affects behaviour change. High-school students were randomly given one of three versions of a 15-minute illustrated lecture on dental hygiene: strong fear (vivid images and warnings of pain, infection and decay), moderate fear, or minimal fear; a control group heard a lecture on a different topic. Dental hygiene practices were measured by questionnaire before and one week after. The minimal-fear group showed the greatest change towards the recommended practices and the strong-fear group the least. Conclusion: too much fear may make people avoid or dismiss the message.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 points: aim; sample (high-school students in the USA); three fear levels; control group; self-report questionnaire before and after; result (minimal most change, strong least); conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the 'Food Dudes' health promotion programme (Tapper et al.) for increasing children's fruit and vegetable consumption, including a discussion about generalisability.
parts.answer: Strengths: high ecological validity – carried out in real schools during normal lunchtimes; objective measures of food eaten (weighing what is left) give reliable quantitative data; clear practical application – combines modelling by admired peers (the Food Dudes videos) with rewards, using social learning and operant principles; effects were maintained at follow-up. Weaknesses / issues: generalisability – UK primary schools may not represent other cultures or older children, and food preferences and school meal systems differ (e.g. in Pakistan); rewards may produce extrinsic motivation that fades once rewards stop; ethical issues are minor but involve children; difficult to separate the effect of the videos from the rewards.
