parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced evaluation with at least four developed points, generalisability discussed in depth, linked to Food Dudes throughout. Level 3 (6–8): mostly developed points, generalisability included. Level 2 (3–5): basic points, little elaboration. Level 1 (1–2): vague or descriptive. Max 6 without generalisability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by 'unrealistic optimism' in health psychology.
parts.answer: A belief that you are less likely than other people to experience negative health events (and more likely to experience positive ones), so you may ignore health warnings.
parts.working: 1 mark: less likely than others; 1 mark: effect on health behaviour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way unrealistic optimism could make a health promotion campaign about road safety less effective.
parts.answer: Young drivers may accept that speeding causes accidents but believe 'it won't happen to me' because they think they are better drivers than average, so they do not change their behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark: 'not me' thinking; 1 mark: applied to the campaign.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the determinism versus free will debate.
parts.answer: Determinism is the view that behaviour is caused by forces outside our control (e.g. reinforcement, biology); free will is the view that people choose their own behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark each side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why using a token economy to improve worksite safety (Fox et al.) is deterministic.
parts.answer: It assumes miners' safe behaviour is controlled by rewards: giving trading stamps for accident-free periods reinforced safety, so behaviour is seen as shaped by consequences rather than chosen freely.
parts.working: 1 mark: behaviour caused by reinforcement; 1 mark: link to Fox et al. (stamps / mines / fewer days lost).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a field experiment to investigate whether a health promotion programme increases handwashing before lunch in primary schools in Lahore. Your plan must include a named sampling technique and a way of measuring handwashing.
parts.answer: Example: IV – schools receiving a 4-week programme (cartoon video of child 'hygiene heroes', posters and sticker rewards for washing) vs schools continuing as normal. DV – percentage of pupils who wash hands with soap before lunch, recorded by trained observers using a checklist (washes with soap for at least 20 seconds), plus soap used (grams) per week. Sample: stratified sample of 8 government and private schools, randomly assigned to conditions; pupils aged 7–9. Procedure: baseline observation for a week, programme, observation immediately after and 3 months later. Controls: same observation times, observers blind to condition. Ethics: permission from head teachers and parents, children's assent, anonymity. Data: compare mean percentages; bar chart.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): clear, detailed, replicable plan with IV/DV, named and justified sampling technique, operationalised measure, procedure, controls and ethics. Level 3 (6–8): most features with some detail. Level 2 (3–5): basic plan. Level 1 (1–2): little relevant content.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the psychological knowledge on which your plan is based.
parts.answer: Health promotion strategies: modelling (social learning) as in the Food Dudes programme, where children copied admired peer models and received small rewards, increasing fruit and vegetable consumption; positive reinforcement and token economies (Fox et al.) increasing safe behaviour; fear appeals (Janis and Feshbach) showing that strong fear is not the most effective, so a positive, low-fear message is used; health promotion in schools reaching many children at an age when habits form.
parts.working: Level 4 (7–8): accurate, detailed description of relevant theory/studies clearly linked to the plan. Level 3 (5–6): accurate with some detail. Level 2 (3–4): limited. Level 1 (1–2): vague.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason for your choice of sampling technique.
parts.answer: Stratified sampling ensures both government and private schools are represented in proportion, because hygiene facilities (soap, water) and family background differ between them; this increases generalisability to Lahore's schools. It also reduces bias compared with an opportunity sample of schools that volunteer, which may already be more health-conscious. Weakness acknowledged: it needs a full list of schools and takes time.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): reason well explained, linked to the plan and to the psychology, with evaluation. Level 2 (3–4): reason explained with some link. Level 1 (1–2): reason stated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate health promotion in worksites and communities, including a discussion about individual and situational explanations.
parts.answer: Strengths: worksite token economies (Fox et al.) produced large, lasting reductions in days lost through accidents – real-world, objective data, high ecological validity; community campaigns reach many people and can change norms. Issues: situational – these programmes assume behaviour can be changed by altering the environment (rewards, information, social norms), which ignores individual differences such as unrealistic optimism, personality or motivation, so some people will not respond; individual approaches (e.g. tailored advice) may be needed alongside. Other weaknesses: extrinsic rewards may stop working when removed; difficult to control extraneous variables in field settings, so cause and effect is uncertain; cultural generalisability.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, at least four developed points, individual/situational debate discussed thoroughly with examples. Level 3 (6–8). Level 2 (3–5). Level 1 (1–2). Max 6 without the debate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal is a bank manager in Karachi. He has frequent headaches, sleeps badly and feels tense all day. Suggest how stress inoculation training could be used to help him.
parts.answer: Phase 1 (conceptualisation): a therapist helps Bilal identify his stressors (e.g. targets, difficult customers) and how he thinks about them. Phase 2 (skills acquisition and rehearsal): he learns coping skills such as relaxation, positive self-statements and time management and practises them in role-plays. Phase 3 (application and follow-through): he uses the skills in real situations at the bank, starting with milder stressors, with booster sessions.
parts.working: 1 mark per phase correctly applied (max 3); 1 mark for clear application to Bilal throughout.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the General Adaptation Syndrome (Selye).
parts.answer: Selye proposed that the body responds to any prolonged stressor in the same three stages. Alarm reaction: the stressor is detected, the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal glands release adrenaline, heart rate and blood pressure rise – 'fight or flight'. Resistance: if the stressor continues, the body adapts, with stress hormones such as cortisol staying high; the person seems to cope but resources are being used up. Exhaustion: after long-term stress, the body's resources are depleted, the immune system is weakened and stress-related illnesses (e.g. ulcers, high blood pressure) can develop. Based on experiments in which rats were exposed to different stressors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 points: same response to all stressors; alarm stage with detail; resistance stage with detail; exhaustion stage with detail; link to illness/immune suppression; based on animal research.

stem: Usman, a university student in Peshawar, completes the Social Readjustment Rating Scale. In the past year he experienced: death of a close family member (63), change in living conditions (25), begin or end school (26), change in residence (20), change in sleeping habits (16) and a vacation (13). Holmes and Rahe suggested that 150–299 LCU indicates moderate risk of stress-related illness, and 300 or more indicates high risk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate Usman's total life change units (LCU).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the guideline given, state Usman's level of risk.
parts.answer: Moderate risk (150–299).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using the Social Readjustment Rating Scale to measure Usman's stress.
parts.answer: Each event is given a fixed value, but the same event affects people differently (e.g. moving house may be exciting for Usman, not stressful), so the score may not validly measure his stress; it also ignores daily hassles.
parts.working: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark explanation applied to Usman.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of measuring stress using physiological measures such as heart rate or cortisol in saliva.
parts.answer: Strength: objective and quantitative – the reading cannot be faked or affected by social desirability, so it is reliable and easy to compare. Weakness: physiological arousal can be caused by things other than stress (e.g. caffeine, exercise, excitement), and the equipment/setting may itself cause anxiety, so the measure may lack validity.
parts.working: 2 marks each: point + explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one self-report measure that could be used alongside it.
parts.answer: A daily hassles diary/scale on which participants tick which minor everyday stressors (e.g. traffic, losing things) they experienced and rate how severe each was.
parts.working: 1 mark named/clear measure; 1 mark detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the nomothetic versus idiographic debate.
parts.answer: The nomothetic approach studies large groups to find general laws that apply to everyone; the idiographic approach studies individuals in depth to understand their unique experience.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the study of work stress in civil servants (Chandola et al.) is nomothetic.
parts.answer: It used a very large sample of London civil servants and statistical analysis to find a general relationship between work stress and coronary heart disease, rather than studying any one person's experience in depth.
parts.working: 1 mark large sample/general law; 1 mark link to the study.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why daily hassles may be a better predictor of psychological health than major life events, referring to research by Kanner et al.
parts.answer: Kanner et al. found that scores on a hassles scale (minor everyday irritations such as misplacing things, traffic, concerns about weight) were a better predictor of psychological symptoms than life-events scores. Hassles happen often and accumulate, so they produce continuous low-level stress; major life events are rare and their effect may operate partly through the hassles they create (e.g. divorce leads to cooking, money worries). Uplifts may also buffer the effect of hassles.
parts.working: 1 mark Kanner finding; 1 mark frequency/accumulation; 1 mark life events act via hassles; 1 mark further point (uplifts / individual appraisal).

stem: Ms Mehwish, a teacher in Hyderabad, has tension headaches caused by stress.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how biofeedback could be used to help Ms Mehwish manage her tension headaches.
parts.answer: Electrodes on her forehead measure muscle tension (EMG) and turn it into a tone or a display; she learns relaxation techniques and watches/hears the signal fall as she relaxes the muscles; the feedback rewards successful relaxation (operant conditioning); with practice she can relax without the machine and use the skill at work when she feels tension starting.
parts.working: 1 mark each: physiological measure; feedback signal; learning to control it by relaxation/reinforcement; transfer to everyday life.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of biofeedback compared with stress inoculation training.
parts.answer: Biofeedback deals only with the physical symptoms and does not address the thoughts or situations causing her stress, so the headaches may return; SIT also teaches cognitive coping skills.
parts.working: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark comparison.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the difference between acute pain and chronic pain.
parts.answer: Acute pain is short-term (usually less than about 3 months) and linked to a specific injury that heals; chronic pain lasts longer than about 3 months and may continue after the tissue has healed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why chronic pain may need psychological as well as medical treatment.
parts.answer: Chronic pain is often linked to anxiety, depression and changed behaviour (e.g. avoiding activity), which can make the pain feel worse; psychological methods such as CBT address these thoughts and behaviours where painkillers alone do not.
parts.working: 1 mark psychological factors; 1 mark how treatment helps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the gate control theory of pain (Melzack and Wall).
parts.answer: Pain is not simply a direct signal from injury to brain. A 'gate' in the spinal cord (dorsal horn, substantia gelatinosa) controls whether pain signals reach the brain. Small fibres (A-delta and C) carrying pain signals open the gate. Large fibres (A-beta) carrying touch/pressure, e.g. rubbing a bump, close it. Messages descending from the brain can also open or close the gate: anxiety and attention to pain open it; distraction, relaxation and positive emotion close it. This explains why the same injury causes different pain in different situations and why phantom limb pain and episodic analgesia occur.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 points: gate in spinal cord; small fibres open; large fibres close (example); descending control from brain; psychological factors that open/close; explains individual/situational differences or examples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nurse Rabia works in a children's hospital in Peshawar. Five-year-old Ali has just had an operation and cannot describe his pain in words. Suggest two ways Nurse Rabia could measure Ali's pain.
parts.answer: 1) Paediatric self-report scale: show Ali the Wong-Baker FACES scale, six cartoon faces from 'no hurt' (0) to 'hurts worst' (10), and ask him to point to the face that shows how he feels. 2) Behavioural observation: use an observational pain scale designed for young children (e.g. the FLACC scale: face, legs, activity, cry, consolability), or a pain behaviour checklist like the UAB scale, to rate observed behaviours such as crying, guarding the wound, grimacing and reluctance to move.
parts.working: 2 marks each: method + application to Ali. Accept other paediatric self-report scales (e.g. a pain thermometer or colour scale) and any named or clearly described observational checklist.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two strengths of the McGill Pain Questionnaire as a measure of pain.
parts.answer: 1) It measures the quality of pain, not just its intensity, using many descriptive words in sensory, affective and evaluative categories, so it gives a detailed picture that helps diagnosis. 2) It is standardised and produces scores (pain rating index), so pain can be compared over time or between patients, giving reliable quantitative data.
parts.working: 2 marks each: strength + explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of the McGill Pain Questionnaire.
parts.answer: It relies on a good vocabulary and understanding of the descriptor words, so it is unsuitable for children or people with a different first language, which could reduce validity.
parts.working: 1 mark weakness; 1 mark explanation.

stem:
In a hypothetical study, five patients with chronic back pain at a clinic in Islamabad marked their pain on a 100 mm visual analogue scale (0 = no pain, 100 = worst pain imaginable) before and after a 6-week programme of non-pain imagery and attention diversion.
Before (mm): 72, 65, 80, 58, 70
After (mm): 45, 50, 52, 40, 48

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean pain rating before and after the programme, in mm.
parts.answer: Before: 69 mm; after: 47 mm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in the mean pain rating. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the researcher cannot be sure the programme caused the reduction.
parts.answer: There was no control group: pain may have reduced naturally over 6 weeks or because patients expected to improve (placebo effect / demand characteristics).
parts.working: 1 mark no control group; 1 mark alternative explanation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate psychological techniques for managing pain (such as attention diversion, non-pain imagery and cognitive redefinition), including a discussion about individual differences.
parts.answer: Strengths: supported by gate control theory – attention and emotion close the gate; no side effects or addiction risk compared with painkillers; give patients a sense of control and can be used anywhere; useful for chronic pain alongside medical treatment. Weaknesses: individual differences – people vary in imagination, concentration and willingness to engage, and children or very anxious patients may find imagery hard, so effectiveness differs; less effective for severe acute pain; evidence often uses self-report measures, open to demand characteristics; hard to separate which component of a combined programme works.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): balanced, four developed points, individual differences discussed thoroughly with examples. Level 3 (6–8). Level 2 (3–5). Level 1 (1–2). Max 6 without individual differences.

stem: Mr Javed, who lives in Lahore, is prescribed 2 tablets a day for 28 days for high blood pressure. When he returns to the clinic after 28 days, 18 tablets are left in the bottle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of tablets Mr Javed should have taken.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of prescribed tablets that Mr Javed appears to have taken. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why a pill count may not be a valid measure of adherence.
parts.answer: Removed tablets may not have been swallowed – a patient could throw them away or share them – or may have been taken at the wrong times, so the count can overestimate adherence.
parts.working: 1 mark reason; 1 mark explanation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mrs Nasreen has been prescribed tablets for high blood pressure. They make her feel tired and dizzy, and she feels perfectly well without them, so she has stopped taking them. Using the idea of rational non-adherence and the health belief model, explain her behaviour.
parts.answer: Rational non-adherence: she has made a reasoned decision that the costs (side effects such as tiredness and dizziness) outweigh the benefits, because high blood pressure has no symptoms she can feel. Health belief model: her perceived susceptibility and severity are low (she feels well), perceived barriers (side effects) are high and perceived benefits are low, so the likelihood of taking action is low.
parts.working: 2 marks for rational non-adherence applied; 2 marks for HBM components applied.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the study by Watt et al. on using a 'Funhaler' to improve adherence in children with asthma.
parts.answer: Aim: to see whether a novel spacer device that was fun to use would improve young children's adherence to asthma medication. Sample: children aged about 1.5–6 years with asthma in Australia, and their parents. The Funhaler had a spinning toy and a whistle activated by the child's breathing. Children used their normal spacer and then the Funhaler, each for a period of about two weeks. Parents answered questions (including by telephone) about whether the child had been medicated and about problems using the device. Results: adherence was higher and parents reported fewer difficulties with the Funhaler. Conclusion: making medication fun can improve adherence in young children.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 accurate points: aim; sample; description of Funhaler; repeated measures design/procedure; self-report from parents; result; conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline one subjective and one objective way of measuring adherence.
parts.answer: Subjective: asking patients by questionnaire or interview how often they took their medicine. Objective: counting remaining pills / electronic pill-bottle caps / blood or urine tests.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why subjective measures of adherence may lack validity.
parts.answer: Patients may overstate adherence to please the doctor or avoid criticism (social desirability), or may simply forget missed doses.
parts.working: 1 mark reason; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dr Kamran runs a tuberculosis (TB) clinic in Faisalabad. Patients must take antibiotics every day for six months, but many stop early. Suggest two ways of improving adherence, based on psychological research, and explain why each should work.
parts.answer: 1) Behavioural reinforcement and reminders: send daily SMS reminders and give small rewards (e.g. travel vouchers) for attending clinic checks, because reminders and incentives have been shown to increase health behaviours such as attending immunisations (positive reinforcement). 2) Use the health belief model: explain clearly the seriousness of TB and that stopping early can cause drug-resistant TB (increase perceived severity and benefits), and reduce barriers by giving medicines for side effects or supervised dosing near home.
parts.working: 2 marks each: suggestion + psychological explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one ethical issue with using rewards to improve adherence.
parts.answer: Rewards may put pressure on poorer patients so their choice is not entirely free; patients who cannot attend could feel unfairly excluded, so rewards must be fair and not coercive.
parts.working: 1 mark issue; 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dr Imran tells patients what is wrong and what to do without asking for their views. Dr Saba asks patients about their concerns and decides treatment together with them. Identify the style each doctor uses.
parts.answer: Dr Imran: doctor-centred (directive) style; Dr Saba: patient-centred (sharing) style.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline the findings of Savage and Armstrong on patients' satisfaction with these styles.
parts.answer: In a study at a general practice in London, patients randomly given a directive (doctor-centred) consultation were more satisfied than patients given a sharing (patient-centred) consultation, particularly those who were ill and expected a clear diagnosis.
parts.working: 1 mark directive preferred / more satisfied; 1 mark detail (random allocation / questionnaire / patients wanted clear diagnosis).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the study by McKinstry and Wang on doctors' dress.
parts.answer: Aim: to find out patients' attitudes to the way doctors dress. Patients attending general practices in Scotland were shown photographs of a male and a female doctor wearing different styles of clothing, e.g. a formal suit, a white coat, smart informal dress and casual clothes such as jeans. They completed a questionnaire rating how happy they would be to see each doctor and how much confidence they would have in them. Overall, patients preferred more formal dress (suit, white coat) and casual clothes were least preferred. Older patients were especially likely to prefer formal dress. Conclusion: dress is part of a doctor's non-verbal communication and affects patients' confidence.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to 6 points: aim; sample; photographs of male and female doctors; range of dress styles; rating questionnaire; results (formal preferred, older patients especially); conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the individual versus situational explanations debate.
parts.answer: Individual explanations say behaviour is caused by personal characteristics (e.g. beliefs, personality); situational explanations say it is caused by external circumstances (e.g. cost, other people, the environment).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using research on delay in seeking treatment (Safer et al.), explain one example of an individual explanation and one of a situational explanation.
parts.answer: Individual: a person's own appraisal of symptoms – e.g. believing that a lump is not serious (appraisal delay), or fear of what the doctor will find. Situational: practical barriers such as cost of treatment or difficulty getting time off work, which lengthen utilisation delay.
parts.working: 1 mark each, linked to stages of delay.

stem: In a hypothetical screening clinic in Karachi, 200 people were checked for diabetes. Later tests showed that 40 of them really had diabetes. The clinic's doctor diagnosed 50 people as having diabetes, of whom 34 really had it. (A type I error = diagnosing a healthy person as ill; a type II error = diagnosing an ill person as healthy.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of type I errors made.
parts.working: 50 diagnosed ill − 34 truly ill = 16 healthy people diagnosed as ill.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of type II errors made.
parts.working: 40 ill − 34 detected = 6 ill people diagnosed as healthy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of healthy people who were wrongly diagnosed as ill.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why practitioners might make more type I errors than type II errors.
parts.answer: Doctors usually think it is safer to diagnose a healthy person as ill than to miss a real illness, because missing an illness could have serious consequences for the patient (and for the doctor). So when unsure they tend to diagnose illness and order further tests, which increases type I errors. The cost is unnecessary anxiety, tests and treatment for healthy patients.
parts.working: 1 mark: missing illness seen as worse; 1 mark: so err on the side of diagnosing; 1 mark: consequence for patients.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by Munchausen syndrome as a misuse of health services.
parts.answer: A disorder in which a person repeatedly feigns, exaggerates or deliberately causes symptoms of illness in order to receive medical attention and treatment, often visiting many hospitals.
parts.working: 1 mark feigning/causing symptoms; 1 mark to gain medical attention (not money).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why Munchausen syndrome is usually studied using case studies.
parts.answer: It is rare and patients hide their behaviour, so it is not possible to gather a large sample; a case study gives detailed (idiographic) information about one patient's history over time.
parts.working: 1 mark rare/hidden; 1 mark depth of information.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one problem for doctors in diagnosing Munchausen syndrome.
parts.answer: Doctors may make a type I error – diagnosing a healthy person as ill – because the feigned or self-induced symptoms appear real, leading to unnecessary tests, operations and treatments that can harm the patient.
parts.working: 1 mark problem; 1 mark consequence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the aim of Piliavin et al.'s subway Samaritan study.
parts.answer: To investigate, in a natural setting, how the type of victim (ill or drunk), the race of the victim, the presence of a helping model and the number of bystanders affect the speed and frequency of helping a person who collapses.
parts.working: 1 mark: investigating helping behaviour/bystander helping in a real-life (field) setting; 1 mark: naming at least two of the factors: type of victim (cane/drunk), race of victim, model, group size.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what the victim did at the start of each trial.
parts.answer: About 70 seconds after the train passed the first station, the victim (standing near a pole in the critical area) staggered forward and collapsed, then lay on the floor looking up at the ceiling until someone helped him.
parts.working: 1 mark: staggered and collapsed (about 70 seconds after the train left the first station); 1 mark: stayed lying on the floor until helped (the model helped if no passenger did).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how the race of the victim was varied in Piliavin et al.'s study.
parts.answer: There were four teams, each with its own male victim. Three of the victims were white and one was black, so passengers saw either a white or a black victim collapse.
parts.working: 1 mark: different victims in different teams/trials; 1 mark: three white victims and one black victim.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline one finding about the race of the victim.
parts.answer: Race had little effect when the victim carried a cane, but in the drunk condition there was a slight tendency for passengers to help a victim of their own race.
parts.working: 1 mark: same-race helping tendency; 1 mark: mainly/especially in the drunk condition (cane victim helped regardless of race).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A man collapses on a crowded Metrobus in Lahore. Using the cost–reward model from Piliavin et al.'s study, explain whether a passenger standing next to him is likely to help.
parts.answer: Seeing him collapse causes unpleasant arousal in the passenger. The passenger reduces this arousal in the way that costs least and rewards most. Costs of helping (getting dirty, embarrassment, missing a stop) are low if the man looks ill and harmless, and the costs of not helping (guilt, others' disapproval, being next to him) are high because the passenger is close. So the passenger is likely to help directly. If the man seemed drunk or dangerous, costs of helping rise and the passenger might move away or leave it to others.
parts.working: 1 mark: arousal caused by seeing an emergency; 1 mark: arousal reduced by the response with the best cost–reward balance; 1 mark: applied costs of helping (time, effort, embarrassment, disgust, harm); 1 mark: applied costs of not helping (guilt, blame) / conclusion linked to scenario (close passenger, ill victim → likely to help).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two ethical guidelines that were not followed in Piliavin et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Informed consent was not obtained; passengers were deceived (they thought the collapse was real). (Also accept: no right to withdraw, no debrief.)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: informed consent, deception, right to withdraw, debriefing, protection from (psychological) harm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the researchers might argue that the study was still justified.
parts.answer: The study could only produce valid, natural helping behaviour if passengers did not know it was a study; the distress was brief and similar to events passengers might meet anyway, and the findings about when people help in emergencies are useful to society.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (realism needed / brief and mild distress / everyday event / usefulness); 1 mark: explained in context of the study.

stem:
Hypothetical replication: researchers repeated Piliavin et al.'s procedure on a commuter train in Karachi. A male victim collapsed on 60 trials.
Condition | Trials | Trials with spontaneous help
Cane (ill) | 30 | 27
Drunk | 30 | 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of trials with spontaneous help (help before the model acted) in each condition of the hypothetical replication. Give your answers to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: Cane: 90 %; drunk: 40 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare these results with the pattern found in Piliavin et al.'s original study.
parts.answer: The pattern is the same: the cane (ill) victim was helped more often than the drunk victim. In the original study the figures were about 95 % (62 of 65 trials) for the cane victim and 50 % (19 of 38) for the drunk victim, so both conditions were helped a little less often in the replication, and the gap is slightly larger (50 percentage points rather than about 45).
parts.working: 1 mark: same direction (ill/cane victim helped more than drunk victim in both); 1 mark: correct comparison of size, e.g. replication slightly lower in both conditions / gap similar.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one reason why the replication cannot be compared directly with the original study.
parts.answer: The replication was carried out in a different culture, decades later, on a different kind of train with different passengers, so differences may be due to cultural norms about helping strangers (or crowding, gender norms) rather than to the victim conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: a valid difference (culture, era, setting, sample, number of trials, victim characteristics); 1 mark: explanation of how it could change helping.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shock generator used in Milgram's (1963) study.
parts.answer: It had a row of 30 switches running from 15 volts to 450 volts in 15-volt steps. Groups of switches had verbal labels from 'Slight Shock' up to 'Danger: Severe Shock', and the last two switches were labelled 'XXX'. It looked realistic but gave no real shocks (the teacher received one genuine 45 V shock as a sample before the study).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: 30 switches; 15 V to 450 V; increases of 15 V; verbal labels from 'Slight Shock' to 'Danger: Severe Shock'; last switches marked XXX; not real/fake.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline the learning task the 'learner' was supposed to do in Milgram's study.
parts.answer: It was a word-pair (paired-associate) task. The teacher read pairs of words, then gave one word and four options; the learner chose an answer by pressing one of four switches, which lit up a light on the teacher's panel.
parts.working: 1 mark: memorising word pairs; 1 mark: chose from four options by pressing a switch/light.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what the teacher was told to do each time the learner gave a wrong answer.
parts.answer: Give the learner an electric shock and move one level (15 volts) higher on the generator for each wrong answer, announcing the voltage level before giving the shock.
parts.working: 1 mark: give a shock; 1 mark: increase by one level/15 V each time (announce the voltage).

stem: In Milgram's (1963) study, 26 of the 40 participants continued to the maximum of 450 volts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Five of the 40 participants stopped at 300 volts. Calculate this as a percentage of the sample.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of participants who stopped before reaching 450 volts.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why 300 volts was an important point in the procedure.
parts.answer: At 300 volts the learner pounded on the wall and stopped answering, which was the first clear sign of protest. No participant had stopped before this point, so it was where defiance first appeared.
parts.working: 1 mark: learner pounded on wall/no more answers at 300 V; 1 mark: no participant stopped below 300 V / first refusals happened here.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Milgram suggested that features of the setting may have increased obedience. Explain two features of the setting at Yale University that could have increased obedience.
parts.answer:
1. Yale was a respected university, so participants trusted that the experimenter was a legitimate authority and that the study was safe and worthwhile. 2. Participants had volunteered and been paid, so they felt an obligation to carry on and not spoil the study.
(Also accept: the study seemed to have a worthy purpose — improving learning; the procedure was new to them, so they did not know what was normal.)
parts.working: For each feature: 1 mark identified (prestige of Yale / payment / volunteering / worthy purpose / unfamiliar situation); 1 mark explained in terms of why it increases obedience. Max 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how obedience might change if the same study were run in an ordinary rented office with no university link.
parts.answer: Obedience would probably be lower, because the experimenter would seem less legitimate and participants would be less sure the study was trustworthy and safe.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower obedience; 1 mark: reason linked to reduced legitimacy/prestige of authority.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Junior nurses in a busy hospital in Rawalpindi sometimes give a dose of a drug that a senior doctor orders by phone, even when it looks wrong. Explain how Milgram's findings could be used to reduce this harmful obedience.
parts.answer: Milgram showed that ordinary people obey a legitimate authority even when they believe they are causing harm, so the hospital should not rely on nurses' personal judgement alone. It could train nurses about the power of authority and give them a set rule (e.g. never give a dose above the safe limit without a written order or a second check), so that refusing is part of the system. Because the experimenter's prods ('you have no other choice') kept people obeying, nurses should be told clearly that they always have the right to question an order.
parts.working: 1 mark: link — Milgram showed people obey legitimate authority even when it causes harm; up to 3 marks for applied strategies explained (training/awareness, rules/second check, empowering refusal, removing authority pressure, supportive peers).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of applying Milgram's findings to this situation.
parts.answer: Milgram studied American men in a laboratory with a stranger as the authority, whereas nurses are trained professionals who know the doctor and have their own medical knowledge, so their obedience may work differently.
parts.working: 1 mark: difference in sample/setting/relationship; 1 mark: why this limits application.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some critics have argued that participants in Milgram's study did not really believe the shocks were real. Use evidence from the study to argue against this criticism.
parts.answer: Many participants showed extreme tension: they sweated, trembled, stuttered, bit their lips, groaned and dug their fingernails into their flesh. Fourteen showed nervous laughter and three had uncontrollable seizures. Many argued with the experimenter and some refused to continue. This level of distress suggests that most believed they were really hurting the learner.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any of: signs of tension (sweating, trembling, stuttering, lip-biting, groaning, nails in flesh); 14 nervous laughter; 3 full seizures; protests/refusals; plus 1 mark for the conclusion that this shows belief. Max 4.

parts.label: b

parts.label: a
parts.text: To what extent can the findings of Yamamoto et al.'s study be generalised to human helping?
parts.answer: Chimpanzees are closely related to humans, so their ability to understand another's needs may show where human targeted helping comes from (evolutionary roots). However, the sample was very small, from one institute, and the animals had long experience of human testing and tool use, so they may not be typical even of chimpanzees. Humans also help without being asked and use language, cultural norms and costs/rewards (as Piliavin showed), so generalisation is limited.
parts.working: 1 mark: argument for (close evolutionary relative / shared ability); up to 2 marks: arguments against (small/captive/trained sample; human helping involves language, norms, proactive help); 1 mark: reasoned judgement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the two assumptions of the social approach.
parts.answer: 1. Behaviour, cognitions and emotions can be influenced by other individuals. 2. Behaviour, cognitions and emotions can be influenced by groups, social contexts, culture and society.
parts.working: 1 mark each: influence of other individuals; influence of groups/social context/culture/society.

parts.label: b
parts.text: At home Hira speaks quietly, but at her cousin's mehndi she sings and dances loudly. Explain how one assumption of the social approach explains this.
parts.answer: Her behaviour changes with the social context: at a wedding celebration the group and cultural norms expect singing and dancing, so she joins in.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies the group/social context/culture assumption; 1 mark: applied to the mehndi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal is a quiet student, but at a cricket match in a packed stadium he stands, shouts and chants with the crowd. Explain how the social approach would explain Bilal's behaviour.
parts.answer: The social approach assumes behaviour is shaped by the groups and social situation we are in. In the crowd, Bilal follows the group norm of chanting and cheering, and he feels part of the crowd, so his behaviour is different from how he acts alone. The same person behaves differently in different social contexts.
parts.working: 1 mark: assumption about groups/social context; 1 mark: crowd norms/others' behaviour influence him; 1 mark: contrast with behaviour when alone/situation not personality.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using an example, how culture can influence behaviour.
parts.answer: Culture gives shared norms about how to behave. For example, in Pakistan people usually greet elders first and stand when they enter a room, so a young person's behaviour depends on the cultural rules they have learned, not only on their personality.
parts.working: 1 mark: culture = shared norms/values/rules; 1 mark: relevant example; 1 mark: link to the social approach assumption that culture/society influences behaviour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the finding that every participant in Milgram's study went to at least 300 volts supports an assumption of the social approach.
parts.answer: It shows that the presence and orders of another individual (the experimenter) changed how ordinary people behaved, supporting the assumption that behaviour is influenced by other individuals.
parts.working: 1 mark: names the 'other individuals' assumption; 1 mark: link to experimenter's influence on all participants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one difference between the assumptions of the social approach and the biological approach.
parts.answer: The social approach assumes behaviour is shaped by other people, groups and culture (external, situational causes), whereas the biological approach assumes behaviour is caused by internal factors such as genes, hormones and brain structure. For example, the social approach explains helping by the costs and rewards of the situation, while the biological approach would look at hormones such as oxytocin.
parts.working: 1 mark: social = other people/groups/culture; 1 mark: biological = genes/brain/hormones/evolution; 1 mark: clear contrast or example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength of the social approach, using an example of how it has been applied.
parts.answer: It has useful applications. For example, Piliavin et al. showed that an ill person is helped more than a drunk one and that helping depends on costs and rewards, so public campaigns can reduce the costs of helping (e.g. teaching first aid) to increase bystander help in emergencies.
parts.working: 1 mark: strength (useful applications); 1 mark: example study/finding; 1 mark: how it is applied in real life.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one weakness of the social approach, using evidence from Milgram's study.
parts.answer: It can ignore individual differences. Although the situation produced high obedience, 14 of the 40 participants defied the experimenter in the same situation, which shows that personality or personal values also matter. The social approach may therefore over-emphasise situational causes.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness (situational determinism/ignores individual or biological factors); 1 mark: evidence (14 defied / 35 % stopped); 1 mark: explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the social approach often uses field experiments and observations, using one core study as an example.
parts.answer: Because it assumes that behaviour depends on real social situations, researchers want to study people in natural settings with real others present. For example, Piliavin et al. studied real passengers on a New York subway, so the helping they saw was natural and could not be explained by an artificial laboratory.
parts.working: 1 mark: link to assumption (behaviour depends on social context); 1 mark: natural settings/real others → validity; 1 mark: example from a core study (Piliavin).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the assumptions of the social approach.
parts.answer: Behaviour, cognitions and emotions can be influenced by other individuals, e.g. an authority figure giving orders or a stranger approaching. They can also be influenced by groups, social contexts, culture and society, e.g. the number of bystanders present or cultural norms about helping.
parts.working: 1 mark for each assumption (2); 1 mark for each relevant example/elaboration (2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare Milgram's study and Piliavin et al.'s study in terms of how well each supports the assumptions of the social approach.
parts.answer: Both studies support the idea that other people change behaviour. Milgram shows the influence of one individual (the experimenter) and of a social context (a prestigious university); 65 % went to 450 V. Piliavin shows the influence of the situation (type of victim, the model) on helping in a crowd. However, Milgram was a laboratory study with one authority figure, while Piliavin studied whole groups of strangers in a natural setting, so Piliavin gives stronger support to the group/social-context assumption, but did not find diffusion of responsibility. Both show individual differences (35 % defied; mostly male first helpers), which limits support for purely social explanations. Both were carried out in the USA, so support for the 'culture' assumption is limited. Comparison of methods, samples and validity should be made point by point.
parts.working: Level 3 (6–8): at least two well-explained comparison points (similarities and/or differences) linking each study to the assumptions, with detail from both studies; Level 2 (3–5): some comparison but partly descriptive or one-sided; Level 1 (1–2): basic, mostly description of one study. Possible points: other individuals vs groups; lab vs field; individual differences in both; culture/US samples; ecological validity of social context.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the social approach relates to the determinism versus free will debate. Use Milgram's study in your answer.
parts.answer: The social approach is mainly situationally deterministic: it suggests the situation (orders from an authority, the setting) causes behaviour. Milgram's finding that 65 % obeyed to 450 V supports this. However, 35 % refused, showing people can choose to resist pressure, which supports some free will. So the approach is better described as 'soft' determinism.
parts.working: 1 mark: social approach = situational determinism; 1 mark: Milgram's obedience as support; 1 mark: defiance as evidence of free will; 1 mark: conclusion/soft determinism.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the assumption that culture influences behaviour makes it difficult to generalise the social approach core studies.
parts.answer: If culture shapes behaviour, then findings from one culture may not apply in another. Milgram and Piliavin studied Americans and Perry et al. tested one specific group of participants from a single country, so their levels of obedience, helping and personal space reflect those cultures' norms. In a more collectivist culture such as Pakistan, respect for authority or norms about helping strangers and personal space could be different, so the results could be ethnocentric.
parts.working: 1 mark: assumption implies cultural differences; 1 mark: core studies use single (mostly Western) cultures; 1 mark: example of how another culture could differ; 1 mark: idea of ethnocentrism/limited generalisability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way researchers could test whether a social approach finding is universal.
parts.answer: Replicate the same standardised procedure in several different countries (cross-cultural research) and compare the results.
parts.working: 1 mark: cross-cultural replication; 1 mark: same standardised procedure/compare results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline what is meant by 'oxytocin'.
parts.answer: A hormone (neuropeptide) produced in the hypothalamus and released by the pituitary gland, linked to social behaviour such as bonding and trust.
parts.working: 1 mark: hormone/neuropeptide (from hypothalamus/pituitary); 1 mark: linked to social behaviour/bonding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how oxytocin was given to participants in Perry et al.'s study.
parts.answer: As a nasal spray (sniffed up the nose).
parts.working: 1 mark: nasal spray.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Perry et al.'s study was double-blind. Explain what this means.
parts.answer: Neither the participants nor the researchers testing them knew whether the spray given on that occasion was oxytocin or the placebo.
parts.working: 1 mark: participants did not know; 1 mark: researchers/experimenters did not know.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a double-blind procedure was used.
parts.answer: It stops participants' expectations (demand characteristics) and researchers' expectations (experimenter bias) from affecting the distances recorded, so any difference is due to the oxytocin.
parts.working: 1 mark: reduces demand characteristics/expectations of participants; 1 mark: reduces experimenter bias.

parts.label: a
parts.text: All the participants in Perry et al.'s study were male. Suggest one reason for this.
parts.answer: Hormone levels in women change during the menstrual cycle and can interact with oxytocin, so using only men removed this extra variable.
parts.working: 1 mark: female hormonal changes/menstrual cycle (or pregnancy risk); 1 mark: would act as a confounding/extraneous variable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of using an all-male sample.
parts.answer: The findings cannot be generalised to women, whose response to oxytocin and personal space preferences may be different.
parts.working: 1 mark: cannot generalise to females; 1 mark: explained (women may respond differently).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Perry et al. measured empathy with a questionnaire. Explain one strength of using a questionnaire to measure empathy.
parts.answer: It gives a standardised numerical score for each participant, so participants can be compared and divided into high- and low-empathy groups objectively.
parts.working: 1 mark: strength (standardised/quantitative/quick/easy to compare); 1 mark: applied to grouping participants by empathy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of measuring empathy with a questionnaire.
parts.answer: Participants may give socially desirable answers, describing themselves as more caring than they really are, so the empathy score may not be valid.
parts.working: 1 mark: social desirability / poor self-insight / fixed answers; 1 mark: consequence for validity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each participant was tested once after oxytocin and once after a placebo, on different days. Explain why the two tests were carried out on different days.
parts.answer: So that the oxytocin had fully worn off before the placebo session (or vice versa), meaning the hormone from one session could not affect behaviour in the other.
parts.working: 1 mark: effect of the hormone wears off / washout; 1 mark: avoids carry-over between conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how counterbalancing could be used in this design and why it is needed.
parts.answer: Half the participants receive oxytocin on the first day and placebo on the second; the other half receive them in the opposite order. This balances out order effects such as being more relaxed with the task the second time.
parts.working: 1 mark: half each order (ABBA/AB-BA); 1 mark: controls order effects (practice/familiarity).

Hypothetical study based on Perry et al.: six male students in Islamabad stood still while a researcher walked slowly towards them and said 'stop' when they began to feel uncomfortable. The distance (cm) was recorded after a placebo spray and, on another day, after an oxytocin spray.
Participant | Placebo | Oxytocin
1 | 62 | 58
2 | 70 | 66
3 | 55 | 57
4 | 68 | 61
5 | 74 | 70
6 | 59 | 54

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean preferred distance in each condition. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Placebo: 64.7 cm; oxytocin: 61.0 cm
parts.working: Placebo: 388 ÷ 6 = 64.7 cm (B1); oxytocin: 366 ÷ 6 = 61.0 cm (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many participants chose a smaller distance after oxytocin than after placebo.
parts.working: Participants 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 had smaller distances; participant 3 increased (55 → 57). (B1)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it would be useful to know each participant's empathy score before drawing a conclusion from these data.
parts.answer: Perry et al. found that the effect of oxytocin depended on empathy, so the small average difference might hide different responses in high- and low-empathy people (for example participant 3, whose distance increased).
parts.working: 1 mark: oxytocin effect depends on empathy (individual differences); 1 mark: means could hide opposite responses / reference to participant 3.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Perry et al. found that the effect of oxytocin on personal space depended on the participant's level of empathy. Explain what this finding means.
parts.answer: Oxytocin did not change personal space in the same way for everyone. Participants high in empathy and those low in empathy responded differently to the hormone, so empathy (an individual characteristic) changed — moderated — the effect of oxytocin on the distance they preferred.
parts.working: 1 mark: oxytocin effect not the same for everyone; 1 mark: high- vs low-empathy participants responded differently; 1 mark: empathy as moderating/interacting factor (biology + personality + social situation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one strength of measuring personal space as a distance in centimetres.
parts.answer: It is an objective, quantitative measure, so it is not affected by the researcher's interpretation and the results for oxytocin and placebo can be compared statistically.
parts.working: 1 mark: objective/quantitative; 1 mark: consequence (reliable, easy to compare, less bias).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one type of qualitative data that could be collected in a study like Perry et al.'s, and explain why it might be useful.
parts.answer: Asking participants, after each trial, to describe how they felt as the other person came closer. This could explain why they chose a certain distance (e.g. anxiety or friendliness), which a number alone cannot show.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable qualitative data (description of feelings/reasons); 1 mark: usefulness (explains reasons/depth).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ethical issues that researchers must deal with when giving participants a hormone such as oxytocin, and how each could be dealt with.
parts.answer: 1. Protection from harm: the hormone could have side effects, so participants should be screened for medical problems, a safe standard dose used and a doctor available. 2. Informed consent: participants cannot be told which spray they are getting on each day, so they should be told in advance that they will receive oxytocin on one occasion and a placebo on another, and agree to this; they should be debriefed afterwards and be free to withdraw.
parts.working: For each issue: 1 mark identified (protection from harm, informed consent, deception, right to withdraw, debrief, confidentiality); 1 mark for how it is dealt with in this context.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A psychologist wants to find out whether Perry et al.'s findings apply to women in Pakistan. Suggest how she could carry out a study, and explain one problem she might face.
parts.answer: Recruit female university students (e.g. by volunteer sampling at a university in Lahore), screen for health, and use a double-blind, placebo-controlled repeated measures design with oxytocin and placebo sessions on separate days, counterbalanced. Measure empathy by questionnaire, and measure preferred distance in cm when a female researcher walks towards each participant until she says 'stop'. Test all women at the same stage of the menstrual cycle if possible. Problem: hormone changes across the cycle are hard to control and cultural norms about closeness to strangers (especially men) could affect distances, so the approaching person's gender must be controlled.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for the plan: sample/sampling; design (repeated measures, double-blind, placebo, counterbalanced); measurement of DV (distance in cm) and empathy; one control (time of cycle, gender of approacher, same room). Up to 2 marks for a problem identified and explained (hormonal variation, cultural norms, ethics of giving hormones, recruitment).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate Perry et al.'s study of oxytocin and personal space in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about generalisability.
parts.answer: Strengths: double-blind, placebo-controlled design reduces bias, so differences can be put down to oxytocin; repeated measures design removes participant variables; distance measured objectively in cm (quantitative, reliable); standardised procedure makes it replicable. Weaknesses: all-male student sample from one country, so findings may not generalise to women, other ages or cultures (generalisability); laboratory task in which a person approaches on request lacks ecological validity; empathy measured by self-report may be affected by social desirability; giving hormones raises ethical issues.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): two strengths and two weaknesses, well explained with detail from the study, including a clear generalisability point; Level 3 (6–8): four points, some less developed, or three well explained; Level 2 (3–5): limited/generic points; Level 1 (1–2): mainly description. parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a pie chart is suitable for these data but would not be suitable for showing the mean revision time of each group.
parts.answer: The data are counts in separate categories that add up to a whole (all 120 students), so each slice shows a share of the total. Mean revision times are not parts of a whole, so they should be shown as bars in a bar chart.
parts.working: 1 mark: categories/parts of a whole (frequencies adding to 100 %); 1 mark: means are not parts of a whole → bar chart.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Twenty first-year students at a college in Sialkot rated how anxious they felt before a presentation (1 = not at all, 5 = extremely). Hypothetical ratings:
3, 4, 2, 5, 3, 3, 1, 4, 2, 3, 4, 5, 3, 2, 4, 3, 1, 3, 4, 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw up a frequency table for these data, showing each rating and its frequency.
parts.answer:
Rating | Frequency
1 | 2
2 | 4
3 | 7
4 | 5
5 | 2
parts.working: 2 marks: all five frequencies correct (1 mark if one error); table must have headings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the modal rating.
parts.working: 3 occurs 7 times (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name a suitable graph for showing the frequency of each rating and give one reason.
parts.answer: A bar chart (frequency on the y-axis, each rating as a separate bar), because the ratings are separate whole-number categories rather than continuous data.
parts.working: 1 mark: bar chart; 1 mark: discrete/separate categories.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In a hypothetical study in Hyderabad, groups of participants learned 25 unrelated words and were tested after different delays.
Time since learning (hours) | Mean words recalled
0 | 18
1 | 14
6 | 11
24 | 8
48 | 7

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the most suitable type of graph for these data and explain your choice.
parts.answer: A line graph, because time since learning is a continuous variable and the graph shows how recall changes across time.
parts.working: 1 mark: line graph; 1 mark: x variable continuous / showing change over time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in mean recall between 0 hours and 24 hours. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the pattern shown by the data.
parts.answer: Recall falls quickly at first (most loss in the first 24 hours) and then falls only slowly between 24 and 48 hours.
parts.working: 1 mark: recall decreases over time; 1 mark: fast fall then levelling off.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A hypothetical field experiment in a supermarket in Islamabad recorded the mean time (minutes) shoppers spent in the store on days with slow or fast background music, for two age groups.
Age group | Slow music | Fast music
Under 30 | 26 | 24
Over 30 | 31 | 22

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of graph that should be used to show all four means on one graph, and describe how it should be set out.
parts.answer: A grouped (clustered) bar chart: type of music on the x-axis with two bars side by side for each (one for under-30s and one for over-30s), mean time in store (minutes) on the y-axis starting at 0, a key showing the two age groups, and a title naming both IVs and the DV.
parts.working: 1 mark: grouped/clustered bar chart; 1 mark: one IV on x-axis with bars for the other IV + key; 1 mark: y-axis = mean minutes (from 0) / title.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much longer, on average, the over-30s stayed with slow music than with fast music, and do the same for the under-30s.
parts.answer: Over-30s: 9 minutes longer; under-30s: 2 minutes longer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answers, state one conclusion from the data.
parts.answer: Slow music increased time in the store for both age groups, but the effect was much larger for shoppers over 30 than for those under 30.
parts.working: 1 mark: slow music → longer time for both; 1 mark: effect bigger for over-30s (age changes the effect).

author: HomiLabs

stem: A researcher studying the new metro line in Lahore counts how many passengers give up their seat for an elderly person, and later interviews some passengers about why they did or did not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which method collects quantitative data and which collects qualitative data.
parts.answer: Quantitative: counting the number of passengers who give up their seat. Qualitative: the interviews about why they did or did not give up their seat.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one strength of each type of data in this study.
parts.answer: Counts are easy to compare between rush hour and quiet times (objective, quick to analyse). The interviews give detailed reasons for passengers' choices, which the counts cannot explain.
parts.working: 1 mark: quantitative strength (easy to compare/analyse/objective); 1 mark: qualitative strength (detail/reasons/insight).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write one closed question that would produce quantitative data about students' sleep.
parts.answer: e.g. 'How many hours did you sleep last night? ___ hours' or 'Do you use your phone in bed? Yes / No'.
parts.working: 1 mark: closed question with fixed/numerical answer about sleep.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write one open question that would produce qualitative data about students' sleep.
parts.answer: e.g. 'Describe what usually stops you from falling asleep.'
parts.working: 1 mark: open question inviting a free answer in the participant's own words.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one weakness of the data produced by your closed question.
parts.answer: It gives only a number or yes/no, so it does not show why students sleep that amount; the fixed answer may force students to choose something that does not fit them, reducing validity.
parts.working: 1 mark: lacks detail/reasons or forced choice; 1 mark: consequence (lower validity/insight).

stem:
A hypothetical mental-health awareness campaign in Karachi posted a video online. Eight viewer comments were collected:
1 'This helped me talk to my sister about stress.'
2 'Too long and boring.'
3 'Posted at 9 pm on Tuesday.'
4 'Great idea, please make one in Urdu too.'
5 'It made mental illness seem like a joke.'
6 'I shared it with my class.'
7 'I watched it.'
8 'Thank you, I feel less alone.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sort the eight comments into three categories: positive, negative and neutral. Give the number of comments in each category.
parts.answer: Positive: 1, 4, 6, 8 (4 comments). Negative: 2, 5 (2 comments). Neutral: 3, 7 (2 comments).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct category count (positive 4, negative 2, neutral 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of comments that were positive.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one problem with sorting qualitative comments into categories in this way.
parts.answer: Some comments are hard to place (e.g. comment 7 could be read as mildly negative), so the category chosen depends on the researcher's interpretation, making the counts subjective and possibly unreliable; detail is also lost.
parts.working: 1 mark: problem (subjective interpretation / loss of detail / ambiguous comments); 1 mark: explained with reference to the data.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why qualitative data are often said to have high validity but lower reliability.
parts.answer: Qualitative data let participants explain their thoughts and feelings in their own words, so the data reflect what they really mean rather than a forced choice — higher validity. However, the answers are unique and must be interpreted by the researcher; another researcher might interpret them differently and the same answers are unlikely to be repeated in the same form, so the data are less consistent — lower reliability.
parts.working: 1 mark: own words/detail; 1 mark: so captures real meaning (validity); 1 mark: requires interpretation/subjective; 1 mark: hard to replicate or get consistent coding (reliability).

stem: A hypothetical study at a clinic in Multan investigates whether heavy smartphone use is linked to anxiety in 200 young adult patients.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one piece of quantitative data and one piece of qualitative data that could be collected in this study.
parts.answer: Quantitative: number of hours spent on the phone per day / anxiety rating 1–10. Qualitative: each patient's description of how they feel when they cannot check their phone.
parts.working: 1 mark each, must fit the study.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the researcher might decide to collect only quantitative data in this study.
parts.answer: With 200 patients, numerical data would be much quicker to collect and analyse, and could be compared statistically between people with high and low phone use.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (large sample, time, ease of analysis, objectivity); 1 mark: applied to the study.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a hypothetical study, 15 new mothers in Islamabad kept a diary for four weeks about how they felt about returning to work. The researcher, who believes returning to work causes guilt, reads the diaries and identifies themes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways the researcher could reduce bias when analysing the diaries.
parts.answer: 1. Use a coding scheme agreed in advance with clear definitions of each theme, so she does not just see what she expects. 2. Ask a second researcher, who does not know the aim, to code the same diaries independently and compare (inter-rater reliability). (Also accept: using direct quotes as evidence; checking interpretations with the mothers.)
parts.working: For each way: 1 mark identified; 1 mark explained in context.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one ethical issue raised by the diaries and how it could be dealt with.
parts.answer: The diaries contain personal, sensitive feelings, so confidentiality must be protected by removing names and storing diaries securely; mothers should be able to withdraw their diary.
parts.working: 1 mark: issue (confidentiality/privacy/psychological harm/withdrawal); 1 mark: how it is dealt with.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher plans an observation of how shoppers choose fruit in an open-air market in Peshawar. Describe how she could collect both quantitative and qualitative data, and explain why using both would be better than using only one.
parts.answer: Quantitative: use event sampling with behavioural categories such as 'touches fruit', 'smells fruit', 'asks the seller about price', tallying each shopper's behaviours (and timing how long they spend at a stall). Qualitative: write descriptive notes of what shoppers say to sellers and how they bargain, or briefly interview some shoppers about how they choose. Both: the counts show how common each behaviour is and can be compared (e.g. men vs women), while the notes explain why shoppers act as they do and may reveal behaviours not on the checklist, so the findings are more valid and complete.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks: quantitative method described (categories/tally/time); up to 2 marks: qualitative method described (notes/interview/quotes); up to 2 marks: why both is better (complementary strengths, triangulation, validity).

stem: Nine participants in a hypothetical study in Quetta were timed (seconds) completing a jigsaw puzzle: 34, 41, 29, 41, 38, 45, 36, 41, 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean, the median and the mode of these times. Give the mean to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Mean 37.2 s; median 38 s; mode 41 s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of the mode for these data.
parts.answer: It only shows the most common time and ignores the other values; here the mode (41 s) is higher than five of the nine times, so it does not represent the typical time well.
parts.working: 1 mark: ignores most data / not representative / can be at an extreme.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A hypothetical class of 25 students in Gujranwala reported how many siblings they have.
Number of siblings | Frequency
0 | 3
1 | 7
2 | 9
3 | 5
4 | 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the modal number of siblings.
parts.working: Frequency 9 is the highest (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the median number of siblings.
parts.working: n = 25, so median is the 13th value; cumulative frequencies 3, 10, 19 → 13th value is 2 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of siblings.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Eight drivers in a hypothetical simulator study in Dubai pressed a brake pedal when a hazard appeared. Reaction times (ms): 412, 385, 450, 398, 520, 405, 430, 390

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the median reaction time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean reaction time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the mean is higher than the median for these data.
parts.answer: One very slow time (520 ms) pulls the mean up, but the median only depends on the middle values, so it is not affected by this extreme score.
parts.working: 1 mark: 520 ms is extreme/outlier; 1 mark: mean uses all values, median does not.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a hypothetical memory study in Rawalpindi, eight participants recalled these numbers of words from a list of 40: 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 9, 10, 31

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the median for all eight participants.
parts.answer: Mean 10.875 (10.9 to 1 d.p.); median 8.5

parts.label: b
parts.text: The researcher discovers that the participant who scored 31 had seen the list before. Calculate the mean and median of the other seven scores.
parts.answer: Mean 8; median 8

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain which measure was more affected by the score of 31.
parts.answer: The mean fell by 2.875 but the median fell by only 0.5, so the mean was much more affected by the extreme score.
parts.working: 1 mark: mean changed more (with figures); 1 mark: because mean uses actual values of all scores / median uses position.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two hypothetical groups of students in Bahawalpur were taught a maths topic in different ways and then tested (score out of 40).
Group A (worksheets): 22, 25, 19, 24, 27, 21, 23
Group B (online game): 18, 30, 12, 29, 15, 31, 26

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the median for each group.
parts.answer: Group A: mean 23, median 23. Group B: mean 23, median 26.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A newspaper reports that 'the two teaching methods worked equally well'. Explain why this conclusion, based only on the means, may be misleading.
parts.answer: Although the means are equal, the scores in Group B are much more spread out (12 to 31) and its median is higher, so the methods did not have the same effect: Group B worked very well for some students and poorly for others.
parts.working: 1 mark: same mean hides different spread/distribution; 1 mark: reference to data (range or median).

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a hypothetical study, 12 participants from Lahore had a mean score of 15 on a puzzle task and 8 participants from Karachi had a mean score of 20.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean score of all 20 participants together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the answer is not simply the average of 15 and 20.
parts.answer: The groups are different sizes; the group of 12 has more weight, so the overall mean is pulled closer to 15 than the simple average of 17.5.
parts.working: 1 mark: unequal group sizes; 1 mark: larger group carries more weight (17 not 17.5).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In a hypothetical repeated measures experiment in Abbottabad, six participants proofread a text in three conditions and the number of errors they missed was recorded.
Participant | Silence | Music | Television
1 | 8 | 11 | 7
2 | 6 | 9 | 5
3 | 9 | 12 | 8
4 | 7 | 10 | 8
5 | 10 | 13 | 9
6 | 8 | 11 | 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of errors in each condition.
parts.answer: Silence 8; music 11; television 7
parts.working: Silence 48 ÷ 6 = 8; music 66 ÷ 6 = 11; television 42 ÷ 6 = 7 (B1 each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the means, state which condition produced the fewest errors and suggest one reason why this result may need to be checked.
parts.answer: Television (mean 7). This is unexpected because television is usually distracting, so the result might be due to an order effect or chance with only six participants; the study should be replicated.
parts.working: 1 mark: television; 1 mark: sensible reason (small sample, order effects, unexpected result, need for replication/statistics).

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a hypothetical study, ten participants in Mardan scored: 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18, 34. The mean is 16.4. The score of 34 was later found to be a recording error.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean of the nine scores that remain when the error is removed. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the median before and after removing the score of 34.
parts.answer: Before: 15; after: 15

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what your answers show about the mean and the median.
parts.answer: Removing one extreme value changed the mean by almost 2 points but did not change the median at all, showing that the median is resistant to extreme values while the mean is sensitive to them.
parts.working: 1 mark: mean changed, median did not; 1 mark: conclusion about sensitivity to outliers.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ten viewers in a hypothetical study in Faisalabad rated a new television drama from 1 (very bad) to 5 (very good): 2, 5, 4, 2, 5, 3, 5, 2, 1, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the median and the mode of these ratings.
parts.answer: Median 3.5; modes 2 and 5 (bimodal)
parts.working: Ordered: 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5; median (3 + 4) ÷ 2 = 3.5 (B1); 2 and 5 each occur 3 times (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the median gives a misleading picture of these ratings.
parts.answer: The median of 3.5 suggests people felt neutral, but in fact opinions were split: many disliked it (2) and many liked it (5), and few gave a middle rating.
parts.working: 1 mark: median suggests middle/neutral view; 1 mark: data show two clusters/polarised opinions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest the most useful way of summarising these data and explain why.
parts.answer: Report both modes (or show a bar chart of frequencies for each rating), because this shows the two groups of opinion clearly.
parts.working: 1 mark: both modes / frequency table or bar chart; 1 mark: reason (shows polarisation).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each of the following sets of data, state the most appropriate measure of central tendency and explain your choice.
(i) The favourite fast-food chain chosen by 50 teenagers.
(ii) Self-rated happiness on a scale from 1 to 7 by 40 workers.
(iii) Times taken by 30 people to solve a puzzle, where two people took over 20 minutes and the rest took 2–5 minutes.
parts.answer: (i) Mode — the data are categories (names), so only the most frequent choice can be found. (ii) Median — ratings are ordered but the gaps between points may not be equal, so a mean of them may not be meaningful. (iii) Median — the two very slow times would distort the mean, but the median is not affected by extreme values.
parts.working: For each set: 1 mark correct measure; 1 mark justified reason.

stem: A hypothetical reasoning test was designed so that scores in a large population are normally distributed with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the range of scores within which about 68 % of people would be expected to fall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the range of scores within which about 95 % of people would be expected to fall.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what percentage of people would be expected to score above 130.
parts.answer: About 2.5 %

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the heights of 1000 adult women in Pakistan would be expected to show a normal distribution.
parts.answer: Most women are close to the average height, with fewer and fewer very short or very tall women, so the frequencies form a symmetrical bell shape around the mean.
parts.working: 1 mark: most scores near mean; 1 mark: fewer at the extremes, symmetrical.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the number of times people in the same sample have been abroad would probably not be normally distributed.
parts.answer: Most people would have been abroad zero or very few times and a small number would have travelled many times, so the data would bunch at the low end with a long tail to the right (positive skew).
parts.working: 1 mark: many scores at/near zero (floor); 1 mark: long tail to the right / positively skewed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'positively skewed' distribution.
parts.answer: A distribution where most scores are at the low end and a few high scores form a long tail to the right, so it is not symmetrical.
