parts.working: 1 mark: most scores low / peak to left; 1 mark: long tail to the right (towards high values).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the usual order of the mean, median and mode in a positively skewed distribution.
parts.answer: Mode < median < mean (the mean is highest).
parts.working: 1 mark: correct order.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of data in psychology that are likely to be positively skewed.
parts.answer: Reaction times, or the number of errors on an easy task.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Data set X: mean 24, median 24, mode 24. Data set Y: mean 31, median 36, mode 39. Data set Z: mean 52, median 45, mode 41. State which data set is most likely to be normally distributed and explain why.
parts.answer: X, because in a normal distribution the mean, median and mode are all equal (the distribution is symmetrical).
parts.working: 1 mark: X; 1 mark: mean = median = mode.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether data set Y is positively or negatively skewed and give a reason.
parts.answer: Negatively skewed, because the mean (31) is lower than the median (36) and the mode (39), so a few low scores pull the mean down.
parts.working: 1 mark: negative; 1 mark: mean < median < mode / tail to the left.

stem: A hypothetical attention test was given to 600 secondary-school students in Lahore. Scores were normally distributed with a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Approximately how many students would you expect to score between 42 and 58?
parts.working: 42 and 58 are 1 SD either side of the mean → 68 % of 600 = 408 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Approximately how many students would you expect to score above 66?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Approximately how many students would you expect to score below 42?

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A hypothetical problem-solving task was given to students in Sukkur (score out of 9).
Score | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9
Frequency | 1 | 3 | 7 | 12 | 15 | 12 | 7 | 3 | 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of participants and the mean score.
parts.answer: 61 participants; mean 5

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the mode and the median.
parts.answer: Mode 5; median 5
parts.working: Mode: frequency 15 at score 5 (B1); median: 31st value = 5 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether these data appear to be normally distributed.
parts.answer: Yes: the frequencies are symmetrical around 5, they rise to a single peak and fall evenly, and the mean, median and mode are equal.
parts.working: 1 mark: symmetrical/bell shape; 1 mark: mean = median = mode.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ten hypothetical scores on a visual memory test: 41, 47, 50, 52, 53, 55, 56, 58, 62, 76

parts.label: a
parts.text: The mean of these scores is 55 and the standard deviation is 9.4 (to 1 decimal place). How many of the ten scores lie within one standard deviation of the mean?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare your answer with what you would expect for a normal distribution.
parts.answer: 8 out of 10 is 80 %, which is higher than the 68 % expected within 1 SD in a normal distribution; with only ten scores and one extreme score (76) inflating the SD, this is not surprising.
parts.working: 1 mark: 80 % vs 68 %; 1 mark: comment (small sample / extreme value).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of a distribution in which mean = 74, median = 80 and mode = 85.
parts.answer: Negatively skewed: most scores are high, with the peak towards the right, and a long tail of a few low scores to the left.
parts.working: 1 mark: negatively skewed; 1 mark: description (bunched at high end, tail to the left).

parts.label: b
parts.text: These are scores (out of 90) on a hypothetical spelling test given to children in Mirpur. Suggest why the scores might have this shape.
parts.answer: The test was too easy, so many children scored near the maximum (a ceiling effect) and only a few children who struggled scored low.
parts.working: 1 mark: ceiling effect / test too easy; 1 mark: explained (scores cannot go above 90, many near top).

stem: In a hypothetical study, Group A (no training) had normally distributed scores with mean 60 and SD 5. Group B (memory training) had normally distributed scores with mean 70 and SD 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the approximate percentage of Group B who scored below 60.
parts.answer: About 2.5 %
parts.working: 60 = 70 − 2 × 5, i.e. 2 SD below B's mean → 2.5 % (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the approximate percentage of Group A who scored above 65.
parts.answer: About 16 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the difference between these two groups is likely to be meaningful, using the means and standard deviations.
parts.answer: The means are 10 points apart, which is two standard deviations, and both groups are quite consistent (SD 5), so the distributions overlap only a little; the difference is unlikely to be due to chance variation alone.
parts.working: 1 mark: difference = 2 SD; 1 mark: small overlap/low spread → meaningful difference.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a normally distributed set of scores, about 95 % lie between 34 and 66. Calculate the mean and the standard deviation.
parts.answer: Mean 50; SD 8

parts.label: b
parts.text: A participant scores 74. Explain what this tells you about the score.
parts.answer: 74 is 3 SD above the mean (50 + 24), so only about 0.1 % of people would score this high (roughly 1 in 750); it is a very unusual score.
parts.working: 1 mark: 3 SD above mean; 1 mark: very rare (≈0.1 %, beyond the 99.7 % range).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher designed a test of knowledge of road signs for new drivers in Islamabad, but the results were strongly positively skewed. Explain what this suggests about the test and suggest one way of improving it.
parts.answer: Most drivers scored very low with a few high scorers, so the test was probably too difficult — a floor effect — and it cannot tell apart drivers at the lower end. It could be improved by adding easier items (and fewer very hard ones), piloting it with a small group first, so that scores spread out around a middle mean.
parts.working: 1 mark: most scores low / tail to the right; 1 mark: test too hard / floor effect; 1 mark: consequence (cannot discriminate); 1 mark: improvement (easier items / pilot study).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the mean and standard deviation are the best summary statistics when data are normally distributed, but the median and range may be better when data are skewed.
parts.answer: In a normal distribution the data are symmetrical, so the mean is the typical value (equal to the median and mode) and the SD tells you where about 68 % and 95 % of scores lie. In a skewed distribution a few extreme scores in the tail pull the mean towards them and inflate the SD, so the mean is no longer typical; the median is not affected by extreme scores, so it better represents the middle (with the range showing the full spread).
parts.working: 1 mark: normal → symmetrical so mean is central/typical; 1 mark: SD meaningful (68/95 % rule); 1 mark: skew → extreme scores distort mean/SD; 1 mark: median resistant to extremes.

stem:
Hypothetical number of customers served per hour by two teams of cashiers at a supermarket in Lahore.
Team P: 18, 22, 25, 20, 27, 24
Team Q: 13, 30, 21, 35, 16, 28

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the range for each team.
parts.answer: Team P: 9; Team Q: 22

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the ranges, state which team was more consistent.
parts.answer: Team P, because its range is smaller.
parts.working: 1 mark: P with reason.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a hypothetical study in Peshawar, two groups of 15 students completed an exam-stress questionnaire (score out of 50). Group A (no revision plan) had a mean of 31 and a standard deviation of 6.8. Group B (weekly revision plan) had a mean of 27 and a standard deviation of 1.4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'measure of spread'.
parts.answer: A statistic that shows how much the scores in a data set vary from each other or from the average.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the standard deviations show about the two groups.
parts.answer: Group B's scores (SD 1.4) were close to their mean, so the group was consistent; Group A's scores (SD 6.8) were much more spread out, so individuals varied a lot.
parts.working: 1 mark: B small SD = scores clustered/consistent; 1 mark: A large SD = more varied.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Seven participants in a hypothetical study in Gilgit counted the number of times they checked their phone in an hour: 12, 9, 14, 11, 40, 17, 13

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the range of these scores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the range without the score of 40.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain one weakness of the range.
parts.answer: The range uses only the two most extreme scores, so one unusual score (40) made the spread look almost four times bigger than it is for most participants.
parts.working: 1 mark: uses only highest and lowest; 1 mark: easily distorted by an outlier (with reference to data).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one strength of the range as a measure of spread.
parts.answer: It is quick and easy to calculate.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one strength of the standard deviation compared with the range.
parts.answer: It uses every score in the data set, so it is more representative and less distorted by one extreme value.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the standard deviation of a set of scores can never be negative.
parts.answer: It is based on squared differences from the mean, which are always zero or positive; the square root of a positive number is taken, so the result is zero or positive.
parts.working: 1 mark: squared deviations (non-negative); 1 mark: square root is positive / zero only if all scores equal.

stem: Six hypothetical participants in Jhelum rated their confidence after a public-speaking workshop (out of 20): 12, 15, 9, 18, 16, 14

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean of these scores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation using s = √(Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Five hypothetical scores on a hand-eye coordination task in Larkana: 20, 22, 25, 27, 31

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copy and complete the calculation: find the mean, each deviation (x − mean), each squared deviation, and Σ(x − mean)².
parts.answer: Mean = 25. Deviations: −5, −3, 0, 2, 6. Squared: 25, 9, 0, 4, 36. Σ(x − mean)² = 74.
parts.working: 1 mark: mean 25; 1 mark: deviations; 1 mark: squares and sum 74.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the standard deviation using the sample formula (divide by n − 1). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Two hypothetical sets of six scores (mean 20 for both):
Set A: 10, 20, 20, 20, 20, 30
Set B: 10, 10, 10, 30, 30, 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the range for each set.
parts.answer: Both ranges are 20

parts.label: b
parts.text: The standard deviations are 6.32 for Set A and 10.95 for Set B. Explain why the standard deviation gives a better description of these data than the range.
parts.answer: The ranges are the same, which suggests equal spread, but in Set A four of the six scores are exactly at the mean (20), while in Set B every score is 10 away from the mean. The SD uses every score, so it correctly shows that Set B is much more spread out.
parts.working: 1 mark: ranges identical; 1 mark: describes difference in the data (A clustered at 20, B all at extremes); 1 mark: SD uses all scores so shows B more variable.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A hypothetical repeated measures experiment in Muzaffarabad compared the number of anagrams solved in 10 minutes in the morning and at night.
Condition | Mean | Standard deviation
Morning | 18 | 2.0
Night | 14 | 5.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the two conditions using the means and the standard deviations.
parts.answer: Participants solved more anagrams in the morning (mean 18) than at night (mean 14), and their scores were more consistent in the morning (SD 2.0) than at night (SD 5.5), when scores varied much more.
parts.working: 1 mark: comparison of means; 1 mark: comparison of SDs (spread).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why scores varied more at night.
parts.answer: People differ in how tired they get at night (some are 'night owls' and others are very sleepy), so tiredness affects some participants much more than others.
parts.working: 1 mark: individual differences in tiredness/sleep habits; 1 mark: explained.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Hypothetical results of a study with 8 participants per condition.
Condition | Mean score | SD
X | 18 | 6.5
Y | 16 | 1.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher claims that condition X is better than condition Y. Using the data, explain why this claim is not well supported.
parts.answer: The means differ by only 2 points, but condition X has a very large SD (6.5), so scores in X ranged widely and overlapped heavily with Y. The difference in means could easily be due to a few high scorers in X rather than a real effect, especially with only 8 per group.
parts.working: 1 mark: small difference in means (2); 1 mark: large SD in X → big overlap/inconsistent; 1 mark: conclusion (could be chance / small sample / need inferential test).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what the researcher should do before drawing a conclusion.
parts.answer: Use a larger sample (or an inferential statistical test) to see whether the difference is significant.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Five hypothetical participants in Nawabshah scored 11, 14, 9, 16 and 10 on a vocabulary test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean and range of these scores.
parts.answer: Mean 12; range 7

parts.label: b
parts.text: Because the scoring sheet was printed wrongly, every participant's score needs 3 marks added. State the new mean, the new range and what happens to the standard deviation, and explain why.
parts.answer: New mean 15; range still 7; SD unchanged (2.92). Adding the same amount to every score moves the whole distribution up by 3, but the distances between scores, and between each score and the mean, stay the same, so measures of spread do not change.
parts.working: 1 mark: mean 15; 1 mark: range 7; 1 mark: SD unchanged; 1 mark: explanation (all deviations the same).

author: HomiLabs

stem:
In a hypothetical repeated measures study in Chitral, six participants recalled items from a shopping list in a quiet room and with traffic noise.
Participant | Quiet | Noise
1 | 14 | 9
2 | 17 | 18
3 | 15 | 12
4 | 16 | 20
5 | 18 | 7
6 | 16 | 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean, range and standard deviation (sample formula, n − 1) for each condition. Give standard deviations to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Quiet: mean 16, range 4, SD 1.41. Noise: mean 13, range 13, SD 5.06.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a conclusion that uses both the means and the measures of spread.
parts.answer: On average, participants recalled more in quiet (16) than with noise (13), and noise also made performance much less consistent (SD 5.06 vs 1.41): some were badly affected and a few (e.g. scores of 18 and 20) were not.
parts.working: 1 mark: mean comparison; 1 mark: spread comparison with interpretation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Ten hypothetical scores on a stress questionnaire completed by bank employees in Karachi: 31, 35, 28, 33, 30, 36, 52, 29, 34, 32

parts.label: a
parts.text: The mean of these scores is 34 and the standard deviation is 6.83. Identify any score that lies more than two standard deviations from the mean.
parts.working: Mean ± 2 SD = 20.34 to 47.66 (M1); only 52 lies outside (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a score more than two standard deviations from the mean is described as unusual.
parts.answer: If data are normally distributed, about 95 % of scores lie within 2 SD of the mean, so a score beyond this is found in fewer than 5 % of people.
parts.working: 1 mark: 95 % within 2 SD; 1 mark: so fewer than 5 % beyond → unusual.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the researcher should investigate this score before deciding whether to remove it.
parts.answer: It might be a recording error or from a participant who misunderstood the task (then removal is justified), but it could also be a genuine score from someone who really is different; removing real data would bias the results.
parts.working: 1 mark: possible error/misunderstanding; 1 mark: may be genuine — removal would bias/reduce validity.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a standardised procedure helps to make a study reliable.
parts.answer: If every participant is given exactly the same instructions, materials and conditions, the procedure can be repeated in the same way by the same or other researchers, so results should be consistent if the study is replicated.
parts.working: 1 mark: same procedure for all participants; 1 mark: allows replication / consistent results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical study in Lahore measured how long shoppers looked at a shop window. The researcher timed them with a hand-held stopwatch. Suggest one reason why this measurement may not be reliable and how it could be improved.
parts.answer: The researcher's reaction time in starting and stopping the watch would vary from shopper to shopper, so times would be inconsistent. Video-record the window and time the looks frame by frame (or use two timers and compare).
parts.working: 1 mark: human timing error/inconsistent judgement of start and stop; 1 mark: improvement (video, automatic sensor, two timers).

stem: In a hypothetical observation of turn-taking among children playing ludo in Hyderabad, two observers coded the same 50 one-minute intervals. They agreed on 46 intervals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage agreement between the two observers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what this result suggests about the observation.
parts.answer: Agreement above 80 % is usually seen as good, so the observers were coding behaviour consistently: the behavioural categories had good inter-rater reliability.
parts.working: 1 mark: high/good agreement (above 80 %); 1 mark: inter-rater reliability is good / categories clear.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by test–retest reliability.
parts.answer: Giving the same test to the same participants on two occasions, separated by a suitable time, and checking that their scores are similar (strongly positively correlated).
parts.working: 1 mark: same test, same people, twice; 1 mark: results compared/correlated for consistency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the time between the two tests should be neither too short nor too long.
parts.answer: If too short, participants may remember their earlier answers and copy them, making the test look more reliable than it is; if too long, the thing being measured (e.g. mood or skill) may have really changed.
parts.working: 1 mark: too short → remembering answers/practice; 1 mark: too long → genuine change in the trait.

stem:
A hypothetical self-confidence questionnaire (score out of 40) was completed by six students in Sargodha and repeated two weeks later.
Participant | Test 1 | Test 2
1 | 24 | 25
2 | 31 | 29
3 | 18 | 20
4 | 27 | 28
5 | 35 | 30
6 | 22 | 23

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which participant's score changed most between the two tests and by how much.
parts.answer: Participant 5, by 5 points (35 to 30).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many participants' scores changed by 2 points or fewer.
parts.working: Changes: 1, 2, 2, 1, 5, 1 → five participants ≤ 2 (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what these data suggest about the test–retest reliability of the questionnaire.
parts.answer: Most participants scored almost the same on both occasions and kept their rank order, suggesting good test–retest reliability; participant 5's drop may be a real change in confidence or a sign that some items are unclear.
parts.working: 1 mark: mostly consistent → reliable; 1 mark: comment on participant 5 / small sample.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher is interviewing 30 shopkeepers in Rawalpindi about stress at work. Describe two ways she could make the interviews more reliable.
parts.answer: 1. Use a structured interview with the same questions in the same order for every shopkeeper, so all are asked the same thing. 2. Train all interviewers to use the same neutral tone and the same prompts (or record and code answers with a fixed scheme by two coders), so the way answers are obtained and scored is consistent.
parts.working: For each way: 1 mark identified (structured/standard questions, same order, interviewer training, recording, coding scheme, two coders); 1 mark explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a pilot study could improve the reliability of a new observation checklist.
parts.answer: The researchers could try out the checklist on a small group first and have two observers use it independently. Where they disagree, unclear categories can be redefined or merged and observers trained, so in the main study observers record behaviour consistently.
parts.working: 1 mark: small trial before main study; 1 mark: find unclear categories/disagreements; 1 mark: revise categories/train observers → consistency.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A psychologist in Pakistan has written a new Urdu questionnaire to measure test anxiety in secondary-school students. Describe how she could check the test–retest reliability of the questionnaire, and explain one difficulty she might face.
parts.answer: Give the questionnaire to a sample of students (e.g. 50 students from several schools) under standardised conditions. Repeat it with the same students after a suitable gap (e.g. two to three weeks), at a time with similar exam pressure. Compare each student's two scores using a correlation; a strong positive correlation (e.g. +0.8 or above) indicates good reliability. Difficulty: test anxiety may genuinely change if an exam gets closer, or students may remember and repeat their answers, so differences or similarities may not reflect the questionnaire itself.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for the method: same participants; same questionnaire and conditions; suitable time gap; correlate scores / strong positive correlation needed. Up to 2 marks: difficulty identified and explained (real change, memory of answers, drop-out, timing of exams).

stem:
In a hypothetical study, two judges rated the creativity of eight short stories written by students in Islamabad (1–10).
Essay | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8
Judge A | 7 | 5 | 8 | 4 | 6 | 9 | 3 | 6
Judge B | 7 | 6 | 8 | 2 | 6 | 8 | 3 | 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: For how many essays did the two judges give exactly the same rating?
parts.working: Essays 1, 3, 5 and 7 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of essays for which the two ratings were within 1 point of each other.
parts.working: Differences 0, 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 1 → 7 of 8 within 1 point; 7 ÷ 8 × 100 = 87.5 % (B1).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean difference between the two judges' ratings, ignoring direction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate the inter-rater reliability of the creativity ratings and suggest one improvement.
parts.answer: Agreement is fairly good (7 of 8 within one point) but exact agreement is only 50 % and essay 4 differs by 2 points, so the judges may understand 'creativity' differently. They should agree a detailed marking scheme with examples of each rating and practise together on other essays before rating.
parts.working: 1 mark: good/moderate overall with data; 1 mark: weakness identified with data (50 % exact, essay 4); 1 mark: improvement (operational definitions/rubric, training, more judges).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using examples, why a measure can be reliable without being valid, but cannot be valid without being reliable.
parts.answer: A measure is reliable if it gives consistent results. A bathroom scale that always reads 2 kg too heavy is reliable (same result each time) but not valid (it does not measure true weight). Similarly, measuring intelligence by head size would give consistent but meaningless results. However, if a measure gives different results each time (e.g. a questionnaire with vague questions), it cannot be accurately measuring what it should, so validity needs reliability.
parts.working: 1 mark: definitions of reliability/validity; 1 mark: example of reliable but not valid; 1 mark: explanation why unreliable cannot be valid; 1 mark: example/elaboration.

stem: A hypothetical study of work stress among teachers in government schools in Punjab asked for volunteers at two schools in Multan; 22 teachers took part.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the target population of this study.
parts.answer: Teachers in government schools in Punjab.
parts.working: 1 mark (accept: teachers in Punjab).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the results may not be generalisable to all teachers in Punjab.
parts.answer: The sample came from only two schools in one city (Multan), so they may not represent teachers in rural areas or other cities, whose workload and stress may be different.
parts.working: 1 mark: limited/unrepresentative sample (two schools, one city, volunteers); 1 mark: why they may differ from the population.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a volunteer (self-selected) sample may reduce generalisability.
parts.answer: People who volunteer tend to be more interested, confident or helpful than others, so the sample may not be typical of the target population.
parts.working: 1 mark: volunteers share particular characteristics; 1 mark: so not representative.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a very small sample reduces generalisability.
parts.answer: With few participants, individual differences (e.g. one unusual person) have a big effect on the results, and the sample is unlikely to include the variety of people in the population.
parts.working: 1 mark: unusual individuals have a large effect; 1 mark: unlikely to represent the range of the population.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the sample in Milgram's (1963) study.
parts.answer: 40 men aged 20 to 50 from New Haven and the surrounding area, with a range of jobs, recruited by a newspaper advertisement and direct mailing (volunteer sample).
parts.working: 1 mark: 40 males, aged 20–50; 1 mark: New Haven area / range of occupations / volunteers via advert.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the findings may not be generalised to women.
parts.answer: Only men were tested, and women may respond differently to an order to harm someone (for example they may be more empathetic or more conforming), so the 65 % obedience level may not apply to them.
parts.working: 1 mark: all-male sample; 1 mark: reason women might behave differently.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study in Germany found that students who studied in short bursts remembered more than those who studied for one long session. Explain one reason why a teacher in Karachi should be careful before applying this finding to her students.
parts.answer: The study was done in a different culture and education system; Pakistani students may study in different conditions (e.g. tuition, exam style, home environment), so the result may not generalise to them.
parts.working: 1 mark: different culture/country/education system; 1 mark: how this might change the result.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one reason why Piliavin et al.'s findings can be generalised to many people.
parts.answer: About 4450 passengers were observed, a large sample of men and women of different races and ages who used the subway on weekdays, so the results represent a wide range of ordinary people.
parts.working: 1 mark: large/varied sample (about 4450 passengers); 1 mark: explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the findings may not be generalised to all emergency situations.
parts.answer: The study was on one stretch of a New York subway where passengers could not leave the train between stations; in an open street people can walk away, so helping may be lower there.
parts.working: 1 mark: specific setting (closed train, no escape, one city, 1968); 1 mark: how other settings differ.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why random sampling usually gives more generalisable results than opportunity sampling.
parts.answer: In random sampling every member of the target population has an equal chance of being chosen, so the sample is not biased by the researcher's choices and is likely to include a range of people. In opportunity sampling the researcher picks whoever is available (e.g. people in one café at one time), who may share characteristics that are not typical of the population.
parts.working: 1 mark: equal chance in random sampling; 1 mark: reduces researcher bias/more representative; 1 mark: opportunity sample biased to those available.

stem: In a hypothetical school in Sialkot, 60 % of the pupils are girls. A researcher studying homework habits recruited 40 pupils, of whom 18 were girls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of girls in the sample.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether the sample is representative of the school in terms of gender.
parts.answer: Not fully: girls are 60 % of the school but only 45 % of the sample, so girls are under-represented and boys over-represented.
parts.working: 1 mark: compares 45 % with 60 %; 1 mark: conclusion — girls under-represented.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the sample could be chosen to match the school's gender balance.
parts.answer: Use stratified sampling: select 24 girls and 16 boys (60 % and 40 % of 40) at random.
parts.working: 1 mark: stratified sampling with correct numbers or description.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study found that rats learned a maze faster when rewarded with sugar. Explain one reason why this finding should be generalised to human learning with caution.
parts.answer: Humans have more complex brains and use language, thinking and social motivation when learning, so what works for rats may not work in the same way for people.
parts.working: 1 mark: species differences; 1 mark: specific difference explained (cognition, language, culture, motivation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why animal findings may still tell us something about human behaviour.
parts.answer: Rats and humans share basic brain structures and learning processes (such as reinforcement), so basic principles found in rats may apply to humans too.
parts.working: 1 mark: shared biology/learning processes; 1 mark: explained.

stem: A hypothetical college in Peshawar has 1200 students: 480 in science, 420 in arts and 300 in commerce. A researcher wants to survey 60 students about their use of the library.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many students from each faculty should be included in a stratified sample of 60.
parts.answer: Science 24; arts 21; commerce 15

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a stratified sample would improve the generalisability of this study.
parts.answer: Each faculty is represented in the same proportion as in the college, so the views of students in all three faculties are fairly included and the results better reflect the whole college.
parts.working: 1 mark: same proportions as population; 1 mark: so sample represents all subgroups.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between generalisability and ecological validity, using an example of each.
parts.answer: Generalisability is whether the findings can be applied from the sample to the wider target population (or other populations), e.g. whether Milgram's results with American men apply to women. Ecological validity is whether the findings can be applied from the research setting and task to real-life settings, e.g. whether shocking a learner in a laboratory reflects obedience at work. A study can have a representative sample but low ecological validity, or the reverse.
parts.working: 1 mark: definition of generalisability (sample → population); 1 mark: example; 1 mark: definition of ecological validity (setting/task → real life); 1 mark: example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical laboratory experiment with 30 psychology undergraduates found that people made more errors on a typing task when a supervisor watched them. A company in Lahore wants to remove supervisors from its data-entry office. Evaluate whether the findings can be generalised to the company's workers.
parts.answer: For: the task (typing) is similar to data entry, and being watched may have a general effect on performance. Against: the sample was 30 psychology students, who are younger, less experienced and may guess the aim (demand characteristics), unlike experienced office workers who may be used to supervision. The laboratory setting and short task lack ecological validity; in a real office, supervisors may also help or motivate. So the company should test the idea in its own office first.
parts.working: 1 mark: point for generalising; 1 mark: sample problem (students vs workers); 1 mark: setting/task problem; 1 mark: reasoned conclusion/suggestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study investigated whether listening to Qur'an recitation reduces anxiety before surgery. It used 12 female patients aged 30–40 at one private hospital in Islamabad. Suggest three changes that would make the findings more generalisable, and explain each.
parts.answer: 1. Increase the sample size (e.g. 100+), so individual differences have less effect. 2. Include men and women of a wide range of ages, so the results apply to all adult patients. 3. Use several hospitals (government and private, in different cities) and random or stratified sampling, so the sample reflects patients of different income levels and regions.
parts.working: For each change: 1 mark identified; 1 mark explained (link to representativeness).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'objectivity' in research.
parts.answer: Data and conclusions that are not affected by the researcher's own opinions, feelings or expectations, so different researchers would record the same result.
parts.working: 1 mark: not influenced by personal views/bias; 1 mark: same result from different researchers / based on fact.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of an objective measure in a study of driving skill.
parts.answer: Number of cones knocked over on a driving course (or reaction time measured by a computer).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each measure, state whether it is objective or subjective.
(i) Heart rate measured by a monitor.
(ii) A teacher's rating of how hard a child is trying.
(iii) Number of words recalled from a list.
(iv) A participant's description of how lonely they feel.
parts.answer: (i) objective (ii) subjective (iii) objective (iv) subjective
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how an interviewer's own views could make the data collected in an interview subjective.
parts.answer: The interviewer might ask leading questions, react positively to answers they agree with, or interpret and record answers in a way that fits what they believe, so the data reflect the interviewer's views as well as the participant's.
parts.working: 1 mark: way the interviewer influences answers or interpretation; 1 mark: consequence (data biased/subjective).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing this problem.
parts.answer: Use a standardised (structured) interview schedule, or record the interview and have a second person, unaware of the aim, code the answers.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how using operationalised behavioural categories makes an observation more objective.
parts.answer: Each behaviour is defined in clear, observable terms (e.g. 'hits another child with an open hand'), so observers record what actually happens instead of making personal judgements about what the behaviour means.
parts.working: 1 mark: clear observable definitions; 1 mark: less need for observer interpretation/personal judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one objective measure and one subjective measure used in Milgram's study.
parts.answer: Objective: the maximum voltage each participant gave (shock level). Subjective: observers' descriptions of participants' tension, such as nervous laughter or sweating.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of having both kinds of data in this study.
parts.answer: The voltage shows how many obeyed and can be compared, while the descriptions of tension show that participants were distressed and believed the shocks were real, which explains why the obedience was important.
parts.working: 1 mark: what objective data add; 1 mark: what subjective/qualitative data add.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Patients in a hypothetical study at a clinic in Quetta rate their back pain from 0 to 10. Explain one strength and one weakness of measuring pain in this way.
parts.answer: Strength: pain is a private experience, so the patient's own rating is the only direct way to measure how much it hurts, and the number is easy to compare across days. Weakness: the rating is subjective — different patients may use the scale differently (one person's 6 may be another's 3), and they may exaggerate or play down their pain.
parts.working: 1 mark: strength identified; 1 mark: explained; 1 mark: weakness identified (subjective/scale used differently/social desirability); 1 mark: explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'blind' observer and why using one increases objectivity.
parts.answer: A blind observer does not know the aim of the study or which condition each participant is in. This means their expectations cannot influence what they notice or how they record behaviour, so the data are more objective.
parts.working: 1 mark: does not know aim/condition/hypothesis; 1 mark: expectations cannot bias recording; 1 mark: data more objective/less observer bias.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher uses a 1–7 scale for observers to rate how 'friendly' customers are towards shop staff. Explain why these ratings are subjective.
parts.answer: 'Friendly' is not defined, so each observer uses their own idea of friendliness and their own standards for what counts as a 5 or a 6.
parts.working: 1 mark: vague/undefined term; 1 mark: depends on personal judgement of each observer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways of making the ratings more objective.
parts.answer: 1. Define each point of the scale with observable behaviours (e.g. 7 = smiles, greets staff and thanks them). 2. Replace the rating with counts of specific behaviours such as smiles and 'thank you's.
parts.working: 1 mark each: anchored/defined scale points; counting behaviours; training observers with examples; using two observers and comparing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why thematic analysis of interview transcripts can be subjective, and suggest one way of reducing this.
parts.answer: The researcher decides which themes exist and which quotes belong to each theme; their own expectations and background may lead them to notice themes that fit their views and ignore others. To reduce this, a second researcher could analyse the same transcripts independently and the two sets of themes could be compared (or the themes could be checked with the participants).
parts.working: 1 mark: researcher chooses themes/interprets meaning; 1 mark: influenced by expectations/background; 1 mark: method to reduce (second analyst, agreed coding, participant checks); 1 mark: explained.

stem:
In a hypothetical study in Karachi, six children were filmed playing after watching a cartoon. Two observers rated each child's aggression from 1 to 10. Observer A knew the children had watched a violent cartoon; Observer B did not know which cartoon they had watched.
Child | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
Observer A | 6 | 7 | 7 | 9 | 5 | 8
Observer B | 4 | 6 | 5 | 7 | 3 | 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean aggression rating given by each observer.
parts.answer: Observer A: 7; Observer B: 5

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data, explain what may have caused the difference between the two observers.
parts.answer: Observer A knew that the children had watched a violent cartoon and expected them to be aggressive, so may have interpreted ambiguous play as aggression (observer bias); Observer B did not know, so gave lower ratings.
parts.working: 1 mark: A's expectations / knowledge of condition; 1 mark: interpretation of ambiguous behaviour → higher ratings (observer bias).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain which observer's data should be used and why.
parts.answer: Observer B's, because the blind observer's ratings are less likely to be influenced by expectations, so they are more objective (although both should ideally use defined behavioural categories).
parts.working: 1 mark: Observer B; 1 mark: blind → more objective.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: 'Subjectivity is always a weakness in psychological research.' To what extent do you agree?
parts.answer: Partly disagree. Subjective data from the researcher (e.g. biased interpretation) are a weakness because they reduce validity and reliability. But participants' subjective experiences, such as feelings, pain or reasons for behaviour, are often what psychologists need to study, and self-reports or qualitative descriptions are the only way to access them; they can give more valid insight than objective numbers alone. So subjectivity of the participant's experience can be a strength, provided the researcher's analysis is kept as objective as possible.
parts.working: 1 mark: why researcher subjectivity is a weakness; 1 mark: some topics are subjective by nature (feelings, pain); 1 mark: subjective data can increase validity/insight; 1 mark: balanced conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the objectivity of the data collected in Perry et al.'s study with the data collected in Piliavin et al.'s study.
parts.answer: Perry et al. measured preferred distance in centimetres in a controlled laboratory with a double-blind procedure, so the main data were highly objective and not affected by researchers' expectations. Piliavin et al.'s observers recorded behaviour in a busy carriage and had to judge features such as passengers' race, sex and location, and how long it took for help to arrive, so some recording involved judgement in difficult conditions. Both collected mainly quantitative data, but Perry's measurement was more objective; Piliavin's observers recorded in a busy, unpredictable setting where judgements could be biased, so observer bias is possible.
parts.working: 1 mark: Perry's measure objective (distance/double-blind); 1 mark: Piliavin's observers making judgements in a natural setting; 1 mark: similarity (both quantitative); 1 mark: conclusion comparing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher plans to investigate whether children in Lahore who play outdoors are more cooperative at school. Teachers who know which children play outdoors will rate each child's cooperation. Explain two problems with the objectivity of this plan and suggest how each could be solved.
parts.answer: 1. Teachers' expectations: teachers who know which children play outdoors may expect them to be more cooperative and rate them higher (observer/researcher bias). Solution: use raters who do not know which children play outdoors (blind ratings). 2. 'Cooperation' is vague, so each teacher will judge it differently (subjective rating). Solution: operationalise it as observable behaviours (e.g. number of times the child shares materials or helps a classmate in a 30-minute lesson), recorded with a checklist by two observers whose agreement is checked.
parts.working: For each problem: 1 mark identified; 1 mark explained in context; 1 mark suitable solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the experimental design used in each of the following hypothetical studies.
(i) Each of 20 cyclists in Lahore is timed riding 1 km with music and, on another day, without music.
(ii) 30 shoppers are randomly split: 15 taste a drink from a red cup and 15 from a blue cup.
(iii) Students are put into pairs with the same O Level maths grade; one of each pair learns with flashcards, the other with notes.
parts.answer: (i) repeated measures (ii) independent measures (iii) matched pairs
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment compares how fast bilingual students in Karachi read a passage in Urdu and an equivalent passage in English. Each student reads both passages. Explain one strength of this design for this study.
parts.answer: Each student is compared with themselves, so differences in general reading ability or eyesight between students cannot explain the difference between the two languages.
parts.working: 1 mark: removes participant variables; 1 mark: applied (reading ability, speed, eyesight).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of this design for this study.
parts.answer: Order effects: reading the first passage may give practice (or tiredness) that changes speed on the second, so the difference may be due to order rather than language.
parts.working: 1 mark: order/practice/fatigue effect; 1 mark: applied.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'participant variables' in an independent measures design.
parts.answer: Differences between the people in each group, such as age, ability or motivation, which might affect the DV and make the groups differ for reasons other than the IV.
parts.working: 1 mark: individual differences between participants in different groups; 1 mark: may affect the DV/confound.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how a researcher can reduce the effect of participant variables in an independent measures design.
parts.answer: Randomly allocate participants to the conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical matched pairs experiment compares two revision apps for O Level chemistry students in Faisalabad. Suggest two variables the students should be matched on and give a reason for each.
parts.answer: 1. Previous chemistry test score, because students who already know more will score higher whichever app they use. 2. Hours of tuition per week, because extra teaching would also improve scores. (Also accept: age, school, English reading level, access to a phone.)
parts.working: For each: 1 mark relevant variable; 1 mark reason it could affect the DV.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical experiment, each participant does the conditions in the order A, B, B, A (for example, typing with a keyboard, then a touch screen, then the touch screen again, then the keyboard). Explain how this controls order effects.
parts.answer: Each condition appears once early and once late in the sequence, so any practice or tiredness effect is spread equally across both conditions. The mean of each participant's two A trials can then be compared with the mean of the two B trials.
parts.working: 1 mark: each condition in early and late positions; 1 mark: practice/fatigue affects both equally; 1 mark: compare averaged scores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one weakness of the ABBA method.
parts.answer: It takes longer and each participant does more trials, so boredom or fatigue increases; participants may also guess the aim.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study in Islamabad tests whether drinking strong coffee in the evening reduces the number of hours people sleep. Explain why a repeated measures design might cause problems, and how the researcher could still use it.
parts.answer: Effects of caffeine may carry over: if the coffee night comes first, the person may sleep badly and then sleep more the following night, which would affect the no-coffee condition. The researcher could leave a gap of several days between the two nights (washout) and counterbalance the order, so that half the participants have coffee first and half no-coffee first.
parts.working: 1 mark: carry-over/order effect identified; 1 mark: explained; 1 mark: time gap between conditions; 1 mark: counterbalancing.

stem:
In a hypothetical matched pairs experiment in Gujranwala, pairs of students with the same English grade learned vocabulary by a new game-based method or the old list method, and were tested (score out of 25).
Pair | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
New method | 15 | 18 | 12 | 20 | 16 | 14
Old method | 13 | 17 | 12 | 16 | 15 | 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in score for each pair (new method minus old method) and the mean difference.
parts.answer: Differences: 2, 1, 0, 4, 1, 4; mean difference 2
parts.working: Differences correct (B1); 12 ÷ 6 = 2 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of pairs in which the new method gave the higher score.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it is useful to compare the two members of each pair, rather than just the overall means.
parts.answer: Because pairs were matched on ability, comparing within pairs removes the effect of ability, so the difference in each pair is more likely to be due to the teaching method.
parts.working: 1 mark: matching controls participant variable (ability); 1 mark: within-pair difference reflects IV.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: A researcher needs 20 scores in each of two conditions. State how many participants are needed with (i) a repeated measures design and (ii) an independent measures design.
parts.working: (i) each participant gives a score in both conditions → 20 (B1); (ii) different people in each condition → 2 × 20 = 40 (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a researcher might still choose the independent measures design even though it needs more participants.
parts.answer: There are no order effects, and participants see only one condition so they are less likely to guess the aim (fewer demand characteristics); the same materials can also be used in both conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: reason (no order effects / fewer demand characteristics / same materials / no carry-over); 1 mark: explained.

stem:
In a hypothetical repeated measures experiment in Bahawalpur, 20 participants solved puzzles in condition A (quiet) and condition B (with a ticking clock). Ten did A then B; ten did B then A. Mean scores:
Group | First test | Second test
Group 1 (A then B) | A = 12 | B = 16
Group 2 (B then A) | B = 13 | A = 15

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the overall mean score for condition A and for condition B.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean score for the first test and for the second test that participants did, whatever the condition.
parts.answer: First test: 12.5; second test: 15.5

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answers, explain what the data show about order effects and about the IV.
parts.answer: Scores were 3 points higher on the second test whatever the condition, showing a strong practice effect. The difference between conditions was only 1 point, so the IV had little effect; counterbalancing stopped the practice effect from making one condition look better.
parts.working: 1 mark: practice effect of 3; 1 mark: small condition effect / counterbalancing balanced it out.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hypothetical independent measures experiment in Lahore compared two ways of training adults to use a mobile banking app (video or face-to-face). 40 volunteers were randomly allocated to the two groups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After random allocation, the mean ages of the two groups were 34 years (group A) and 21 years (group B). Explain why this is a problem for this study.
parts.answer: Age could affect learning to use a smartphone banking app (younger people may already be more familiar with apps), so any difference in performance could be due to age rather than the type of training: age is a confounding participant variable.
parts.working: 1 mark: age may affect the DV; 1 mark: confounds the IV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the researcher could have avoided this problem, and explain one weakness of your suggestion.
parts.answer: Use a matched pairs design: pair participants of similar age (and app experience), then randomly assign one of each pair to each training type. Weakness: matching takes time, and if one member of a pair drops out, the other's data cannot be used; participants can only be matched on a few variables.
parts.working: 1 mark: matched pairs on age / stratified random allocation; 1 mark: described; 1 mark: weakness.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why studies comparing identical twins can be seen as a natural form of matched pairs design.
parts.answer: Identical twins share all their genes and usually the same upbringing, so they are matched on many participant variables at once; giving one twin each condition controls these variables.
parts.working: 1 mark: twins share genes/environment; 1 mark: so matched on participant variables.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one limitation of using twins in this way.
parts.answer: Twins are a small and possibly unusual group (they grow up together and may influence each other), so the results may not generalise to non-twins, and twins may still differ in experiences.
parts.working: 1 mark: limitation (unrepresentative/hard to find/still differ/influence each other); 1 mark: explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan a field experiment using a repeated measures design to investigate whether the tempo of background music affects how fast people walk through a shopping arcade in Karachi. Your plan must include the hypothesis, the variables, how you will deal with order effects and how you will collect the data.
parts.answer: Hypothesis: shoppers walk faster through the arcade when fast music (e.g. 140 bpm) is played than when slow music (e.g. 70 bpm) is played. IV: tempo of music (fast/slow) — same volume, same type of instrumental music. DV: time (s) taken to walk a marked 20 m stretch, recorded by a hidden observer with a stopwatch or by video. Design: repeated measures by using the same regular shoppers (e.g. staff or regular visitors) who agree to walk the route each day; or the same arcade/time slots. Order effects: counterbalance — half do fast first, half slow first, on different days; same time of day. Controls: same weekday times, similar crowd levels, observers blind to hypothesis. Ethics: public place, no personal data, debrief where possible. Sampling: opportunity/volunteer sample of e.g. 30 regular visitors.
parts.working: Level 4 (9–10): detailed, coherent plan with hypothesis, operationalised IV and DV, repeated measures clearly explained, counterbalancing, data collection and several controls/ethics, all applied to the arcade; Level 3 (6–8): most features with some detail; Level 2 (3–5): basic plan, some features missing or not applied; Level 1 (1–2): minimal. Single long answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one weakness of your plan and suggest how it could be improved.
parts.answer: Weakness: participants who walk the route repeatedly may guess the aim and change their speed (demand characteristics), or learn the route and walk faster the second time. Improvement: use an independent measures design with random passers-by each session (and a larger sample), or use a cover story and add filler days with no music change.
parts.working: 1 mark: weakness identified; 1 mark: explained in context; 1 mark: improvement; 1 mark: how it would help.

stem: A hypothetical simulator study in Lahore compares the braking reaction times of young drivers (18–25 years) and older drivers (60–70 years), each driving with and without a hands-free phone conversation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: This study has two independent variables. For each IV, state which experimental design should be used and explain why.
parts.answer: Age group: independent measures — a participant cannot be both young and older, so different people must be in each age group. Phone conversation: repeated measures — each driver can drive with and without a conversation, which removes individual differences in driving skill and reaction speed (with the order counterbalanced).
parts.working: Age: 1 mark independent measures; 1 mark reason (cannot be in both groups/pre-existing characteristic). Phone: 1 mark repeated measures; 1 mark reason (controls participant variables/fewer participants) or matched pairs with justification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the age-group comparison cannot show that age itself causes any difference in reaction time.
parts.answer: Age was not manipulated or randomly allocated, so the two groups may also differ in other ways, such as driving experience, eyesight or familiarity with phones, any of which could explain the difference.
parts.working: 1 mark: IV not manipulated / no random allocation (quasi-experiment); 1 mark: other variables differ between age groups.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an 'extraneous variable'.
parts.answer: Any variable other than the IV that might affect the DV, if it is not controlled.
parts.working: 1 mark: variable other than the IV; 1 mark: could affect the DV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A hypothetical experiment in Multan tests whether chewing gum helps students concentrate during a test. Suggest one extraneous variable and how it could be controlled.
parts.answer: Noise in the room — test all students in the same quiet room. (Also accept: time of day, test difficulty, hunger.)
parts.working: 1 mark: relevant variable; 1 mark: suitable control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between an extraneous variable and a confounding variable.
parts.answer: An extraneous variable is any variable that could affect the DV. A confounding variable is an extraneous variable that has actually varied with the IV (e.g. one condition was always tested in the morning), so it is mixed up with the IV and we cannot tell which caused the change.
parts.working: 1 mark: extraneous = could affect DV; 1 mark: confounding = varies systematically with IV/has affected results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write two sentences of standardised instructions for participants in a hypothetical experiment where they must spot spelling mistakes in a page of text in 3 minutes.
parts.answer: e.g. 'You will see a page of text that contains some spelling mistakes. You have 3 minutes to circle as many mistakes as you can; please work in silence and stop when I say "stop".'
parts.working: 1 mark: explains the task clearly; 1 mark: gives time limit/what to do, same for everyone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why standardised instructions are a form of control.
parts.answer: Every participant receives the same information, so differences in performance cannot be caused by differences in what they were told.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why participants in a laboratory experiment should be tested in the same room at the same time of day.
parts.answer: Conditions such as light, noise, temperature and tiredness can affect performance; keeping room and time the same means these situational variables cannot explain differences between conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: room/time can affect performance (situational variables); 1 mark: keeping them constant controls them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'single-blind' procedure.
parts.answer: Participants do not know which condition they are in (or the aim of the study), although the researcher does.
parts.working: 1 mark: participants unaware of condition/aim; 1 mark: researcher knows.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a single-blind procedure is used.
parts.answer: It reduces demand characteristics, because participants cannot change their behaviour to fit what they think is expected.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hypothetical study in Hyderabad tests whether a vitamin tablet improves memory in older adults. Explain why a placebo group is needed.
parts.answer: People who believe they have taken something helpful may try harder or feel more confident, which could improve memory scores. A placebo group (an identical-looking tablet with no vitamin) shows how much improvement comes from belief alone, so the real effect of the vitamin can be found.
parts.working: 1 mark: expectation/belief can change the DV; 1 mark: placebo separates the effect of the vitamin from expectation.

stem: A hypothetical study in a school in Sukkur compared a new English textbook with the old one. Class 1 used the old textbook with Mr Ahmed; Class 2 used the new textbook with Ms Rubina. After a term, Class 2 scored higher.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify one uncontrolled variable in this study.
parts.answer: The teacher (each class had a different teacher). (Also accept: the class itself / class ability.)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this variable could affect the conclusion.
parts.answer: If the teacher of class 2 is more experienced or enthusiastic, class 2 may score higher because of the teacher, not the textbook, so the researcher cannot conclude that the new textbook is better.
parts.working: 1 mark: teacher could affect scores; 1 mark: so the IV is confounded / conclusion invalid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the study could be improved to control this variable.
parts.answer: Have the same teacher teach both classes (one with each textbook), or randomly allocate students and teachers to the textbooks.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by 'demand characteristics'.
parts.answer: Cues in a study that help participants guess its aim, which may lead them to change their behaviour (e.g. to help or to spoil the study).
parts.working: 1 mark: cues that reveal the aim; 1 mark: participants change behaviour as a result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways of reducing demand characteristics in a hypothetical experiment testing whether people eat more snacks while watching television.
parts.answer: 1. Use an independent measures design so each participant sees only one condition and is less able to guess the aim. 2. Use a single-blind procedure, telling participants the study is about rating the TV programme while secretly weighing the snack bowls.
parts.working: 1 mark each: independent measures; single-blind/cover story; covert measurement; filler tasks.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each variable, state whether it is a situational variable or a participant variable.
(i) Temperature of the testing room.
(ii) Participants' age.
(iii) Background noise from traffic.
(iv) Participants' previous experience of the task.
parts.answer: (i) situational (ii) participant (iii) situational (iv) participant
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical experiment, Researcher 1 tested all the participants in condition A and Researcher 2 tested all the participants in condition B. Explain why this is a problem.
parts.answer: The researchers may differ in manner, tone or expectations (experimenter effects), so differences between conditions could be caused by the researcher rather than the IV: researcher is confounded with condition.
parts.working: 1 mark: researchers differ/experimenter effects; 1 mark: confounded with the IV.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways of solving this problem.
parts.answer: 1. Have each researcher test equal numbers of participants in both conditions. 2. Give both researchers the same script and training, and keep them blind to the hypothesis (double-blind).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which Milgram standardised his procedure.
parts.answer: 1. The experimenter used the same four prods in the same order whenever a participant hesitated. 2. The same learner, 'Mr Wallace' (a confederate who was never really shocked), and the same experimenter were used, and the learner's protests followed the same script (pounding on the wall at 300 volts, then silence). (Also accept: same rigged draw, same shock generator, same 45-volt sample shock, same room at Yale.)
parts.working: For each way: 1 mark identified; 1 mark described with detail.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why standardisation was important in this study.
parts.answer: Because every participant had the same experience, the level of obedience could be compared fairly across participants and the study could be replicated by other researchers to check reliability.
parts.working: 1 mark: fair comparison/consistency; 1 mark: allows replication/reliability.

stem:
In a hypothetical study in Islamabad, 40 university students were randomly allocated to use a sleep-tracking app or no app (control) for a month. Mean nightly sleep (hours):
Group | Before | After
App | 5.8 | 6.9
Control | 5.9 | 6.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in sleep for each group.
parts.answer: App: 1.1 hours; control: 0.6 hours

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using your answers, explain why the control group was important.
parts.answer: The control group also slept more (perhaps because they were in a study or because exams finished), so without it the researcher might have thought the app caused all 1.1 hours. The app's effect is better estimated as about 0.5 hours.
parts.working: 1 mark: control group improved too; 1 mark: true effect = difference (0.5 h).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the control group's sleep improved.
parts.answer: Being in a study made them think about sleep more (or a change in season/exam pressure affected everyone).
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A hypothetical field experiment at a shopping mall in Karachi tests whether passers-by are more likely to help a woman who drops a bag of oranges if she is carrying a baby than if she is not.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two variables that the researchers could control in this field experiment, and explain how.
parts.answer: 1. The confederate: use the same confederate, wearing the same clothes, dropping the same bag of oranges in the same way each time. 2. Time and place: run all trials at the same entrance, at the same time on weekdays, so crowd levels are similar.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark variable; 1 mark how it is controlled.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one variable that the researchers could not control, and its possible effect.
parts.answer: The number and type of people nearby (e.g. some passers-by in a hurry, groups of friends) — this could affect whether help is given, independently of the IV.
parts.working: 1 mark: uncontrollable variable; 1 mark: its effect on helping.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a placebo and a double-blind procedure could be used in a hypothetical experiment to test whether an energy drink improves exam performance among students in Lahore.
parts.answer: Recruit students and randomly allocate them to two groups. One group drinks the energy drink; the other drinks a placebo drink that looks, smells and tastes the same but contains no caffeine or sugar. Drinks are prepared in identical coded cans by a third person, so neither the students nor the researchers giving the drink and marking the test know who had which (double-blind). All take the same practice exam in the same room at the same time 30 minutes later. The codes are revealed after marking, and scores compared.
parts.working: 1 mark: random allocation into two groups; 1 mark: placebo identical in appearance/taste; 1 mark: participants unaware; 1 mark: researchers/markers unaware (third party codes); 1 mark: standardised test conditions; 1 mark: codes broken after marking / compare scores.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a hypothetical memory experiment, all participants see the same 30 words in the same order. Explain why this might be a problem and how presenting the words in a randomised order for each participant would solve it.
parts.answer: Words at the start and end of a list are usually remembered better (primacy and recency), so in a fixed order the same words always benefit and features of those particular words could affect results. Randomising the order for each participant means each word appears in different positions, so position effects are spread evenly and do not bias the results towards particular words or conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: problem — position (primacy/recency) effects; 1 mark: fixed order means the same words always advantaged / confound; 1 mark: randomising spreads positions; 1 mark: bias removed/results fairer.

stem: In a hypothetical experiment in Abbottabad, 30 students revised with flashcards and were tested at 9 am (mean score 72 %). Another 30 students revised by watching videos and were tested at 3 pm (mean score 64 %).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the mean scores of the two conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the researcher cannot conclude that the type of revision caused this difference.
parts.answer: All the flashcard group were tested in the morning and all the video group in the afternoon, so time of day is a confounding variable: students may be more alert in the morning, which could explain the higher scores.
parts.working: 1 mark: time of day varies with condition; 1 mark: alertness/tiredness could cause the difference.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a better procedure.
parts.answer: Test half of each group in the morning and half in the afternoon (or test everyone at the same time), so time of day is balanced across conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: balance or hold constant the time of day; 1 mark: explanation.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a hypothetical experiment in Rawalpindi, 50 participants were randomly allocated to a 'smiling faces' or a 'neutral faces' condition. All were tested in the same room at 10 am. The researcher read the same instructions from a card. Each participant saw 20 faces on a screen for 2 seconds each and then tried to recognise them among 40 faces. The researcher knew the hypothesis and recorded the answers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three controls used in this procedure.
parts.answer: Any three of: same room; same time of day; standardised instructions read from a card; same 20 faces for everyone; same 2-second presentation time; random allocation to conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one important variable that has not been controlled and suggest how to control it.
parts.answer: The participants' familiarity with the faces — some could recognise a famous or local face. Use only faces of unknown people (pre-tested in a pilot). (Also accept: the researcher's expectations — use a double-blind procedure.)
parts.working: 1 mark: relevant uncontrolled variable; 1 mark: suitable control.

author: HomiLabs
